title: 1. Exam at a glance (2026-27)
text: 1. Exam at a glance (2026-27)          Item   Details           Theory paper   80 marks, 3 hours (plus 15 minutes reading time)       Internal Assessment (IA)   20 marks (done in school)       Total   100       Number of questions   38, all compulsory, with internal choice in some questions       Section A   Q1-18 MCQ + Q19-20 Assertion-Reason (A-R), 1 mark each =  20 marks        Section B   Q21-25: very short answer, 2 marks each =  10 marks        Section C   Q26-31: short answer, 3 marks each =  18 marks        Section D   Q32-35: long answer, 5 marks each =  20 marks        Section E   Q36-38: case-study, 4 marks each (1 + 1 + 2) =  12 marks        Calculator    Not allowed.  Take π = 22/7 unless told otherwise. Learn √2 = 1.414, √3 = 1.732.        Pass mark     33 out of 100  (theory 80 + IA 20 combined), per CBSE Controller of Examinations FAQ (2025) and CBSE's October 2026 clarification for the 2027 exams        Safe target in theory     32 out of 80  (40%). With a normal IA score this gives a big safety buffer.          Standard (041) vs Basic (241):  Both have the  same syllabus, same chapters and same paper design . The Basic paper has more easy questions (about 75% "remember / understand" type, against about 54% in Standard). A weak student should take  Basic (241)  unless they plan to take Maths in Class XI. (A Basic student may still take Maths 041 in Class XI with the school head's approval, CBSE circular of 27.05.2025.)    Two board exams from 2026:  The main exam is in  February . An optional  second exam in May  lets a student improve marks in up to  3 subjects . If Maths goes badly in February, the May exam is a second chance. Do not plan to fail, but do not panic either.    The SQP note says:  "There is no change in the Question Paper Design and Assessment Pattern for Academic Session 2026-27."    Internal Assessment 20 marks (2026-27 curriculum):          Part   Marks           Pen-paper tests and multiple assessment (5 + 5)   10       Portfolio (class work, worksheets, notebook)   5       Lab practical (activities from the prescribed lab manual)   5          Deleted, not in the board paper (skip old PYQs from these):  Euclid's division lemma / algorithm, decimal expansions of rationals, division algorithm for polynomials, cross-multiplication method, equations reducible to linear form, completing the square, area of a triangle by coordinates, Pythagoras theorem proof and areas of similar triangles theorem, complementary-angle trigonometry (sin(90° - A) etc.), constructions, frustum of a cone, conversion of solids (melting / recasting, canal water), and ogives.

title: 3. The 33-mark plan (target 32/80 in theory)
text: 3. The 33-mark plan (target 32/80 in theory)     Main idea:  You do  not  need the whole book. Learn the  fixed-pattern  questions that come every year: formulas you just plug in, and 4-5 proofs that are always the same. Attempt  every  MCQ: there is  no negative marking .

title: 3a. Study order (easiest and highest return first)
text: 3a. Study order (easiest and highest return first)       Probability (5) : dice, cards, coins and balls. Only one formula: P = favourable / total. Learn the 36 dice outcomes.    Statistics (6) : mean, median, mode of grouped data. Same table method every year, plus Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean.    Real Numbers (6) : HCF/LCM by prime factors, HCF × LCM = product, and the "prove √2 / √3 / √5 irrational" proof (same proof every time).    Coordinate Geometry (6) : just 3 formulas (distance, section, mid-point).    Arithmetic Progressions (4) + one case study (4) : a_n = a + (n - 1)d and S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d]. The AP case study comes almost every year.    Trigonometry (6) + Heights and Distances (6) : learn the table of values (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°), 3 identities and the "two angles" tower method.    Circles (7) : two theorems (tangent ⟂ radius; tangents from an outside point are equal) and 3 standard proofs.    Bonus if time:  Quadratic (discriminant, word problems), Pair of linear equations (elimination method), Areas of sectors, Surface areas and volumes, Triangles (BPT proof).

Aim for  12 correct out of 20  = 12 marks from Section A alone.

title: 3c. How internal assessment helps
text: 3c. How internal assessment helps      IA is  20 marks , and most students who attend school and submit work score  15-18 . Because Class X passing is  33 out of 100 combined , a student with 17/20 in IA needs only  16/80 in theory  to pass.  Do not lose IA marks.     Portfolio (5):  keep the maths notebook complete and neat, with every class worksheet. Get it checked and signed.    Lab practical (5):  do the activities from the lab manual (e.g. verifying BPT by paper cutting, finding area of a circle by cutting sectors, probability by tossing coins). Write aim, material, procedure, observation and result in the lab file.    Pen-paper tests (10):  periodic tests in school. Treat them as practice for the board paper.    Still aim for 32/80 in theory.  It protects you if IA marks come lower than expected.

title: 5. Must-do question bank (80 questions)
text: 5. Must-do question bank (80 questions)    ★ = asked many times, so do this first. Years in brackets are papers where the same or a very similar question appeared. "SQP" = 2026-27 Sample Paper. "NCERT" = textbook question (no board year claimed).

title: Chapter 1: Real Numbers
text: Chapter 1: Real Numbers       Q1 ★ (MCQ, SQP; same idea 2023)  The greatest number which divides both 134 and 188, leaving remainders 4 and 6 respectively, is: (A) 13 (B) 26 (C) 39 (D) 65     Ans: (B) 26.  Subtract the remainders: 134 - 4 = 130 and 188 - 6 = 182. HCF(130, 182): 130 = 2 × 5 × 13, 182 = 2 × 7 × 13, so HCF = 2 × 13 =  26 .        Q2 (MCQ, 2025)  If HCF(98, 28) = m and LCM(98, 28) = n, then the value of n - 7m is: (A) 0 (B) 28 (C) 98 (D) 198     Ans: (C) 98.  98 = 2 × 7², 28 = 2² × 7. HCF = 2 × 7 = 14 = m. LCM = 2² × 7² = 196 = n. n - 7m = 196 - 98 =  98 .        Q3 (MCQ, 2019)  Two positive integers a and b can be written as a = x³y² and b = xy³, where x, y are prime numbers. Find LCM(a, b).     Ans: x³y³.  LCM = product of the  highest  power of each prime. (HCF would be the lowest powers: xy².)        Q4 ★ (3 marks, 2019; √5 in 2023)  Prove that √2 is an irrational number.     Ans:      Suppose √2 is rational. Then √2 = a/b, where a and b are co-prime integers and b ≠ 0.   Squaring: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b². So 2 divides a², hence 2 divides a. Let a = 2c.   Then 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c². So 2 divides b², hence 2 divides b.   Now 2 divides both a and b. This  contradicts  that a and b are co-prime.   So our assumption is wrong.  √2 is irrational.  (For √3 or √5, replace 2 by 3 or 5 in every line.)          Q5 ★ (3 marks, SQP; 2 + 3√5 in 2026; (2 + √3)/5 in 2019)  Given that √3 is irrational, prove that (2 + 3√3) is irrational.     Ans:      Suppose 2 + 3√3 is rational. Then 2 + 3√3 = p/q, where p, q are integers, q ≠ 0.   So 3√3 = p/q - 2 = (p - 2q)/q, and √3 = (p - 2q)/(3q).   The right side is rational (integers divided by a non-zero integer), so √3 would be rational.   But √3 is irrational. This is a  contradiction . So  2 + 3√3 is irrational.           Q6 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  Three bells toll at intervals of 5, 6 and 8 minutes. They all toll together at 10:00 a.m. when the park opens. How many more times do they toll together till the park closes at 7:00 p.m.?     Ans:      LCM(5, 6, 8): 5 = 5, 6 = 2 × 3, 8 = 2³. LCM = 2³ × 3 × 5 = 120 minutes = 2 hours.   They toll together every 2 hours: 12 noon, 2 p.m., 4 p.m., 6 p.m. (8 p.m. is after closing).   So they toll together  4 more times .  (Other OR in SQP: hall 9.75 m × 6.75 m × 5.25 m, longest ruler = HCF(975, 675, 525) cm =  75 cm .)

title: Chapter 2: Polynomials
text: Chapter 2: Polynomials       Q7 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  If f(x) = px² + qx + r, p ≠ 0 and p + r = q, then one of the zeroes of f(x) is: (A) q/p (B) r/p (C) -r/p (D) -q/p     Ans: (C) -r/p.  Put x = -1: f(-1) = p - q + r = 0 (because q = p + r). So -1 is a zero. Product of zeroes = r/p, so the other zero = (r/p) ÷ (-1) =  -r/p .        Q8 ★ (A-R, SQP)  A: If the zeroes of (2k - 1)x² + 4x - 3 are reciprocal of each other, then k = -1. R: If a = c, then the zeroes of ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0) are reciprocal of each other.     Ans: (A)  Both true and R explains A. Reciprocal zeroes means product = 1, so c/a = 1, i.e. a = c: 2k - 1 = -3, k = -1.        Q9 (A-R, 2024)  A: If the graph of a polynomial touches the x-axis at only one point, then the polynomial cannot be a quadratic polynomial. R: A polynomial of degree n (n > 1) can have at most n zeroes.     Ans: (D)  A is false (y = x² touches the x-axis only at (0, 0) and is quadratic). R is true.        Q10 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  Find the value of k such that the polynomial x² - (k + 6)x + 2(2k - 1) has sum of its zeroes equal to half of their product.     Ans:      a = 1, b = -(k + 6), c = 2(2k - 1)   Sum = -b/a = k + 6; Product = c/a = 2(2k - 1)   k + 6 = ½ × 2(2k - 1) = 2k - 1    k = 7       (SQP similar, 3 marks: if α, β are zeroes of 2x² - 8x + 5, find (α + 1/β)(β + 1/α). Expand: αβ + 1 + 1 + 1/(αβ). αβ = 5/2, so the value = 5/2 + 2 + 2/5 =  49/10 .)

title: Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
text: Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables       Q11 (MCQ, 2025)  If x = 1 and y = 2 is a solution of the pair of linear equations 2x - 3y + a = 0 and 2x + 3y - b = 0, then: (A) a = 2b (B) 2a = b (C) a + 2b = 0 (D) 2a + b = 0     Ans: (B) 2a = b.  Put x = 1, y = 2: 2 - 6 + a = 0 gives a = 4; 2 + 6 - b = 0 gives b = 8. So b = 2a.        Q12 ★ (2 marks, 2019)  Find c if the system cx + 3y + (3 - c) = 0, 12x + cy - c = 0 has infinitely many solutions.     Ans:      Condition: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, so c/12 = 3/c = (3 - c)/(-c)   c/12 = 3/c gives c² = 36, c = ±6   3/c = (3 - c)/(-c) gives -3 = 3 - c, so c = 6    c = 6  (satisfies both)  (Remember: unique solution a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2; no solution a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2.)           Q13 (2 marks, 2024)  Solve 7x - 2y = 5 and 8x + 7y = 15 and verify your answer.     Ans (elimination):      Multiply the first by 7: 49x - 14y = 35. Multiply the second by 2: 16x + 14y = 30.   Add: 65x = 65, so  x = 1 . Then 7(1) - 2y = 5, so  y = 1 .   Verify: 7 - 2 = 5 ✓ and 8 + 7 = 15 ✓.          Q14 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  A father's age is three times the sum of the ages of his two children. After 5 years his age will be two times the sum of their ages. Find the present age of the father.     Ans:      Let father = x years, sum of children's ages = y years. So x = 3y.   After 5 years: father x + 5; children's sum y + 10 (each child gets 5 years older).   x + 5 = 2(y + 10), so x - 2y = 15. Put x = 3y: y = 15.    Father = 45 years.           Q15 ★ (5 marks, 2025)  Vijay invested money in two schemes A and B at 8% and 9% per annum. He received ₹1,860 total annual interest. Had he interchanged the amounts, he would have received ₹20 more. How much did he invest in each scheme?     Ans:      Let ₹x in A and ₹y in B. 8x/100 + 9y/100 = 1860, so 8x + 9y = 186000 ...(1)   Interchanged: 9x + 8y = 188000 ...(2)   Add: 17x + 17y = 374000, so x + y = 22000 ...(3)   Subtract (1) from (2): x - y = 2000 ...(4)   From (3) and (4): x = 12000, y = 10000.    ₹12,000 in scheme A and ₹10,000 in scheme B.   (SQP case study similar: x + y = 1000 and 10x + 15y = 12750 give 450 small and 550 large bottles in June.)

title: Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations
text: Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations       Q16 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  If (1 - p) is a root of x² + px + 1 - p = 0, then its roots are: (A) 0, 1 (B) -1, 1 (C) 0, -1 (D) -1, 2     Ans: (C) 0, -1.  Put x = 1 - p: (1 - p)² + p(1 - p) + (1 - p) = (1 - p)(1 - p + p + 1) = 2(1 - p) = 0, so p = 1. The equation becomes x² + x = 0, i.e. x(x + 1) = 0, roots  0 and -1 .        Q17 ★ (2 marks, 2017)  Find the value of k for which x² + k(2x + k - 1) + 2 = 0 has real and equal roots.     Ans:      x² + 2kx + (k² - k + 2) = 0. So a = 1, b = 2k, c = k² - k + 2.   Equal roots: D = b² - 4ac = 0   4k² - 4(k² - k + 2) = 0, so 4k - 8 = 0    k = 2   (2019 MCQ: for real roots of x² + 4x + k = 0, D ≥ 0 gives 16 - 4k ≥ 0, so  k ≤ 4 .)           Q18 (2 marks, 2026)  Verify that the roots of (p - q)x² + (q - r)x + (r - p) = 0 are equal when q + r = 2p.     Ans:      D = (q - r)² - 4(p - q)(r - p)   If q + r = 2p, then r = 2p - q, so q - r = 2q - 2p = -2(p - q) and r - p = p - q.   D = 4(p - q)² - 4(p - q)(p - q) = 0. So the  roots are equal .          Q19 ★ (5 marks, 2025)  A train travels 480 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 8 km/h less, it would have taken 3 hours more. Find the speed of the train.     Ans:      Let speed = x km/h. Time = 480/x. New time = 480/(x - 8).   480/(x - 8) - 480/x = 3   480 × 8 = 3x(x - 8), so 3840 = 3x² - 24x, so x² - 8x - 1280 = 0   (x - 40)(x + 32) = 0, so x = 40 or -32 (speed cannot be negative)    Speed = 40 km/h           Q20 ★ (5 marks, SQP)  A rectangular park is 50 m × 40 m. A rectangular pool is built in the middle with a grass strip of uniform width around it. The area of the grass strip is 1184 m². Find the dimensions of the pool.     Ans:      Let the strip width = x m. Pool = (50 - 2x) by (40 - 2x).   Pool area = 2000 - 1184 = 816 m²   (50 - 2x)(40 - 2x) = 816, so 4x² - 180x + 2000 = 816, so x² - 45x + 296 = 0   (x - 8)(x - 37) = 0. x = 37 is impossible (50 - 74 < 0), so x = 8.    Pool = 34 m × 24 m  (check: 34 × 24 = 816 ✓)  (Also asked: 2019 taps fill a tank in 15/8 h, one takes 2 h less →  3 h and 5 h ; 2026 tour ₹5,400, extend 5 days, cut ₹180/day → x² + 5x - 150 = 0 →  10 days, ₹540/day ; 2025 right triangle perimeter 60 cm, hypotenuse 25 cm → sides  15 cm and 20 cm .)

title: Chapter 5: Arithmetic Progressions
text: Chapter 5: Arithmetic Progressions       Q21 (MCQ, SQP)  The middle term of the AP 10, 7, 4, ..., -62 is: (A) -26 (B) -29 (C) -32 (D) -35     Ans: (A) -26.  a = 10, d = -3. -62 = 10 + (n - 1)(-3), so n - 1 = 24, n = 25. Middle term = 13th = 10 + 12(-3) =  -26 .        Q22 ★ (MCQ, 2025; S_n given in 2019 too)  If the sum of the first m terms of an AP is 2m² + 3m, then its second term is: (A) 10 (B) 9 (C) 12 (D) 4     Ans: (B) 9.  S1 = 2 + 3 = 5 = a1. S2 = 8 + 6 = 14. a2 = S2 - S1 =  9 .  (2019: if S_n = 3n² - 4n, then a_n = S_n - S_(n-1) =  6n - 7 .)         Q23 ★ (2 marks, 2019; same type 2017)  How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 3?     Ans:      AP: 12, 15, 18, ..., 99. a = 12, d = 3, a_n = 99   99 = 12 + (n - 1) × 3, so (n - 1) = 29,  n = 30   (2019 Set III: two-digit numbers divisible by 7: 14, ..., 98 gives  13 . 2017: integers between 200 and 500 divisible by 8: 208, ..., 496 gives  37 .)           Q24 ★ (2 marks, 2019)  Which term of the AP 3, 15, 27, 39, ... will be 120 more than its 21st term?     Ans:      a = 3, d = 12. a21 = 3 + 20 × 12 = 243   Required term = 243 + 120 = 363 = 3 + (n - 1) × 12, so n - 1 = 30    31st term           Q25 (3 marks, SQP)  Find the sum of integers between 1 and 400 that are multiples of 4 as well as of 5.     Ans:      Multiples of both 4 and 5 = multiples of 20: 20, 40, ..., 380 (400 is not "between")   380 = 20 + (n - 1) × 20, so n = 19   S19 = 19/2 × (20 + 380) = 19 × 200 =  3800           Q26 ★ (Case study 4 marks, 2025)  A charity run: the first round is 300 m and each next round is 50 m longer. There are 10 rounds. (i) Write the 4th, 5th and 6th terms. (ii) Find the distance of the 8th round. (iii)(a) Total distance after 10 rounds. OR (iii)(b) Total distance of the first 6 rounds.     Ans:      (i) a = 300, d = 50:  450 m, 500 m, 550 m    (ii) a8 = 300 + 7 × 50 =  650 m    (iii)(a) S10 = 10/2 [2 × 300 + 9 × 50] = 5 × 1050 =  5250 m    (iii)(b) S6 = 6/2 [600 + 5 × 50] = 3 × 850 =  2550 m   (2026 "Kolam" case: 4, 8, 12, ... dots; a = 4, d = 4, a_n = 4n; S_n = 2n(n + 1) = 220 gives  n = 10  squares; 2n(n + 1) = 100 has no whole-number answer, so  100 dots is not possible .)

title: Chapter 6: Triangles
text: Chapter 6: Triangles       Q27 (MCQ, SQP)  The perimeters of two similar triangles are 56 cm and 70 cm. If one side of the first triangle is 14 cm, the corresponding side of the second is: (A) 5 (B) 7.5 (C) 10 (D) 17.5     Ans: (D) 17.5.  Ratio of perimeters = ratio of sides: 14/x = 56/70, so x = 14 × 70/56 =  17.5 cm .        Q28 (MCQ, 2025)  In triangles ABC and DEF, ∠B = ∠E, ∠F = ∠C and AB = 3DE. Then the two triangles are: (A) congruent but not similar (B) congruent as well as similar (C) neither congruent nor similar (D) similar but not congruent     Ans: (D).  Two equal angles give similarity (AA). Sides are in ratio 3 : 1, so they are not congruent.  (2025 Section B similar: if ΔABC ~ ΔPQR, AB = 6, BC = 4, AC = 8 and PR = 6 cm, the ratio is 6/8 = 3/4, so PQ = 4.5, QR = 3 and  PQ + QR = 7.5 cm .)         Q29 ★ (5 marks, SQP; BPT used in 2023 and 2026 MCQs/short answers)  Prove that a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, divides the other two sides in the same ratio (Basic Proportionality Theorem).     Ans:       Given:  In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC, D on AB and E on AC.  To prove:  AD/DB = AE/EC.    Construction:  Join BE and CD. Draw EN ⟂ AB and DM ⟂ AC.   ar(ADE) = ½ × AD × EN, ar(BDE) = ½ × DB × EN. So ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB ...(1)   ar(ADE) = ½ × AE × DM, ar(DEC) = ½ × EC × DM. So ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC ...(2)   ΔBDE and ΔDEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC, so ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) ...(3)   From (1), (2), (3):  AD/DB = AE/EC.  Hence proved.    Draw the figure  (triangle with DE parallel to BC, the two joins and two perpendiculars). The figure alone carries marks.          Q30 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. Its diagonals meet at O. Show that AO/BO = CO/DO.     Ans:      In ΔAOB and ΔCOD: ∠OAB = ∠OCD (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC) and ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite).   So ΔAOB ~ ΔCOD (AA). Hence AO/CO = BO/DO.   Rearranging:  AO/BO = CO/DO.   (SQP OR: if ∠PQR = ∠QSP, PQ = 6 cm, PS = 3 cm, then ΔPRQ ~ ΔPQS, so PQ/PR = PS/PQ, 36 = 3 × PR,  PR = 12 cm .)

title: Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry       Q31 ★ (MCQ, SQP and 2024)  PM is a median of ΔPQR with vertices P(5, -6), Q(6, 4) and R(0, 0). The length of PM is: (A) 2√17 (B) 2√15 (C) √101 (D) 10 units     Ans: (A) 2√17.  M = mid-point of QR = ((6 + 0)/2, (4 + 0)/2) = (3, 2). PM = √[(5 - 3)² + (-6 - 2)²] = √(4 + 64) = √68 =  2√17 .        Q32 (MCQ, SQP)  The point which lies on the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining A(-3, -4) and B(3, 4) is: (A) (0, 0) (B) (0, 3) (C) (3, 0) (D) (0, 4)     Ans: (A) (0, 0).  It is the mid-point of AB, and the mid-point lies on the perpendicular bisector.        Q33 (MCQ, 2024; same type 2017)  If the distance between (3, -5) and (x, -5) is 15 units, then x is: (A) 12, -18 (B) -12, 18 (C) 18, 5 (D) -9, -12     Ans: (B).  √[(x - 3)² + 0] = 15, so x - 3 = ±15,  x = 18 or -12 .  (2017: distance between (4, k) and (1, 0) is 5 gives 9 + k² = 25,  k = ±4 .)         Q34 ★ (3 marks, SQP; same type 2019, 2023)  In what ratio does the x-axis divide the line segment joining (-4, -6) and (-1, 7)? Find the point of division.     Ans:      Let the ratio be k : 1. The point on the x-axis has y = 0.   y = (k × 7 + 1 × (-6))/(k + 1) = 0, so 7k = 6, k = 6/7.  Ratio 6 : 7.    x = (6 × (-1) + 7 × (-4))/(6 + 7) = (-6 - 28)/13 = -34/13    Point = (-34/13, 0)   (2019: x-axis divides (1, -3) and (4, 5) in ratio  3 : 5  at (17/8, 0).)           Q35 ★ (3 marks, 2025; NCERT)  Find the ratio in which the y-axis divides the line segment joining (5, -6) and (-1, -4). Also find the point of intersection.     Ans:      On the y-axis x = 0. Let ratio k : 1: x = (k × (-1) + 5)/(k + 1) = 0, so k = 5.  Ratio 5 : 1.    y = (5 × (-4) + 1 × (-6))/6 = -26/6 = -13/3    Point = (0, -13/3)           Q36 (3 marks, 2019)  Find the point on the y-axis which is equidistant from (5, -2) and (-3, 2).     Ans:      Let P = (0, y). PA² = PB²: 25 + (y + 2)² = 9 + (y - 2)²   25 + y² + 4y + 4 = 9 + y² - 4y + 4, so 8y = -16, y = -2    P = (0, -2)           Q37 ★ (A-R, SQP)  A: If three vertices of a parallelogram taken in order are (-1, -6), (2, -5) and (7, 2), then its fourth vertex is (4, 1). R: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.     Ans: (A)  Both true and R explains A. Mid-point of AC = ((-1 + 7)/2, (-6 + 2)/2) = (3, -2) = mid-point of BD. So D = (2 × 3 - 2, 2 × (-2) + 5) = (4, 1).  (2019 1-mark: centre (2, -3), one end B(1, 4) of a diameter; other end A = (2 × 2 - 1, 2 × (-3) - 4) =  (3, -10) .)

title: Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry
text: Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry       Q38 (MCQ, 2025)  If θ is an acute angle and 7 + 4 sin θ = 9, then θ is: (A) 90° (B) 30° (C) 45° (D) 60°     Ans: (B) 30°.  4 sin θ = 2, so sin θ = 1/2, θ = 30°.        Q39 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  If tan(A + B) = √3 and tan(A - B) = 1/√3, 0° < A + B < 90°, A > B, then A and B are: (A) 60°, 30° (B) 60°, 45° (C) 45°, 15° (D) 60°, 15°     Ans: (C) 45°, 15°.  A + B = 60° and A - B = 30°. Adding: 2A = 90°, A = 45°, B = 15°.        Q40 (MCQ, 2024)  If sec θ - tan θ = m, then sec θ + tan θ = ?     Ans: 1/m.  Because (sec θ - tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ) = sec²θ - tan²θ = 1.        Q41 ★ (2 marks, 2024)  Evaluate: 2√2 cos 45° sin 30° + 2√3 cos 30°.     Ans:      = 2√2 × (1/√2) × (1/2) + 2√3 × (√3/2)   = 1 + 3 =  4   (2024 OR: for A = 60°, B = 30°, verify sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B. LHS = sin 90° = 1. RHS = (√3/2)(√3/2) + (1/2)(1/2) = 3/4 + 1/4 = 1 ✓.)           Q42 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  If tan θ = 1/√5, find the value of (cosec²θ - sec²θ)/(cosec²θ + sec²θ).     Ans:      cot θ = √5, so cosec²θ = 1 + cot²θ = 1 + 5 = 6   sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ = 1 + 1/5 = 6/5   Value = (6 - 6/5)/(6 + 6/5) = (24/5)/(36/5) =  2/3           Q43 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  Prove that (sin θ + cosec θ)² + (cos θ + sec θ)² = 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ.     Ans:      LHS = sin²θ + cosec²θ + 2 sin θ cosec θ + cos²θ + sec²θ + 2 cos θ sec θ   sin θ cosec θ = 1 and cos θ sec θ = 1, so LHS = (sin²θ + cos²θ) + cosec²θ + sec²θ + 2 + 2   = 1 + (1 + cot²θ) + (1 + tan²θ) + 4   =  7 + tan²θ + cot²θ  = RHS. Hence proved.          Q44 ★ (3 marks, SQP)  A student simplified cos θ/(1 - sin θ) + (1 - sin θ)/cos θ as follows: Step 1: [cos²θ + (1 - sin θ)²] / [(1 - sin θ) cos θ]; Step 2: [cos²θ + cos²θ] / [(1 - sin θ) cos θ]; Step 3: 2cos²θ / [(1 - sin θ) cos θ]; Step 4: 2cos θ/(1 - sin θ). Find the error and the correct answer.     Ans:       Error in Step 2:  (1 - sin θ)² is NOT cos²θ. (1 - sin²θ = cos²θ, but (1 - sin θ)² = 1 - 2 sin θ + sin²θ.)   Correct: numerator = cos²θ + 1 - 2 sin θ + sin²θ = 1 + 1 - 2 sin θ = 2(1 - sin θ)   So the expression = 2(1 - sin θ)/[(1 - sin θ) cos θ] = 2/cos θ =  2 sec θ           Q45 (3 marks, 2023)  Prove that (tan θ + sec θ - 1)/(tan θ - sec θ + 1) = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ.     Ans:      Write 1 = sec²θ - tan²θ in the numerator: tan θ + sec θ - (sec²θ - tan²θ)   = (sec θ + tan θ) - (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ - tan θ) = (sec θ + tan θ)(1 - sec θ + tan θ)   Denominator = (tan θ - sec θ + 1), the same bracket, so it cancels.   LHS = sec θ + tan θ = 1/cos θ + sin θ/cos θ =  (1 + sin θ)/cos θ  = RHS.

title: Chapter 9: Some Applications of Trigonometry (Heights and Distances)
text: Chapter 9: Some Applications of Trigonometry (Heights and Distances)       Q46 (MCQ, 2025; 1-mark 2017)  A kite is flying at a height of 150 m. Its string is inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The length of the string is: (A) 100 m (B) 300 m (C) 150 m (D) 150√3 m     Ans: (B) 300 m.  sin 30° = height/string, so 1/2 = 150/L, L = 300 m.  (2017: tower : shadow = √3 : 1, so tan θ = √3, angle of elevation of the sun =  60° . SQP: string 52 m with tan θ = 12/5, so sin θ = 12/13 and height = 52 × 12/13 =  48 m .)         Q47 ★ (5 marks, SQP)  The angles of depression of two ships from the top of a lighthouse, on the same side, are 45° and 30°. The ships are 200 m apart, one exactly behind the other. Find the height of the lighthouse.     Ans:      Let height = h, distance of the nearer ship = x. Draw the figure (lighthouse, two ships on a line).   Near ship (45°): tan 45° = h/x, so x = h.   Far ship (30°): tan 30° = h/(x + 200), so x + 200 = h√3.   h + 200 = h√3, so h(√3 - 1) = 200, h = 200/(√3 - 1) = 200(√3 + 1)/2 = 100(√3 + 1)    h = 100(√3 + 1) ≈ 273.2 m           Q48 ★ (4 marks, 2019; 2017 same idea with a 150 m cliff)  A man in a boat rowing away from a 100 m high lighthouse takes 2 minutes to change the angle of elevation of its top from 60° to 30°. Find the speed of the boat (√3 = 1.732).     Ans:      First position: tan 60° = 100/d1, so d1 = 100/√3   Second position: tan 30° = 100/d2, so d2 = 100√3   Distance moved = 100√3 - 100/√3 = (300 - 100)/√3 = 200/√3 = 115.47 m   Speed = 115.47/2 =  57.73 m per minute           Q49 ★ (3 marks, 2017 Set II)  From the top of a 7 m high building, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 60° and the angle of depression of its foot is 45°. Find the height of the tower.     Ans:      Depression 45° to the foot: distance between building and tower = 7 m (tan 45° = 7/d).   Elevation 60° to the top: extra height above the building level = 7 tan 60° = 7√3 m.   Tower = 7 + 7√3 = 7(√3 + 1) ≈  19.12 m           Q50 (5 marks, 2026)  A kite is flying 60 m above the ground. Ravi, on the roof of a house, holds the string straight and sees the kite at an angle of elevation of 30°. From the bottom of the same building the angle of elevation of the kite is 45°. Find the length of the string and the height of the roof (√3 = 1.73).     Ans:      From the bottom (45°): horizontal distance to the kite = 60 m.   From the roof (height r): tan 30° = (60 - r)/60, so 60 - r = 60/√3 = 20√3 = 34.6 m.  Roof height r = 60 - 34.6 = 25.4 m.    String: sin 30° = (60 - r)/L, so L = 2 × 34.6 =  69.2 m  (exactly 40√3 m).  (2022 also asked: tower 50 m, elevation of the building top from the tower's foot 30°, of the tower top from the building's foot 60°; distance = 50/√3, building = (50/√3) × (1/√3) =  50/3 = 16.67 m .)

title: Chapter 10: Circles
text: Chapter 10: Circles       Q51 (MCQ, 2025; proof in 2017)  The tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are always: (A) parallel (B) perpendicular (C) equal (D) intersecting     Ans: (A) parallel.  Both tangents are ⟂ to the same diameter, so they are parallel (alternate angles 90° each).        Q52 (MCQ, 2026)  PQ and PR are tangents to a circle with centre O and radius 4 cm such that ∠QPR = 90°. Then OP is: (A) 4 cm (B) 4√2 cm (C) 8 cm (D) 2√2 cm     Ans: (B) 4√2 cm.  OQPR is a square of side 4 cm; OP is its diagonal = 4√2.        Q53 ★ (2 marks, 2025; same idea SQP case, 2022)  A person standing at P is 26 m from the centre of a circular ground. His tangent distances PA and PB to the ground are 10 m each. Find the radius.     Ans:      Radius ⟂ tangent, so ΔOAP is right-angled at A.   OA² = OP² - PA² = 26² - 10² = 676 - 100 = 576    Radius = 24 m   (2022: concentric circles of radii 4 cm and 3 cm; chord of the bigger circle touching the smaller = 2√(16 - 9) =  2√7 cm .)           Q54 ★ (3 marks, NCERT theorem; used in every tangent question)  Prove that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.     Ans:       Given:  PQ and PR are tangents from P to a circle with centre O.  To prove:  PQ = PR.   Join OP, OQ, OR. In ΔOQP and ΔORP:   OQ = OR (radii); OP = OP (common); ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (radius ⟂ tangent)   So ΔOQP ≅ ΔORP (RHS). Hence  PQ = PR  (CPCT).          Q55 ★ (3 marks, 2017; 2023)  Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.     Ans:      Let ∠PTQ = θ. TP = TQ (tangents from T), so ∠TPQ = ∠TQP = (180° - θ)/2 = 90° - θ/2.   ∠OPT = 90° (radius ⟂ tangent).   ∠OPQ = ∠OPT - ∠TPQ = 90° - (90° - θ/2) = θ/2.   So  ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ . Hence proved.          Q56 ★ (3 marks, SQP)  Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.     Ans:      Let ABCD be a parallelogram whose sides touch the circle at P (on AB), Q (BC), R (CD), S (DA).   Tangents from a point are equal: AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS.   Add: (AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ), i.e. AB + CD = AD + BC.   In a parallelogram AB = CD and AD = BC, so 2AB = 2AD, AB = AD.   So all four sides are equal:  ABCD is a rhombus.           Q57 ★ (Case study 4 marks, SQP)  P is outside a circular garden with centre O and radius 9 m; OP = 18 m. PA and PB are tangents. (i) ∠OAP = ? (ii) Find PA. (iii)(A) Find ∠AOB. OR (iii)(B) If PA and PB were inclined at 60°, find their length.     Ans:      (i)  ∠OAP = 90°  (radius ⟂ tangent)   (ii) PA = √(18² - 9²) = √(324 - 81) = √243 =  9√3 m    (iii)(A) cos ∠AOP = OA/OP = 9/18 = 1/2, so ∠AOP = 60°, and  ∠AOB = 120°    (iii)(B) ∠APO = 30°, tan 30° = OA/PA, so PA = 9/(1/√3) =  9√3 m   (2019: incircle of ΔABC with AB = 10, BC = 8, AC = 12 cm; using equal tangents x + y = 8, y + z = 12, x + z = 10 gives  BL = 3, CM = 5, AN = 7 cm .)

title: Chapter 11: Areas Related to Circles
text: Chapter 11: Areas Related to Circles       Q58 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  The diameter of a car wheel is 21 cm. The number of complete revolutions it makes in moving 66 km is: (A) 10⁴ (B) 10⁵ (C) 10⁶ (D) 10⁷     Ans: (B) 10⁵.  Circumference = πd = 22/7 × 21 = 66 cm. 66 km = 66,00,000 cm. Revolutions = 66,00,000/66 = 1,00,000 =  10⁵ . (In the printed SQP the options appear as "104, 105 ...": they mean powers of 10.)        Q59 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  An arc of a circle is 6π cm long and the sector it bounds has area 24π cm². The radius is: (A) 4 (B) 8 (C) 16 (D) 18 cm     Ans: (B) 8 cm.  Area of sector = ½ × arc length × r: 24π = ½ × 6π × r, so r = 8.  (2025 MCQ: sector of area 40π sq. units and angle 72°: (72/360) πr² = 40π, r² = 200,  r = 10√2 .)         Q60 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  Find the area of a sector of a circle with diameter 28 cm if the length of the corresponding arc is 22 cm.     Ans:      r = 14 cm. Area of sector = ½ × l × r = ½ × 22 × 14 =  154 cm²    (Or: θ/360 × 2πr = 22 gives θ = 90°; area = ¼ × 22/7 × 196 = 154 cm².)          Q61 ★ (Case study 4 marks, 2025)  A brooch is a circle of diameter 35 mm made of silver wire. 5 diameters divide it into 10 equal sectors. (i) Central angle of each sector? (ii) Length of arc ACB (one sector)? (iii)(a) Area of each sector? OR (iii)(b) Total length of silver wire?     Ans:      (i) 360°/10 =  36°    (ii) Arc = circumference/10 = (22/7 × 35)/10 = 110/10 =  11 mm    (iii)(a) Sector area = (1/10) × 22/7 × 17.5 × 17.5 = 962.5/10 =  96.25 mm²    (iii)(b) Wire = circumference + 5 diameters = 110 + 5 × 35 =  285 mm           Q62 (3 marks, 2019 Set II; similar 2017)  Find the area of the segment of a circle of radius 21 cm with ∠AOB = 120° (π = 22/7, √3 = 1.732).     Ans:      Area of sector = 120/360 × 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 462 cm²   Area of ΔAOB = ½ r² sin 120° = ½ × 441 × (√3/2) = 441√3/4 = 190.95 cm²   Segment = 462 - 190.95 =  271.05 cm²   (2017: chord subtending 60° in a circle of radius 10 cm, π = 3.14: sector 52.33, equilateral triangle (√3/4) × 100 = 43.30,  minor segment ≈ 9.03 cm² , major segment = 314 - 9.03 ≈  304.97 cm² .)

title: Chapter 12: Surface Areas and Volumes
text: Chapter 12: Surface Areas and Volumes       Q63 (MCQ, SQP)  Two cubes, each of volume 64 cm³, are joined end to end. The surface area of the resulting cuboid is: (A) 192 (B) 160 (C) 96 (D) 80 cm²     Ans: (B) 160 cm².  Side = 4 cm. Cuboid 8 × 4 × 4: SA = 2(8×4 + 4×4 + 8×4) = 2(32 + 16 + 32) = 160 cm².        Q64 (A-R, 2025)  A: If we join two hemispheres of the same radius along their bases, we get a sphere. R: Total surface area of a sphere of radius r is 3πr².     Ans: (C)  A is true; R is false (TSA of a sphere is 4πr²; 3πr² is the TSA of a solid hemisphere).  (2024 MCQ: a solid sphere cut into two hemispheres; ratio of surface areas = 4πr² : 2 × 3πr² =  2 : 3 . 2026 MCQ: three balls of radius r packed in a cylinder of radius r and height 6r; air = 6πr³ - 3 × (4/3)πr³ =  2πr³ .)         Q65 ★ (5 marks, SQP)  A tent is a cylinder (height 3 m, radius 14 m) surmounted by a cone. Total height is 13.5 m. Find the canvas needed, keeping 26 m² extra for stitching and wastage, and its cost at ₹250 per m².     Ans:      Cone height = 13.5 - 3 = 10.5 m. Slant height l = √(14² + 10.5²) = √(196 + 110.25) = √306.25 = 17.5 m   CSA of cylinder = 2πrh = 2 × 22/7 × 14 × 3 = 264 m²   CSA of cone = πrl = 22/7 × 14 × 17.5 = 770 m²   Canvas = 264 + 770 + 26 =  1060 m²    Cost = 1060 × 250 =  ₹2,65,000    (No base: the floor of a tent is not covered with canvas.)          Q66 ★ (5 marks, SQP OR; 2022 similar)  A solid toy is a hemisphere surmounted by a cone of the same radius 3.5 cm. Total volume is 166 5/6 cm³. Find the height of the cone, and the cost of painting the hemispherical part at ₹15 per cm².     Ans:      Volume of hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = 2/3 × 22/7 × 3.5³ = 539/6 cm³ (= 89 5/6)   Volume of cone = 1001/6 - 539/6 = 462/6 = 77 cm³   (1/3) × 22/7 × 3.5 × 3.5 × h = 77, so (77/6) h = 77,  h = 6 cm    CSA of hemisphere = 2πr² = 2 × 22/7 × 3.5 × 3.5 = 77 cm². Cost = 77 × 15 =  ₹1,155   (2022: a cone of height 24 cm, radius 7 cm hollowed out of a cylinder of height 30 cm, radius 7 cm. TSA left = cylinder CSA 1320 + top circle 154 + cone CSA (l = 25) 550 =  2024 cm² .)

title: Chapter 13: Statistics
text: Chapter 13: Statistics       Q67 ★ (MCQ, SQP; 2025, 2026 same idea)  The mean and median of a data are 35.5 and 32. The mode is: (A) 23 (B) 26 (C) 25 (D) 30     Ans: (C) 25.  Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean = 96 - 71 =  25 .  (2025: mode 15x, mean 18x gives median = (Mode + 2 Mean)/3 = (15x + 36x)/3 =  17x . 2026: mean 43, median 40 gives mode = 120 - 86 =  34 .)         Q68 (MCQ, SQP)  The mean age of a combined group of men and women is 35 years. The mean ages of men and women are 38 and 30 years. The percentage of women is: (A) 15 (B) 25.5 (C) 35 (D) 37.5     Ans: (D) 37.5.  38m + 30w = 35(m + w), so 3m = 5w, m : w = 5 : 3. Women = 3/8 =  37.5% .        Q69 ★ (Case study 4 marks, SQP)  Marks (out of 50): 0-10: 3, 10-20: 6, 20-30: 12, 30-40: 15, 40-50: 14. (i) Modal class? (ii) Median class? (iii)(A) Mean? OR (iii)(B) Mode?     Ans:      (i) Highest frequency 15, so modal class =  30-40    (ii) N = 50, N/2 = 25. Cumulative frequencies 3, 9, 21, 36, 50. 25 first falls in 36, so median class =  30-40    (iii)(A) Class marks 5, 15, 25, 35, 45; fx = 15, 90, 300, 525, 630; Σfx = 1560. Mean = 1560/50 =  31.2    (iii)(B) l = 30, f1 = 15, f0 = 12, f2 = 14, h = 10. Mode = 30 + [(15 - 12)/(30 - 12 - 14)] × 10 = 30 + (3/4) × 10 =  37.5           Q70 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  Find the mode: the modal class is 30-40 with frequency 16; the class before has 10 and the class after has 12 (class size 10).     Ans:      Mode = l + [(f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)] × h   = 30 + [(16 - 10)/(32 - 10 - 12)] × 10 = 30 + (6/10) × 10 =  36           Q71 ★ (5 marks, 2025)  Find the missing frequency f if the mean is 18. Hence find the mode. Daily allowance: 11-13: 7, 13-15: 6, 15-17: 9, 17-19: 13, 19-21: f, 21-23: 5, 23-25: 4     Ans:      Class marks x: 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24   fx: 84, 84, 144, 234, 20f, 110, 96. Σfx = 752 + 20f. Σf = 44 + f   Mean = (752 + 20f)/(44 + f) = 18, so 752 + 20f = 792 + 18f,  f = 20    Modal class = 19-21 (f1 = 20), f0 = 13, f2 = 5, h = 2   Mode = 19 + [(20 - 13)/(40 - 13 - 5)] × 2 = 19 + (7/22) × 2 = 19 + 0.64 =  19.64           Q72 ★ (5 marks, 2026)  The median of the following data is 50 and the total frequency is 90. Find p and q. Class: 20-30: p, 30-40: 15, 40-50: 25, 50-60: 20, 60-70: q, 70-80: 8, 80-90: 10     Ans:      p + 15 + 25 + 20 + q + 8 + 10 = 90, so  p + q = 12    Median 50 lies in 50-60. l = 50, f = 20, h = 10, N/2 = 45, cf before = p + 40   50 = 50 + [(45 - (p + 40))/20] × 10, so 45 - p - 40 = 0,  p = 5 ,  q = 7   (2026 OR: mean and mode of 0-15: 4, 15-30: 8, 30-45: 11, 45-60: 14, 60-75: 10, 75-90: 7, 90-105: 6. Σf = 60, Σfx = 3195,  mean = 53.25 ; modal class 45-60, mode = 45 + (3/7) × 15 =  51.43 .)

title: Chapter 14: Probability
text: Chapter 14: Probability       Q73 ★ (MCQ, SQP; 2026 same)  Two dice are rolled together. The probability of getting a number less than 4 on each die is: (A) 1/4 (B) 1/9 (C) 1/36 (D) 1/6     Ans: (A) 1/4.  Each die must show 1, 2 or 3: 3 × 3 = 9 outcomes out of 36. 9/36 =  1/4 .        Q74 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  2 diamond cards and 4 spade cards are missing from a pack of 52. A card is drawn at random. P(heart) = ? (A) 13/52 (B) 13/46 (C) 11/52 (D) 11/46     Ans: (B) 13/46.  Cards left = 52 - 6 = 46. All 13 hearts are still there.  (2025: P(red face card) from 52 cards = 6/52 =  3/26 . 2024: one black card is lost; P(queen of hearts) =  1/51 .)         Q75 (MCQ, SQP)  T-shirts numbered 4 to 99 are in a box. One is taken at random. P(number is a perfect square or a perfect cube) = ? (A) 1/12 (B) 1/32 (C) 11/96 (D) 5/48     Ans: (D) 5/48.  Total = 96. Squares: 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 (8). Cubes: 8, 27, 64 (3). 64 is counted twice, so favourable = 8 + 3 - 1 = 10. P = 10/96 =  5/48 .        Q76 (MCQ, 2024; 2023 similar)  If the probability of a player winning a game is 0.79, the probability of his losing is:     Ans: 0.21  (1 - 0.79).  (2023: a girl's probability of winning a lottery prize is 0.08; 6000 tickets were sold, so she bought 0.08 × 6000 =  480  tickets. 2023: 5 of 20 people can't swim, P(can swim) = 15/20 =  3/4 .)         Q77 (A-R, 2026)  A: If the probability of an event is 0.2p, p > 0, then p cannot be more than 5. R: P(not E) = 1 - P(E) for an event E.     Ans: (B)  Both true, but R does not explain A. (A is true because a probability is at most 1: 0.2p ≤ 1 gives p ≤ 5.)        Q78 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that the product of the numbers is a prime number.     Ans:      A product is prime only when one die shows 1 and the other a prime: (1,2), (2,1), (1,3), (3,1), (1,5), (5,1) = 6 outcomes   P = 6/36 =  1/6           Q79 ★ (3 marks, 2025; 2017 similar)  Two dice are thrown at the same time. Find the probability that the difference of the numbers on the two dice is 2.     Ans:      Favourable: (1,3), (3,1), (2,4), (4,2), (3,5), (5,3), (4,6), (6,4) = 8   P = 8/36 =  2/9   (2017: sum less than 7: 15 outcomes, P =  5/12 ; product less than 16: 25 outcomes, P =  25/36 ; doublet of odd numbers (1,1), (3,3), (5,5): P = 3/36 =  1/12 . 2024 MCQ: sum 2, 3 or 5: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 outcomes, P =  7/36 .)           Q80 ★ (2 marks, 2019)  A game consists of tossing a coin 3 times and noting the outcome each time. Getting the same result in all tosses is a success. Find the probability of losing the game.     Ans:      Outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT = 8   Success: HHH, TTT = 2. P(win) = 2/8 = 1/4    P(lose) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4   (2019: a die is thrown once; P(prime) = 3/6 =  1/2 ; P(number between 2 and 6, i.e. 3, 4, 5) =  1/2 . 2023: bag with 4 red, 3 blue, 2 yellow balls; P(yellow) =  2/9 , P(red) =  4/9 .)

title: 6. Quick revision sheet
text: 6. Quick revision sheet

title: 6a. Formulas (learn these and you can do most of the paper)
text: 6a. Formulas (learn these and you can do most of the paper)          Chapter   Formula           Real Numbers   HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers (for 2 numbers only). HCF = lowest powers of common primes; LCM = highest powers of all primes       Polynomials   For ax² + bx + c: sum of zeroes α + β = -b/a; product αβ = c/a. Quadratic with given zeroes: x² - (sum)x + (product)       Linear equations   Unique: a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2. No solution (parallel): a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2. Infinite (coincident): a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2       Quadratic   D = b² - 4ac. D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: equal roots; D < 0: no real roots. Roots x = [-b ± √D]/(2a)       AP   a_n = a + (n - 1)d. S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (a + l). a_n = S_n - S_(n-1)       Coordinates   Distance = √[(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²]. Mid-point = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2). Section (m : n) = ((mx2 + nx1)/(m + n), (my2 + ny1)/(m + n)). On x-axis y = 0; on y-axis x = 0       Triangles   BPT: if DE ∥ BC then AD/DB = AE/EC. Similar triangles: sides in same ratio, perimeters in same ratio       Trigonometry   sin = P/H, cos = B/H, tan = P/B; cosec = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos, cot = 1/tan; tan = sin/cos       Identities   sin²A + cos²A = 1; 1 + tan²A = sec²A; 1 + cot²A = cosec²A       Circles   Tangent ⟂ radius at point of contact. Tangents from an outside point are equal. Tangent length = √(d² - r²)       Areas   Circumference 2πr; area πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr; sector = (θ/360) × πr² = ½ × arc × r; segment = sector - triangle (triangle = ½ r² sin θ)       Volumes   Cube a³; cuboid lbh; cylinder πr²h; cone (1/3)πr²h; sphere (4/3)πr³; hemisphere (2/3)πr³       Surface areas   Cylinder CSA 2πrh; cone CSA πrl, l = √(r² + h²); sphere 4πr²; hemisphere CSA 2πr², TSA 3πr²; cuboid 2(lb + bh + hl); cube 6a²       Statistics   Mean = Σfx/Σf. Median = l + [(N/2 - cf)/f] × h. Mode = l + [(f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)] × h.  3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean        Probability   P(E) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; P(not E) = 1 - P(E). Sure event P = 1; impossible event P = 0

title: 6b. Trigonometry table (write it on the first page of your rough work)
text: 6b. Trigonometry table (write it on the first page of your rough work)          Angle   0°   30°   45°   60°   90°           sin   0   1/2   1/√2   √3/2   1       cos   1   √3/2   1/√2   1/2   0       tan   0   1/√3   1   √3   not defined         Trick: sin row is √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. The cos row is the sin row backwards. tan = sin/cos.

title: 6c. Key definitions (1-mark favourites)
text: 6c. Key definitions (1-mark favourites)       Rational number:  can be written as p/q, p and q integers, q ≠ 0.  Irrational:  cannot (√2, √3, π). Rational + irrational = irrational; non-zero rational × irrational = irrational.    Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic:  every composite number can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way (apart from order).    Zero of a polynomial:  value of x that makes p(x) = 0. On a graph, the number of zeroes = number of times the graph  meets the x-axis .    Consistent pair:  has at least one solution.  Inconsistent:  no solution.    Tangent:  a line that touches a circle at exactly one point.  Secant:  cuts it at two points.    Angle of elevation:  angle above the horizontal when looking up.  Angle of depression:  angle below the horizontal when looking down. (Angle of elevation from A to B = angle of depression from B to A.)    Median:  the middle-most observation.  Mode:  the most frequent value.  Modal class:  the class with the highest frequency.   A 52-card pack: 4 suits (hearts ♥, diamonds ♦ red; spades ♠, clubs ♣ black), 13 each;  12 face cards  (J, Q, K of each suit); 26 red, 26 black; 4 aces.

title: 6d. Two dice: the 36 outcomes (draw this grid in every dice question)
6e. Diagrams to learn (draw neatly in pencil; the figure itself earns marks)
text: 6e. Diagrams to learn (draw neatly in pencil; the figure itself earns marks)       BPT figure:  ΔABC, line DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC; join BE and CD; drop EN ⟂ AB and DM ⟂ AC.    Two tangents from an external point:  circle with centre O, point P outside, tangents PA and PB, radii OA and OB with right-angle marks at A and B, and the line OP.    Quadrilateral / parallelogram around a circle:  four sides touching the circle at P, Q, R, S; mark the equal tangent pieces with the same letter.    Heights and distances (two angles):  vertical tower/lighthouse, horizontal ground line, two observation points on the same side, angles marked at the ground (elevation) or at the top with a horizontal line drawn (depression). Label h, x and the given distance.    Combined solid:  cylinder with cone on top (tent), or hemisphere with cone on top (toy). Mark r, h and slant height l.    Sector and segment:  circle, two radii making angle θ, chord joining their ends; shade the part asked.

title: 7. Answer-writing tips (to collect step marks) and a 30-day timetable
text: 7. Answer-writing tips (to collect step marks) and a 30-day timetable

title: 7a. Tips
text: 7a. Tips       Write the formula first.  In a 3-mark sum, the formula alone often gets ½-1 mark, substitution another 1 mark. Never write only the final number.    Proofs:  always write  Given, To prove, Construction (if any), Proof  with a reason in brackets after every line ("radius ⟂ tangent", "tangents from an external point are equal", "AA similarity").    Draw the figure  in every geometry, circles and heights-and-distances question. A correct, labelled figure is usually worth ½-1 mark.    Word problems (linear / quadratic):  start with "Let ... = x". Writing the correct equation is half the marks even if you cannot solve it.    Reject impossible answers in words:  "speed cannot be negative, so x = 40". This line carries marks.    Statistics:  make the full table (class, x, f, fx or cf). Write the formula with l, f1, f0, f2, h listed separately before substituting.    Probability:  write the total outcomes and  list  the favourable outcomes. Give the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.    MCQ and A-R:  never leave one blank; there is no negative marking. In A-R, first decide "Is A true? Is R true?", then "Does R explain A?".    Case studies (Section E):  parts (i) and (ii) are 1 mark each and usually very easy. Always attempt them, even if you skip (iii).    Choose the easier OR option.  Usually pick the numerical over the proof, unless it is one of the standard proofs you have learnt (√2 irrational, BPT, tangent proofs).    Order of attempting:  Section A (25 min) → case-study (i), (ii) parts → questions you know from this pack → the rest. Keep 10 minutes to check signs and units.    Units:  cm, cm², cm³, m/min. Write them in the final answer.

Write each proof 3 times.       8   Coordinate Geometry: distance and mid-point (Q31-Q33, Q36)       9   Coordinate Geometry: section formula, axis ratio, parallelogram (Q34, Q35, Q37)       10   AP: a_n and "how many terms" (Q21, Q23, Q24)       11   AP: S_n, sum questions and case studies (Q22, Q25, Q26)       12   Trigonometry: table of values, evaluate questions (Q38-Q42)       13   Trigonometry: identities (Q43-Q45)       14   Heights and distances: one-angle and two-angle sums (Q46-Q47, Q49)       15   Heights and distances: speed and roof problems (Q48, Q50). title: Q1 · Chapter 1: Real Numbers
text: Q1 ★ (MCQ, SQP; same idea 2023)  The greatest number which divides both 134 and 188, leaving remainders 4 and 6 respectively, is: (A) 13 (B) 26 (C) 39 (D) 65    Ans: (B) 26.  Subtract the remainders: 134 - 4 = 130 and 188 - 6 = 182. HCF(130, 182): 130 = 2 × 5 × 13, 182 = 2 × 7 × 13, so HCF = 2 × 13 =  26 .

title: Q3 · Chapter 1: Real Numbers
text: Q3 (MCQ, 2019)  Two positive integers a and b can be written as a = x³y² and b = xy³, where x, y are prime numbers. Find LCM(a, b).    Ans: x³y³.  LCM = product of the  highest  power of each prime. (HCF would be the lowest powers: xy².)

title: Q4 · Chapter 1: Real Numbers
text: Q4 ★ (3 marks, 2019; √5 in 2023)  Prove that √2 is an irrational number.    Ans:      Suppose √2 is rational. Then √2 = a/b, where a and b are co-prime integers and b ≠ 0.   Squaring: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b². So 2 divides a², hence 2 divides a. Let a = 2c.   Then 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c². So 2 divides b², hence 2 divides b.   Now 2 divides both a and b. This  contradicts  that a and b are co-prime.   So our assumption is wrong.  √2 is irrational.  (For √3 or √5, replace 2 by 3 or 5 in every line.)

title: Q5 · Chapter 1: Real Numbers
text: Q5 ★ (3 marks, SQP; 2 + 3√5 in 2026; (2 + √3)/5 in 2019)  Given that √3 is irrational, prove that (2 + 3√3) is irrational.    Ans:      Suppose 2 + 3√3 is rational. Then 2 + 3√3 = p/q, where p, q are integers, q ≠ 0.   So 3√3 = p/q - 2 = (p - 2q)/q, and √3 = (p - 2q)/(3q).   The right side is rational (integers divided by a non-zero integer), so √3 would be rational.   But √3 is irrational. This is a  contradiction . So  2 + 3√3 is irrational.

title: Q6 · Chapter 1: Real Numbers
text: Q6 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  Three bells toll at intervals of 5, 6 and 8 minutes. They all toll together at 10:00 a.m. when the park opens. How many more times do they toll together till the park closes at 7:00 p.m.?    Ans:      LCM(5, 6, 8): 5 = 5, 6 = 2 × 3, 8 = 2³. LCM = 2³ × 3 × 5 = 120 minutes = 2 hours.   They toll together every 2 hours: 12 noon, 2 p.m., 4 p.m., 6 p.m. (8 p.m. is after closing).   So they toll together  4 more times .  (Other OR in SQP: hall 9.75 m × 6.75 m × 5.25 m, longest ruler = HCF(975, 675, 525) cm =  75 cm .)

title: Q7 · Chapter 2: Polynomials
text: Q7 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  If f(x) = px² + qx + r, p ≠ 0 and p + r = q, then one of the zeroes of f(x) is: (A) q/p (B) r/p (C) -r/p (D) -q/p    Ans: (C) -r/p.  Put x = -1: f(-1) = p - q + r = 0 (because q = p + r). So -1 is a zero. Product of zeroes = r/p, so the other zero = (r/p) ÷ (-1) =  -r/p .

title: Q8 · Chapter 2: Polynomials
text: Q8 ★ (A-R, SQP)  A: If the zeroes of (2k - 1)x² + 4x - 3 are reciprocal of each other, then k = -1. R: If a = c, then the zeroes of ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0) are reciprocal of each other.    Ans: (A)  Both true and R explains A. Reciprocal zeroes means product = 1, so c/a = 1, i.e. a = c: 2k - 1 = -3, k = -1.

title: Q9 · Chapter 2: Polynomials
text: Q9 (A-R, 2024)  A: If the graph of a polynomial touches the x-axis at only one point, then the polynomial cannot be a quadratic polynomial. R: A polynomial of degree n (n > 1) can have at most n zeroes.    Ans: (D)  A is false (y = x² touches the x-axis only at (0, 0) and is quadratic). R is true.

title: Q10 · Chapter 2: Polynomials
text: Q10 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  Find the value of k such that the polynomial x² - (k + 6)x + 2(2k - 1) has sum of its zeroes equal to half of their product.    Ans:      a = 1, b = -(k + 6), c = 2(2k - 1)   Sum = -b/a = k + 6; Product = c/a = 2(2k - 1)   k + 6 = ½ × 2(2k - 1) = 2k - 1    k = 7       (SQP similar, 3 marks: if α, β are zeroes of 2x² - 8x + 5, find (α + 1/β)(β + 1/α). Expand: αβ + 1 + 1 + 1/(αβ). αβ = 5/2, so the value = 5/2 + 2 + 2/5 =  49/10 .)

title: Q11 · Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
text: Q11 (MCQ, 2025)  If x = 1 and y = 2 is a solution of the pair of linear equations 2x - 3y + a = 0 and 2x + 3y - b = 0, then: (A) a = 2b (B) 2a = b (C) a + 2b = 0 (D) 2a + b = 0    Ans: (B) 2a = b.  Put x = 1, y = 2: 2 - 6 + a = 0 gives a = 4; 2 + 6 - b = 0 gives b = 8. So b = 2a.

title: Q12 · Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
text: Q12 ★ (2 marks, 2019)  Find c if the system cx + 3y + (3 - c) = 0, 12x + cy - c = 0 has infinitely many solutions.    Ans:      Condition: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, so c/12 = 3/c = (3 - c)/(-c)   c/12 = 3/c gives c² = 36, c = ±6   3/c = (3 - c)/(-c) gives -3 = 3 - c, so c = 6    c = 6  (satisfies both)  (Remember: unique solution a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2; no solution a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2.)

title: Q13 · Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
text: Q13 (2 marks, 2024)  Solve 7x - 2y = 5 and 8x + 7y = 15 and verify your answer.    Ans (elimination):      Multiply the first by 7: 49x - 14y = 35. Multiply the second by 2: 16x + 14y = 30.   Add: 65x = 65, so  x = 1 . Then 7(1) - 2y = 5, so  y = 1 .   Verify: 7 - 2 = 5 ✓ and 8 + 7 = 15 ✓.

title: Q14 · Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
text: Q14 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  A father's age is three times the sum of the ages of his two children. After 5 years his age will be two times the sum of their ages. Find the present age of the father.    Ans:      Let father = x years, sum of children's ages = y years. So x = 3y.   After 5 years: father x + 5; children's sum y + 10 (each child gets 5 years older).   x + 5 = 2(y + 10), so x - 2y = 15. Put x = 3y: y = 15.    Father = 45 years.

title: Q15 · Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
text: Q15 ★ (5 marks, 2025)  Vijay invested money in two schemes A and B at 8% and 9% per annum. He received ₹1,860 total annual interest. Had he interchanged the amounts, he would have received ₹20 more. How much did he invest in each scheme?    Ans:      Let ₹x in A and ₹y in B. 8x/100 + 9y/100 = 1860, so 8x + 9y = 186000 ...(1)   Interchanged: 9x + 8y = 188000 ...(2)   Add: 17x + 17y = 374000, so x + y = 22000 ...(3)   Subtract (1) from (2): x - y = 2000 ...(4)   From (3) and (4): x = 12000, y = 10000.    ₹12,000 in scheme A and ₹10,000 in scheme B.   (SQP case study similar: x + y = 1000 and 10x + 15y = 12750 give 450 small and 550 large bottles in June.)

title: Q16 · Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations
text: Q16 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  If (1 - p) is a root of x² + px + 1 - p = 0, then its roots are: (A) 0, 1 (B) -1, 1 (C) 0, -1 (D) -1, 2    Ans: (C) 0, -1.  Put x = 1 - p: (1 - p)² + p(1 - p) + (1 - p) = (1 - p)(1 - p + p + 1) = 2(1 - p) = 0, so p = 1. The equation becomes x² + x = 0, i.e. x(x + 1) = 0, roots  0 and -1 .

title: Q17 · Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations
text: Q17 ★ (2 marks, 2017)  Find the value of k for which x² + k(2x + k - 1) + 2 = 0 has real and equal roots.    Ans:      x² + 2kx + (k² - k + 2) = 0. So a = 1, b = 2k, c = k² - k + 2.   Equal roots: D = b² - 4ac = 0   4k² - 4(k² - k + 2) = 0, so 4k - 8 = 0    k = 2   (2019 MCQ: for real roots of x² + 4x + k = 0, D ≥ 0 gives 16 - 4k ≥ 0, so  k ≤ 4 .)

title: Q18 · Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations
text: Q18 (2 marks, 2026)  Verify that the roots of (p - q)x² + (q - r)x + (r - p) = 0 are equal when q + r = 2p.    Ans:      D = (q - r)² - 4(p - q)(r - p)   If q + r = 2p, then r = 2p - q, so q - r = 2q - 2p = -2(p - q) and r - p = p - q.   D = 4(p - q)² - 4(p - q)(p - q) = 0. So the  roots are equal .

title: Q19 · Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations
text: Q19 ★ (5 marks, 2025)  A train travels 480 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 8 km/h less, it would have taken 3 hours more. Find the speed of the train.    Ans:      Let speed = x km/h. Time = 480/x. New time = 480/(x - 8).   480/(x - 8) - 480/x = 3   480 × 8 = 3x(x - 8), so 3840 = 3x² - 24x, so x² - 8x - 1280 = 0   (x - 40)(x + 32) = 0, so x = 40 or -32 (speed cannot be negative)    Speed = 40 km/h

title: Q20 · Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations
text: Q20 ★ (5 marks, SQP)  A rectangular park is 50 m × 40 m. A rectangular pool is built in the middle with a grass strip of uniform width around it. The area of the grass strip is 1184 m². Find the dimensions of the pool.    Ans:      Let the strip width = x m. Pool = (50 - 2x) by (40 - 2x).   Pool area = 2000 - 1184 = 816 m²   (50 - 2x)(40 - 2x) = 816, so 4x² - 180x + 2000 = 816, so x² - 45x + 296 = 0   (x - 8)(x - 37) = 0. x = 37 is impossible (50 - 74 < 0), so x = 8.    Pool = 34 m × 24 m  (check: 34 × 24 = 816 ✓)  (Also asked: 2019 taps fill a tank in 15/8 h, one takes 2 h less →  3 h and 5 h ; 2026 tour ₹5,400, extend 5 days, cut ₹180/day → x² + 5x - 150 = 0 →  10 days, ₹540/day ; 2025 right triangle perimeter 60 cm, hypotenuse 25 cm → sides  15 cm and 20 cm .)

title: Q22 · Chapter 5: Arithmetic Progressions
text: Q22 ★ (MCQ, 2025; S_n given in 2019 too)  If the sum of the first m terms of an AP is 2m² + 3m, then its second term is: (A) 10 (B) 9 (C) 12 (D) 4    Ans: (B) 9.  S1 = 2 + 3 = 5 = a1. S2 = 8 + 6 = 14. a2 = S2 - S1 =  9 .  (2019: if S_n = 3n² - 4n, then a_n = S_n - S_(n-1) =  6n - 7 .)

title: Q23 · Chapter 5: Arithmetic Progressions
text: Q23 ★ (2 marks, 2019; same type 2017)  How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 3?    Ans:      AP: 12, 15, 18, ..., 99. a = 12, d = 3, a_n = 99   99 = 12 + (n - 1) × 3, so (n - 1) = 29,  n = 30   (2019 Set III: two-digit numbers divisible by 7: 14, ..., 98 gives  13 . 2017: integers between 200 and 500 divisible by 8: 208, ..., 496 gives  37 .)

title: Q24 · Chapter 5: Arithmetic Progressions
text: Q24 ★ (2 marks, 2019)  Which term of the AP 3, 15, 27, 39, ... will be 120 more than its 21st term?    Ans:      a = 3, d = 12. a21 = 3 + 20 × 12 = 243   Required term = 243 + 120 = 363 = 3 + (n - 1) × 12, so n - 1 = 30    31st term

title: Q25 · Chapter 5: Arithmetic Progressions
text: Q25 (3 marks, SQP)  Find the sum of integers between 1 and 400 that are multiples of 4 as well as of 5.    Ans:      Multiples of both 4 and 5 = multiples of 20: 20, 40, ..., 380 (400 is not "between")   380 = 20 + (n - 1) × 20, so n = 19   S19 = 19/2 × (20 + 380) = 19 × 200 =  3800

title: Q26 · Chapter 5: Arithmetic Progressions
text: Q26 ★ (Case study 4 marks, 2025)  A charity run: the first round is 300 m and each next round is 50 m longer. There are 10 rounds. (i) Write the 4th, 5th and 6th terms. (ii) Find the distance of the 8th round. (iii)(a) Total distance after 10 rounds. OR (iii)(b) Total distance of the first 6 rounds.    Ans:      (i) a = 300, d = 50:  450 m, 500 m, 550 m    (ii) a8 = 300 + 7 × 50 =  650 m    (iii)(a) S10 = 10/2 [2 × 300 + 9 × 50] = 5 × 1050 =  5250 m    (iii)(b) S6 = 6/2 [600 + 5 × 50] = 3 × 850 =  2550 m   (2026 "Kolam" case: 4, 8, 12, ... dots; a = 4, d = 4, a_n = 4n; S_n = 2n(n + 1) = 220 gives  n = 10  squares; 2n(n + 1) = 100 has no whole-number answer, so  100 dots is not possible .)

title: Q27 · Chapter 6: Triangles
text: Q27 (MCQ, SQP)  The perimeters of two similar triangles are 56 cm and 70 cm. If one side of the first triangle is 14 cm, the corresponding side of the second is: (A) 5 (B) 7.5 (C) 10 (D) 17.5    Ans: (D) 17.5.  Ratio of perimeters = ratio of sides: 14/x = 56/70, so x = 14 × 70/56 =  17.5 cm .

title: Q28 · Chapter 6: Triangles
text: Q28 (MCQ, 2025)  In triangles ABC and DEF, ∠B = ∠E, ∠F = ∠C and AB = 3DE. Then the two triangles are: (A) congruent but not similar (B) congruent as well as similar (C) neither congruent nor similar (D) similar but not congruent    Ans: (D).  Two equal angles give similarity (AA). Sides are in ratio 3 : 1, so they are not congruent.  (2025 Section B similar: if ΔABC ~ ΔPQR, AB = 6, BC = 4, AC = 8 and PR = 6 cm, the ratio is 6/8 = 3/4, so PQ = 4.5, QR = 3 and  PQ + QR = 7.5 cm .)

title: Q29 · Chapter 6: Triangles
text: Q29 ★ (5 marks, SQP; BPT used in 2023 and 2026 MCQs/short answers)  Prove that a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, divides the other two sides in the same ratio (Basic Proportionality Theorem).    Ans:       Given:  In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC, D on AB and E on AC.  To prove:  AD/DB = AE/EC.    Construction:  Join BE and CD. Draw EN ⟂ AB and DM ⟂ AC.   ar(ADE) = ½ × AD × EN, ar(BDE) = ½ × DB × EN. So ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB ...(1)   ar(ADE) = ½ × AE × DM, ar(DEC) = ½ × EC × DM. So ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC ...(2)   ΔBDE and ΔDEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC, so ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) ...(3)   From (1), (2), (3):  AD/DB = AE/EC.  Hence proved.    Draw the figure  (triangle with DE parallel to BC, the two joins and two perpendiculars). The figure alone carries marks.

title: Q30 · Chapter 6: Triangles
text: Q30 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. Its diagonals meet at O. Show that AO/BO = CO/DO.    Ans:      In ΔAOB and ΔCOD: ∠OAB = ∠OCD (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC) and ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite).   So ΔAOB ~ ΔCOD (AA). Hence AO/CO = BO/DO.   Rearranging:  AO/BO = CO/DO.   (SQP OR: if ∠PQR = ∠QSP, PQ = 6 cm, PS = 3 cm, then ΔPRQ ~ ΔPQS, so PQ/PR = PS/PQ, 36 = 3 × PR,  PR = 12 cm .)

title: Q31 · Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Q31 ★ (MCQ, SQP and 2024)  PM is a median of ΔPQR with vertices P(5, -6), Q(6, 4) and R(0, 0). The length of PM is: (A) 2√17 (B) 2√15 (C) √101 (D) 10 units    Ans: (A) 2√17.  M = mid-point of QR = ((6 + 0)/2, (4 + 0)/2) = (3, 2). PM = √[(5 - 3)² + (-6 - 2)²] = √(4 + 64) = √68 =  2√17 .

title: Q32 · Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Q32 (MCQ, SQP)  The point which lies on the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining A(-3, -4) and B(3, 4) is: (A) (0, 0) (B) (0, 3) (C) (3, 0) (D) (0, 4)    Ans: (A) (0, 0).  It is the mid-point of AB, and the mid-point lies on the perpendicular bisector.

title: Q33 · Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Q33 (MCQ, 2024; same type 2017)  If the distance between (3, -5) and (x, -5) is 15 units, then x is: (A) 12, -18 (B) -12, 18 (C) 18, 5 (D) -9, -12    Ans: (B).  √[(x - 3)² + 0] = 15, so x - 3 = ±15,  x = 18 or -12 .  (2017: distance between (4, k) and (1, 0) is 5 gives 9 + k² = 25,  k = ±4 .)

title: Q34 · Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Q34 ★ (3 marks, SQP; same type 2019, 2023)  In what ratio does the x-axis divide the line segment joining (-4, -6) and (-1, 7)? Find the point of division.    Ans:      Let the ratio be k : 1. The point on the x-axis has y = 0.   y = (k × 7 + 1 × (-6))/(k + 1) = 0, so 7k = 6, k = 6/7.  Ratio 6 : 7.    x = (6 × (-1) + 7 × (-4))/(6 + 7) = (-6 - 28)/13 = -34/13    Point = (-34/13, 0)   (2019: x-axis divides (1, -3) and (4, 5) in ratio  3 : 5  at (17/8, 0).)

title: Q35 · Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Q35 ★ (3 marks, 2025; NCERT)  Find the ratio in which the y-axis divides the line segment joining (5, -6) and (-1, -4). Also find the point of intersection.    Ans:      On the y-axis x = 0. Let ratio k : 1: x = (k × (-1) + 5)/(k + 1) = 0, so k = 5.  Ratio 5 : 1.    y = (5 × (-4) + 1 × (-6))/6 = -26/6 = -13/3    Point = (0, -13/3)

title: Q36 · Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Q36 (3 marks, 2019)  Find the point on the y-axis which is equidistant from (5, -2) and (-3, 2).    Ans:      Let P = (0, y). PA² = PB²: 25 + (y + 2)² = 9 + (y - 2)²   25 + y² + 4y + 4 = 9 + y² - 4y + 4, so 8y = -16, y = -2    P = (0, -2)

title: Q37 · Chapter 7: Coordinate Geometry
text: Q37 ★ (A-R, SQP)  A: If three vertices of a parallelogram taken in order are (-1, -6), (2, -5) and (7, 2), then its fourth vertex is (4, 1). R: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.    Ans: (A)  Both true and R explains A. Mid-point of AC = ((-1 + 7)/2, (-6 + 2)/2) = (3, -2) = mid-point of BD. So D = (2 × 3 - 2, 2 × (-2) + 5) = (4, 1).  (2019 1-mark: centre (2, -3), one end B(1, 4) of a diameter; other end A = (2 × 2 - 1, 2 × (-3) - 4) =  (3, -10) .)

title: Q38 · Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry
text: Q38 (MCQ, 2025)  If θ is an acute angle and 7 + 4 sin θ = 9, then θ is: (A) 90° (B) 30° (C) 45° (D) 60°    Ans: (B) 30°.  4 sin θ = 2, so sin θ = 1/2, θ = 30°.

title: Q40 · Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry
text: Q40 (MCQ, 2024)  If sec θ - tan θ = m, then sec θ + tan θ = ?    Ans: 1/m.  Because (sec θ - tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ) = sec²θ - tan²θ = 1.

title: Q42 · Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry
text: Q42 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  If tan θ = 1/√5, find the value of (cosec²θ - sec²θ)/(cosec²θ + sec²θ).    Ans:      cot θ = √5, so cosec²θ = 1 + cot²θ = 1 + 5 = 6   sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ = 1 + 1/5 = 6/5   Value = (6 - 6/5)/(6 + 6/5) = (24/5)/(36/5) =  2/3

title: Q43 · Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry
text: Q43 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  Prove that (sin θ + cosec θ)² + (cos θ + sec θ)² = 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ.    Ans:      LHS = sin²θ + cosec²θ + 2 sin θ cosec θ + cos²θ + sec²θ + 2 cos θ sec θ   sin θ cosec θ = 1 and cos θ sec θ = 1, so LHS = (sin²θ + cos²θ) + cosec²θ + sec²θ + 2 + 2   = 1 + (1 + cot²θ) + (1 + tan²θ) + 4   =  7 + tan²θ + cot²θ  = RHS. Hence proved.

title: Q44 · Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry
text: Q44 ★ (3 marks, SQP)  A student simplified cos θ/(1 - sin θ) + (1 - sin θ)/cos θ as follows: Step 1: [cos²θ + (1 - sin θ)²] / [(1 - sin θ) cos θ]; Step 2: [cos²θ + cos²θ] / [(1 - sin θ) cos θ]; Step 3: 2cos²θ / [(1 - sin θ) cos θ]; Step 4: 2cos θ/(1 - sin θ). Find the error and the correct answer.    Ans:       Error in Step 2:  (1 - sin θ)² is NOT cos²θ. (1 - sin²θ = cos²θ, but (1 - sin θ)² = 1 - 2 sin θ + sin²θ.)   Correct: numerator = cos²θ + 1 - 2 sin θ + sin²θ = 1 + 1 - 2 sin θ = 2(1 - sin θ)   So the expression = 2(1 - sin θ)/[(1 - sin θ) cos θ] = 2/cos θ =  2 sec θ

title: Q45 · Chapter 8: Introduction to Trigonometry
text: Q45 (3 marks, 2023)  Prove that (tan θ + sec θ - 1)/(tan θ - sec θ + 1) = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ.    Ans:      Write 1 = sec²θ - tan²θ in the numerator: tan θ + sec θ - (sec²θ - tan²θ)   = (sec θ + tan θ) - (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ - tan θ) = (sec θ + tan θ)(1 - sec θ + tan θ)   Denominator = (tan θ - sec θ + 1), the same bracket, so it cancels.   LHS = sec θ + tan θ = 1/cos θ + sin θ/cos θ =  (1 + sin θ)/cos θ  = RHS.

title: Q46 · Chapter 9: Some Applications of Trigonometry (Heights and Distances)
text: Q46 (MCQ, 2025; 1-mark 2017)  A kite is flying at a height of 150 m. Its string is inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The length of the string is: (A) 100 m (B) 300 m (C) 150 m (D) 150√3 m    Ans: (B) 300 m.  sin 30° = height/string, so 1/2 = 150/L, L = 300 m.  (2017: tower : shadow = √3 : 1, so tan θ = √3, angle of elevation of the sun =  60° . SQP: string 52 m with tan θ = 12/5, so sin θ = 12/13 and height = 52 × 12/13 =  48 m .)

title: Q47 · Chapter 9: Some Applications of Trigonometry (Heights and Distances)
text: Q47 ★ (5 marks, SQP)  The angles of depression of two ships from the top of a lighthouse, on the same side, are 45° and 30°. The ships are 200 m apart, one exactly behind the other. Find the height of the lighthouse.    Ans:      Let height = h, distance of the nearer ship = x. Draw the figure (lighthouse, two ships on a line).   Near ship (45°): tan 45° = h/x, so x = h.   Far ship (30°): tan 30° = h/(x + 200), so x + 200 = h√3.   h + 200 = h√3, so h(√3 - 1) = 200, h = 200/(√3 - 1) = 200(√3 + 1)/2 = 100(√3 + 1)    h = 100(√3 + 1) ≈ 273.2 m

title: Q48 · Chapter 9: Some Applications of Trigonometry (Heights and Distances)
text: Q48 ★ (4 marks, 2019; 2017 same idea with a 150 m cliff)  A man in a boat rowing away from a 100 m high lighthouse takes 2 minutes to change the angle of elevation of its top from 60° to 30°. Find the speed of the boat (√3 = 1.732).    Ans:      First position: tan 60° = 100/d1, so d1 = 100/√3   Second position: tan 30° = 100/d2, so d2 = 100√3   Distance moved = 100√3 - 100/√3 = (300 - 100)/√3 = 200/√3 = 115.47 m   Speed = 115.47/2 =  57.73 m per minute

title: Q49 · Chapter 9: Some Applications of Trigonometry (Heights and Distances)
text: Q49 ★ (3 marks, 2017 Set II)  From the top of a 7 m high building, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 60° and the angle of depression of its foot is 45°. Find the height of the tower.    Ans:      Depression 45° to the foot: distance between building and tower = 7 m (tan 45° = 7/d).   Elevation 60° to the top: extra height above the building level = 7 tan 60° = 7√3 m.   Tower = 7 + 7√3 = 7(√3 + 1) ≈  19.12 m

title: Q50 · Chapter 9: Some Applications of Trigonometry (Heights and Distances)
text: Q50 (5 marks, 2026)  A kite is flying 60 m above the ground. Ravi, on the roof of a house, holds the string straight and sees the kite at an angle of elevation of 30°. From the bottom of the same building the angle of elevation of the kite is 45°. Find the length of the string and the height of the roof (√3 = 1.73).    Ans:      From the bottom (45°): horizontal distance to the kite = 60 m.   From the roof (height r): tan 30° = (60 - r)/60, so 60 - r = 60/√3 = 20√3 = 34.6 m.  Roof height r = 60 - 34.6 = 25.4 m.    String: sin 30° = (60 - r)/L, so L = 2 × 34.6 =  69.2 m  (exactly 40√3 m).  (2022 also asked: tower 50 m, elevation of the building top from the tower's foot 30°, of the tower top from the building's foot 60°; distance = 50/√3, building = (50/√3) × (1/√3) =  50/3 = 16.67 m .)

title: Q51 · Chapter 10: Circles
text: Q51 (MCQ, 2025; proof in 2017)  The tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are always: (A) parallel (B) perpendicular (C) equal (D) intersecting    Ans: (A) parallel.  Both tangents are ⟂ to the same diameter, so they are parallel (alternate angles 90° each).

title: Q52 · Chapter 10: Circles
text: Q52 (MCQ, 2026)  PQ and PR are tangents to a circle with centre O and radius 4 cm such that ∠QPR = 90°. Then OP is: (A) 4 cm (B) 4√2 cm (C) 8 cm (D) 2√2 cm    Ans: (B) 4√2 cm.  OQPR is a square of side 4 cm; OP is its diagonal = 4√2.

title: Q53 · Chapter 10: Circles
text: Q53 ★ (2 marks, 2025; same idea SQP case, 2022)  A person standing at P is 26 m from the centre of a circular ground. His tangent distances PA and PB to the ground are 10 m each. Find the radius.    Ans:      Radius ⟂ tangent, so ΔOAP is right-angled at A.   OA² = OP² - PA² = 26² - 10² = 676 - 100 = 576    Radius = 24 m   (2022: concentric circles of radii 4 cm and 3 cm; chord of the bigger circle touching the smaller = 2√(16 - 9) =  2√7 cm .)

title: Q54 · Chapter 10: Circles
text: Q54 ★ (3 marks, NCERT theorem; used in every tangent question)  Prove that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.    Ans:       Given:  PQ and PR are tangents from P to a circle with centre O.  To prove:  PQ = PR.   Join OP, OQ, OR. In ΔOQP and ΔORP:   OQ = OR (radii); OP = OP (common); ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (radius ⟂ tangent)   So ΔOQP ≅ ΔORP (RHS). Hence  PQ = PR  (CPCT).

title: Q55 · Chapter 10: Circles
text: Q55 ★ (3 marks, 2017; 2023)  Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.    Ans:      Let ∠PTQ = θ. TP = TQ (tangents from T), so ∠TPQ = ∠TQP = (180° - θ)/2 = 90° - θ/2.   ∠OPT = 90° (radius ⟂ tangent).   ∠OPQ = ∠OPT - ∠TPQ = 90° - (90° - θ/2) = θ/2.   So  ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ . Hence proved.

title: Q56 · Chapter 10: Circles
text: Q56 ★ (3 marks, SQP)  Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.    Ans:      Let ABCD be a parallelogram whose sides touch the circle at P (on AB), Q (BC), R (CD), S (DA).   Tangents from a point are equal: AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS.   Add: (AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ), i.e. AB + CD = AD + BC.   In a parallelogram AB = CD and AD = BC, so 2AB = 2AD, AB = AD.   So all four sides are equal:  ABCD is a rhombus.

title: Q57 · Chapter 10: Circles
text: Q57 ★ (Case study 4 marks, SQP)  P is outside a circular garden with centre O and radius 9 m; OP = 18 m. PA and PB are tangents. (i) ∠OAP = ? (ii) Find PA. (iii)(A) Find ∠AOB. OR (iii)(B) If PA and PB were inclined at 60°, find their length.    Ans:      (i)  ∠OAP = 90°  (radius ⟂ tangent)   (ii) PA = √(18² - 9²) = √(324 - 81) = √243 =  9√3 m    (iii)(A) cos ∠AOP = OA/OP = 9/18 = 1/2, so ∠AOP = 60°, and  ∠AOB = 120°    (iii)(B) ∠APO = 30°, tan 30° = OA/PA, so PA = 9/(1/√3) =  9√3 m   (2019: incircle of ΔABC with AB = 10, BC = 8, AC = 12 cm; using equal tangents x + y = 8, y + z = 12, x + z = 10 gives  BL = 3, CM = 5, AN = 7 cm .)

title: Q58 · Chapter 11: Areas Related to Circles
text: Q58 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  The diameter of a car wheel is 21 cm. The number of complete revolutions it makes in moving 66 km is: (A) 10⁴ (B) 10⁵ (C) 10⁶ (D) 10⁷    Ans: (B) 10⁵.  Circumference = πd = 22/7 × 21 = 66 cm. 66 km = 66,00,000 cm. Revolutions = 66,00,000/66 = 1,00,000 =  10⁵ . (In the printed SQP the options appear as "104, 105 ...": they mean powers of 10.)

title: Q59 · Chapter 11: Areas Related to Circles
text: Q59 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  An arc of a circle is 6π cm long and the sector it bounds has area 24π cm². The radius is: (A) 4 (B) 8 (C) 16 (D) 18 cm    Ans: (B) 8 cm.  Area of sector = ½ × arc length × r: 24π = ½ × 6π × r, so r = 8.  (2025 MCQ: sector of area 40π sq. units and angle 72°: (72/360) πr² = 40π, r² = 200,  r = 10√2 .)

title: Q60 · Chapter 11: Areas Related to Circles
text: Q60 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  Find the area of a sector of a circle with diameter 28 cm if the length of the corresponding arc is 22 cm.    Ans:      r = 14 cm. Area of sector = ½ × l × r = ½ × 22 × 14 =  154 cm²    (Or: θ/360 × 2πr = 22 gives θ = 90°; area = ¼ × 22/7 × 196 = 154 cm².)

title: Q61 · Chapter 11: Areas Related to Circles
text: Q61 ★ (Case study 4 marks, 2025)  A brooch is a circle of diameter 35 mm made of silver wire. 5 diameters divide it into 10 equal sectors. (i) Central angle of each sector? (ii) Length of arc ACB (one sector)? (iii)(a) Area of each sector? OR (iii)(b) Total length of silver wire?    Ans:      (i) 360°/10 =  36°    (ii) Arc = circumference/10 = (22/7 × 35)/10 = 110/10 =  11 mm    (iii)(a) Sector area = (1/10) × 22/7 × 17.5 × 17.5 = 962.5/10 =  96.25 mm²    (iii)(b) Wire = circumference + 5 diameters = 110 + 5 × 35 =  285 mm

title: Q62 · Chapter 11: Areas Related to Circles
text: Q62 (3 marks, 2019 Set II; similar 2017)  Find the area of the segment of a circle of radius 21 cm with ∠AOB = 120° (π = 22/7, √3 = 1.732).    Ans:      Area of sector = 120/360 × 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 462 cm²   Area of ΔAOB = ½ r² sin 120° = ½ × 441 × (√3/2) = 441√3/4 = 190.95 cm²   Segment = 462 - 190.95 =  271.05 cm²   (2017: chord subtending 60° in a circle of radius 10 cm, π = 3.14: sector 52.33, equilateral triangle (√3/4) × 100 = 43.30,  minor segment ≈ 9.03 cm² , major segment = 314 - 9.03 ≈  304.97 cm² .)

title: Q63 · Chapter 12: Surface Areas and Volumes
text: Q63 (MCQ, SQP)  Two cubes, each of volume 64 cm³, are joined end to end. The surface area of the resulting cuboid is: (A) 192 (B) 160 (C) 96 (D) 80 cm²    Ans: (B) 160 cm².  Side = 4 cm. Cuboid 8 × 4 × 4: SA = 2(8×4 + 4×4 + 8×4) = 2(32 + 16 + 32) = 160 cm².

title: Q64 · Chapter 12: Surface Areas and Volumes
text: Q64 (A-R, 2025)  A: If we join two hemispheres of the same radius along their bases, we get a sphere. R: Total surface area of a sphere of radius r is 3πr².    Ans: (C)  A is true; R is false (TSA of a sphere is 4πr²; 3πr² is the TSA of a solid hemisphere).  (2024 MCQ: a solid sphere cut into two hemispheres; ratio of surface areas = 4πr² : 2 × 3πr² =  2 : 3 . 2026 MCQ: three balls of radius r packed in a cylinder of radius r and height 6r; air = 6πr³ - 3 × (4/3)πr³ =  2πr³ .)

title: Q65 · Chapter 12: Surface Areas and Volumes
text: Q65 ★ (5 marks, SQP)  A tent is a cylinder (height 3 m, radius 14 m) surmounted by a cone. Total height is 13.5 m. Find the canvas needed, keeping 26 m² extra for stitching and wastage, and its cost at ₹250 per m².    Ans:      Cone height = 13.5 - 3 = 10.5 m. Slant height l = √(14² + 10.5²) = √(196 + 110.25) = √306.25 = 17.5 m   CSA of cylinder = 2πrh = 2 × 22/7 × 14 × 3 = 264 m²   CSA of cone = πrl = 22/7 × 14 × 17.5 = 770 m²   Canvas = 264 + 770 + 26 =  1060 m²    Cost = 1060 × 250 =  ₹2,65,000    (No base: the floor of a tent is not covered with canvas.)

title: Q66 · Chapter 12: Surface Areas and Volumes
text: Q66 ★ (5 marks, SQP OR; 2022 similar)  A solid toy is a hemisphere surmounted by a cone of the same radius 3.5 cm. Total volume is 166 5/6 cm³. Find the height of the cone, and the cost of painting the hemispherical part at ₹15 per cm².    Ans:      Volume of hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = 2/3 × 22/7 × 3.5³ = 539/6 cm³ (= 89 5/6)   Volume of cone = 1001/6 - 539/6 = 462/6 = 77 cm³   (1/3) × 22/7 × 3.5 × 3.5 × h = 77, so (77/6) h = 77,  h = 6 cm    CSA of hemisphere = 2πr² = 2 × 22/7 × 3.5 × 3.5 = 77 cm². Cost = 77 × 15 =  ₹1,155   (2022: a cone of height 24 cm, radius 7 cm hollowed out of a cylinder of height 30 cm, radius 7 cm. TSA left = cylinder CSA 1320 + top circle 154 + cone CSA (l = 25) 550 =  2024 cm² .)

title: Q67 · Chapter 13: Statistics
text: Q67 ★ (MCQ, SQP; 2025, 2026 same idea)  The mean and median of a data are 35.5 and 32. The mode is: (A) 23 (B) 26 (C) 25 (D) 30    Ans: (C) 25.  Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean = 96 - 71 =  25 .  (2025: mode 15x, mean 18x gives median = (Mode + 2 Mean)/3 = (15x + 36x)/3 =  17x . 2026: mean 43, median 40 gives mode = 120 - 86 =  34 .)

title: Q68 · Chapter 13: Statistics
text: Q68 (MCQ, SQP)  The mean age of a combined group of men and women is 35 years. The mean ages of men and women are 38 and 30 years. The percentage of women is: (A) 15 (B) 25.5 (C) 35 (D) 37.5    Ans: (D) 37.5.  38m + 30w = 35(m + w), so 3m = 5w, m : w = 5 : 3. Women = 3/8 =  37.5% .

title: Q69 · Chapter 13: Statistics
text: Q69 ★ (Case study 4 marks, SQP)  Marks (out of 50): 0-10: 3, 10-20: 6, 20-30: 12, 30-40: 15, 40-50: 14. (i) Modal class? (ii) Median class? (iii)(A) Mean? OR (iii)(B) Mode?    Ans:      (i) Highest frequency 15, so modal class =  30-40    (ii) N = 50, N/2 = 25. Cumulative frequencies 3, 9, 21, 36, 50. 25 first falls in 36, so median class =  30-40    (iii)(A) Class marks 5, 15, 25, 35, 45; fx = 15, 90, 300, 525, 630; Σfx = 1560. Mean = 1560/50 =  31.2    (iii)(B) l = 30, f1 = 15, f0 = 12, f2 = 14, h = 10. Mode = 30 + [(15 - 12)/(30 - 12 - 14)] × 10 = 30 + (3/4) × 10 =  37.5

title: Q70 · Chapter 13: Statistics
text: Q70 ★ (3 marks, 2019)  Find the mode: the modal class is 30-40 with frequency 16; the class before has 10 and the class after has 12 (class size 10).    Ans:      Mode = l + [(f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)] × h   = 30 + [(16 - 10)/(32 - 10 - 12)] × 10 = 30 + (6/10) × 10 =  36

title: Q73 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q73 ★ (MCQ, SQP; 2026 same)  Two dice are rolled together. The probability of getting a number less than 4 on each die is: (A) 1/4 (B) 1/9 (C) 1/36 (D) 1/6    Ans: (A) 1/4.  Each die must show 1, 2 or 3: 3 × 3 = 9 outcomes out of 36. 9/36 =  1/4 .

title: Q74 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q74 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  2 diamond cards and 4 spade cards are missing from a pack of 52. A card is drawn at random. P(heart) = ? (A) 13/52 (B) 13/46 (C) 11/52 (D) 11/46    Ans: (B) 13/46.  Cards left = 52 - 6 = 46. All 13 hearts are still there.  (2025: P(red face card) from 52 cards = 6/52 =  3/26 . 2024: one black card is lost; P(queen of hearts) =  1/51 .)

title: Q75 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q75 (MCQ, SQP)  T-shirts numbered 4 to 99 are in a box. One is taken at random. P(number is a perfect square or a perfect cube) = ? (A) 1/12 (B) 1/32 (C) 11/96 (D) 5/48    Ans: (D) 5/48.  Total = 96. Squares: 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 (8). Cubes: 8, 27, 64 (3). 64 is counted twice, so favourable = 8 + 3 - 1 = 10. P = 10/96 =  5/48 .

title: Q76 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q76 (MCQ, 2024; 2023 similar)  If the probability of a player winning a game is 0.79, the probability of his losing is:    Ans: 0.21  (1 - 0.79).  (2023: a girl's probability of winning a lottery prize is 0.08; 6000 tickets were sold, so she bought 0.08 × 6000 =  480  tickets. 2023: 5 of 20 people can't swim, P(can swim) = 15/20 =  3/4 .)

title: Q77 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q77 (A-R, 2026)  A: If the probability of an event is 0.2p, p > 0, then p cannot be more than 5. R: P(not E) = 1 - P(E) for an event E.    Ans: (B)  Both true, but R does not explain A. (A is true because a probability is at most 1: 0.2p ≤ 1 gives p ≤ 5.)

title: Q78 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q78 ★ (2 marks, SQP)  Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that the product of the numbers is a prime number.    Ans:      A product is prime only when one die shows 1 and the other a prime: (1,2), (2,1), (1,3), (3,1), (1,5), (5,1) = 6 outcomes   P = 6/36 =  1/6

title: Q79 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q79 ★ (3 marks, 2025; 2017 similar)  Two dice are thrown at the same time. Find the probability that the difference of the numbers on the two dice is 2.    Ans:      Favourable: (1,3), (3,1), (2,4), (4,2), (3,5), (5,3), (4,6), (6,4) = 8   P = 8/36 =  2/9   (2017: sum less than 7: 15 outcomes, P =  5/12 ; product less than 16: 25 outcomes, P =  25/36 ; doublet of odd numbers (1,1), (3,3), (5,5): P = 3/36 =  1/12 . 2024 MCQ: sum 2, 3 or 5: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 outcomes, P =  7/36 .)

title: Q80 · Chapter 14: Probability
text: Q80 ★ (2 marks, 2019)  A game consists of tossing a coin 3 times and noting the outcome each time. Getting the same result in all tosses is a success. Find the probability of losing the game.    Ans:      Outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT = 8   Success: HHH, TTT = 2. P(win) = 2/8 = 1/4    P(lose) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4   (2019: a die is thrown once; P(prime) = 3/6 =  1/2 ; P(number between 2 and 6, i.e. 3, 4, 5) =  1/2 . 2023: bag with 4 red, 3 blue, 2 yellow balls; P(yellow) =  2/9 , P(red) =  4/9 .)
