(c)  Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar  (Punjab). (d)  Champaran  (north Bihar). Mark it with a dot and write the name on the line given.

title: Q12 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q12. ★ Explain any three changes Napoleon brought into the territories under his control. (3)  Seen: 2019, 2025    Answer:      The  Civil Code of 1804  (Napoleonic Code) ended privileges based on birth, gave equality before the law and secured the right to property.   He simplified administrative divisions and  abolished the feudal system , so peasants were freed from serfdom and manorial dues.   In towns, guild restrictions were removed. Transport and communication were improved, and he brought in uniform laws, standard weights and measures and a common currency, which helped businessmen.

title: Q13 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q13. ★ Explain the ideas of economic liberalism, or the steps taken towards economic unity, in 19th-century Germany. (3)  Seen: 2020, 2024, 2025, 2026    Answer:      Economic liberalism meant  freedom of markets  and the end of state restrictions on the movement of goods and capital.   Before unity, German areas had 39 states, each with its own currency, weights, measures and customs barriers. This made trade slow and costly.   In  1834 the Zollverein , a customs union started by Prussia, removed tariff barriers and cut the number of currencies from over 30 to two. A network of  railways  also linked markets. Economic unity became a step towards national unity.

title: Q14 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q14. Explain what liberalism stood for politically in early 19th-century Europe. (3)     Answer:  Liberalism comes from the Latin word  liber , meaning free. For the middle classes it meant:     Freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law.   Government by consent, a constitution and a representative government elected by people.   The end of autocracy and clerical privileges.  Limit:  voting rights were given only to property-owning men. Women and men without property had no vote.

title: Q15 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q15. ★ "The formation of the nation-state in Britain was not the result of a sudden upheaval." Explain. (5)  Seen: 2024, 2026    Answer:      Before the 18th century there was no British nation. People saw themselves as English, Welsh, Scot or Irish.   The English nation grew in wealth and power and spread its influence over the other islands. In  1688  the English Parliament took power from the monarchy.   The  Act of Union (1707)  between England and Scotland formed the "United Kingdom of Great Britain". In practice, England dominated Scotland.   Scottish culture was suppressed: the Gaelic language was forbidden, Highlanders could not wear their national dress, and many were driven out of their land.   Ireland, divided between Catholics and Protestants, was forcibly brought in in  1801  after a failed revolt led by Wolfe Tone (1798).   A new "British nation" was spread through symbols: the  Union Jack  flag, the national anthem  God Save Our Noble King , and the  English language .

title: Q16 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q16. ★ Who were Marianne and Germania? What was the importance of the way they were shown? (2)  Seen: 2023, 2026E2    Answer:  They were  female allegories  (figures standing for an idea) of the nation:  Marianne for France  and  Germania for Germany . Marianne wore a red cap and the tricolour, and her statues stood in public squares and appeared on coins and stamps. Germania wore a crown of  oak leaves , because the German oak stands for heroism. They made the abstract idea of the nation easy for ordinary people to see and love.

title: Q17 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q17. ★ Why were the Balkans called "a big powder keg" after 1871? (3)  Seen: 2018, 2024    Answer:      The Balkans had many ethnic groups (Slavs, Greeks and others), and a large part was under the  Ottoman Empire . As that empire broke up, romantic nationalism spread and each group wanted independence.   The Balkan states were  jealous of each other , and each wanted more territory at the cost of the others.    Big powers  (Russia, Germany, England and Austria-Hungary) competed for control of the region, which led to a series of wars and finally the  First World War (1914) .

title: Q18 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q18. Describe the Greek War of Independence. (3)  Seen: 2020    Answer:      Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the 15th century. The struggle for independence began in  1821 .   Greek nationalists got support from Greeks living in exile and from many West Europeans who admired ancient Greek culture. Poets and artists praised Greece as the cradle of European civilisation. The English poet  Lord Byron  raised funds and died in the war in 1824.   The  Treaty of Constantinople (1832)  recognised Greece as an independent nation.

title: Q19 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q19. ★ Why did Gandhiji start the Non-Cooperation Movement? How was it to unfold? (5)  Seen: 2018, 2020, 2024, 2025    Answer:      In  Hind Swaraj  (1909) Gandhiji wrote that British rule survived only because Indians cooperated. If Indians refused to cooperate, British rule would collapse within a year.    Causes:  the  Rowlatt Act (1919) , the  Jallianwala Bagh massacre  (13 April 1919) and the  Khilafat issue . Gandhiji wanted Hindus and Muslims to unite.    Stages:  first, the surrender of titles given by the government. Then a boycott of the civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils and schools.    Boycott of foreign goods , and a full civil disobedience campaign if the government used repression.   The Congress accepted the programme at the  Nagpur session in December 1920 .

title: Q20 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q20. ★ Explain the economic effects of the Non-Cooperation Movement. (3)  Seen: 2018, 2020, 2024, 2025    Answer:      Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires.   The  import of foreign cloth halved  between 1921 and 1922, and its value fell from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore. Merchants refused to trade in foreign goods.   People wore only Indian clothes, so the  production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up .

title: Q21 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q21. Why did the Non-Cooperation Movement slow down in the cities? (3)     Answer:       Khadi  cloth was more expensive than mill cloth, and poor people could not afford it.   Boycotting British institutions needed  Indian institutions to replace them , and these came up slowly.   So students and teachers went back to government schools, and lawyers went back to government courts.

title: Q22 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q22. ★ How did different social groups take part in the Civil Disobedience Movement? (5)  Seen: 2018, 2019, 2024, 2026E2    Answer:       Rich peasants  (Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP) were hit by the trade depression and falling prices, so they wanted lower revenue. They were disappointed when the movement was called off in 1931 without the revenue rates being revised.    Poor peasants  wanted unpaid rent to the landlord to be remitted. The Congress did not support "no rent" campaigns, so their relationship stayed uncertain.    Business classes  (FICCI, 1927; Purshottamdas Thakurdas, G.D. Birla) wanted protection against foreign imports and gave financial help. After the failure of the Round Table Conference they lost enthusiasm.    Industrial workers  took part in a small way, for example in Nagpur, by boycotting foreign goods.    Women  took part in large numbers: they joined the salt march, made salt and picketed liquor and foreign-cloth shops. The Congress was reluctant to give them positions of authority.

title: Q23 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q23. ★ Why did Gandhiji choose salt to start the Civil Disobedience Movement? (3)  Seen (Dandi): 2018, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026E2    Answer:      Salt was eaten by  both rich and poor , so it was one of the most essential items of food. It could unite everyone.   The  tax on salt  and the government's  monopoly  over making it were very oppressive. Gandhiji's letter to Viceroy Irwin (31 January 1930) had 11 demands, and abolishing the salt tax was one of them.   On  12 March 1930  he marched about 240 miles from  Sabarmati to Dandi  in 24 days, and broke the salt law on  6 April 1930 . This started the movement.

title: Q24 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q24. ★ Explain the effects of the First World War on India. (3)  Seen: 2023    Answer:       Defence spending rose sharply . It was paid for by war loans and higher taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax was introduced.    Prices doubled  between 1913 and 1918, which caused hardship for common people.    Forced recruitment  of soldiers from villages caused anger. Crop failures in 1918-19 and 1920-21 caused food shortages, and an influenza epidemic killed 12 to 13 million people.

title: Q25 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q25. How did folklore, songs and symbols create a sense of collective belonging? (3)  Seen: 2023    Answer:       Image of Bharat Mata:  Bankim Chandra wrote  Vande Mataram , and Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata as a calm, divine figure.    Folklore:  Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths. Natesa Sastri published  The Folklore of Southern India . They saw these as the true picture of Indian culture.    Flags:  the Swadeshi flag (red, green, yellow) had 8 lotuses for 8 provinces. By 1921 Gandhiji's tricolour (red, green, white) had a  spinning wheel  in the centre. Carrying the flag became a symbol of defiance. (Also:  reinterpreting history  to show India's glorious past and to tell Indians to be proud.)

title: Q26 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q26. What was the Rowlatt Act? What happened at Jallianwala Bagh? (3)  Seen (Jallianwala): 2019, 2020, 2026; SQP    Answer:      The  Rowlatt Act (1919)  let the government  detain political prisoners without trial for two years . Gandhiji started a nationwide satyagraha against it.   On  13 April 1919 , a crowd gathered in  Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar , some to protest and some for the Baisakhi fair.  General Dyer  blocked the exits and opened fire, killing hundreds.   His aim was to create fear (a "moral effect"). Instead, it caused strikes, clashes and attacks on government buildings across north India.

title: Q27 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q27. ★ "Silk routes are a good example of pre-modern trade and cultural links." Explain. (2)  Seen: 2024; SQP    Answer:      The name shows the importance of  Chinese silk cargoes  that went west along these routes. Indian and South-East Asian  textiles and spices  also travelled, and  gold and silver  flowed from Europe to Asia.   They also carried  culture and religion : Christian missionaries, Muslim preachers and Buddhism spread along them. The routes existed before the Christian era and thrived until the 15th century.

title: Q28 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q28. ★ "The most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors was not a conventional military weapon at all." Justify. (2)  Seen: 2026; SQP    Answer:      It was  germs, such as smallpox , that the Spanish carried with them.   America had long been cut off from the rest of the world, so its people had  no immunity  to these diseases. Smallpox spread deep into the continent and killed whole communities, even before the Europeans reached them. This made the conquest easy.

title: Q29 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q29. ★ How did Gutenberg develop the printing press? (3)  Seen (print): 2018, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2026E2    Answer:      Gutenberg, the son of a merchant, grew up on a large farm and saw  wine and olive presses  from childhood. He also learned to polish stones, became a master goldsmith, and learned to make lead moulds for trinkets.   Using this knowledge, he  adapted the olive press  to make the printing press, and used moulds to cast  metal type  for the letters of the alphabet.   By  1448  he had perfected the system. The first book he printed was the  Bible : about 180 copies took 3 years, which was very fast for that time.

title: Q30 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q30. ★ How did print help the Protestant Reformation? (2)  Seen (print): 2018, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2026E2    Answer:      In  1517 Martin Luther  wrote the  Ninety-Five Theses , criticising many practices of the Roman Catholic Church, and posted them on a church door in Wittenberg.   They were  printed in large numbers  and read widely, which led to the division of the Church and the  Protestant Reformation . Luther said, "Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one."

title: Q31 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q31. ★ How did print culture create the conditions for the French Revolution? (3)  Seen (print): 2018, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2026E2    Answer:      Print  spread the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers  such as Voltaire and Rousseau, who attacked tradition, superstition and despotism and asked people to use reason.   Print created a new  culture of dialogue and debate . People questioned existing values and institutions.   By the 1780s there was a lot of  literature mocking the royalty  (especially Marie Antoinette) and criticising its morals, which raised questions about the monarchy. (Note: print did not directly shape minds, but it opened up the possibility of thinking differently.)

title: Q32 · Part 2: History (Section A)
text: Q32. ★ What was the Vernacular Press Act? Why was it passed? (3)  Seen (censorship): 2018, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2026E2    Answer:      After the revolt of 1857, the British grew afraid of Indian newspapers that criticised them and supported nationalism.   In  1878  the  Vernacular Press Act  was passed, modelled on the Irish Press Laws. It gave the government wide powers to  censor reports and editorials  in the vernacular (Indian-language) press.   If a report was judged seditious, the newspaper was warned. If the warning was ignored, the  press could be seized and the printing machinery confiscated . Even so, nationalist newspapers grew in number.

title: Q33 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q33. ★ MAP (3 marks). Locate and label on the outline map of India:  Seen: every paper read; SQP (a) The largest water resource project on the Narmada in Gujarat. (b) An iron and steel plant in Tamil Nadu. (c) A cotton textile centre in the capital of Maharashtra. (d) Meenambakkam International Airport. (e) A nuclear power plant in Gujarat. (f) A major port in Odisha.    Answer:  (a)  Sardar Sarovar Dam , Gujarat. (b)  Salem . (c)  Mumbai . (d)  Chennai . (e)  Kakrapara . (f)  Paradip . Use a clear symbol (a triangle for a dam, a dot for a city, an anchor for a port, a plane for an airport) and write the name beside it.

title: Q34 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q34. ★ Explain the three main steps of resource planning in India. (3)  Seen: 2020, 2025    Answer:       Identification and inventory  of resources across the regions of the country: surveying, mapping, and measuring their quality and quantity.    Evolving a planning structure  with the right technology, skills and institutions to put the plans into action.    Matching resource development plans with overall national development plans .

title: Q35 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q35. ★ Write any three features of black soil. (3)  Seen (soils): 2023, 2024, 2026    Answer:      It is black in colour and is also called  regur soil . It formed from  lava rocks  (Deccan trap) and covers Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.   It is  ideal for cotton , so it is also called black cotton soil. It is made of very fine clay and  holds moisture  well.   It is rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime, but  poor in phosphoric content . It develops deep cracks in the hot season, which helps the soil get air.

title: Q36 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q36. ★ Write features of alluvial soil and laterite soil. (3)  Seen (soils): 2023, 2024, 2026    Answer:       Alluvial soil:  the most widespread soil, covering the northern plains (deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra) and the eastern coastal deltas. It is rich in  potash, phosphoric acid and lime , and good for sugarcane, paddy and wheat. Old alluvium is  bangar ; new alluvium is  khadar  (more fertile).    Laterite soil:  forms in areas of  high temperature and heavy rainfall , through  intense leaching . It is poor in humus, but with manures and fertilisers it is good for  tea, coffee and cashew . It is found in Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh and the hills of Odisha and Assam.

title: Q37 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q37. What causes soil erosion? Suggest three ways to conserve soil. (3)  Seen (soils): 2023, 2024, 2026    Answer:       Causes:  deforestation, overgrazing, construction, mining, and wrong farming methods. Running water makes  gullies  (badlands); water flowing as a sheet causes  sheet erosion ; wind blows away the top soil.    Conservation:  (1)  Contour ploughing  across hill slopes slows the flow of water. (2)  Terrace farming  on slopes (western and central Himalayas). (3)  Strip cropping  (grass strips between crops) and  shelter belts  (rows of trees) to break the force of the wind (western India).

title: Q38 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q38. ★ How do local communities help conserve forests? Give examples. (3)  Seen in SQP case study    Answer:      The  Chipko Movement  in the Himalayas: villagers hugged trees to stop them being cut.   In Rajasthan, the  Bishnois  protect blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks. Villagers of Sariska fought mining and declared 1,200 hectares as the  Bhairodev Dakav Sonchuri .    Joint Forest Management  (Odisha, 1988) involves local communities in protecting and restoring degraded forests; in return they get forest produce.  Sacred groves  have also been protected by communities.

title: Q39 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q39. ★ Why is water scarcity growing in India even though water is renewable? (3)  Seen: 2018, 2019, 2026E2    Answer:      A  large and growing population  needs more water for drinking and for growing more food. Irrigated farming is the biggest user.    Industrialisation and urbanisation  use more water and more power. Cities have many housing societies with their own groundwater pumps.    Over-exploitation of groundwater  has lowered water tables. Water is also  polluted  by sewage, chemicals and fertilisers, so good-quality water is scarce even where there is plenty of water.

title: Q40 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q40. ★ Suggest two traditional rainwater harvesting methods for a drought-prone area. (2)  SQP    Answer:       Rooftop rainwater harvesting:  rain from roofs is stored in underground tanks ( tankas ), as in Phalodi, Bikaner and Barmer in Rajasthan.    Khadins and johads:  rain-fed storage structures in Rajasthan where water stands and moistens the soil for growing crops. (Other examples:  guls or kuls  in the Western Himalayas,  bamboo drip irrigation  in Meghalaya,  inundation channels  in Bengal.)

title: Q41 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q41. What are multipurpose river projects? Why are they being opposed? (5)     Answer:  These are dams that serve many purposes at once: irrigation, electricity, water supply, flood control, fishing and inland navigation. Nehru called them the  "temples of modern India" . They are opposed because:     They  stop the natural flow  of rivers, so the riverbed gets more  sediment  and aquatic life suffers.   They  displace large numbers of people , who often get no proper compensation (Narmada Bachao Andolan, Tehri Dam Andolan).   Big dams have sometimes  caused floods  instead of controlling them, because of excess sediment and heavy rain.   Over-irrigation causes  salinisation  of soil, and benefits often go to rich landowners.   They can cause earthquakes and water-borne diseases, and lead to pollution from excess use of water.

title: Q42 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q42. ★ Compare the growing conditions of rice and wheat. (5)  Seen: 2018, 2019, 2024, 2026; SQP    Answer:          Point   Rice   Wheat           Season   Kharif   Rabi       Temperature   High, above 25 °C, with high humidity   Cool growing season, with bright sunshine at ripening time       Rainfall   Above 100 cm (less only with irrigation)   50-75 cm, evenly spread over the season       Main areas   Plains of north and north-east India, coastal areas and deltas; Punjab and Haryana through canals   Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil areas of the Deccan       Leading states   West Bengal, UP, Punjab   Punjab, Haryana, UP, MP, Bihar, Rajasthan         India is the second-largest producer of rice in the world, after China.

title: Q43 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q43. ★ Describe the conditions needed to grow tea, and name the tea and coffee areas. (5)  Seen (agriculture): 2018, 2019, 2024, 2026; SQP    Answer:      Tea is a  plantation crop  and a beverage crop, brought to India by the British.   It needs a  tropical or sub-tropical climate  and  deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus and organic matter .   It needs a  warm, moist, frost-free climate all year , with frequent showers spread evenly over the year so that tender leaves keep growing.   It is  labour-intensive  and needs plenty of cheap, skilled labour. It is processed in the tea garden itself.    Tea areas:  Assam, the Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri hills (West Bengal), Tamil Nadu and Kerala.  Coffee:  the  Arabica  variety from Yemen was first grown in the  Baba Budan Hills . Today it is grown in the  Nilgiris  in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

title: Q44 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q44. ★ Explain any three types of farming in India. (3)  Seen: 2018, 2019, 2024, 2026    Answer:       Primitive subsistence farming:  done on small patches with simple tools (hoe, dao, digging sticks) and family labour. It includes  "slash and burn"  (jhumming): land is cleared, crops are grown, and the farmer moves on when the soil loses fertility.    Intensive subsistence farming:  in densely populated areas. High doses of fertilisers and irrigation are used to get maximum output from a small plot.    Commercial farming:  high doses of modern inputs (HYV seeds, fertilisers, pesticides) are used to grow crops for sale.  Plantation  is one type, where a single crop such as tea, coffee, rubber or banana is grown on a large area.

title: Q45 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q45. ★ Why is it necessary to conserve energy resources? Suggest ways. (3)  Seen: 2023, 2024, 2026    Answer:  Energy is needed for every sector, but coal, oil and gas are  limited and non-renewable , and burning them pollutes the air. Ways to conserve:     Use  public transport  instead of private vehicles. Switch off lights and fans when they are not needed.   Use  power-saving devices  such as LED bulbs and star-rated appliances.   Use  non-conventional sources  such as solar, wind, biogas and tidal energy. Remember: "energy saved is energy produced".

title: Q46 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q46. ★ "Manufacturing industries are the backbone of economic development." Explain. (3)  Seen: 2018, 2024, 2026E2    Answer:      They help  modernise agriculture  and reduce people's heavy dependence on farming by creating jobs in the secondary and tertiary sectors.   They help remove  unemployment and poverty , and reduce  regional disparities  when industries are set up in tribal and backward areas.    Export  of manufactured goods expands trade and brings in  foreign exchange . Countries that turn raw materials into a wide range of higher-value finished goods become prosperous.

title: Q47 · Part 3: Geography (Section B)
text: Q47. Case-based (4), a practice passage modelled on the board flood-safety cases. Read: "During heavy rain, the water level in a dam rose quickly. The authorities opened the gates in advance and warned villages downstream to move to higher ground."  Seen (flood-safety case): 2024, 2026 (a) Name one benefit of a dam, apart from flood control. (1) (b) Why must people downstream be warned before the gates are opened? (1) (c) Suggest two flood-safety steps for families living near rivers. (2)    Answer:  (a) Irrigation, or hydroelectricity. (b) Released water suddenly raises river levels and can flood low-lying villages, so warnings save lives. (c) Move to higher ground with an emergency kit (water, food, torch, medicines, documents), and follow official alerts and avoid walking or driving through flood water.

title: Q48 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q48. ★ Explain the steps Belgium took to accommodate its different communities. (5)  Seen (power sharing): 2019, 2020, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2026E2; SQP    Answer:  (In Belgium, Dutch speakers are 59%, French speakers 40% and German speakers 1%. In Brussels, 80% speak French and 20% speak Dutch.)     The Constitution says the  number of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers  in the central government must be equal. Some special laws need the support of a majority of each language group.   Many powers of the central government were given to the  state governments  of the two regions. State governments are not under the central government.    Brussels has a separate government  in which both communities have equal representation.   A  "community government"  is elected by people of one language community. It has power over cultural, educational and language matters.   Result: Belgium avoided civil war and a split of the country.

title: Q49 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q49. ★ What majoritarian measures did Sri Lanka adopt? What was the result? (3)  Seen (power sharing): 2019, 2020, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2026E2    Answer:  (Sinhalas are about 74% of the population; Tamils about 18%.)     In  1956  an Act made  Sinhala the only official language , ignoring Tamil.   The government gave  preference to Sinhala applicants  for university places and government jobs. The Constitution said the state would  protect and foster Buddhism .    Result:  Sri Lankan Tamils felt alienated. They demanded autonomy and an independent Tamil Eelam, and the conflict turned into a  civil war .

title: Q50 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q50. ★ Describe the different forms of power sharing in modern democracies. (5)  Seen: 2019, 2020, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2026E2    Answer:       Horizontal sharing among organs of government  (legislature, executive and judiciary). Each checks the others: a system of  checks and balances .    Vertical sharing among levels of government : central (union), state and local governments. This is  federal  government.    Sharing among social groups , such as religious and linguistic groups: for example, the community government in Belgium and reserved seats for weaker sections in India.    Sharing among political parties, pressure groups and movements : for example,  coalition governments  and the influence of pressure groups.

title: Q51 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q51. Give one prudential and one moral reason for power sharing. (2)     Answer:   Prudential:  it  reduces conflict  between social groups and ensures  political stability .  Moral:  it is the  very spirit of democracy : people affected by a policy have a right to be consulted.

title: Q52 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q52. ★ What makes India a federal country? (5)  Seen (federalism): 2020, 2026; SQP    Answer:       Two-tier government  (Union and States), later a  third tier  of Panchayats and Municipalities.   The Constitution divides powers into three lists. The  Union List  covers defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency. The  State List  covers police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation. The  Concurrent List  covers education, forests, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession.  Residuary subjects  go to the Union.   The basic division of power  cannot be changed by one level alone . A change needs a two-thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament and the approval of at least half the state legislatures.    Courts (the judiciary)  settle disputes over the division of powers.   Sources of revenue for each level are clearly specified.  Linguistic states , the  language policy  (no single national language) and  centre-state relations  have also strengthened federalism.

title: Q53 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q53. ★ Explain the provisions of the 1992 constitutional amendment that strengthened local government. (5)  Seen: 2018, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026; SQP    Answer:      It is now  constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections  to local government bodies.    Seats are reserved  in the elected bodies and in executive heads for  Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes .    At least one-third of all positions are reserved for women .   An independent  State Election Commission  in each state conducts panchayat and municipal elections.   State governments must  share some powers and revenue  with local bodies. (Structure:  Gram Panchayat  (with the Gram Sabha), then  Panchayat Samiti  (block level), then  Zilla Parishad  (district). In towns: Municipalities and Municipal Corporations.)

title: Q54 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q54. ★ What is secularism? Explain the provisions that make India a secular state. (3)  Seen: 2018, 2020, 2023, 2026    Answer:      There is  no official religion  for the Indian state, unlike Buddhism in Sri Lanka or Islam in Pakistan.   The Constitution gives all individuals and communities the  freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion , or not to follow any.   It  prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion , and it allows the state to  intervene in religious matters to ensure equality  (for example, banning untouchability).

title: Q55 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q55. Describe the various forms communalism can take in politics. (3)  Seen (secularism/communalism): 2018, 2020, 2023, 2026    Answer:       Everyday beliefs : religious prejudice, stereotypes of other communities, and the belief that one's own religion is superior.    Majoritarian dominance  by the majority community, or the desire of a minority to form a separate political unit.    Political mobilisation on religious lines , using sacred symbols and religious leaders to appeal to voters.    Communal violence , riots and massacres (for example, at the time of Partition).

title: Q56 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q56. ★ "Elections are not all about caste." Give three arguments. (3)  SQP    Answer:       No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste , so every candidate must win the trust of more than one caste.    No party wins the votes of all the voters of one caste . People vote on many issues.   Many constituencies have  several candidates from the same caste , while many voters have no candidate from their caste. Also, ruling parties and sitting MPs often  lose elections , which would not happen if caste decided everything.

title: Q57 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q57. ★ Describe the functions of political parties in a democracy. (5)  Seen: 2018, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026; SQP    Answer:  A political party is a group of people who come together to  contest elections and hold power  in the government.      Contest elections : parties choose candidates.    Put forward policies and programmes  for voters to choose from.   Play a decisive role in  making laws .    Form and run governments . Parties that lose play the role of the  opposition , criticise the government and raise people's issues.    Shape public opinion , and give people  access to government machinery and welfare schemes .

title: Q58 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q58. ★ What are the challenges political parties face? (3)  Seen: 2018, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026    Answer:       Lack of internal democracy : power is concentrated in one or a few leaders, and there are no regular organisational elections.    Dynastic succession : top positions go to members of one family.    Growing role of money and muscle power , especially during elections.    Lack of meaningful choice : the policies of major parties look very similar.

title: Q59 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q59. ★ How is democracy an accountable, responsive and legitimate government? (5)  Seen (outcomes of democracy): 2018, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026    Answer:       Accountable:  citizens can choose their rulers and control them through  free and fair elections  held regularly.   Decisions are taken through  norms and procedures , after discussion. They may be slower, but they are  more acceptable and effective .    Transparency:  a citizen has the  right and the means to examine how decisions are made .    Responsive:  governments must attend to people's needs and demands, and there is open public debate on major policies.    Legitimate:  a democratic government is the  people's own government . People everywhere want to be ruled by representatives they elect. Democracy may be slow and imperfect, but it is legitimate.

title: Q60 · Part 4: Political Science (Section C)
text: Q60. ★ "Democracy accommodates social diversity and promotes the dignity and freedom of citizens." Explain. (3)  Seen (outcomes): 2018, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026    Answer:      Democracies develop ways to  handle differences and conflicts  peacefully. The majority must work with the minority, and  majority rule does not mean the rule of one religious or ethnic group .   Democracy has strengthened the claims of  women to equal treatment , and of the  disadvantaged and discriminated castes  to equal status and opportunity.   It respects  individual freedom and dignity . Even where discrimination remains, democracy gives people a legal and moral basis to fight it. (Limit: on  economic growth and reducing inequality , democracies have not done as well as hoped. Dictatorships have had a slightly higher growth rate, but democracy is still preferred.)

title: Q61 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q61. ★ "Different people can have different, even conflicting, development goals." Explain with examples. (3)  Seen: SQP    Answer:      People have  different life situations , so they want different things. A landless rural labourer wants more days of work and better wages; a rich farmer wants higher prices for crops.   Goals can  conflict : an industrialist wants more electricity from a big dam, but tribal people who would be displaced by it want to keep their land.   Besides income, people also want  equal treatment, freedom, security and respect . So what is development for one person may be destruction for another.

title: Q62 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q62. ★ What is per capita income? What are its limitations as an indicator of development? (3)     Answer:       Per capita (average) income = Total income of the country / Total population.  The  World Bank  uses it to compare countries.    Limitation:  an average  hides inequality . Two countries with the same average income can have very different distributions.   It does not show  non-material things  such as health, education, a clean environment or security. So the  UNDP's Human Development Index (HDI)  uses  per capita income, education and health (life expectancy) . Example: Kerala has a lower infant mortality rate than richer states because of better basic health and education facilities.

title: Q63 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q63. ★ Why is the issue of sustainability important for development? (3)  Seen: 2018, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026    Answer:      Development must meet the needs of the present  without harming future generations .   Resources are being overused:  groundwater  levels are falling in many parts of India, and  non-renewable resources  such as crude oil will run out.    Environmental damage  (pollution, soil erosion, global warming) does not respect state or national borders, so it affects everyone. Development that destroys the environment cannot last.

title: Q64 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q64. ★ Why is the tertiary sector becoming so important in India? (3)  Seen: 2019, 2020, 2026    Answer:       Basic services  such as hospitals, schools, post and telegraph, police, courts, transport, banks and insurance are needed by everyone, and the government provides many of them.    Growth of agriculture and industry  increases the need for transport, trade and storage.    Rising incomes  create demand for services such as eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals and schools. New  IT-based services  have also grown fast. (Note: not all service jobs are good. Many people work in small shops and repair jobs with low pay and no job security.)

title: Q65 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q65. ★ Distinguish between the organised and the unorganised sector. (3)  Seen: 2018    Answer:          Organised sector   Unorganised sector           Registered with the government; follows rules such as the Factories Act and the Minimum Wages Act   Small, scattered units, mostly outside government control       Job security, regular salary, fixed working hours, paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits   Low pay, no job security, no paid leave, long hours       Example: government employees, large factory workers   Example: street vendors, small workshops, daily-wage labourers

title: Q66 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q66. ★ Distinguish between the public and the private sector. (3)  Seen: 2020, 2024, 2025    Answer:          Public sector   Private sector           The  government owns  most of the assets and provides the services   Ownership of assets and delivery of services are in the hands of  private individuals or companies        Main aim:  public welfare , not profit   Main aim:  earning profit        Example: Indian Railways, Post Office   Example: Tata Iron and Steel Company, Reliance Industries         The government also provides things that the private sector won't supply at a reasonable cost: roads, bridges, electricity, health and education.

title: Q67 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q67. What is disguised unemployment? What is MGNREGA 2005? (3)     Answer:       Disguised unemployment:  more people are working than are needed, so if some are removed, output does not fall. Example: 5 family members working on a small farm that needs only 3.    MGNREGA 2005:  guarantees  100 days of employment in a year  to every rural household that needs work. If work is not given, the government pays an  unemployment allowance . One-third of the jobs are reserved for women.

title: Q68 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q68. ★ "Money is a medium of exchange." Explain. What are demand deposits? (3)  Seen (demand deposit/cheque): 2026E2    Answer:      In the barter system, both parties must want each other's goods: a  double coincidence of wants . Money acts as an  intermediate  in exchange, so this is no longer needed.    Demand deposits  are deposits in bank accounts that can be  withdrawn on demand . They share the features of money.   A  cheque  is a paper instructing the bank to pay a certain amount from the account to the person named on it. So payments can be made without cash.

title: Q69 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q69. ★ Distinguish between formal and informal sources of credit. Why should formal credit expand? (5)  Seen: 2018, 2019, 2024, 2025, 2026    Answer:          Formal sources   Informal sources           Banks and cooperatives   Moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends        Supervised by the RBI     No organisation supervises  them       Lower rate of interest    High rate of interest , often with no fixed rules       Need collateral and documents   Little paperwork, but borrowers can be forced to sell land or fall into a  debt trap           Why expand formal credit:  cheap and affordable credit raises incomes, lets people start small businesses and farm better, and protects poor households from exploitation by moneylenders. Formal credit should reach  poor households  too, not only the rich.

title: Q70 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q70. ★ What is the role of the RBI in supervising formal loans? (3)  Seen (banks & RBI): 2020, 2023    Answer:      The RBI  issues currency  on behalf of the government (only the RBI can issue currency notes).   It makes sure banks  keep a minimum cash balance  out of their deposits.   It checks that banks  give loans to small farmers, small industries and small borrowers , not only to profit-making businesses. Banks must report how much they lend, to whom, and at what rate of interest.

title: Q71 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q71. ★ What are self-help groups (SHGs)? How do they help the rural poor? (3)  Seen (cooperatives/SHGs): 2025    Answer:      An SHG has  15-20 members , usually women from one area, who  save regularly  and pool their savings.   Members get  small loans from the group  at reasonable interest,  without collateral . After one or two years, the group can get  bank loans .   SHGs free the poor from moneylenders, help them start small businesses, and make women  financially independent and self-confident . (Example: Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, founded by Muhammad Yunus.)

title: Q72 · Part 5: Economics (Section D)
text: Q72. ★ What is globalisation? Explain the factors that enabled it. (5)  Seen: 2024, 2025, 2026    Answer:  Globalisation is the  rapid integration or interconnection between countries  through more foreign trade, more foreign investment by  MNCs  (companies that own or control production in more than one country), and the movement of technology and people.      Technology (transport):  faster and cheaper delivery of goods over long distances.  Containers  cut port handling costs, and air transport became cheaper.    Information and communication technology:  telecommunications, computers and the  internet  let a company in one country instantly share information and services with another (for example, a news magazine designed in Delhi and printed in Mumbai, or call centres serving clients abroad).    Liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policy:  removing  trade barriers  (such as taxes on imports) set by the government. Around  1991 , India removed many barriers to foreign trade and investment.   As a result, goods from around the world reached Indian markets, and Indian producers had to compete with world producers.

text: 3a. Study order (highest return first)       Formal letter format (Q4):  learn the 8-part layout in Section 6. Format = 1 sure mark; a simple, correct body gives 2-3 more. title: 3c. How internal assessment helps
text: 3c. How internal assessment helps      IA is 20 marks. Most regular students score 14-18. If you score even 12 in IA, you need only  21 out of 80  in theory to reach 33 overall.    ALS (5 marks):  speak clearly, finish your sentences, answer the teacher's questions about the listening text. Practise a 1-minute talk on a familiar topic (my school, my favourite festival).
