title: 5. Must-do question bank (115 questions)
text: 5. Must-do question bank (115 questions)    Tags: years = board papers listed above where this or a very close version appeared. "SQP" = CBSE Sample Paper 2026-27. "Practice" = standard NCERT-type question, no year claimed. Constants (as given in the paper): c = 3 × 10^8 m/s, h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, 1/(4πε0) = 9 × 10^9 N m²/C², μ0 = 4π × 10^-7 T m/A. Handy: E(eV) = 1240 / λ(nm).

title: Chapter 1 – Electric Charges and Fields
text: Chapter 1 – Electric Charges and Fields       Q1. (MCQ) A point charge +Q is at the centre of a spherical Gaussian surface of radius R. If the radius is doubled, the flux will: (A) halve (B) double (C) remain the same (D) become four times.  [SQP; similar 2015]    Answer: (C). Flux = q(enclosed)/ε0. It does not depend on size or shape of the closed surface.        Q2. (1 mark) What is the electric flux through a cube of side 1 cm which encloses an electric dipole?  [2015]    Answer: Zero, because net charge enclosed = +q − q = 0.        Q3. (2 marks) Define electric flux. Is it scalar or vector? Give its SI unit.  [2018]    Answer: Electric flux through a surface = number of field lines crossing it = ∮ E·dA (= EA cos θ for uniform field). It is a scalar. Unit: N m² C^-1 (or V m).        Q4. (Derivation, 3–5 marks) Derive the electric field of a dipole at a point on its axial line. Show that for r >> a, E = 2p / (4πε0 r³).  [2015, 2017]    Steps:     Dipole: −q at A, +q at B, AB = 2a, p = q × 2a (from −q to +q). Point P on axis at distance r from centre O, on the side of +q.   Field due to +q: E+ = kq/(r − a)², directed away from +q (along p).   Field due to −q: E− = kq/(r + a)², directed towards −q (opposite to p).   Net E = kq [1/(r − a)² − 1/(r + a)²] = kq × 4ar / (r² − a²)².   E = k × 2p r / (r² − a²)², along p.   For r >> a: E = 2kp / r³ = 2p / (4πε0 r³). Direction: along p. Diagram: straight line with −q, O, +q, and P to the right; arrows E+ (right) bigger than E− (left).          Q5. (Derivation, 3–5 marks) Derive the field at a point on the equatorial line of a dipole.  [2019, 2023; 2025 asked field at (0, y) for charges at (±a, 0)]    Steps:     P on perpendicular bisector at distance r from O. Distance from each charge = √(r² + a²).   Magnitudes: E+ = E− = kq/(r² + a²).   Components perpendicular to the axis cancel. Components parallel to the axis add (both point from +q side towards −q side, i.e. opposite to p).   E = 2 E+ cos θ, with cos θ = a/√(r² + a²).   E = kq × 2a / (r² + a²)^(3/2) = kp / (r² + a²)^(3/2), direction opposite to p.   For r >> a: E = p / (4πε0 r³). (Half of axial value. If distance is halved, E becomes 8 times – 2023 part.)          Q6. (3 marks) Write the torque on a dipole in a uniform field. Show stable and unstable equilibrium.  [2017; SQP-type]    Answer: τ = p × E, magnitude τ = pE sin θ. Net force on dipole in uniform field = 0. Stable: p parallel to E (θ = 0°), τ = 0. Unstable: p antiparallel (θ = 180°), τ = 0. Maximum torque pE at θ = 90°.        Q7. (Numerical, 2 marks) A dipole: −1.0 pC at (0, 0) and +1.0 pC at (3 mm, 4 mm). Field E = 1000 V/m along +x is switched on. Find the torque.  [2024]    Steps:     p = q × (vector from −q to +q) = 10^-12 × (3 × 10^-3 î + 4 × 10^-3 ĵ) = (3î + 4ĵ) × 10^-15 C m.   τ = p × E = (3î + 4ĵ) × 10^-15 × 1000 î.   î × î = 0, ĵ × î = −k̂. So τ = −4 × 10^-12 k̂ N m.   Magnitude 4 × 10^-12 N m, along −z.          Q8. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Gauss's law find E due to an infinitely long straight wire of linear charge density λ. Draw E vs r graph.  [2018; 2026 used it for force between two line charges]    Steps:     Gaussian surface: cylinder of radius r, length l, coaxial with wire.   Flux through flat ends = 0 (E parallel to them). Flux through curved surface = E × 2πrl.   Charge enclosed = λl. Gauss: E × 2πrl = λl/ε0.   E = λ / (2πε0 r), radially outward for λ > 0. Graph: E vs r is a falling curve (E ∝ 1/r), like a hyperbola.          Q9. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Gauss's law, find E due to an infinite plane sheet of charge density σ.  [2016, 2017]    Steps: Take a cylinder (pillbox) of cross-section A crossing the sheet. Flux only through the two flat faces: EA + EA = 2EA. Charge enclosed = σA. So 2EA = σA/ε0 →  E = σ / (2ε0) , perpendicular to sheet, away for +σ, towards for −σ. E does not depend on distance.        Q10. (Derivation, 3 marks) Field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell (radius R, charge q) (i) outside (r > R) (ii) inside (r < R).  [2025; 2026 (shell flux parts)]    Steps:     Outside: Gaussian sphere of radius r > R. E × 4πr² = q/ε0 → E = q / (4πε0 r²) (as if all charge at centre).   Inside: Gaussian sphere r < R encloses no charge → E × 4πr² = 0 →  E = 0 .   Graph: E = 0 up to R, jumps to maximum at R, then falls as 1/r².          Q11. (Numerical, 3 marks) Electric field E = 500x î N/C (x in m). A cube of side 0.1 m has its faces at x = 0.1 m and x = 0.2 m (other faces parallel to the x-axis). Find the flux through the cube and charge inside.  [2024 – figure positions assumed here as above]    Steps:     Only the two faces perpendicular to x have flux. Area A = 0.01 m².   At x = 0.1 m: E = 50 N/C, flux in = −50 × 0.01 = −0.5 N m²/C.   At x = 0.2 m: E = 100 N/C, flux out = +100 × 0.01 = +1.0 N m²/C.   Net flux = 0.5 N m²/C.   q = ε0 × flux = 8.854 × 10^-12 × 0.5 ≈ 4.4 × 10^-12 C.

title: Chapter 2 – Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
text: Chapter 2 – Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance       Q12. (Numerical, 2 marks) Two charges +q and +q are a distance d apart. How much work is needed to bring another +q from infinity to the midpoint?  [SQP]    Steps: Potential at midpoint V = kq/(d/2) + kq/(d/2) = 4kq/d. Work W = qV = 4kq²/d = q² / (πε0 d).        Q13. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive the potential due to a dipole at a point on its axis; show V = p / (4πε0 r²) for r >> a.  [2019; 2024 (far point)]    Steps: V = kq/(r − a) − kq/(r + a) = kq × 2a/(r² − a²) = kp/(r² − a²). For r >> a, V = kp/r² = p/(4πε0 r²). On the equatorial line V = 0 (equal and opposite contributions).        Q14. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive the potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field. When is it maximum and minimum?  [2024]    Steps:     Torque τ = pE sin θ. Work to rotate from θ0 to θ: W = ∫ pE sin θ dθ = pE (cos θ0 − cos θ).   Take θ0 = 90° as zero energy: U(θ) = −pE cos θ = −p·E.   Minimum U = −pE at θ = 0° (stable). Maximum U = +pE at θ = 180° (unstable).          Q15. (2 marks) Define equipotential surface. Draw them for (i) a point charge (ii) uniform field along z. Why is E always perpendicular to them?  [2016, 2019]    Answer: Surface where potential is the same at every point. (i) concentric spheres around the charge, getting farther apart outward. (ii) equally spaced planes parallel to the x-y plane. No work is done moving a charge on it (ΔV = 0), so E has no component along the surface; E ⟂ surface.        Q16. (Numerical, 2 marks) How will you connect 6 μF, 9 μF and 18 μF capacitors to get (i) minimum (ii) maximum capacitance?  [SQP]    Steps: (i) Series: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/9 + 1/18 = (3 + 2 + 1)/18 = 1/3 → C = 3 μF (minimum). (ii) Parallel: C = 6 + 9 + 18 = 33 μF (maximum).        Q17. (MCQ) Ten capacitors of 1 μF each are joined in parallel to 100 V. Total energy stored = ?  [2024]    Answer: C = 10 μF. U = ½CV² = ½ × 10^-5 × 10^4 = 5.0 × 10^-2 J.        Q18. (Numerical, 3 marks) Two capacitors C1 and C2, first in series then in parallel across 100 V, store 0.045 J and 0.25 J. Find C1 and C2 and charge on each in parallel.  [2015]    Steps:     Parallel: ½(C1 + C2)(100)² = 0.25 → C1 + C2 = 5 × 10^-5 F = 50 μF.   Series: ½  C1C2/(C1 + C2) ² = 0.045 → C1C2/(C1 + C2) = 9 μF → C1C2 = 450 (μF)².   Solve x² − 50x + 450 = 0 → x = 38.2 μF and 11.8 μF.   Charges (parallel, V = 100 V): Q = CV → 3.82 × 10^-3 C and 1.18 × 10^-3 C.          Q19. (2 marks) What factors does the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor depend on? Why can an isolated conductor not have a large capacitance?  [SQP]    Answer: C = Kε0A/d → depends on plate area A, separation d (C ∝ 1/d), and dielectric constant K of medium. Isolated sphere C = 4πε0R; even a sphere as big as the Earth has only about 711 μF, so a single conductor cannot have large C.        Q20. (Numerical, 2 marks) Show E = −dV/dr. Air breaks down at 2.5 × 10^6 V/m. A metal sphere must reach 5 × 10^5 V. Minimum radius?  [SQP]    Steps: Work done moving unit charge by dr against E: dV = −E dr → E = −dV/dr. For a sphere, V = kQ/R and E = kQ/R² → E = V/R. R = V/E = 5 × 10^5 / 2.5 × 10^6 = 0.2 m.        Q21. (Numerical, 2 marks) Two isolated metal spheres of radii 1 cm and 3 cm have the same surface charge density 10^-9 C/m². They are joined by a thin wire. Find the new charge on the smaller sphere.  [2024; 2016 similar idea]    Steps:     Q1 = σ × 4πr1² = 10^-9 × 4π × 10^-4 = 4π × 10^-13 C; Q2 = 10^-9 × 4π × 9 × 10^-4 = 36π × 10^-13 C. Total Q = 40π × 10^-13 C.   After joining, potentials equal: Q1'/r1 = Q2'/r2 → Q1' : Q2' = 1 : 3.   Q1' = Q/4 = 10π × 10^-13 ≈ 3.14 × 10^-12 C. (Charge flows from the larger sphere to the smaller, since with equal σ the larger sphere is at higher potential.)

title: Chapter 3 – Current Electricity
text: Chapter 3 – Current Electricity       Q22. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive the relation I = neAvd. Also derive vd = eEτ/m.  [2016, 2026]    Steps:     Electron acceleration a = −eE/m. Averaged over relaxation time τ: vd = −eEτ/m (magnitude eEτ/m).   In time Δt, electrons in length vdΔt cross area A: number = n A vd Δt; charge = neAvdΔt.   I = charge/time = neAvd. (2026 part: if length doubled at same V, E = V/l halves, so vd halves.)          Q23. (Derivation, 3 marks) Show j = σE with σ = ne²τ/m, and resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ).  [2018, 2024, 2025]    Steps: j = I/A = nevd = ne(eEτ/m) = (ne²τ/m)E. So σ = ne²τ/m and ρ = 1/σ = m/(ne²τ). Current density is a vector; unit A/m².        Q24. (Numerical, 2 marks) At what temperature will a silver wire have twice its resistance at 20 °C? α = 4.0 × 10^-3 /K.  [2024]    Steps: R = R0[1 + α(T − 20)]. 2R0 = R0[1 + 4 × 10^-3 (T − 20)] → T − 20 = 1/(4 × 10^-3) = 250 → T = 270 °C.        Q25. (MCQ) Cell's open-circuit pd is 8 V; it falls to 4 V when 4 A is drawn. Internal resistance = ?  [2023]    Answer: r = (E − V)/I = (8 − 4)/4 = 1 Ω.        Q26. (Numerical, 2 marks) A battery of emf 21 V, internal resistance 3 Ω gives 3 A through a resistor. Find (i) resistor (ii) terminal voltage.  [2026]    Steps: I = E/(R + r) → 3 = 21/(R + 3) → R = 4 Ω. V = E − Ir = 21 − 9 = 12 V (check: IR = 3 × 4 = 12 V).        Q27. (Numerical, 3 marks) With R = 4 Ω the current is 1 A; with R = 9 Ω it is 0.5 A. Find E and r. Draw V vs I.  [2015]    Steps: E = 1(4 + r) and E = 0.5(9 + r). So 4 + r = 4.5 + 0.5r → r = 1 Ω, E = 5 V. Graph: V = E − Ir is a straight line falling from V = E (at I = 0) with slope −r.        Q28. (Numerical, 2 marks) Battery 12 V, r = 2 Ω, connected to 4 Ω. Show voltmeter across cell and across resistor read the same. Why is voltmeter in parallel and ammeter in series?  [2016; 2017 similar]    Steps: I = 12/(4 + 2) = 2 A. Across resistor: 2 × 4 = 8 V. Across cell: 12 − 2 × 2 = 8 V. Same. Ammeter has very low resistance (does not change current); voltmeter has very high resistance (draws almost no current).        Q29. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Kirchhoff's rules, get the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge.  [2015, 2024; 2026 A-R; SQP MCQ]    Steps:     Arms P (AB), Q (BC), R (AD), S (DC); galvanometer between B and D; cell across A and C.   At balance Ig = 0, so current I1 in P and Q, I2 in R and S.   Loop ABDA: −I1P + I2R = 0 (Ig = 0) → I1P = I2R.   Loop BCDB: −I1Q + I2S = 0 → I1Q = I2S.   Divide:  P/Q = R/S . (Swapping cell and galvanometer does not change balance.) Kirchhoff rules: Junction rule – sum of currents at a junction = 0 (charge conservation). Loop rule – sum of emfs = sum of IR drops in a closed loop (energy conservation).          Q30. (MCQ) Bulbs rated 200 V–60 W and 200 V–100 W. Ratio R1/R2 = ?  [SQP]    Answer: R = V²/P. R1/R2 = P2/P1 = 100/60 = 5 : 3.        Q31. (MCQ) Two identical heaters (1000 W, 220 V) in parallel across 220 V. Total power?  [SQP]    Answer: Each works at rated voltage, P = 1000 + 1000 = 2000 W.        Q32. (2 marks) Bulbs P and Q have resistances in ratio 1 : 2 and are in series. Ratio of powers?  [2018]    Answer: Same current in series, P = I²R → PP : PQ = 1 : 2. (In parallel it would be 2 : 1, since P = V²/R.)        Q33. (2 marks) Describe the path of free electrons in a conductor (a) with an electric field (b) without it.  [SQP]    Answer: (a) Random zig-zag motion with collisions, plus a slow net drift opposite to E → current flows. (b) Only random thermal motion in all directions; average velocity zero → no current.

title: Chapter 4 – Moving Charges and Magnetism
text: Chapter 4 – Moving Charges and Magnetism       Q34. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Biot–Savart law, find B at the centre of a circular loop of radius R carrying I (and state B on the axis).  [2016, 2017, 2023; 2025 asked vector form]    Steps:     Biot–Savart: dB = (μ0/4π) I (dl × r) / r³, magnitude dB = (μ0/4π) I dl sin θ / r².   At centre, every element is at distance R and dl ⟂ r (θ = 90°), all dB in the same direction.   B = (μ0/4π)(I/R²) × ∮dl = (μ0/4π)(I/R²)(2πR) =  μ0I / (2R) .   On the axis at distance x: B = μ0IR² / [2(R² + x²)^(3/2)], along the axis (right-hand thumb rule). Diagram: loop with field lines passing through centre like a small bar magnet.          Q35. (MCQ) A long wire with a semicircular loop of radius 10 cm carries 5 A. B at centre of the semicircle?  [SQP]    Answer: B = μ0I/(4R) = 4π × 10^-7 × 5/(4 × 0.1) = 5π × 10^-6 T = 5π μT. (Straight parts pass through the centre line, so give zero.)        Q36. (2 marks) State Ampere's circuital law and use it to find B due to a long straight wire.  [syllabus; 2015 used Ampere's law]    Answer: ∮B·dl = μ0 I(enclosed). Take a circle of radius r around the wire: B × 2πr = μ0I →  B = μ0I/(2πr) . Field lines are concentric circles (2025 MCQ).        Q37. (Numerical, 3 marks) A proton (KE 1.3384 × 10^-14 J) moving horizontally north to south enters B = 2.0 mT pointing east. q/m = 1.0 × 10^8 C/kg. Find (a) speed (b) acceleration (c) radius.  [2024]    Steps:     m = q/(q/m) = 1.6 × 10^-19 / 10^8 = 1.6 × 10^-27 kg.   v = √(2K/m) = √(2 × 1.3384 × 10^-14 / 1.6 × 10^-27) = √(1.673 × 10^13) ≈ 4.09 × 10^6 m/s.   a = qvB/m = (q/m)vB = 10^8 × 4.09 × 10^6 × 2 × 10^-3 ≈ 8.2 × 10^11 m/s².   r = mv/(qB) = v/[(q/m)B] = 4.09 × 10^6 / (2 × 10^5) ≈ 20.4 m.          Q38. (Numerical, 3 marks) An alpha particle (m = 6.4 × 10^-27 kg, q = 3.2 × 10^-19 C) of energy 8.0 MeV enters B = 0.5 T at right angles. Find radius. When does it move in a helix / go undeviated?  [2026]    Steps:     K = 8 × 1.6 × 10^-13 = 1.28 × 10^-12 J.   p = √(2mK) = √(2 × 6.4 × 10^-27 × 1.28 × 10^-12) = 1.28 × 10^-19 kg m/s.   r = p/(qB) = 1.28 × 10^-19 / (3.2 × 10^-19 × 0.5) = 0.8 m.   Helix: velocity at an angle (not 0°, 90°, 180°) to B. Undeviated: velocity parallel or antiparallel to B (F = qvB sin θ = 0).          Q39. (2 marks) Find the condition for a charged particle to pass undeviated through crossed E and B fields (velocity selector).  [2017]    Answer: v, E and B mutually perpendicular with electric and magnetic forces opposite. qE = qvB →  v = E/B . Only particles with this speed go straight.        Q40. (Numerical, 3 marks) Two long parallel wires A and B, 2.5 cm apart, carry 5.0 A and 2.5 A in opposite directions. Find force on 10 cm of wire B. Define 1 ampere.  [2023; 2019, 2024 A-R similar]    Steps: F = μ0 I1 I2 L / (2πd) = 2 × 10^-7 × 5 × 2.5 × 0.1 / 0.025 = 1.0 × 10^-5 N,  repulsive  (opposite currents repel; like currents attract). 1 ampere: the current which, flowing in two infinitely long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10^-7 N per metre length on each.        Q41. (Numerical, 3 marks) A coil of 30 turns, radius 8.0 cm, carries 6 A in a horizontal B = 1.0 T. Field lines make 30° with the plane of the coil. Find the torque. What if the coil is of irregular shape with same area?  [2026; NCERT]    Steps: Angle between B and normal (area vector) = 90° − 30° = 60°. τ = NIAB sin 60° = 30 × 6 × π(0.08)² × 1 × 0.866 ≈ 3.1 N m. For any planar shape of the same area the torque is the same (τ depends only on area).        Q42. (Numerical, 3 marks) An ammeter of resistance 13 Ω reads up to 100 A. What shunt extends its range to 750 A? Why is the coil wound on a metal frame?  [SQP]    Steps: Shunt carries 750 − 100 = 650 A, same pd as meter: 100 × 13 = 650 × S → S = 2 Ω. Metal frame: eddy currents in the frame damp the oscillations so the pointer comes to rest quickly (electromagnetic damping).        Q43. (MCQ) A galvanometer (resistance G) is converted to an ammeter of range I; galvanometer current is 0.1% of I. Resistance of the ammeter?  [2024]    Answer: Ig = 0.001I. Shunt S = IgG/(I − Ig) = G/999. Ammeter resistance = GS/(G + S) = G/1000. Voltmeter conversion: high resistance R in series, R = V/Ig − G.

title: Chapter 5 – Magnetism and Matter
text: Chapter 5 – Magnetism and Matter       Q44. (2 marks) A material has relative permeability 800. Identify it and write two properties.  [SQP]    Answer: μr >> 1 → ferromagnetic. Strongly attracted by magnets; retains magnetism (can make permanent magnets); shows hysteresis; becomes paramagnetic above Curie temperature.        Q45. (3 marks) Give three differences between dia-, para- and ferromagnetic substances with examples.  [2019; 2016, 2018, 2025 similar] | Property | Dia | Para | Ferro | |---|---|---|---| | Behaviour near magnet | Weakly repelled | Weakly attracted | Strongly attracted | | Susceptibility χ | Small, negative | Small, positive | Very large, positive | | μr | Slightly < 1 | Slightly > 1 | Very large (>> 1) | | Field lines | Pushed out | Slightly concentrated | Strongly concentrated | | Temperature effect | Almost none | χ ∝ 1/T (Curie law) | Becomes para above Curie point | | Examples | Bismuth, copper, water | Aluminium, sodium, oxygen | Iron, cobalt, nickel |        Q46. (MCQ / A-R) Assertion: When a copper bar is placed in a magnetic field, field lines get concentrated inside it. Reason: Copper is paramagnetic.  [2023]    Answer: (D) Both false. Copper is diamagnetic, so lines are pushed out of it.        Q47. (MCQ) A superconducting ball (cooled in liquid nitrogen) is placed near a bar magnet. It moves ______ and its magnetic moment is ______ the magnet's.  [SQP]    Answer: Away from the magnet; opposite (a superconductor is a perfect diamagnet).        Q48. (2 marks) State Gauss's law for magnetism and its significance.  [SQP; 2019]    Answer: Net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: ∮B·dA = 0. Significance: isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist; magnetic field lines form closed loops.

title: Chapter 6 – Electromagnetic Induction
text: Chapter 6 – Electromagnetic Induction       Q49. (2 marks) State Faraday's laws and Lenz's law. Show Lenz's law follows conservation of energy.  [2026; SQP]    Answer: Faraday: induced emf e = −dΦ/dt (N turns: −N dΦ/dt). Lenz: the induced current opposes the change that produces it. If a magnet's N-pole is pushed towards a coil, the near face becomes N and repels it; we must do work against this repulsion, and that work appears as electrical energy. If the current helped the motion, we would get energy for nothing – impossible.        Q50. (2 marks) A bar magnet falls through a metal ring. Why is its acceleration less than g?  [SQP]    Answer: Changing flux induces a current in the ring. By Lenz's law this current opposes the motion (repels when approaching, attracts when leaving), so there is an upward force → a < g.        Q51. (Numerical, 1–2 marks) A square loop of side 50 cm is in B = 3.0 T perpendicular to its plane. It is rotated by 90° in 0.3 s. Average emf?  [2026]    Steps: Φ initial = BA = 3 × 0.25 = 0.75 Wb; final = 0. e = ΔΦ/Δt = 0.75/0.3 = 2.5 V.        Q52. (Numerical, 2 marks) Current in a coil changes from 8.0 A to 2.0 A in 0.6 s; induced emf is 50 V. Find L. Write the dimensional formula of L.  [2026]    Steps: e = L(ΔI/Δt) → 50 = L × (6/0.6) = 10L → L = 5 H. Dimensions: [M L² T^-2 A^-2].        Q53. (Derivation, 3 marks) Define mutual inductance. Derive M for two long coaxial solenoids of the same length l.  [2015, 2017, 2023 (coil on solenoid)]    Steps:     Inner solenoid S1: n1 turns/m, area A1. Outer S2: n2 turns/m.   Current I2 in S2 gives B2 = μ0n2I2 inside it.   Flux linked with S1 (N1 = n1 l turns): N1Φ1 = n1 l × A1 × μ0n2I2.   M = N1Φ1/I2 =  μ0 n1 n2 A1 l . (M12 = M21 = M.) Unit: henry (H). Definition: M = flux linked with one coil per unit current in the other (or emf in one coil per unit rate of change of current in the other).          Q54. (3 marks) State the principle of an AC generator and derive e = NBAω sin ωt.  [2016, 2017, 2018]    Steps: Principle – electromagnetic induction. A coil (N turns, area A) rotates with angular speed ω in uniform B. Flux Φ = NBA cos ωt. e = −dΦ/dt = NBAω sin ωt. Peak emf e0 = NBAω (= 2πf NBA).

title: Chapter 7 – Alternating Current
text: Chapter 7 – Alternating Current       Q55. (MCQ) An ac ammeter reads 10 A. Peak current = ?  [2025]    Answer: Meter reads rms. I0 = √2 × Irms = 10√2 A.        Q56. (MCQ) A capacitor has reactance X. If C is doubled and frequency tripled, new reactance = ?  [2024]    Answer: XC = 1/(2πfC) → new X = X/(2 × 3) = X/6.        Q57. (Derivation, 3–5 marks) Using a phasor diagram, get the impedance of a series LCR circuit and the resonance condition.  [2023, 2025, 2026, SQP; 2019]    Steps:     Same current i = i0 sin ωt in all. VR in phase with i; VL leads i by 90°; VC lags i by 90°.   Phasors: VR along i; (VL − VC) perpendicular.   V² = VR² + (VL − VC)² → V = i √[R² + (XL − XC)²].    Z = √[R² + (XL − XC)²] , tan φ = (XL − XC)/R, XL = ωL, XC = 1/(ωC).   Resonance: XL = XC →  ω0 = 1/√(LC) , f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). Then Z = R (minimum), current maximum, circuit acts purely resistive, VL and VC are 180° out of phase.   Use: radio tuning – changing C changes f0; the station whose frequency equals f0 gives maximum current (SQP). Graph: current vs ω rises to a sharp peak at ω0.          Q58. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive average power in an ac circuit; show it is zero for an ideal inductor.  [2024, 2016]    Steps: v = v0 sin ωt, i = i0 sin(ωt − φ). p = vi = v0i0 sin ωt sin(ωt − φ) = (v0i0/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ)]. Average of cos(2ωt − φ) over a cycle = 0. So  P = Vrms Irms cos φ . Ideal inductor: φ = 90°, cos φ = 0 → P = 0 (wattless current). Power factor = cos φ = R/Z.        Q59. (Numerical, 3 marks) A lamp is designed for 110 V dc and 11 A. To run it on 220 V, 50 Hz ac, a coil is put in series. Find the inductance.  [2024]    Steps:     Lamp R = 110/11 = 10 Ω.   Needed Z = 220/11 = 20 Ω.   XL = √(Z² − R²) = √(400 − 100) = √300 ≈ 17.3 Ω.   L = XL/(2πf) = 17.3/314 ≈ 0.055 H (55 mH).          Q60. (Numerical, 3 marks) An inductor draws 1 A from 200 V dc but only 0.5 A from 200 V, 50 Hz ac. Why? Find L.  [2019]    Steps: With dc, XL = 0, so R = 200 Ω. With ac, Z = 200/0.5 = 400 Ω. XL = √(400² − 200²) = √120000 ≈ 346 Ω. L = 346/(2π × 50) ≈ 1.1 H. Current falls because the inductor offers reactance to ac.        Q61. (3 marks) A bulb is in series with an inductor and an ac source. What happens to brightness if (i) an iron rod is put inside the coil (ii) a capacitor with XC = XL is added (iii) frequency is decreased?  [2015, 2016, 2026]    Answer: (i) L increases → XL increases → current falls → dimmer. (ii) XL − XC = 0 → Z = R, maximum current → brightest. (iii) XL = 2πfL decreases → current increases → brighter.        Q62. (Long, 5 marks) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer, state its principle and working, and give three energy losses. Does it violate energy conservation? Numerical: Np = 200, Ns = 3000, Vp = 90 V, Is = 2.0 A; find Vs and Ip.  [2024; 2015, 2016, 2018, 2019, SQP]    Answer:     Diagram: soft iron laminated core, primary (few turns) connected to ac input, secondary (many turns) to output.   Principle: mutual induction – changing current in primary changes flux in core, which induces emf in secondary.   Relations: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; ideal: VpIp = VsIs so Ip/Is = Ns/Np.   Losses: (1) copper loss (I²R heating of windings), (2) eddy current loss (reduced by laminated core), (3) hysteresis loss, (4) flux leakage.   No violation: voltage goes up but current goes down in the same ratio; power out ≤ power in.   Numerical: Vs = 90 × 3000/200 = 1350 V. Ip = Is × Ns/Np = 2 × 15 = 30 A.   Works only on ac (dc gives no changing flux) – asked 2015.

title: Chapter 8 – Electromagnetic Waves
text: Chapter 8 – Electromagnetic Waves       Q63. (3 marks) Name the EM waves used for (a) radar/aircraft navigation (b) treating muscular strain (physiotherapy) (c) diagnosis of bone fracture (d) water purification / LASIK eye surgery. How are they produced?  [2015, 2018, 2019; 2016, 2017 similar]    Answer: (a) Microwaves – klystron, magnetron, Gunn diode. (b) Infrared – hot bodies, vibrating molecules. (c) X-rays – fast electrons hitting a metal target. (d) Ultraviolet – very hot bodies, sun, special lamps. Order of increasing frequency: radio < microwave < infrared < visible < UV < X-ray < gamma.        Q64. (3 marks) What is displacement current? Where does it exist while a capacitor is charging?  [2025; 2017, 2016]    Answer: Id = ε0 dΦE/dt – a current due to a changing electric field (no charges move). While charging, conduction current flows in the wires; between the plates there is no conduction current, but E is changing, so displacement current exists there. Id = conduction current, so current is continuous. In steady state ΦE is constant → no current.        Q65. (MCQ) Electric field amplitude of an EM wave in free space is 1000 V/m. Magnetic field amplitude = ?  [2025]    Answer: B0 = E0/c = 1000/(3 × 10^8) = 3.33 × 10^-6 T.        Q66. (Numerical, 2 marks) E = 30 sin(2π × 10^18 t + π × 10^10 x), B = 10^-7 sin(same). Find refractive index of the medium, frequency, and name the wave.  [SQP]    Steps: v = ω/k = 2π × 10^18 / (π × 10^10) = 2 × 10^8 m/s. n = c/v = 1.5. f = ω/2π = 10^18 Hz → X-rays. (Wave travels along −x.)        Q67. (2 marks) Write three characteristics of EM waves.  [2025, 2026]    Answer: (1) Transverse – E and B perpendicular to each other and to direction of travel. (2) Travel in vacuum with speed c = 1/√(μ0ε0) = 3 × 10^8 m/s. (3) E0/B0 = c; they carry energy and momentum; no medium needed.

title: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
text: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments       Q68. (Numerical, 2 marks) Object 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius 40 cm. Find image position and magnification.  [2024]    Steps: f = −20 cm, u = −30 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/30 = −1/60 → v = −60 cm (real, in front). m = −v/u = −(−60)/(−30) = −2 → real, inverted, twice as big.        Q69. (Numerical, 2 marks) A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms the image of an object 30 cm away. Position and nature?  [2026]    Steps: u = −30, f = +20. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 → v = +60 cm. m = v/u = −2 → real, inverted, magnified, on the other side.        Q70. (Numerical, 2 marks) A plano-convex lens of focal length 16 cm is made of material n = 1.4. Radius of the curved surface?  [2024]    Steps: Lens maker: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R1 − 1/R2), R2 = ∞. 1/16 = 0.4/R → R = 6.4 cm.        Q71. (Numerical, 2 marks) An equiconvex lens of glass n = 1.55 has f = 15 cm. Radius of each surface?  [2025; 2017 had f = 20 cm]    Steps: 1/f = (n − 1)(2/R) → 1/15 = 0.55 × 2/R → R = 1.1 × 15 = 16.5 cm. (For f = 20 cm, R = 22 cm.)        Q72. (Derivation, 5 marks) Derive n2/v − n1/u = (n2 − n1)/R for refraction at a convex spherical surface; hence derive the lens maker's formula.  [2015, 2016, 2023, 2026]    Steps:     Point object O in medium n1 on axis; convex surface (centre C, radius R) into medium n2; image I. Ray ON hits surface at N, refracts along NI. Angles with axis: α (at O), β (at I), γ (at C). Small angles.   In triangles: i = α + γ, r = γ − β.   Snell (small angles): n1 i = n2 r → n1(α + γ) = n2(γ − β).   With tan ≈ angle: α = MN/OM, β = MN/MI, γ = MN/MC.   n1/OM + n2/MI = (n2 − n1)/MC. Signs: OM = −u, MI = +v, MC = +R →  n2/v − n1/u = (n2 − n1)/R .   Lens: first surface (R1) forms image I1 at v1: n2/v1 − n1/u = (n2 − n1)/R1. I1 is object for second surface (R2): n1/v − n2/v1 = (n1 − n2)/R2.   Add: n1(1/v − 1/u) = (n2 − n1)(1/R1 − 1/R2). For object at infinity v = f:    1/f = (n21 − 1)(1/R1 − 1/R2) , n21 = n2/n1.          Q73. (Numerical, 2 marks) Light from a point source in air falls on a convex glass surface (n = 1.5, R = 20 cm). Source is 100 cm away. Find image position.  [2016]    Steps: 1.5/v − 1/(−100) = (1.5 − 1)/20 → 1.5/v = 0.025 − 0.010 = 0.015 → v = 100 cm (real image inside glass).        Q74. (3 marks) State conditions for total internal reflection and relate critical angle to n. A ray inside diamond (n = 2.42) hits the surface at 30°. Refraction or TIR? Why do diamonds sparkle?  [SQP; 2016, 2018, 2019, 2023, 2026]    Answer: Conditions: (1) light goes from denser to rarer medium; (2) angle of incidence > critical angle. sin C = 1/n. Diamond: sin C = 1/2.42 = 0.413 → C ≈ 24.4°. 30° > 24.4° → total internal reflection. Diamonds are cut so light undergoes many TIRs inside before coming out → sparkle. Other uses: optical fibres, prisms in binoculars. (Twinkling of stars is due to refraction, not TIR – 2026 MCQ.)        Q75. (Numerical, 3 marks) Prism of refractive index √2 and angle 60°. Find angle of minimum deviation and angle of incidence. Draw the i–δ graph.  [2024; 2025, 2017, 2019]    Steps: n = sin[(A + Dm)/2] / sin(A/2). √2 = sin[(60 + Dm)/2] / sin 30° → sin[(60 + Dm)/2] = √2 × 0.5 = 1/√2 → (60 + Dm)/2 = 45° → Dm = 30°. At minimum deviation i = (A + Dm)/2 = 45°. Graph: δ vs i is a U-shaped curve; its lowest point is Dm (at Dm, ray passes symmetrically, i = e, r1 = r2 = A/2).        Q76. (Numerical, 3 marks) A compound microscope: fo = 2 cm, fe = 5 cm, object 2.2 cm from objective. Find (i) image by objective (ii) magnifying power with final image at infinity.  [SQP]    Steps: (i) 1/v = 1/fo + 1/u = 1/2 − 1/2.2 = 0.1/2.2 → v = 22 cm. (ii) m = (vo/|uo|) × (D/fe) = (22/2.2) × (25/5) = 10 × 5 = 50.        Q77. (Numerical, 3 marks) Telescope: objective 15 m, eyepiece 1.0 cm. (i) angular magnification (ii) diameter of the Moon's image by objective (Moon diameter 3.48 × 10^6 m, orbit radius 3.8 × 10^8 m). Draw the ray diagram (normal adjustment). Why large objective aperture?  [2015, 2019; 2016, 2017, 2026 MCQ (fo = 144 cm, fe = 6 cm → m = 24, tube length 150 cm)]    Steps: (i) m = fo/fe = 1500/1 = 1500. (ii) angle subtended by Moon α = 3.48 × 10^6 / 3.8 × 10^8; image size = fo × α = 15 × 9.16 × 10^-3 ≈ 0.137 m = 13.7 cm. Large aperture: gathers more light (bright image) and gives higher resolving power. Objective: large f; eyepiece: small f. Near-point adjustment: m = (fo/fe)(1 + fe/D). Reflecting telescope advantages: no chromatic aberration, cheaper large mirror, more light, better resolution.        Q78. (MCQ set) (a) Two convex lenses of 60 cm and 20 cm in contact: power? (b) An equiconvex lens of power P is cut into two halves perpendicular to the axis: power of each part? (c) Convex lens immersed in water: focal length? Derive 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2.  [2024 case; 2017, 2026 derivation; SQP A-R] Answers: (a) P = 1/0.6 + 1/0.2 = 1.67 + 5 = 6.67 D. (b) Each half is plano-convex with one curved face → P/2. (c) Increases (relative refractive index n(glass)/n(water) is smaller, so (n − 1) term smaller).    Derivation: Lens 1 alone: 1/v1 − 1/u = 1/f1. Image of lens 1 is object for lens 2 (in contact): 1/v − 1/v1 = 1/f2. Add: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f1 + 1/f2 = 1/f. So P = P1 + P2.

title: Chapter 10 – Wave Optics
text: Chapter 10 – Wave Optics       Q79. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Huygens' principle, derive Snell's law of refraction. Which prediction of wave theory was later verified?  [SQP; 2017, 2019 (or), 2016]    Steps:     Plane wavefront AB (in medium 1, speed v1) strikes surface PP' at angle i. While B travels BC = v1t to reach the surface at C, a secondary wavelet from A travels AE = v2t in medium 2.   Tangent CE from C to the wavelet (radius v2t) is the refracted wavefront, at angle r.   In triangle ABC: sin i = BC/AC = v1t/AC. In triangle AEC: sin r = AE/AC = v2t/AC.   sin i / sin r = v1/v2 = constant = n21 (= n2/n1) → Snell's law.   Prediction: speed of light in a denser medium is less than in air (v2 < v1 when light bends towards normal) – later verified experimentally (Foucault). Diagram: incident wavefront AB, surface, arc of radius v2t from A, refracted wavefront EC.          Q80. (Derivation, 3 marks) State Huygens' principle; prove i = r for reflection using it.  [2018, 2019, 2024]    Answer: Huygens: (1) every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets moving with the wave's speed; (2) the forward envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets gives the new wavefront. Proof: Wavefront AB hits mirror at A. In time t, B reaches C (BC = vt). Wavelet from A has radius AE = vt. Tangent CE is the reflected wavefront. Triangles ABC and CEA are congruent (common AC, right angles at B and E, BC = AE) → i = r.        Q81. (A-R) YDSE: d = 0.25 mm, D = 1.0 m, λ = 500 nm. A: fringe width is 2.0 mm. R: fringe width is directly proportional to slit separation and inversely to wavelength.  [SQP]    Answer: β = λD/d = 500 × 10^-9 × 1 / 0.25 × 10^-3 = 2 × 10^-3 m = 2 mm. A true; R false (β ∝ λ and ∝ 1/d) → (C).        Q82. (Numerical, 2 marks) In YDSE, light has a known wavelength 520 nm and an unknown λ'. The 4th bright fringe of λ' coincides with the 5th bright fringe of 520 nm. Find λ'.  [2024]    Steps: Bright fringe position y = nλD/d. 4λ'D/d = 5 × 520 × D/d → λ' = 650 nm.        Q83. (Numerical, 2 marks) Two coherent beams of intensities I and 4I superpose. Find Imax/Imin.  [2023; 2018 similar]    Steps: Amplitude ∝ √I: a1 = 1, a2 = 2 (in units). Imax ∝ (2 + 1)² = 9, Imin ∝ (2 − 1)² = 1 → 9 : 1.        Q84. (2 marks) What are coherent sources? Can two independent sodium lamps be coherent? Why is sustained interference needed?  [2024]    Answer: Sources with the same frequency and a constant phase difference. Two independent lamps cannot be coherent – each emits from millions of atoms whose phases change randomly about every 10^-8 s, so the pattern shifts too fast to see. Coherent sources are made from one source (e.g. two slits lit by one source).        Q85. (3 marks) A YDSE set-up in water is moved to a liquid of higher refractive index. Effect on (a) speed, frequency, wavelength of light (b) fringe width, shape, position of central maximum.  [2025]    Answer: (a) Speed decreases, frequency unchanged, wavelength decreases. (b) Fringe width β = λD/d decreases; fringes remain straight lines; central maximum stays at the same place (centre).        Q86. (Numerical, 2 marks) A teacher uses a 633 nm laser; screen 5.0 m away; wants fringe width 5 mm. Slit separation?  [2026]    Steps: d = λD/β = 633 × 10^-9 × 5 / 5 × 10^-3 = 6.33 × 10^-4 m ≈ 0.63 mm.        Q87. (2–3 marks) Give two differences between interference and diffraction patterns. In single-slit diffraction, what happens to the central band if slit width is doubled?  [2017, 2018, 2019, 2023]    Answer: Interference: superposition of waves from two coherent sources; fringes of equal width; all bright fringes equally bright. Diffraction: superposition of wavelets from different parts of the same wavefront; central maximum twice as wide as others; brightness falls quickly away from centre. Doubling slit width: central band width (2λD/a) halves; it becomes brighter (more light passes, energy in a smaller area). Diffraction of sound is common because its wavelength (≈ 1 m) is comparable to doors/obstacles, while light's wavelength is very small (2026 Q).

title: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
text: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter       Q88. (3 marks) Write Einstein's photoelectric equation. Explain using photon picture: (a) threshold frequency (b) Kmax independent of intensity (c) V0 vs ν is a straight line of slope h/e.  [2025; 2015, 2017, 2019, SQP]    Answer: hν = φ0 + Kmax, i.e. Kmax = hν − φ0 = eV0. (a) One photon frees one electron. If hν < φ0 (ν < ν0 = φ0/h), no electron can escape however intense the light. (b) Intensity = number of photons; it increases current, not energy per photon. Kmax depends only on ν. (c) eV0 = hν − φ0 → V0 = (h/e)ν − φ0/e: straight line, slope h/e (same for all metals), intercept on ν-axis = ν0. Also: emission is instantaneous – wave theory cannot explain (a), (b) or this.        Q89. (MCQ) Radiation of 200 nm falls on a surface of work function 4.2 eV. Kmax ≈ ?  [2026]    Steps: E = 1240/200 = 6.2 eV. Kmax = 6.2 − 4.2 = 2.0 eV.        Q90. (MCQ) Photons of 3.3 eV and 11.3 eV fall on a metal (φ = 2.3 eV). Ratio of maximum speeds of electrons?  [2024]    Steps: K1 = 1.0 eV, K2 = 9.0 eV. v ∝ √K → v1/v2 = √(1/9) = 1/3.        Q91. (Graphs, 3 marks) Plot (a) photocurrent vs collector plate potential for two intensities (same frequency) (b) same for two frequencies (same intensity) (c) photocurrent vs intensity.  [2023; 2017, 2018]    Answer: (a) Two curves with the same stopping potential (same point on negative axis) but different saturation currents – higher intensity, higher saturation. (b) Same saturation current, higher frequency → more negative stopping potential. (c) Straight line through the origin (current ∝ intensity).        Q92. (MCQ) An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. They have the same: momentum / speed / energy / angular momentum?  [2024]    Answer: Momentum (λ = h/p).        Q93. (MCQ) A proton and an alpha particle have equal momentum. Ratio of their kinetic energies Kp/Kα and wavelengths λp/λα?  [2026]    Steps: K = p²/2m → Kp/Kα = mα/mp = 4. λ = h/p → λp/λα = 1. Answer: 4, 1.        Q94. (2 marks) De Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V?  [Practice; 2019 asked the λ vs 1/√V graph]    Steps: λ = h/√(2meV) = 1.227/√V nm = 1.227/10 = 0.123 nm. Graph λ vs 1/√V is a straight line through origin with slope h/√(2mq): smaller slope means larger charge (for same mass).        Q95. (2 marks) A neutron (mass m) of kinetic energy E and a photon of the same energy. Find λn/λp.  [2024]    Steps: λn = h/√(2mE). λp = hc/E. λn/λp = E / (c√(2mE)) = √(E/(2mc²)) = (1/c)√(E/2m).        Q96. (MCQ) Red and blue beams have equal intensity. Which is true?  [2025]    Answer: The red beam has more photons (each red photon has less energy, so more photons are needed for the same intensity). Photons and electrons both show dual nature.

title: Chapter 12 – Atoms
text: Chapter 12 – Atoms       Q97. (2 marks) State Bohr's quantisation condition. How does de Broglie's hypothesis explain it?  [SQP; 2018]    Answer: mvr = nh/2π (angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/2π); electrons in these orbits do not radiate. De Broglie: electron is a wave, λ = h/mv. A stable orbit holds a standing wave, so circumference = nλ: 2πr = nh/mv → mvr = nh/2π.        Q98. (Derivation, 3 marks) Show that radius of nth Bohr orbit ∝ n² (also give v and E).  [2015; 2023 MCQ]    Steps:     Centripetal force = Coulomb force: mv²/r = ke²/r².   Bohr: mvr = nh/2π → v = nh/(2πmr).   Substitute: m[n²h²/(4π²m²r²)]/r = ke²/r² → r = n²h²/(4π²mke²) = ε0n²h²/(πme²).   So rn ∝ n² (r1 = 0.53 Å). vn = 2πke²/(nh) ∝ 1/n. En = −13.6/n² eV.   Total energy E = −ke²/2r; KE = +ke²/2r; PE = −ke²/r (2025 case).          Q99. (Numerical, 2 marks) Ground-state energy of H is −13.6 eV. Find KE and PE in the third excited state.  [2023]    Steps: Third excited state = n = 4. E = −13.6/16 = −0.85 eV. KE = −E = 0.85 eV. PE = 2E = −1.70 eV.        Q100. (Numerical, 2 marks) H atom in ground state absorbs a photon and goes to n = 4. Frequency of photon?  [2018; 2023 (n = 5)]    Steps: ΔE = 13.6(1 − 1/16) = 12.75 eV = 12.75 × 1.6 × 10^-19 J. ν = ΔE/h = 2.04 × 10^-18 / 6.63 × 10^-34 ≈ 3.1 × 10^15 Hz.        Q101. (Numerical, 2 marks) An electron jumps from −1.51 eV to −3.4 eV. Wavelength emitted and series?  [2017]    Steps: ΔE = 1.89 eV. λ = 1240/1.89 ≈ 656 nm (red). −1.51 eV is n = 3, −3.4 eV is n = 2 → Balmer series (visible).        Q102. (MCQ) The second line of the Balmer series in H corresponds to the transition:  [2024]    Answer: ni = 4 → nf = 2. (First line: 3 → 2.) Series: Lyman (to n = 1, UV), Balmer (to n = 2, visible), Paschen (to n = 3, IR) – energy-level diagram asked 2023.        Q103. (A-R / 3 marks) Rutherford's α-scattering: why do most α-particles pass undeflected? Give drawbacks of Rutherford's model and how Bohr removed them.  [SQP (A-R answer B); 2024; 2015]    Answer: Most of the atom is empty space; the positive charge and mass are in a tiny nucleus (≈ 10^-15 m vs atom ≈ 10^-10 m). (In the SQP A-R, both statements are true but R is not the correct reason → B.) Drawbacks: (1) an accelerating (revolving) electron should radiate energy, spiral into the nucleus – atom would be unstable; (2) it predicts a continuous spectrum, but hydrogen gives a line spectrum. Bohr: electrons move only in certain stationary orbits without radiating; radiation is emitted only during a jump, hν = Ei − Ef. Ionisation energy of H = 13.6 eV (SQP).

title: Chapter 13 – Nuclei
text: Chapter 13 – Nuclei       Q104. (Numerical, 3 marks) Atomic mass of O-16 is 15.99493 u. mp = 1.00727 u, mn = 1.00866 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV. Find binding energy per nucleon.  [SQP]    Steps:     8 protons + 8 neutrons: 8(1.00727) + 8(1.00866) = 8.05816 + 8.06928 = 16.12744 u.   Mass defect Δm = 16.12744 − 15.99493 = 0.13251 u.   BE = 0.13251 × 931.5 ≈ 123.4 MeV.   BE per nucleon = 123.4/16 ≈ 7.71 MeV.          Q105. (Derivation, 2–3 marks) Using R = R0 A^(1/3), show nuclear density is the same for all nuclei.  [2015, 2019, 2023, 2024]    Steps: Mass ≈ mA (m = mass of a nucleon). Volume = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)πR0³A. Density = mA / [(4/3)πR0³A] = 3m/(4πR0³) – no A, so same for all nuclei (≈ 2.3 × 10^17 kg/m³). Nuclear density >> atomic density because nearly all mass is packed in a tiny nucleus. 2026 MCQ: r1/r2 for A = 64 and 27 = (64/27)^(1/3) = 4/3.        Q106. (3 marks) Draw the BE/A vs mass number curve. Give two features. Why do light nuclei fuse and heavy nuclei split?  [2023, 2018; SQP MCQ]    Answer: Curve rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.75 MeV near A = 56 (iron – most stable), then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV at A = 238. Features: (1) nearly constant (≈ 8 MeV) for A = 30–170 – nuclear force is short-range (saturation); (2) lower for very light and very heavy nuclei. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move towards higher BE/A, so energy is released.        Q107. (3 marks) Differentiate between nuclear fission and fusion with one example each.  [2026; 2015]    Answer: Fission – a heavy nucleus splits into two medium nuclei: 235U + 1n → 144Ba + 89Kr + 3 1n + about 200 MeV. Happens with slow neutrons, used in reactors. Fusion – light nuclei join to form a heavier one: 2H + 3H → 4He + 1n + 17.6 MeV. Needs very high temperature (~10^7 K), powers the Sun.        Q108. (2 marks) Define mass defect and binding energy. Give two properties of nuclear force.  [2026; 2024]    Answer: Mass defect Δm = (Zmp + Nmn) − M(nucleus). Binding energy = Δm c² = energy needed to separate the nucleus into its nucleons. Nuclear force: very strong (much stronger than Coulomb), short range (a few fm), charge-independent, attractive at 0.8–2 fm but repulsive below about 0.8 fm. (2026 A-R "nuclear forces are always attractive / R: nuclear force is weak" → both false → D.)

title: Chapter 14 – Semiconductor Electronics
text: Chapter 14 – Semiconductor Electronics       Q109. (3 marks) Draw energy band diagrams of a conductor, insulator and semiconductor. Why is diamond an insulator but tin a conductor (both group IV)? Why is Si used, not diamond?  [SQP; 2025 MCQ (Sn conducts)]    Answer: Conductor – valence and conduction bands overlap (or partly filled conduction band). Insulator – large gap Eg > 3 eV (diamond 5.4 eV). Semiconductor – small gap, Eg < 3 eV (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV). Diamond's gap is too big for thermal excitation at room temperature; in tin the bands overlap so free electrons are available. Silicon's small gap lets electrons cross with thermal energy, and conduction can be controlled by doping.        Q110. (2 marks) Distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors. How are charge carriers created in an intrinsic semiconductor?  [2015, 2023, 2026]    Answer: Intrinsic: pure; ne = nh = ni; conductivity depends only on temperature. Extrinsic: doped; ne ≠ nh; conductivity depends on doping and temperature. In intrinsic, thermal energy breaks some covalent bonds; each freed electron goes to the conduction band and leaves a hole in the valence band (electron-hole pairs).        Q111. (2 marks) Ge is doped with arsenic. What type is formed? What are majority/minority carriers in n- and p-type?  [2024 MCQ; 2025, 2023]    Answer: As is pentavalent (donor) → n-type; number of conduction electrons increases. n-type: majority electrons, minority holes. p-type (trivalent dopant: B, Al, Ga, In – acceptor): majority holes, minority electrons. Even so, n-type is electrically neutral (each donor ion is positive, balancing the extra electron) – 2025 A-R answer (A). Donor level is about 0.01 eV (Ge) to 0.05 eV (Si) below the conduction band (2023 MCQ: order 0.01 eV).        Q112. (Numerical, 2 marks) Pure Si has ni = 1.5 × 10^16 m^-3. On doping, hole concentration becomes 4.5 × 10^22 m^-3. Identify dopant type and find electron concentration.  [Type seen 2025; NCERT values]    Steps: Holes increase → trivalent (acceptor) dopant → p-type. ne × nh = ni² → ne = (1.5 × 10^16)² / 4.5 × 10^22 = 2.25 × 10^32 / 4.5 × 10^22 = 5 × 10^9 m^-3.        Q113. (3 marks) Explain formation of depletion region and potential barrier in a p-n junction (role of diffusion and drift currents).  [2016, 2023, 2025]    Answer: Electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n (concentration difference) → diffusion current (p to n). They leave behind fixed positive donor ions on the n-side and fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side near the junction → a layer with no free carriers = depletion region. These ions set up an electric field from n to p, which pushes minority carriers across → drift current (n to p). At equilibrium diffusion current = drift current; the potential difference across the layer is the barrier potential (≈ 0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge). Diagram: p | depletion layer (− ions on p side, + ions on n side) | n, with field arrow from n to p.        Q114. (3 marks) With circuit diagrams, explain forward and reverse bias. Draw the V–I characteristic of a Si diode.  [2026, 2023]    Answer: Forward bias: p to + terminal, n to −. Barrier and depletion width decrease; current rises sharply after about 0.7 V (knee/threshold voltage); current in mA. Reverse bias: p to −, n to +. Barrier and depletion width increase; tiny reverse current (μA) due to minority carriers, almost constant until breakdown. Graph: forward curve in first quadrant rising steeply after 0.7 V; reverse curve in third quadrant almost flat and close to the axis. Minority carrier injection happens in forward bias (2026 MCQ). Forward resistance = ΔV/ΔI, e.g. (1.0 − 0.8) V / 2 mA = 100 Ω (2026 MCQ).        Q115. (3 marks) Draw a full-wave rectifier circuit and explain its working with input and output waveforms. What is the output ripple frequency for 50 Hz input in half-wave and full-wave?  [2017, 2018, 2019, 2024 case; 2016 half-wave]    Answer: Centre-tap transformer, two diodes D1, D2 and load RL. In the first half cycle top end A is +ve: D1 forward biased conducts, D2 reverse biased; current through RL in one direction. In the next half, B is +ve: D2 conducts, D1 off; current through RL in the same direction. So both halves give output in one direction – pulsating dc. At any instant one diode is forward and the other reverse biased (2024 MCQ); each diode conducts for half a cycle. Half-wave (one diode) gives output only in alternate half cycles. Ripple frequency: half-wave 50 Hz, full-wave 100 Hz. Waveforms: input sine; half-wave output = only positive humps with gaps; full-wave output = continuous positive humps.

title: Key definitions (one line each)
text: Key definitions (one line each)      Electric flux: Φ = ∮E·dA (scalar, N m² C^-1).   Gauss's law: Φ = q(enclosed)/ε0.   Electric dipole moment: p = q × 2a, from −q to +q (C m).   Equipotential surface: surface with the same potential everywhere; E ⟂ to it.   Capacitance: C = Q/V (farad). Dielectric constant K = C(with)/C(air).   Drift velocity: average velocity of electrons in a conductor under E: vd = eEτ/m.   Relaxation time τ: average time between two collisions.   Mobility μ = vd/E = eτ/m.   Resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ); depends on material and temperature, not on size.   EMF: work done per unit charge by the cell in moving charge round the whole circuit; terminal voltage V = E − Ir.   Current sensitivity of galvanometer: deflection per unit current = NAB/k. Voltage sensitivity: deflection per unit voltage = NAB/(kG).   Magnetic dipole moment of a loop: m = NIA (A m²).   Self-inductance L = NΦ/I; Mutual inductance M = N2Φ2/I1 (henry).   RMS value: Irms = I0/√2 (the dc that gives the same heat).   Power factor: cos φ = R/Z. Wattless current: when cos φ = 0, P = 0.   Resonance: XL = XC, Z = R minimum, current maximum.   Displacement current: Id = ε0 dΦE/dt.   Wavefront: locus of points vibrating in the same phase.   Coherent sources: same frequency, constant phase difference.   Critical angle: angle of incidence in denser medium for which angle of refraction is 90°.   Power of lens: P = 1/f (f in m), unit dioptre (D).   Work function: minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal surface.   Threshold frequency: minimum frequency for photoemission, ν0 = φ0/h.   Stopping potential: minimum negative potential on the collector that stops the fastest photoelectrons: eV0 = Kmax.   Mass defect: (Zmp + Nmn) − M. Binding energy = Δm c².   Depletion region: region near junction without free carriers.

title: 7. Answer-writing tips and 30-day timetable
text: 7. Answer-writing tips and 30-day timetable

title: How to grab step marks
text: How to grab step marks       Numericals:  Write "Given:" (with units in SI), the formula, substitution, then the answer with unit. In CBSE marking schemes, formula and substitution each usually carry ½ to 1 mark, even if the final arithmetic is wrong.    Derivations:  Always draw the labelled diagram first (often ½–1 mark). Number your steps. Box the final result.    Graphs:  Label both axes with quantity and unit, mark the special point (threshold frequency, stopping potential, knee voltage, ω0, peak at A = 56).    Definitions:  Write the definition plus formula plus SI unit. That is usually full marks for a 1–2 mark question.    Assertion–Reason:  First decide if A is true, then if R is true, then if R explains A. Write only the option letter clearly.    Case-based:  Most parts are 1-mark MCQs. Read the paragraph – the answer is often written in it.    Choice questions:  In Section E, choose the option with a derivation you know plus a simple numerical.    Never leave blanks.  Write the relevant formula at least – it can get partial credit.    Units and signs:  In optics use sign convention (distances against the light are negative). Convert cm to m for power (P = 100/f(cm)).    Time plan (180 min):  Section A 25 min, B 20 min, C 45 min, D 15 min, E 50 min, revision 25 min.
