title: 5. Must-do question bank (72 questions)
text: 5. Must-do question bank (72 questions)    ★ = asked many times, so do this first. Years in brackets are papers where the same or a very similar question appeared. "SQP" = 2026-27 Sample Paper.

title: Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Chapter 1: Solutions       Q1 ★ (MCQ, 2026)  Which solution will have the lowest freezing point? (A) 0.1 M glucose (B) 0.1 M CaCl2 (C) 0.1 M KCl (D) 0.1 M urea     Ans: (B) CaCl2.  It gives 3 ions (i = 3), so it has the most particles, the largest ΔTf and the lowest freezing point.        Q2 (MCQ, 2025)  Which aqueous solution has the highest freezing point? (A) 1.0 M KCl (B) 1.0 M Na2SO4 (C) 1.0 M glucose (D) 1.0 M AlCl3     Ans: (C) glucose.  It is a non-electrolyte (i = 1), so it has the fewest particles and the smallest ΔTf.        Q3 (MCQ, 2023)  The colligative property used to find the molar mass of polymers and proteins is:     Ans: osmotic pressure.  It is measured at room temperature and gives a measurable value even for very dilute solutions.        Q4 ★ (A-R, 2026)  A: The components of an azeotrope cannot be separated by fractional distillation. R: Components of an azeotrope have the same composition in the liquid and vapour phase and boil at constant temperature.     Ans: (A)  Both are true, and R explains A.        Q5 (A-R, 2025)  A: Henry's law constant KH decreases with increase in temperature. R: As temperature increases, the solubility of gases in liquids decreases.     Ans: (D)  A is false (KH  increases  with temperature), and R is true.        Q6 ★ (2 marks, 2025)  Calculate the elevation in boiling point when 3 g CaCl2 (M = 111) is dissolved in 260 g water (complete dissociation, Kb = 0.52 K kg/mol).     Ans:      Moles of CaCl2 = 3/111 = 0.0270 mol   m = 0.0270 / 0.260 kg = 0.104 mol/kg   CaCl2 → Ca2+ + 2Cl-, so i = 3   ΔTb = i × Kb × m = 3 × 0.52 × 0.104 =  0.162 K           Q7 ★ (3 marks, 2026)  Calculate the boiling point of a solution of 0.61 g benzoic acid (M = 122) in 5 g CS2, if benzoic acid dimerises to the extent of 88%. Boiling point of CS2 = 46.2 °C, Kb = 2.3 K kg/mol.     Ans:      For dimerisation (2A → A2): i = 1 - α/2 = 1 - 0.88/2 =  0.56    m = (0.61/122) / 0.005 kg = 0.005/0.005 = 1 mol/kg   ΔTb = i Kb m = 0.56 × 2.3 × 1 = 1.288 K   Boiling point = 46.2 + 1.288 =  47.49 °C           Q8 ★ (3 marks, 2016)  Calculate the freezing point of a solution of 1.9 g MgCl2 (M = 95) in 50 g water, assuming complete ionisation (Kf = 1.86 K kg/mol).     Ans:  n = 1.9/95 = 0.02 mol; m = 0.02/0.05 = 0.4 mol/kg; i = 3. ΔTf = 3 × 1.86 × 0.4 = 2.23 K. Freezing point = 273.15 - 2.23 =  270.92 K .        Q9 ★ (3 marks, 2019; same idea 2017)  A 4% (w/w) solution of sucrose (M = 342) freezes at 271.15 K. Find the freezing point of a 5% glucose (M = 180) solution. (Pure water freezes at 273.15 K.)     Ans:      Sucrose: ΔTf = 2 K. Here m = (4/342) / 0.096 kg = 0.1218 mol/kg.   Glucose: m = (5/180) / 0.095 kg = 0.2924 mol/kg.   Same Kf, so ΔTf(glucose) = 2 × (0.2924/0.1218) = 4.80 K   Freezing point = 273.15 - 4.80 =  268.35 K           Q10 (3 marks, 2015)  3.9 g benzoic acid in 49 g benzene lowers the freezing point by 1.62 K. Find i and the nature of the solute (M = 122, Kf = 4.9).     Ans:  m = (3.9/122) / 0.049 = 0.652 mol/kg. Normal ΔTf = 4.9 × 0.652 = 3.20 K. i = 1.62/3.20 =  0.51 . Since i < 1, benzoic acid is  associated  (it forms a dimer).        Q11 (2 marks, 2020)  Calculate the osmotic pressure of a 5% (w/v) urea solution (M = 60) at 300 K (R = 0.0821 L atm/K/mol).     Ans:  5 g in 100 mL, so C = (5/60)/0.1 L = 0.833 mol/L. π = CRT = 0.833 × 0.0821 × 300 =  20.5 atm .        Q12 (3 marks, 2023)  30 g urea (M = 60) is dissolved in 846 g water. Find the vapour pressure of water if p° = 23.8 mm Hg.     Ans:  n(urea) = 0.5 mol; n(water) = 846/18 = 47 mol. x(water) = 47/47.5 = 0.9895. p = x × p° = 0.9895 × 23.8 =  23.55 mm Hg .        Q13 (2 marks, 2025)  Liquids X and Y form an ideal solution. p°X = 120 mm Hg and p°Y = 160 mm Hg. Find the vapour pressure of a solution with equal moles of X and Y.     Ans:  xX = xY = 0.5. p = 0.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 160 =  140 mm Hg .        Q14 ★ (2-3 marks, 2025, 2026, SQP)  A student mixes two liquids (10 mL + 10 mL) and the volume becomes 20.2 mL. (i) Why? (ii) Will the temperature rise or fall? (iii) Give an example. Also: what type of deviation does phenol + aniline show?     Ans:      (i) The volume increases because A-B attractions are  weaker  than A-A and B-B attractions. This is a  positive deviation  from Raoult's law (ΔmixV > 0).   (ii) Heat is absorbed (ΔmixH > 0), so the  temperature falls .   (iii) Examples: ethanol + acetone, or acetone + CS2.   Phenol + aniline shows  negative deviation . They form strong H-bonds (O-H...N), so the vapour pressure falls and the  boiling point rises . Volume decreases and heat is released.          Q15 (2 marks, 2025, 2016, 2024)  (i) Why is salt sprinkled on snowy roads? (ii) What happens when RBCs are put in 0.5% NaCl solution? (iii) Give one use of reverse osmosis.     Ans:      (i) Salt lowers the freezing point of water, so the ice melts.   (ii) 0.5% NaCl is  hypotonic  (blood is isotonic with 0.9% NaCl). Water enters the cells and they  swell and may burst . In more than 0.9% NaCl (hypertonic), the cells shrink.   (iii)  Desalination  of sea water.          Q16 (1 mark, SQP, 2023)  Why do people at high altitude have low oxygen in their blood?     Ans:  The atmospheric pressure, and so the partial pressure of O2, is low. By Henry's law (p = KH × x), less O2 dissolves in blood (this is called anoxia).

title: Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Chapter 2: Electrochemistry       Q17 ★ (5 marks, 2026; 2025 similar)  Calculate the emf and ΔG for: Mg | Mg2+ (0.01 M) || Ag+ (0.001 M) | Ag at 298 K. E°(Mg2+/Mg) = -2.37 V, E°(Ag+/Ag) = +0.80 V, 1 F = 96500 C/mol.     Ans:      E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0.80 - (-2.37) = 3.17 V   Reaction: Mg + 2Ag+ → Mg2+ + 2Ag, so n = 2   E = E° - (0.059/n) log([Mg2+]/[Ag+]^2)   = 3.17 - (0.059/2) log(0.01 / (0.001)^2) = 3.17 - 0.0295 × log(10^4) = 3.17 - 0.118 =  3.052 V    ΔG = -nFE = -2 × 96500 × 3.052 = -589036 J =  -589 kJ/mol    2025 version ([Mg2+] = 0.100 M): log(0.1/10^-6) = 5, so E = 3.17 - 0.1475 =  3.02 V           Q18 ★ (2 marks, 2024)  Find the electrode potential of Fe2+ (0.01 M) / Fe at 298 K. E° = -0.45 V.     Ans:  Fe2+ + 2e- → Fe, n = 2. E = E° - (0.059/2) log(1/[Fe2+]) = -0.45 - 0.0295 × log 100 = -0.45 - 0.059 =  -0.509 V .        Q19 ★ (3 marks, 2016)  Calculate the emf at 298 K for 2Cr + 3Fe2+ (0.1 M) → 2Cr3+ (0.01 M) + 3Fe. E°(Cr3+/Cr) = -0.74 V, E°(Fe2+/Fe) = -0.44 V.     Ans:  E° = -0.44 - (-0.74) = 0.30 V; n = 6. E = 0.30 - (0.059/6) log([Cr3+]^2/[Fe2+]^3) = 0.30 - (0.059/6) log(10^-4 / 10^-3) = 0.30 - (0.059/6)(-1) = 0.30 + 0.0098 =  0.3098 V .        Q20 ★ (3 marks, 2020; 2023 similar)  Calculate ΔG° for Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu. E°(Zn2+/Zn) = -0.76 V, E°(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V.     Ans:  E° = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V. ΔG° = -nFE° = -2 × 96500 × 1.10 =  -212300 J = -212.3 kJ/mol . 2023 version: Ni + 2Ag+ → Ni2+ + 2Ag, E° = 0.80 - (-0.25) = 1.05 V. ΔG° = -2 × 96500 × 1.05 = -202.65 kJ, so the maximum work is 202.65 kJ. log Kc = nE°/0.059 = 2 × 1.05/0.059 =  35.6 .        Q21 ★ (3 marks, 2025; 2017 similar)  Λ°m of NH4Cl, NaOH and NaCl are 129.8, 217.4 and 108.9 S cm2/mol. Λm of 0.01 M NH4OH is 9.33 S cm2/mol. Find α.     Ans:  By Kohlrausch's law, Λ°(NH4OH) = Λ°(NH4Cl) + Λ°(NaOH) - Λ°(NaCl) = 129.8 + 217.4 - 108.9 = 238.3 S cm2/mol. α = Λm/Λ°m = 9.33/238.3 =  0.039 . (2017: acetic acid, Λ° = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5; α = 39.05/390.5 = 0.1)        Q22 (2 marks, 2023, 2025)  State Kohlrausch's law and give two uses.     Ans:  The limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion: Λ°m = ν+ λ°+ + ν- λ°-. Uses: (1) to find Λ°m of a weak electrolyte; (2) to find the degree of dissociation α = Λm/Λ°m (and the dissociation constant).        Q23 ★ (3 marks, 2024)  A cell with 0.05 M KCl (κ = 1.35 × 10^-2 S/cm) has R = 100 Ω. With 0.02 M AgNO3 it has R = 90 Ω. Find κ and Λm of AgNO3.     Ans:  Cell constant G* = κ × R = 1.35 × 10^-2 × 100 = 1.35 cm^-1. κ(AgNO3) = G*/R = 1.35/90 = 0.015 S/cm. Λm = κ × 1000/C = 0.015 × 1000/0.02 =  750 S cm2/mol .        Q24 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2025, SQP)  Why does conductivity decrease, but molar conductivity increase, on dilution?     Ans:  Conductivity (κ) depends on the number of ions per unit volume. On dilution there are fewer ions per cm3, so κ  decreases . Molar conductivity (Λm = κ × V) is for 1 mole of electrolyte. On dilution the total volume containing 1 mole increases (and a weak electrolyte ionises more), so Λm  increases .        Q25 (3 marks, 2017; 2019 similar)  A current of 2 A is passed through AgNO3 solution for 15 min. Find the mass of Ag deposited (Ag = 108).     Ans:  Q = I × t = 2 × 900 = 1800 C. Ag+ + e- → Ag, so 96500 C deposits 108 g. Mass = 108 × 1800/96500 =  2.01 g .        Q26 (MCQ, SQP)  The charge needed to get 1 mol of metal M from M2O3 is:     Ans: 3F , because M3+ + 3e- → M.        Q27 (MCQ, 2026)  During electrolysis of aqueous CuCl2 with Pt electrodes:     Ans: Cl2 gas is released at the anode  (and Cu is deposited at the cathode).        Q28 ★ (2-3 marks, 2016, 2020, 2024, 2025, 2026, SQP)  Batteries:      (a) Primary vs secondary battery: In a primary battery the reaction occurs only once and it cannot be recharged (dry cell, mercury cell). A secondary battery can be recharged (lead storage battery).   (b) Mercury cell: used in hearing aids and watches. It gives a constant voltage (1.35 V) because the overall reaction Zn(Hg) + HgO → ZnO + Hg has  no ion in solution  whose concentration changes.   (c) Lead storage battery on  charging : 2PbSO4 + 2H2O → Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4. On discharge H2SO4 is used up, so the specific gravity of the acid  falls ; on charging it  rises .   (d) H2-O2 fuel cell: anode 2H2 + 4OH- → 4H2O + 4e-; cathode O2 + 2H2O + 4e- → 4OH-; overall 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Advantages: high efficiency (about 70%) and pollution-free (it only gives water). It was used in the Apollo space programme.   (e) Cell uses (2025 MCQ): lead storage → inverter/automobile; mercury → wrist watch/hearing aid; dry cell → wall clock; fuel cell → Apollo.          Q29 (1 mark, SQP)  Why are iron pipes connected to Mg?     Ans:  Mg is more reactive. It acts as a  sacrificial anode  and gets oxidised instead of iron, so the iron does not corrode.

title: Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics       Q30 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  The half-life of a first-order reaction is 16 min. The time for 75% completion is:     Ans: 32 min  (75% = 2 half-lives).        Q31 ★ (3 marks, 2015)  A first-order reaction takes 30 min for 50% completion. Find the time for 90% completion.     Ans:  k = 0.693/30 = 0.0231 min^-1. t = (2.303/k) log([R]0/[R]) = (2.303/0.0231) log(100/10) = 99.7 × 1 ≈  100 min . (Shortcut: t90 = 3.32 × t1/2.)        Q32 ★ (3 marks, 2026)  For the first-order reaction C2H5Cl(g) → C2H4(g) + HCl(g), the total pressure is 0.30 atm at t = 0 and 0.50 atm at t = 30 s. Find k (log 3 = 0.48).     Ans:      Let the pressure of C2H5Cl fall by x. Total pressure = 0.30 - x + x + x = 0.30 + x = 0.50, so x = 0.20 atm.   Pressure of C2H5Cl left = 0.30 - 0.20 = 0.10 atm   k = (2.303/t) log(P0/P) = (2.303/30) log(0.30/0.10) = (2.303/30) × 0.48 =  3.68 × 10^-2 s^-1           Q33 ★ (3 marks, 2024; 2025 similar)  For 2NO + Br2 → 2NOBr:          [NO]   [Br2]   Rate           0.05   0.05   1.0 × 10^-3       0.05   0.15   3.0 × 10^-3       0.15   0.05   9.0 × 10^-3         Find the order, k, and the rate at [NO] = 0.4, [Br2] = 0.2.  Ans:      [Br2] × 3 makes the rate × 3, so the order in Br2 = 1.   [NO] × 3 makes the rate × 9, so the order in NO = 2.   Rate = k[NO]^2[Br2] (overall order 3)   k = 1.0 × 10^-3 / (0.05^2 × 0.05) =  8 L2 mol^-2 s^-1    Rate = 8 × 0.4^2 × 0.2 =  0.256 mol L^-1 s^-1           Q34 (2 marks, 2026)  2A + B → 2C takes place in one step. How does the rate change if the volume is reduced to one-third? Does the order change?     Ans:  Rate = k[A]^2[B]. Each concentration becomes 3 times, so the new rate = 3^2 × 3 =  27 times . The order stays  3  (it does not change).        Q35 (3 marks, 2019)  NH3 decomposes on Pt as a zero-order reaction with k = 4 × 10^-3 M/s. How long does it take for [NH3] to fall from 0.1 M to 0.064 M?     Ans:  For zero order, t = ([R]0 - [R])/k = (0.1 - 0.064)/(4 × 10^-3) = 0.036/0.004 =  9 s .        Q36 ★ (3 marks, 2016; SQP similar)  For a first-order reaction, log k = 14.2 - (1.0 × 10^4 K)/T. Find Ea, and find k if t1/2 = 200 min.     Ans:  Compare with log k = log A - Ea/(2.303 RT). So Ea/(2.303 R) = 1.0 × 10^4, giving Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 10^4 = 1.915 × 10^5 J =  191.5 kJ/mol . k = 0.693/200 =  3.47 × 10^-3 min^-1 .        Q37 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2023, 2024, SQP)  What is a pseudo-first-order reaction? Give an example. (SQP: hydrolysis of acetyl chloride with (i) equimolar water, (ii) excess water.)     Ans:  A reaction that has molecularity 2 but behaves as first order because one reactant is in large excess, so its concentration hardly changes. Example: hydrolysis of an ester, CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (excess) → CH3COOH + C2H5OH (H+ catalyst). Rate = k[ester]. SQP: (i) second order, (ii) first order.        Q38 (2 marks, SQP, 2025)  "The rate of reaction stays constant during the reaction." Is this always true?     Ans:  It is true only for a  zero-order  reaction (rate = k, independent of concentration). For first-, second- or other-order reactions, the rate decreases as the concentration of reactants decreases.        Q39 (MCQ, 2024, 2026)  Graph and formula facts:      log k vs 1/T: slope = -Ea/(2.303R), intercept = log A.   The fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea is  e^(-Ea/RT) .   A catalyst lowers  Ea . It does not change ΔG, ΔH or the equilibrium constant.

title: Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements       Q40 (MCQ, 2026)  Which of these is not a transition metal: Sc, Ag, Hg, Cu?     Ans: Hg.  Its d-orbitals are completely filled (5d10) in the atom and in its common ion Hg2+.        Q41 ★ (5 × 1 marks, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). Give reasons:       (a)  Transition metals are good catalysts:  they show variable oxidation states, they form unstable intermediate compounds, and they provide a large surface area for adsorption (examples: Fe in Haber's process, V2O5 in the Contact process).   (b)  Transition metals form complexes:  small size of the metal ions, high ionic charge, and vacant d-orbitals available for bonding.   (c)  Transition metal ions are coloured:  they have unpaired d-electrons, which absorb visible light and undergo  d-d transitions . Sc3+ (3d0) and Zn2+ (3d10) are colourless.   (d)  Zn, Cd and Hg are not transition elements / have low melting points:  they have completely filled d10 orbitals in the ground state and in their common ions. With no unpaired d-electrons, metallic bonding is weak.   (e)  Transition metals have high enthalpy of atomisation:  they have a large number of unpaired electrons, giving strong metallic bonding.          Q42 ★ (3 marks, 2017, 2023, 2024)       (a)  Cr2+ is a reducing agent, Mn3+ is an oxidising agent (both d4):  Cr2+ → Cr3+ gives d3 (t2g3), a stable half-filled t2g level. Mn3+ → Mn2+ gives d5, which is extra-stable because it is half-filled.   (b)  Cu+ is unstable in water:  Cu2+(aq) has a much more negative hydration enthalpy, which more than makes up for the second ionisation enthalpy. So 2Cu+ → Cu2+ + Cu (disproportionation).   (c)  E°(Cu2+/Cu) is positive:  Cu has a high enthalpy of atomisation and high ionisation enthalpies, which its hydration enthalpy cannot balance.          Q43 (2 marks, SQP)  Why does Ti melt at a lower temperature than Cr?     Ans:  Cr has more unpaired d-electrons (3d5 4s1) than Ti, so its metallic bonding is stronger.        Q44 ★ (2-3 marks, 2016, 2017, 2025). Potassium dichromate:       Preparation: 4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 → 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2 (yellow chromate)   Then 2Na2CrO4 + 2H+ → Na2Cr2O7 + 2Na+ + H2O, followed by Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl → K2Cr2O7 (orange) + 2NaCl   Colour change: 2CrO4^2- (yellow) + 2H+ ⇌ Cr2O7^2- (orange) + H2O.  Acid turns yellow to orange  (2025 MCQ: HCl in the test tube).  Alkali turns orange to yellow  (2017).          Q45 ★ (2-3 marks, 2019, 2025, 2026, 2024). Potassium permanganate:       2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2 → 2K2MnO4 (dark green, A) + 2H2O   In acid: 3MnO4^2- + 4H+ → 2MnO4- (purple, B) + MnO2 + 2H2O (disproportionation)   On heating: 2KMnO4 → K2MnO4 + MnO2 + O2   With I-, acidic: 2MnO4- + 10I- + 16H+ → 2Mn2+ + 5I2 + 8H2O   With I-, neutral/alkaline: 2MnO4- + I- + H2O → 2MnO2 + IO3- + 2OH-   With Fe2+, acidic: MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ → Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O   Dichromate with Fe2+: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6Fe2+ → 2Cr3+ + 6Fe3+ + 7H2O (SQP)   Dichromate with I-: Cr2O7^2- + 6I- + 14H+ → 2Cr3+ + 3I2 + 7H2O (2024)          Q46 (2-3 marks, 2015, 2017, 2024, 2025)  Lanthanoids and actinoids:      Lanthanoid contraction: a steady decrease in atomic/ionic size from La to Lu, caused by the poor shielding of 4f electrons. Consequence: Zr and Hf have almost the same size, so they are very hard to separate.   Actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction because 5f electrons shield even more poorly.   Actinoids show more oxidation states because 5f, 6d and 7s have similar energies.   Ce4+ is a good oxidising agent because it prefers to change to the common +3 state.   The most common oxidation state of lanthanoids is  +3  (2023 MCQ).

title: Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds
text: Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds       Q47 ★ (1-2 marks, many years). IUPAC names and formulas:       [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 → pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride (2023)   [Co(NH3)5(CO3)]Cl → pentaamminecarbonatocobalt(III) chloride (2017)   K3[Fe(C2O4)3] → potassium trioxalatoferrate(III) (2026)   [Ag(NH3)2][Ag(CN)2] → diamminesilver(I) dicyanidoargentate(I) (2026)   [Cr(NH3)3Cl3] → triamminetrichloridochromium(III) (2017)   Potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II) → K2[Zn(OH)4] (2020, 2024)   Hexaammineplatinum(IV) chloride → [Pt(NH3)6]Cl4 (2020)   Hexaamminecobalt(III) sulphate → [Co(NH3)6]2(SO4)3 (2019)   Potassium trioxalatochromate(III) → K3[Cr(C2O4)3] (2019)   Iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II) → Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (2023)          Q48 ★ (2-3 marks, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2026). Hybridisation and magnetic behaviour (VBT):           Complex   Metal ion, d-electrons   Ligand   Hybridisation / shape   Magnetic           [Fe(CN)6]3-   Fe3+, d5   CN- strong   d2sp3, octahedral, inner orbital, low spin   Paramagnetic, 1 unpaired (1.73 BM)       [Fe(CN)6]4-   Fe2+, d6   CN- strong   d2sp3, octahedral   Diamagnetic       [Co(NH3)6]3+   Co3+, d6   NH3 strong here   d2sp3, octahedral   Diamagnetic       [CoF6]3-   Co3+, d6   F- weak   sp3d2, octahedral, outer orbital, high spin   Paramagnetic, 4 unpaired       [Ni(CN)4]2-   Ni2+, d8   CN- strong   dsp2, square planar   Diamagnetic       [NiCl4]2-   Ni2+, d8   Cl- weak   sp3, tetrahedral   Paramagnetic, 2 unpaired       [Ni(CO)4]   Ni(0), 3d10 4s0 after pairing   CO strong   sp3, tetrahedral   Diamagnetic           2026: [NiCl4]2- is paramagnetic but [Ni(CO)4] is diamagnetic, though both are tetrahedral. Ni2+ in [NiCl4]2- keeps 2 unpaired electrons (Cl- cannot pair them). In [Ni(CO)4], Ni is in the 0 state and strong-field CO pushes the 4s electrons into 3d, so all electrons are paired.   SQP MCQ: the tetrahedral complex among [Ni(CN)4]2-, [Cu(NH3)4]2+, [NiCl4]2- and [Co(en)3]3+ is  [NiCl4]2- .          Q49 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2025, 2026, SQP). Crystal field theory:       Crystal field splitting energy (Δo): the energy difference between the two sets of d-orbitals (t2g and eg) when ligands approach.   In an octahedral field, the  eg orbitals (dx2-y2, dz2) are raised  because they point directly at the ligands and feel more repulsion (2026).   d4 ion: if Δo < P (weak field), t2g3 eg1; if Δo > P (strong field), t2g4 eg0.   d5 with Δo > P: t2g5 eg0 (SQP).   [CoF6]3-: t2g4 eg2. [Co(NH3)6]3+: t2g6 eg0 (2026).   Low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rare because Δt is small (about 4/9 Δo) and is less than the pairing energy (2023 A-R: answer A; 2025).          Q50 ★ (2 marks, 2016, 2023, 2025, SQP). Werner / AgCl questions:       CrCl3·6H2O gives 2 mol AgCl → [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2O (2016)   CrCl3·4H2O gives 1 mol AgCl → [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl; secondary valency = 6 (2025)   PdCl2·4NH3 gives 2 mol AgCl → [Pd(NH3)4]Cl2; primary valency 2, secondary valency 4 (SQP)   PtCl2·2NH3 does not react with AgNO3 → [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] (2023)   Secondary valency of [Co(en)3]3+ =  6  (en is didentate, 3 × 2) (2023, 2026: [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+ → 6)   Conductivity order (2024, 2025, SQP): [Cr(NH3)3Cl3] (0 ions) < [Cr(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 (3 ions) < [Cr(NH3)6]Cl3 (4 ions)          Q51 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2023, 2024, 2026). Isomerism:       [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+ →  linkage  isomerism (NO2- can bind through N or O)   [Co(NH3)5SO4]Cl and [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 →  ionisation  isomers. Test: the first gives a white precipitate (AgCl) with AgNO3; the second gives a white precipitate (BaSO4) with BaCl2 (2026).   [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] →  coordination  isomerism (2017)   [Co(en)3]3+ →  optical  isomerism (d and l forms) (2017, 2024)   [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] →  geometrical  (cis and trans). Cis-[Pt(en)2Cl2]2+ is optically active (2015, 2016).   Chelate effect: complexes with chelating (di- or polydentate) ligands are more stable than similar complexes with monodentate ligands. Example: [Ni(en)3]2+ is more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]2+.

title: Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
text: Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes       Q52 ★ (3 marks, 2016, 2017, 2019, 2024, 2025, 2026, SQP). SN1 / SN2:       SN2 reactivity: 1° > 2° > 3° (steric hindrance). 1-Bromopentane reacts fastest by SN2. 2-Bromopentane is optically active. 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane (3°) is fastest in elimination and SN1 (2017).   SN1 reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°, depending on carbocation stability. Allylic/benzylic halides are very reactive (resonance-stabilised carbocation). (CH3)3C-I is more reactive than (CH3)3C-Br because C-I is weaker (2019).   SN1 on an optically active halide gives  racemisation : the planar carbocation can be attacked from both sides (2016, 2020, 2025).   SN2 gives  inversion of configuration  (SQP MCQ: (-)-2-bromohexane → (+)-hexan-2-ol is SN2 with inversion).   2026 case:   (a) Rate = k[X], so X reacts by SN1 and is the 3° bromide, X =  (CH3)3C-Br  (2-bromo-2-methylpropane). Y is optically active and rate = k[Y][OH-], so Y reacts by SN2: Y =  CH3CH(Br)CH2CH3  (2-bromobutane, the only chiral C4H9Br).   (b)  Expected answer: X (SN1).  It goes through a flat (planar) carbocation, which the OH- can attack from either side. For a chiral substrate this gives a racemic mixture.   (c)  Y (SN2)  gives inversion of configuration, because OH- attacks from the back side, opposite the Br.   Teacher's note: (CH3)3CBr itself is not chiral, so the racemisation in (b) is the general SN1 rule. Write the reason (planar carbocation, attack from both sides) to get the mark.          Q53 ★ (2-3 marks, 2016, 2024, 2025, 2026). Haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution.  Reasons:      (i)  Resonance  gives the C-Cl bond partial double-bond character.   (ii) The carbon is  sp2  (more s-character), so C-X is shorter and stronger.   (iii) The phenyl cation is unstable.   (iv) The electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile.   Also: the C-Cl bond in chlorobenzene is  shorter  than in CH3Cl for reasons (i) and (ii).   A -NO2 group at the ortho/para position  increases  reactivity: it withdraws electrons and stabilises the carbanion intermediate. So the nitro group activates; the methoxy group does not (SQP).          Q54 ★ (1-2 marks, 2019, 2025, SQP, 2024)       KCN gives an alkyl cyanide (R-CN). AgCN gives an isocyanide (R-NC). KCN is ionic and attacks through C; AgCN is covalent and attacks through N. CN- is an  ambident nucleophile . (SQP: CH3CH2CH2Cl + AgCN → X = CH3CH2CH2NC; + KCN → Y = CH3CH2CH2CN.)   Ethyl bromide + AgNO2 gives  nitroethane  (2025 MCQ). KNO2 gives ethyl nitrite.   Grignard reagents are made in dry conditions because RMgX + H2O → RH + Mg(OH)X.   Aqueous KOH gives an alcohol (substitution). Alcoholic KOH gives an alkene (elimination).          Q55 ★ (MCQ/2 marks, 2023, 2015, 2025)  Name reactions of haloalkanes:      Finkelstein: CH3Cl + NaI → CH3I + NaCl (dry acetone)   Swarts (best for alkyl fluorides, 2023 MCQ): CH3Br + AgF → CH3F + AgBr   Boiling point order RI > RBr > RCl > RF, because van der Waals forces increase with size (2025 A-R: answer A).   n-Butyl bromide has a higher boiling point than t-butyl bromide because it has more surface area (2015).

title: Chapter 7: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
text: Chapter 7: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers       Q56 ★ (2-3 marks, 2017, 2019, 2023, 2024). Mechanism of dehydration of ethanol (conc. H2SO4, 443 K):       Step 1: protonation. CH3CH2-OH + H+ → CH3CH2-OH2+ (fast)   Step 2: carbocation forms. CH3CH2-OH2+ → CH3CH2+ + H2O (slow, rate-determining)   Step 3: loss of H+. CH3CH2+ → CH2=CH2 + H+   Ease of dehydration: 3° > 2° > 1° (2024 MCQ). t-Butyl alcohol dehydrates faster than n-butanol (2020).   Acid-catalysed hydration of ethene (2020, 2025) is the reverse. CH2=CH2 + H3O+ → CH3CH2+ + H2O. Then CH3CH2+ + H2O → CH3CH2OH2+. Finally CH3CH2OH2+ + H2O → CH3CH2OH + H3O+.          Q57 ★ (3 marks, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2026). Named reactions of phenols:        Reimer-Tiemann:  phenol + CHCl3 + aq NaOH (340 K), then H+ →  salicylaldehyde  (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde)    Kolbe:  phenol + NaOH → sodium phenoxide; + CO2 (400 K, 4-7 atm), then H+ →  salicylic acid  (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). Acetylating salicylic acid gives  aspirin  (2026 MCQ).    Friedel-Crafts acylation of anisole:  anisole + CH3COCl (anhydrous AlCl3) → 2-methoxyacetophenone (minor) + 4-methoxyacetophenone (major)    Williamson synthesis  (2024 MCQ): R-X + R'-ONa → R-O-R' + NaX. Use a 1° halide; a 3° halide gives an alkene (2019: t-butyl chloride + CH3ONa gives 2-methylpropene).   Phenol + dil HNO3 at low temperature → o- and p-nitrophenol (2026). Phenol + bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate). Phenol + conc HNO3 → picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol).   Phenol + Zn dust → benzene. Anisole + HBr → phenol + CH3Br (2025).          Q58 ★ (1-2 marks, 2017, 2023, 2025, SQP). Acidity:       Phenol is more acidic than an alcohol because the  phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised ; the alkoxide ion is not.   Electron-withdrawing groups (-NO2) increase acidity. Electron-releasing groups (-CH3, cresol) decrease it.   Order (2025): 4-methylphenol < phenol < 3,5-dinitrophenol < 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.   Order (2017): ethanol < phenol < p-nitrophenol.   -OH directs  ortho/para , not meta (2026 A-R: A false, R true → D).

title: Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
text: Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids       Q59 ★ (3 marks, SQP, 2017, 2019, 2024). Identify and write the named reaction:        Aldol:  2CH3CHO (dil NaOH) → CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO (3-hydroxybutanal); on heating → CH3CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal) + H2O. This is how ethanal is converted to but-2-enal (2023).    Etard:  toluene + CrO2Cl2 in CS2 → chromium complex; + H3O+ → benzaldehyde    Wolff-Kishner:  >C=O + NH2NH2 → >C=N-NH2 (hydrazone); + KOH/ethylene glycol, heat → >CH2 + N2    Clemmensen:  >C=O + Zn-Hg / conc HCl → >CH2 + H2O (for example, butan-2-one → butane; acetophenone → ethylbenzene)    Cannizzaro  (only for aldehydes with no α-H): 2HCHO + conc KOH → CH3OH + HCOOK; 2C6H5CHO + conc NaOH → C6H5CH2OH + C6H5COONa. Of the four aldehydes in the 2025 MCQ, only (CH3)3C-CHO has no α-H.    Rosenmund:  RCOCl + H2 (Pd-BaSO4) → RCHO + HCl. This is how acetyl chloride is converted to acetaldehyde (2025, 2019).    Stephen:  RCN + SnCl2/HCl → RCH=NH; + H3O+ → RCHO. The reagent for ethanenitrile → ethanal is SnCl2 + HCl (2026).    Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ):  RCH2COOH + Cl2 / red P → RCH(Cl)COOH. This converts propanoic acid to 2-chloropropanoic acid (2023, 2017).    Decarboxylation:  RCOONa + NaOH/CaO (heat) → R-H + Na2CO3          Q60 ★ (2 marks, 2016, 2017, 2023, 2025, 2026, SQP). Distinguishing tests:        Aldehyde vs ketone  (propanal vs propanone): Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with the aldehyde; Fehling's solution gives a red-brown precipitate with the aliphatic aldehyde. The ketone gives neither.    Iodoform test  (I2 + NaOH, yellow CHI3 precipitate): given by CH3CO- compounds and CH3CH(OH)- compounds (ethanol, ethanal, acetone, butan-2-one, acetophenone). Not given by pentan-3-one, phenol or methanol (2020, 2017).   CH3COCH2CH3 vs CH3CH2CH2CHO: iodoform test is positive for the first; Tollens' test is positive for the second.    Acid vs aldehyde  (propanoic acid vs propanal; benzoic acid vs ethyl benzoate): NaHCO3 gives brisk effervescence (CO2) with the acid only.          Q61 ★ (3 marks, 2026, 2025, SQP). Give reasons:        Carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols  of similar mass: they form  dimers  through strong intermolecular H-bonding.    α-H of aldehydes/ketones is acidic:  the C=O group withdraws electrons, and the carbanion (enolate) formed is resonance-stabilised.    Ammonia derivatives do not add in strongly acidic medium:  strong acid protonates the NH2 group, so it is no longer a nucleophile. The best pH is about 3.5.    Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones  towards nucleophilic addition: they have fewer bulky groups (less steric hindrance) and fewer electron-releasing groups.   Order towards HCN (2026): di-tert-butyl ketone < acetone < acetaldehyde.   Ease of oxidation (SQP): HCHO > CH3CHO > C6H5CHO.    NaHSO3 purifies aldehydes:  it forms a water-soluble crystalline adduct, which gives back the aldehyde with dilute acid or alkali.          Q62 ★ (3 marks, 2025; 2026, 2015 similar)  A (C8H8O) gives a 2,4-DNP test, does not give Tollens' test, and gives a yellow precipitate B with NaOH + I2. Drastic oxidation gives C (C7H6O2). Identify A, B and C.     Ans:      A =  acetophenone, C6H5COCH3 : it is a ketone, it gives the iodoform test, and it has a CH3CO- group.   B =  iodoform, CHI3 : C6H5COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH → C6H5COONa + CHI3 + 3NaI + 3H2O   C =  benzoic acid, C6H5COOH  (from oxidation with KMnO4/KOH, then H+)          Q63 (5 marks, 2026)  C5H10O: draw X if it (I) does not give Tollens' test but gives a positive iodoform test; (II) gives neither Tollens' nor iodoform but does undergo aldol; (III) undergoes Cannizzaro.     Ans:  (I) pentan-2-one, CH3COCH2CH2CH3 (or 3-methylbutan-2-one). (II) pentan-3-one, CH3CH2COCH2CH3. (III) 2,2-dimethylpropanal, (CH3)3C-CHO (no α-H).

title: Chapter 9: Amines
text: Chapter 9: Amines       Q64 ★ (1-2 marks, 2015, 2017, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, SQP). Basicity:       In water: (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 > C6H5NH2. Increasing pKb is the same order (2025). The strongest base in the 2020 MCQ is  dimethylamine .    Aniline is weaker than NH3 / CH3NH2:  the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is less available for H+.    CH3NH2 is more basic than (CH3)3N in water  (2026): there is less steric hindrance and better H-bonding solvation of the cation (combined inductive, solvation and steric effects).   Boiling point: (CH3)3N < C2H5NH2 < C2H5OH (2015, 2019). Butane < butanamine < butanol (2020).          Q65 ★ (1-2 marks, 2017, 2023, 2025, 2026, SQP)        Aniline on nitration gives about 47% meta product:  in strong acid, aniline is protonated to the  anilinium ion (C6H5NH3+), which is meta-directing . NCERT figures: 51% para, 47% meta, 2% ortho (2026 MCQ).    Aniline is acetylated before nitration or bromination:  -NHCOCH3 is  less activating  than -NH2 (the N lone pair is shared with C=O). This stops multiple substitution, protects -NH2 from oxidation, and gives the mono (para) product. (2023 A-R: A true, R false → C.)    Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts:  it forms a salt with AlCl3 (a Lewis acid). The N becomes positive and deactivates the ring.          Q66 ★ (2 marks, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, SQP). Named tests and reactions of amines:        Carbylamine  (only 1° amines): R-NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH (alc) → R-NC (foul-smelling isocyanide) + 3KCl + 3H2O. 2025 version: C2H5NH2 → C2H5NC. SQP: nitrobenzene reduced → aniline, which gives this test.    Gabriel phthalimide  (only 1° aliphatic amines): phthalimide + KOH → potassium phthalimide; + R-X → N-alkylphthalimide; + NaOH(aq) → R-NH2 + sodium phthalate. (Aniline cannot be made this way.)    Hofmann bromamide:  R-CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → R-NH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O. The amine has  one carbon less . CH3CONH2 → CH3NH2 (2023 MCQ). C6H5CONH2 → aniline.    Hinsberg's test  (C6H5SO2Cl):   1° amine gives a precipitate  soluble  in NaOH. In 2025, C2H7N reacts and the product dissolves in NaOH, so X =  ethanamine, C2H5NH2 .   2° amine gives a precipitate  insoluble  in alkali. In 2026, C3H9N gives an alkali-insoluble product, so X =  N-methylethanamine, CH3NHC2H5  (2°).   3° amine does not react.          Q67 ★ (3 marks, 2020, 2024, 2025, SQP). Conversions using diazonium salts:       Diazotisation: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl (273-278 K) → C6H5N2+Cl- + NaCl + 2H2O    Sandmeyer:  C6H5N2+Cl- + CuCl/HCl → C6H5Cl; + CuBr/HBr → C6H5Br; + CuCN/KCN → C6H5CN (benzonitrile, 2026). C6H5CN + H2O/H+ → C6H5COOH.    Fluorobenzene (SQP):  nitrobenzene + Sn/HCl → aniline; + NaNO2/HCl (0-5 °C) → C6H5N2+Cl-; + HBF4 → C6H5N2+BF4-; heat → C6H5F + BF3 + N2    Phenol:  C6H5N2+Cl- + H2O (warm) → C6H5OH + N2 + HCl    Benzene:  C6H5N2+Cl- + H3PO2 + H2O → C6H6 + N2 + H3PO3 + HCl    Coupling:  C6H5N2+Cl- + phenol (OH-) → p-hydroxyazobenzene (orange dye). This is the test that distinguishes aniline from methylamine/ethanamine: aliphatic amines give N2 gas, not a dye.    p-Bromoaniline:  aniline + (CH3CO)2O → acetanilide; + Br2/CH3COOH → p-bromoacetanilide; + H+/H2O → p-bromoaniline    Benzoic acid → benzylamine (SQP):  C6H5COOH + NH3 (heat) → C6H5CONH2; + LiAlH4 → C6H5CH2NH2

title: Chapter 10: Biomolecules
text: Chapter 10: Biomolecules       Q68 ★ (3 marks, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). Reactions of D-glucose:        HI (long heating) → n-hexane.  Shows that the 6 C atoms are in a  straight chain .    Br2 water → gluconic acid  (CHO → COOH). Shows the  aldehyde group .    Conc HNO3 → saccharic (glucaric) acid , HOOC-(CHOH)4-COOH. Shows a 1° alcohol group as well.    Acetic anhydride → glucose pentaacetate.  Shows  five -OH groups .    HCN → cyanohydrin; NH2OH → oxime.  Show the C=O group.   Glucose does not give the 2,4-DNP test or Schiff's test, and its pentaacetate does not react with NH2OH. This shows the free -CHO is absent: glucose exists in a  cyclic  form. (2026 A-R: A true, R false → C.)          Q69 ★ (2 marks, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). Linkages:        Peptide linkage:  the amide link -CO-NH- formed between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH2 of another, with loss of water. It joins amino acids into proteins.    Glycosidic linkage:  an oxide link (C-O-C) between two monosaccharide units, with loss of water. It joins sugars (for example, C1-C4 α-glycosidic links in amylose, 2023).    Essential amino acids  cannot be made in the body and must come from food (valine, leucine, lysine).  Non-essential  ones are made in the body (glycine, alanine, glutamic acid). SQP: HOOC-CH2-CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH (glutamic acid) is  acidic and non-essential .          Q70 ★ (2 marks, 2016, 2020, 2025, SQP). Nucleic acids:       DNA vs RNA:   Sugar: DNA has 2-deoxyribose; RNA has ribose.   Bases: DNA has A, G, C,  T ; RNA has A, G, C,  U .   Strands: DNA is double-stranded (double helix); RNA is single-stranded.   Role: DNA carries heredity (replication); RNA makes proteins.    Nucleoside  = base + sugar.  Nucleotide  = base + sugar + phosphate.   The two DNA strands are  complementary  (not identical): A pairs with T (2 H-bonds) and G pairs with C (3 H-bonds), held by hydrogen bonds.   The third component of DNA, besides the sugar and base, is  phosphoric acid  (2024).          Q71 ★ (1 mark each, 2015, 2016, 2024, 2026). Vitamins:       Fat-soluble:  A, D, E, K . They are stored in liver and adipose tissue.   Water-soluble:  B group and C . They must be taken daily because they are excreted in urine.   Deficiencies:   A: night blindness, xerophthalmia   B1: beriberi   B12: pernicious anaemia   C: scurvy (bleeding gums)   D: rickets (bone deformities in children)   E:  increased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness  (2026 MCQ)   K: increased blood clotting time          Q72 ★ (2-3 marks, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2025, SQP). Carbohydrates and proteins, short facts:       Hydrolysis products:    Sucrose  → glucose + fructose. It is  non-reducing  because the glycosidic bond joins both reducing groups (C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose). It is called  invert sugar  because sucrose is dextrorotatory, but the mixture formed on hydrolysis is laevorotatory: fructose (-92.4°) outweighs glucose (+52.5°).    Maltose  → 2 glucose    Lactose  → glucose + galactose (β-D-galactose + β-D-glucose)    Starch vs cellulose:  starch is made of α-D-glucose units (amylose: unbranched, C1-C4; amylopectin: branched, C1-C4 + C1-C6). Cellulose is a straight chain of β-D-glucose units (C1-C4).    Anomers:  cyclic forms of a sugar that differ only in the configuration at C1 (α and β glucose).    Fibrous vs globular proteins:  fibrous proteins are thread-like and water-insoluble (keratin, myosin). Globular proteins are spherical and water-soluble (insulin, albumin).   Secondary structure: α-helix and β-pleated sheet. The α-helix is a feature of  polypeptides  (2023 MCQ).    Denaturation  (SQP: lemon juice in milk): a change in pH breaks the H-bonds, so the protein unfolds and loses its biological activity (the casein curdles). The primary structure stays the same.    SQP case:  a sugar that gives a positive Benedict's test (reducing) and gives only one monosaccharide on hydrolysis is  maltose .

title: 6a. Formulas (learn these 20 and you can do every numerical)
text: 6a. Formulas (learn these 20 and you can do every numerical)     Solutions      Raoult's law: p = p° × x. Ideal mixture: P(total) = pA° xA + pB° xB   Relative lowering of vapour pressure: (p° - p)/p° = x(solute) ≈ n2/n1   ΔTb = i Kb m;  ΔTf = i Kf m;  π = i C R T   Molar mass from ΔTf: M2 = (Kf × w2 × 1000) / (ΔTf × w1)   Henry's law: p = KH × x. Higher KH means lower solubility.   van't Hoff factor:   Dissociation: i = 1 + (n - 1)α   Association (dimer): i = 1 - α/2   Examples: NaCl, KCl → i = 2; CaCl2, MgCl2, Na2SO4 → i = 3; AlCl3, K3[Fe(CN)6] → i = 4      Electrochemistry      E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode (both as reduction potentials)   Nernst equation at 298 K: E = E° - (0.059/n) log Q, where Q = [products]/[reactants] (ignore solids)   ΔG = -nFE;  ΔG° = -nFE° = -2.303 RT log K;  log Kc = nE°/0.059   κ = G* / R (cell constant G* = l/A);  Λm = κ × 1000 / C (S cm2 mol^-1)   Strong electrolyte: Λm = Λ°m - A√c   Kohlrausch: Λ°m = ν+ λ°+ + ν- λ°-;  α = Λm / Λ°m   Faraday: Q = I × t; mass = (M × I × t) / (n × 96500)      Kinetics      Zero order: [R] = [R]0 - kt;  t1/2 = [R]0/2k;  unit of k = mol L^-1 s^-1   First order: k = (2.303/t) log([R]0/[R]);  t1/2 = 0.693/k (independent of [R]0);  unit of k = s^-1   Gas-phase first order: k = (2.303/t) log(P0 / (2P0 - Pt))   Unit of k for order n: (mol L^-1)^(1-n) s^-1   Arrhenius: k = A e^(-Ea/RT);  log(k2/k1) = (Ea / 2.303R)(1/T1 - 1/T2)      Coordination      Spin-only magnetic moment μ = √(n(n+2)) BM. For n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: μ = 1.73, 2.83, 3.87, 4.90, 5.92.      Must-know numbers:  log 2 = 0.3010, log 3 = 0.4771, log 4 = 0.6021, log 5 = 0.6990; 2.303RT/F = 0.059 V at 298 K; 1 F = 96500 C mol^-1; R = 8.314 J/K/mol = 0.0821 L atm/K/mol.

title: 6b. Key definitions (1-mark favourites)
text: 6b. Key definitions (1-mark favourites)       Molality (m):  moles of solute per kg of solvent. It does not change with temperature.    Molarity (M):  moles of solute per litre of solution.    Colligative property:  depends only on the number of solute particles, not on their nature.    Azeotrope:  a liquid mixture with the same composition in the liquid and vapour phase that boils at constant temperature.   Positive deviation gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope (95% ethanol + water).   Negative deviation gives a maximum-boiling azeotrope (68% HNO3 + 32% water, SQP).    Ideal solution:  obeys Raoult's law at all concentrations; ΔmixH = 0 and ΔmixV = 0.    Molecularity:  the number of species colliding in an elementary step. It is always a whole number and never zero.    Order:  the sum of the powers of concentration in the rate law. It can be 0 or a fraction.    Limiting molar conductivity (Λ°m):  the molar conductivity at infinite dilution (concentration → 0).    Fuel cell:  a cell that changes the energy of combustion of a fuel (H2, CH4) directly into electricity.    Corrosion:  an electrochemical process in which a metal is oxidised by air and moisture (rusting of iron).    Transition element:  an element with a partly filled d-subshell in the atom or in any common ion.    Ambidentate ligand:  a ligand that can bind through two different atoms (NO2-, SCN-, CN-).    Chelate:  a complex in which a polydentate ligand forms a ring with the metal (e.g. en, C2O4^2-, EDTA).    Racemic mixture:  an equal mixture of d and l forms. It is optically inactive because the two rotations cancel.    Enantiomers:  non-superimposable mirror images. They have the same mp, bp and reactivity, and  opposite  rotation of equal size.

title: 6e. Diagrams to learn (describe and draw neatly)
text: 6e. Diagrams to learn (describe and draw neatly)       Vapour pressure-composition graphs:  a straight line for an ideal solution. With positive deviation the total-pressure curve lies  above  the line; with negative deviation it lies  below .    Λm vs √c:  for a strong electrolyte (KCl) it is a nearly straight line with a small downward slope; extrapolate it to c = 0 to get Λ°m. For a weak electrolyte (CH3COOH) it rises steeply at low concentration and cannot be extrapolated.    Kinetics graphs:     - Zero order: [R] vs t is a straight line with slope -k.    - First order: ln[R] vs t is a straight line with slope -k; log([R]0/[R]) vs t is a straight line with slope k/2.303.    - Arrhenius: log k vs 1/T is a straight line with slope -Ea/(2.303R).    Energy profile with catalyst:  two humps between reactants and products. The catalysed hump is lower (lower Ea); ΔH is the same.    Crystal field splitting (octahedral):  five d-orbitals split into lower t2g (dxy, dyz, dxz), at -0.4Δo, and upper eg (dx2-y2, dz2), at +0.6Δo.    Cis and trans [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]  (square planar): in cis the two Cl are next to each other; in trans they are opposite.    Optical isomers of [Co(en)3]3+:  two mirror-image octahedra with three en "loops".    Ring structure of α-D-glucopyranose:  a six-membered ring with O in the ring. The C1-OH points down (α).    H2-O2 fuel cell:  porous carbon electrodes, concentrated aqueous NaOH, H2 in at the anode, O2 in at the cathode, water out.

title: 7. Answer-writing tips (to collect step marks) and a 30-day timetable
text: 7. Answer-writing tips (to collect step marks) and a 30-day timetable

title: 7a. Tips
text: 7a. Tips       Numericals:  write the  formula first  (½ mark), then substitute values with units (½ mark), then the answer  with units  (½ mark). Even a wrong final answer can still earn 1½-2 of the 3 marks.    Nernst questions:  first write the cell reaction and  n . Then calculate E°cell. Many marks come from these two lines alone.    Organic "identify A, B, C":  write the structures  and  the reactions. Name each reaction ("Hofmann bromamide reaction") even if you are unsure of the product; a correct reagent or name can earn ½ mark.    "Give reasons" (1 mark each):  use a keyword sentence. For example: "due to resonance", "due to the -I effect", "due to steric hindrance", "due to the stable half-filled d5 configuration", "due to H-bonding", "due to unpaired d-electrons".    Coordination questions:  draw the orbital box diagram (3d, 4s, 4p). The examiner gives marks for the hybridisation and the number of unpaired electrons separately.    MCQ and A-R:  never leave one blank. For A-R, first decide if A is true and if R is true, then ask "does R explain A?".    Choose the easier OR option , usually the theory one rather than the numerical, unless the numerical is a Nernst or ΔTf one you have practised.    Start with Section A , then go to the questions you know best. Write the question number clearly. Leave 10 minutes at the end to check units and signs.   Write equations with  arrows and conditions  (catalyst, temperature) above the arrow. Balanced equations score full marks.

title: 7b. 30-day study timetable (about 2 hours a day)
text: 7b. 30-day study timetable (about 2 hours a day)          Day   Task           1   Biomolecules: glucose reactions, structure, linkages (Q68-Q69)       2   Biomolecules: DNA/RNA, vitamins, proteins, sugars (Q70-Q72)       3   Coordination: IUPAC naming rules + 10 formulas (Q47)       4   Coordination: VBT table, magnetic moment, CFT (Q48-Q49)       5   Coordination: Werner/AgCl, isomerism (Q50-Q51). Write a 1-page test.       6   Solutions: concentration terms, Raoult's law, deviations, azeotropes (Q4, Q13, Q14)       7   Solutions: ΔTb, ΔTf, π numericals with i (Q6-Q11)       8   Solutions: Henry's law, osmosis, RBC (Q5, Q15, Q16) + revise formulas       9   Kinetics: rate, order vs molecularity, units of k, pseudo-first-order (Q34, Q37-Q39)       10   Kinetics: first-order numericals, t1/2 (Q30-Q32)       11   Kinetics: order from data, Arrhenius (Q33, Q35, Q36)       12   Electrochemistry: E°cell, Nernst numericals (Q17-Q19)       13   Electrochemistry: ΔG, log K, Faraday (Q20, Q25-Q27)       14   Electrochemistry: conductivity, Kohlrausch, cells, corrosion (Q21-Q24, Q28-Q29)       15    Test 1:  physical chemistry (Ch 1-3) mixed numericals. Revise the formula sheet (6a).       26   Solve the  2026-27 SQP  in 3 hours. Mark it with the official marking scheme.       27   Redo every wrong answer from the SQP. Revise the PYQ trend table topics.       28   Solve the  2026 board paper (56/1/1)  in 3 hours       29   Revise all ★ questions in Section 5       30   Light revision: formulas, named reactions, definitions.
