title: Q1 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q1 ★ (MCQ, 2026)  Which solution will have the lowest freezing point? (A) 0.1 M glucose (B) 0.1 M CaCl2 (C) 0.1 M KCl (D) 0.1 M urea    Ans: (B) CaCl2.  It gives 3 ions (i = 3), so it has the most particles, the largest ΔTf and the lowest freezing point.

title: Q2 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q2 (MCQ, 2025)  Which aqueous solution has the highest freezing point? (A) 1.0 M KCl (B) 1.0 M Na2SO4 (C) 1.0 M glucose (D) 1.0 M AlCl3    Ans: (C) glucose.  It is a non-electrolyte (i = 1), so it has the fewest particles and the smallest ΔTf.

title: Q3 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q3 (MCQ, 2023)  The colligative property used to find the molar mass of polymers and proteins is:    Ans: osmotic pressure.  It is measured at room temperature and gives a measurable value even for very dilute solutions.

title: Q4 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q4 ★ (A-R, 2026)  A: The components of an azeotrope cannot be separated by fractional distillation. R: Components of an azeotrope have the same composition in the liquid and vapour phase and boil at constant temperature.    Ans: (A)  Both are true, and R explains A.

title: Q5 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q5 (A-R, 2025)  A: Henry's law constant KH decreases with increase in temperature. R: As temperature increases, the solubility of gases in liquids decreases.    Ans: (D)  A is false (KH  increases  with temperature), and R is true.

title: Q6 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q6 ★ (2 marks, 2025)  Calculate the elevation in boiling point when 3 g CaCl2 (M = 111) is dissolved in 260 g water (complete dissociation, Kb = 0.52 K kg/mol).    Ans:      Moles of CaCl2 = 3/111 = 0.0270 mol   m = 0.0270 / 0.260 kg = 0.104 mol/kg   CaCl2 → Ca2+ + 2Cl-, so i = 3   ΔTb = i × Kb × m = 3 × 0.52 × 0.104 =  0.162 K

title: Q7 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q7 ★ (3 marks, 2026)  Calculate the boiling point of a solution of 0.61 g benzoic acid (M = 122) in 5 g CS2, if benzoic acid dimerises to the extent of 88%. Boiling point of CS2 = 46.2 °C, Kb = 2.3 K kg/mol.    Ans:      For dimerisation (2A → A2): i = 1 - α/2 = 1 - 0.88/2 =  0.56    m = (0.61/122) / 0.005 kg = 0.005/0.005 = 1 mol/kg   ΔTb = i Kb m = 0.56 × 2.3 × 1 = 1.288 K   Boiling point = 46.2 + 1.288 =  47.49 °C

title: Q8 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q8 ★ (3 marks, 2016)  Calculate the freezing point of a solution of 1.9 g MgCl2 (M = 95) in 50 g water, assuming complete ionisation (Kf = 1.86 K kg/mol).    Ans:  n = 1.9/95 = 0.02 mol; m = 0.02/0.05 = 0.4 mol/kg; i = 3. ΔTf = 3 × 1.86 × 0.4 = 2.23 K. Freezing point = 273.15 - 2.23 =  270.92 K .

title: Q9 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q9 ★ (3 marks, 2019; same idea 2017)  A 4% (w/w) solution of sucrose (M = 342) freezes at 271.15 K. Find the freezing point of a 5% glucose (M = 180) solution. (Pure water freezes at 273.15 K.)    Ans:      Sucrose: ΔTf = 2 K. Here m = (4/342) / 0.096 kg = 0.1218 mol/kg.   Glucose: m = (5/180) / 0.095 kg = 0.2924 mol/kg.   Same Kf, so ΔTf(glucose) = 2 × (0.2924/0.1218) = 4.80 K   Freezing point = 273.15 - 4.80 =  268.35 K

title: Q10 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q10 (3 marks, 2015)  3.9 g benzoic acid in 49 g benzene lowers the freezing point by 1.62 K. Find i and the nature of the solute (M = 122, Kf = 4.9).    Ans:  m = (3.9/122) / 0.049 = 0.652 mol/kg. Normal ΔTf = 4.9 × 0.652 = 3.20 K. i = 1.62/3.20 =  0.51 . Since i < 1, benzoic acid is  associated  (it forms a dimer).

title: Q11 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q11 (2 marks, 2020)  Calculate the osmotic pressure of a 5% (w/v) urea solution (M = 60) at 300 K (R = 0.0821 L atm/K/mol).    Ans:  5 g in 100 mL, so C = (5/60)/0.1 L = 0.833 mol/L. π = CRT = 0.833 × 0.0821 × 300 =  20.5 atm .

title: Q12 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q12 (3 marks, 2023)  30 g urea (M = 60) is dissolved in 846 g water. Find the vapour pressure of water if p° = 23.8 mm Hg.    Ans:  n(urea) = 0.5 mol; n(water) = 846/18 = 47 mol. x(water) = 47/47.5 = 0.9895. p = x × p° = 0.9895 × 23.8 =  23.55 mm Hg .

title: Q13 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q13 (2 marks, 2025)  Liquids X and Y form an ideal solution. p°X = 120 mm Hg and p°Y = 160 mm Hg. Find the vapour pressure of a solution with equal moles of X and Y.    Ans:  xX = xY = 0.5. p = 0.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 160 =  140 mm Hg .

title: Q14 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q14 ★ (2-3 marks, 2025, 2026, SQP)  A student mixes two liquids (10 mL + 10 mL) and the volume becomes 20.2 mL. (i) Why? (ii) Will the temperature rise or fall? (iii) Give an example. Also: what type of deviation does phenol + aniline show?    Ans:      (i) The volume increases because A-B attractions are  weaker  than A-A and B-B attractions. This is a  positive deviation  from Raoult's law (ΔmixV > 0).   (ii) Heat is absorbed (ΔmixH > 0), so the  temperature falls .   (iii) Examples: ethanol + acetone, or acetone + CS2.   Phenol + aniline shows  negative deviation . They form strong H-bonds (O-H...N), so the vapour pressure falls and the  boiling point rises . Volume decreases and heat is released.

title: Q15 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q15 (2 marks, 2025, 2016, 2024)  (i) Why is salt sprinkled on snowy roads? (ii) What happens when RBCs are put in 0.5% NaCl solution? (iii) Give one use of reverse osmosis.    Ans:      (i) Salt lowers the freezing point of water, so the ice melts.   (ii) 0.5% NaCl is  hypotonic  (blood is isotonic with 0.9% NaCl). Water enters the cells and they  swell and may burst . In more than 0.9% NaCl (hypertonic), the cells shrink.   (iii)  Desalination  of sea water.

title: Q16 · Chapter 1: Solutions
text: Q16 (1 mark, SQP, 2023)  Why do people at high altitude have low oxygen in their blood?    Ans:  The atmospheric pressure, and so the partial pressure of O2, is low. By Henry's law (p = KH × x), less O2 dissolves in blood (this is called anoxia).

title: Q21 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q21 ★ (3 marks, 2025; 2017 similar)  Λ°m of NH4Cl, NaOH and NaCl are 129.8, 217.4 and 108.9 S cm2/mol. Λm of 0.01 M NH4OH is 9.33 S cm2/mol. Find α.    Ans:  By Kohlrausch's law, Λ°(NH4OH) = Λ°(NH4Cl) + Λ°(NaOH) - Λ°(NaCl) = 129.8 + 217.4 - 108.9 = 238.3 S cm2/mol. α = Λm/Λ°m = 9.33/238.3 =  0.039 . (2017: acetic acid, Λ° = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5; α = 39.05/390.5 = 0.1)

title: Q22 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q22 (2 marks, 2023, 2025)  State Kohlrausch's law and give two uses.    Ans:  The limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion: Λ°m = ν+ λ°+ + ν- λ°-. Uses: (1) to find Λ°m of a weak electrolyte; (2) to find the degree of dissociation α = Λm/Λ°m (and the dissociation constant).

title: Q23 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q23 ★ (3 marks, 2024)  A cell with 0.05 M KCl (κ = 1.35 × 10^-2 S/cm) has R = 100 Ω. With 0.02 M AgNO3 it has R = 90 Ω. Find κ and Λm of AgNO3.    Ans:  Cell constant G* = κ × R = 1.35 × 10^-2 × 100 = 1.35 cm^-1. κ(AgNO3) = G*/R = 1.35/90 = 0.015 S/cm. Λm = κ × 1000/C = 0.015 × 1000/0.02 =  750 S cm2/mol .

title: Q24 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q24 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2025, SQP)  Why does conductivity decrease, but molar conductivity increase, on dilution?    Ans:  Conductivity (κ) depends on the number of ions per unit volume. On dilution there are fewer ions per cm3, so κ  decreases . Molar conductivity (Λm = κ × V) is for 1 mole of electrolyte. On dilution the total volume containing 1 mole increases (and a weak electrolyte ionises more), so Λm  increases .

title: Q25 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q25 (3 marks, 2017; 2019 similar)  A current of 2 A is passed through AgNO3 solution for 15 min. Find the mass of Ag deposited (Ag = 108).    Ans:  Q = I × t = 2 × 900 = 1800 C. Ag+ + e- → Ag, so 96500 C deposits 108 g. Mass = 108 × 1800/96500 =  2.01 g .

title: Q26 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q26 (MCQ, SQP)  The charge needed to get 1 mol of metal M from M2O3 is:    Ans: 3F , because M3+ + 3e- → M.

title: Q27 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q27 (MCQ, 2026)  During electrolysis of aqueous CuCl2 with Pt electrodes:    Ans: Cl2 gas is released at the anode  (and Cu is deposited at the cathode).

title: Q28 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q28 ★ (2-3 marks, 2016, 2020, 2024, 2025, 2026, SQP)  Batteries:     (a) Primary vs secondary battery: In a primary battery the reaction occurs only once and it cannot be recharged (dry cell, mercury cell). A secondary battery can be recharged (lead storage battery).   (b) Mercury cell: used in hearing aids and watches. It gives a constant voltage (1.35 V) because the overall reaction Zn(Hg) + HgO → ZnO + Hg has  no ion in solution  whose concentration changes.   (c) Lead storage battery on  charging : 2PbSO4 + 2H2O → Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4. On discharge H2SO4 is used up, so the specific gravity of the acid  falls ; on charging it  rises .   (d) H2-O2 fuel cell: anode 2H2 + 4OH- → 4H2O + 4e-; cathode O2 + 2H2O + 4e- → 4OH-; overall 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Advantages: high efficiency (about 70%) and pollution-free (it only gives water). It was used in the Apollo space programme.   (e) Cell uses (2025 MCQ): lead storage → inverter/automobile; mercury → wrist watch/hearing aid; dry cell → wall clock; fuel cell → Apollo.

title: Q29 · Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
text: Q29 (1 mark, SQP)  Why are iron pipes connected to Mg?    Ans:  Mg is more reactive. It acts as a  sacrificial anode  and gets oxidised instead of iron, so the iron does not corrode.

title: Q30 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q30 ★ (MCQ, SQP)  The half-life of a first-order reaction is 16 min. The time for 75% completion is:    Ans: 32 min  (75% = 2 half-lives).

title: Q31 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q31 ★ (3 marks, 2015)  A first-order reaction takes 30 min for 50% completion. Find the time for 90% completion.    Ans:  k = 0.693/30 = 0.0231 min^-1. t = (2.303/k) log([R]0/[R]) = (2.303/0.0231) log(100/10) = 99.7 × 1 ≈  100 min . (Shortcut: t90 = 3.32 × t1/2.)

title: Q32 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q32 ★ (3 marks, 2026)  For the first-order reaction C2H5Cl(g) → C2H4(g) + HCl(g), the total pressure is 0.30 atm at t = 0 and 0.50 atm at t = 30 s. Find k (log 3 = 0.48).    Ans:      Let the pressure of C2H5Cl fall by x. Total pressure = 0.30 - x + x + x = 0.30 + x = 0.50, so x = 0.20 atm.   Pressure of C2H5Cl left = 0.30 - 0.20 = 0.10 atm   k = (2.303/t) log(P0/P) = (2.303/30) log(0.30/0.10) = (2.303/30) × 0.48 =  3.68 × 10^-2 s^-1

title: Q33 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q33 ★ (3 marks, 2024; 2025 similar)  For 2NO + Br2 → 2NOBr:         [NO]   [Br2]   Rate           0.05   0.05   1.0 × 10^-3       0.05   0.15   3.0 × 10^-3       0.15   0.05   9.0 × 10^-3         Find the order, k, and the rate at [NO] = 0.4, [Br2] = 0.2.  Ans:      [Br2] × 3 makes the rate × 3, so the order in Br2 = 1.   [NO] × 3 makes the rate × 9, so the order in NO = 2.   Rate = k[NO]^2[Br2] (overall order 3)   k = 1.0 × 10^-3 / (0.05^2 × 0.05) =  8 L2 mol^-2 s^-1    Rate = 8 × 0.4^2 × 0.2 =  0.256 mol L^-1 s^-1

title: Q34 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q34 (2 marks, 2026)  2A + B → 2C takes place in one step. How does the rate change if the volume is reduced to one-third? Does the order change?    Ans:  Rate = k[A]^2[B]. Each concentration becomes 3 times, so the new rate = 3^2 × 3 =  27 times . The order stays  3  (it does not change).

title: Q35 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q35 (3 marks, 2019)  NH3 decomposes on Pt as a zero-order reaction with k = 4 × 10^-3 M/s. How long does it take for [NH3] to fall from 0.1 M to 0.064 M?    Ans:  For zero order, t = ([R]0 - [R])/k = (0.1 - 0.064)/(4 × 10^-3) = 0.036/0.004 =  9 s .

title: Q36 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q36 ★ (3 marks, 2016; SQP similar)  For a first-order reaction, log k = 14.2 - (1.0 × 10^4 K)/T. Find Ea, and find k if t1/2 = 200 min.    Ans:  Compare with log k = log A - Ea/(2.303 RT). So Ea/(2.303 R) = 1.0 × 10^4, giving Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 10^4 = 1.915 × 10^5 J =  191.5 kJ/mol . k = 0.693/200 =  3.47 × 10^-3 min^-1 .

title: Q37 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q37 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2023, 2024, SQP)  What is a pseudo-first-order reaction? Give an example. (SQP: hydrolysis of acetyl chloride with (i) equimolar water, (ii) excess water.)    Ans:  A reaction that has molecularity 2 but behaves as first order because one reactant is in large excess, so its concentration hardly changes. Example: hydrolysis of an ester, CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (excess) → CH3COOH + C2H5OH (H+ catalyst). Rate = k[ester]. SQP: (i) second order, (ii) first order.

title: Q38 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q38 (2 marks, SQP, 2025)  "The rate of reaction stays constant during the reaction." Is this always true?    Ans:  It is true only for a  zero-order  reaction (rate = k, independent of concentration). For first-, second- or other-order reactions, the rate decreases as the concentration of reactants decreases.

title: Q39 · Chapter 3: Chemical Kinetics
text: Q39 (MCQ, 2024, 2026)  Graph and formula facts:     log k vs 1/T: slope = -Ea/(2.303R), intercept = log A.   The fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea is  e^(-Ea/RT) .   A catalyst lowers  Ea . It does not change ΔG, ΔH or the equilibrium constant.

title: Q40 · Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Q40 (MCQ, 2026)  Which of these is not a transition metal: Sc, Ag, Hg, Cu?    Ans: Hg.  Its d-orbitals are completely filled (5d10) in the atom and in its common ion Hg2+.

title: Q41 · Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Q41 ★ (5 × 1 marks, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). Give reasons:      (a)  Transition metals are good catalysts:  they show variable oxidation states, they form unstable intermediate compounds, and they provide a large surface area for adsorption (examples: Fe in Haber's process, V2O5 in the Contact process).   (b)  Transition metals form complexes:  small size of the metal ions, high ionic charge, and vacant d-orbitals available for bonding.   (c)  Transition metal ions are coloured:  they have unpaired d-electrons, which absorb visible light and undergo  d-d transitions . Sc3+ (3d0) and Zn2+ (3d10) are colourless.   (d)  Zn, Cd and Hg are not transition elements / have low melting points:  they have completely filled d10 orbitals in the ground state and in their common ions. With no unpaired d-electrons, metallic bonding is weak.   (e)  Transition metals have high enthalpy of atomisation:  they have a large number of unpaired electrons, giving strong metallic bonding.

title: Q42 · Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Q42 ★ (3 marks, 2017, 2023, 2024)      (a)  Cr2+ is a reducing agent, Mn3+ is an oxidising agent (both d4):  Cr2+ → Cr3+ gives d3 (t2g3), a stable half-filled t2g level. Mn3+ → Mn2+ gives d5, which is extra-stable because it is half-filled.   (b)  Cu+ is unstable in water:  Cu2+(aq) has a much more negative hydration enthalpy, which more than makes up for the second ionisation enthalpy. So 2Cu+ → Cu2+ + Cu (disproportionation).   (c)  E°(Cu2+/Cu) is positive:  Cu has a high enthalpy of atomisation and high ionisation enthalpies, which its hydration enthalpy cannot balance.

title: Q43 · Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Q43 (2 marks, SQP)  Why does Ti melt at a lower temperature than Cr?    Ans:  Cr has more unpaired d-electrons (3d5 4s1) than Ti, so its metallic bonding is stronger.

title: Q44 · Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Q44 ★ (2-3 marks, 2016, 2017, 2025). Potassium dichromate:      Preparation: 4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 → 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2 (yellow chromate)   Then 2Na2CrO4 + 2H+ → Na2Cr2O7 + 2Na+ + H2O, followed by Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl → K2Cr2O7 (orange) + 2NaCl   Colour change: 2CrO4^2- (yellow) + 2H+ ⇌ Cr2O7^2- (orange) + H2O.  Acid turns yellow to orange  (2025 MCQ: HCl in the test tube).  Alkali turns orange to yellow  (2017).

title: Q45 · Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Q45 ★ (2-3 marks, 2019, 2025, 2026, 2024). Potassium permanganate:      2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2 → 2K2MnO4 (dark green, A) + 2H2O   In acid: 3MnO4^2- + 4H+ → 2MnO4- (purple, B) + MnO2 + 2H2O (disproportionation)   On heating: 2KMnO4 → K2MnO4 + MnO2 + O2   With I-, acidic: 2MnO4- + 10I- + 16H+ → 2Mn2+ + 5I2 + 8H2O   With I-, neutral/alkaline: 2MnO4- + I- + H2O → 2MnO2 + IO3- + 2OH-   With Fe2+, acidic: MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ → Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O   Dichromate with Fe2+: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6Fe2+ → 2Cr3+ + 6Fe3+ + 7H2O (SQP)   Dichromate with I-: Cr2O7^2- + 6I- + 14H+ → 2Cr3+ + 3I2 + 7H2O (2024)

title: Q46 · Chapter 4: d- and f-Block Elements
text: Q46 (2-3 marks, 2015, 2017, 2024, 2025)  Lanthanoids and actinoids:     Lanthanoid contraction: a steady decrease in atomic/ionic size from La to Lu, caused by the poor shielding of 4f electrons. Consequence: Zr and Hf have almost the same size, so they are very hard to separate.   Actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction because 5f electrons shield even more poorly.   Actinoids show more oxidation states because 5f, 6d and 7s have similar energies.   Ce4+ is a good oxidising agent because it prefers to change to the common +3 state.   The most common oxidation state of lanthanoids is  +3  (2023 MCQ).

title: Q47 · Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds
text: Q47 ★ (1-2 marks, many years). IUPAC names and formulas:      [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 → pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride (2023)   [Co(NH3)5(CO3)]Cl → pentaamminecarbonatocobalt(III) chloride (2017)   K3[Fe(C2O4)3] → potassium trioxalatoferrate(III) (2026)   [Ag(NH3)2][Ag(CN)2] → diamminesilver(I) dicyanidoargentate(I) (2026)   [Cr(NH3)3Cl3] → triamminetrichloridochromium(III) (2017)   Potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II) → K2[Zn(OH)4] (2020, 2024)   Hexaammineplatinum(IV) chloride → [Pt(NH3)6]Cl4 (2020)   Hexaamminecobalt(III) sulphate → [Co(NH3)6]2(SO4)3 (2019)   Potassium trioxalatochromate(III) → K3[Cr(C2O4)3] (2019)   Iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II) → Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (2023)

title: Q48 · Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds
text: Q48 ★ (2-3 marks, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2026). Hybridisation and magnetic behaviour (VBT):          Complex   Metal ion, d-electrons   Ligand   Hybridisation / shape   Magnetic           [Fe(CN)6]3-   Fe3+, d5   CN- strong   d2sp3, octahedral, inner orbital, low spin   Paramagnetic, 1 unpaired (1.73 BM)       [Fe(CN)6]4-   Fe2+, d6   CN- strong   d2sp3, octahedral   Diamagnetic       [Co(NH3)6]3+   Co3+, d6   NH3 strong here   d2sp3, octahedral   Diamagnetic       [CoF6]3-   Co3+, d6   F- weak   sp3d2, octahedral, outer orbital, high spin   Paramagnetic, 4 unpaired       [Ni(CN)4]2-   Ni2+, d8   CN- strong   dsp2, square planar   Diamagnetic       [NiCl4]2-   Ni2+, d8   Cl- weak   sp3, tetrahedral   Paramagnetic, 2 unpaired       [Ni(CO)4]   Ni(0), 3d10 4s0 after pairing   CO strong   sp3, tetrahedral   Diamagnetic           2026: [NiCl4]2- is paramagnetic but [Ni(CO)4] is diamagnetic, though both are tetrahedral. Ni2+ in [NiCl4]2- keeps 2 unpaired electrons (Cl- cannot pair them). In [Ni(CO)4], Ni is in the 0 state and strong-field CO pushes the 4s electrons into 3d, so all electrons are paired.   SQP MCQ: the tetrahedral complex among [Ni(CN)4]2-, [Cu(NH3)4]2+, [NiCl4]2- and [Co(en)3]3+ is  [NiCl4]2- .

title: Q49 · Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds
text: Q49 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2025, 2026, SQP). Crystal field theory:      Crystal field splitting energy (Δo): the energy difference between the two sets of d-orbitals (t2g and eg) when ligands approach.   In an octahedral field, the  eg orbitals (dx2-y2, dz2) are raised  because they point directly at the ligands and feel more repulsion (2026).   d4 ion: if Δo < P (weak field), t2g3 eg1; if Δo > P (strong field), t2g4 eg0.   d5 with Δo > P: t2g5 eg0 (SQP).   [CoF6]3-: t2g4 eg2. [Co(NH3)6]3+: t2g6 eg0 (2026).   Low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rare because Δt is small (about 4/9 Δo) and is less than the pairing energy (2023 A-R: answer A; 2025).

title: Q50 · Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds
text: Q50 ★ (2 marks, 2016, 2023, 2025, SQP). Werner / AgCl questions:      CrCl3·6H2O gives 2 mol AgCl → [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2O (2016)   CrCl3·4H2O gives 1 mol AgCl → [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl; secondary valency = 6 (2025)   PdCl2·4NH3 gives 2 mol AgCl → [Pd(NH3)4]Cl2; primary valency 2, secondary valency 4 (SQP)   PtCl2·2NH3 does not react with AgNO3 → [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] (2023)   Secondary valency of [Co(en)3]3+ =  6  (en is didentate, 3 × 2) (2023, 2026: [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+ → 6)   Conductivity order (2024, 2025, SQP): [Cr(NH3)3Cl3] (0 ions) < [Cr(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 (3 ions) < [Cr(NH3)6]Cl3 (4 ions)

title: Q51 · Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds
text: Q51 ★ (2 marks, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2023, 2024, 2026). Isomerism:      [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+ →  linkage  isomerism (NO2- can bind through N or O)   [Co(NH3)5SO4]Cl and [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 →  ionisation  isomers. Test: the first gives a white precipitate (AgCl) with AgNO3; the second gives a white precipitate (BaSO4) with BaCl2 (2026).   [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] →  coordination  isomerism (2017)   [Co(en)3]3+ →  optical  isomerism (d and l forms) (2017, 2024)   [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] →  geometrical  (cis and trans). Cis-[Pt(en)2Cl2]2+ is optically active (2015, 2016).   Chelate effect: complexes with chelating (di- or polydentate) ligands are more stable than similar complexes with monodentate ligands. Example: [Ni(en)3]2+ is more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]2+.

title: Q52 · Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
text: Q52 ★ (3 marks, 2016, 2017, 2019, 2024, 2025, 2026, SQP). SN1 / SN2:      SN2 reactivity: 1° > 2° > 3° (steric hindrance). 1-Bromopentane reacts fastest by SN2. 2-Bromopentane is optically active. 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane (3°) is fastest in elimination and SN1 (2017).   SN1 reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°, depending on carbocation stability. Allylic/benzylic halides are very reactive (resonance-stabilised carbocation). (CH3)3C-I is more reactive than (CH3)3C-Br because C-I is weaker (2019).   SN1 on an optically active halide gives  racemisation : the planar carbocation can be attacked from both sides (2016, 2020, 2025).   SN2 gives  inversion of configuration  (SQP MCQ: (-)-2-bromohexane → (+)-hexan-2-ol is SN2 with inversion).   2026 case:   (a) Rate = k[X], so X reacts by SN1 and is the 3° bromide, X =  (CH3)3C-Br  (2-bromo-2-methylpropane). Y is optically active and rate = k[Y][OH-], so Y reacts by SN2: Y =  CH3CH(Br)CH2CH3  (2-bromobutane, the only chiral C4H9Br).   (b)  Expected answer: X (SN1).  It goes through a flat (planar) carbocation, which the OH- can attack from either side. For a chiral substrate this gives a racemic mixture.   (c)  Y (SN2)  gives inversion of configuration, because OH- attacks from the back side, opposite the Br.   Teacher's note: (CH3)3CBr itself is not chiral, so the racemisation in (b) is the general SN1 rule. Write the reason (planar carbocation, attack from both sides) to get the mark.

title: Q53 · Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
text: Q53 ★ (2-3 marks, 2016, 2024, 2025, 2026). Haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution.  Reasons:     (i)  Resonance  gives the C-Cl bond partial double-bond character.   (ii) The carbon is  sp2  (more s-character), so C-X is shorter and stronger.   (iii) The phenyl cation is unstable.   (iv) The electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile.   Also: the C-Cl bond in chlorobenzene is  shorter  than in CH3Cl for reasons (i) and (ii).   A -NO2 group at the ortho/para position  increases  reactivity: it withdraws electrons and stabilises the carbanion intermediate. So the nitro group activates; the methoxy group does not (SQP).

title: Q54 · Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
text: Q54 ★ (1-2 marks, 2019, 2025, SQP, 2024)      KCN gives an alkyl cyanide (R-CN). AgCN gives an isocyanide (R-NC). KCN is ionic and attacks through C; AgCN is covalent and attacks through N. CN- is an  ambident nucleophile . (SQP: CH3CH2CH2Cl + AgCN → X = CH3CH2CH2NC; + KCN → Y = CH3CH2CH2CN.)   Ethyl bromide + AgNO2 gives  nitroethane  (2025 MCQ). KNO2 gives ethyl nitrite.   Grignard reagents are made in dry conditions because RMgX + H2O → RH + Mg(OH)X.   Aqueous KOH gives an alcohol (substitution). Alcoholic KOH gives an alkene (elimination).

title: Q55 · Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
text: Q55 ★ (MCQ/2 marks, 2023, 2015, 2025)  Name reactions of haloalkanes:     Finkelstein: CH3Cl + NaI → CH3I + NaCl (dry acetone)   Swarts (best for alkyl fluorides, 2023 MCQ): CH3Br + AgF → CH3F + AgBr   Boiling point order RI > RBr > RCl > RF, because van der Waals forces increase with size (2025 A-R: answer A).   n-Butyl bromide has a higher boiling point than t-butyl bromide because it has more surface area (2015).

title: Q56 · Chapter 7: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
text: Q56 ★ (2-3 marks, 2017, 2019, 2023, 2024). Mechanism of dehydration of ethanol (conc. H2SO4, 443 K):      Step 1: protonation. CH3CH2-OH + H+ → CH3CH2-OH2+ (fast)   Step 2: carbocation forms. CH3CH2-OH2+ → CH3CH2+ + H2O (slow, rate-determining)   Step 3: loss of H+. CH3CH2+ → CH2=CH2 + H+   Ease of dehydration: 3° > 2° > 1° (2024 MCQ). t-Butyl alcohol dehydrates faster than n-butanol (2020).   Acid-catalysed hydration of ethene (2020, 2025) is the reverse. CH2=CH2 + H3O+ → CH3CH2+ + H2O. Then CH3CH2+ + H2O → CH3CH2OH2+. Finally CH3CH2OH2+ + H2O → CH3CH2OH + H3O+.

title: Q57 · Chapter 7: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
text: Q57 ★ (3 marks, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2026). Named reactions of phenols:       Reimer-Tiemann:  phenol + CHCl3 + aq NaOH (340 K), then H+ →  salicylaldehyde  (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde)    Kolbe:  phenol + NaOH → sodium phenoxide; + CO2 (400 K, 4-7 atm), then H+ →  salicylic acid  (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). Acetylating salicylic acid gives  aspirin  (2026 MCQ).    Friedel-Crafts acylation of anisole:  anisole + CH3COCl (anhydrous AlCl3) → 2-methoxyacetophenone (minor) + 4-methoxyacetophenone (major)    Williamson synthesis  (2024 MCQ): R-X + R'-ONa → R-O-R' + NaX. Use a 1° halide; a 3° halide gives an alkene (2019: t-butyl chloride + CH3ONa gives 2-methylpropene).   Phenol + dil HNO3 at low temperature → o- and p-nitrophenol (2026). Phenol + bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate). Phenol + conc HNO3 → picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol).   Phenol + Zn dust → benzene. Anisole + HBr → phenol + CH3Br (2025).

title: Q58 · Chapter 7: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
text: Q58 ★ (1-2 marks, 2017, 2023, 2025, SQP). Acidity:      Phenol is more acidic than an alcohol because the  phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised ; the alkoxide ion is not.   Electron-withdrawing groups (-NO2) increase acidity. Electron-releasing groups (-CH3, cresol) decrease it.   Order (2025): 4-methylphenol < phenol < 3,5-dinitrophenol < 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.   Order (2017): ethanol < phenol < p-nitrophenol.   -OH directs  ortho/para , not meta (2026 A-R: A false, R true → D).

title: Q59 · Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
text: Q59 ★ (3 marks, SQP, 2017, 2019, 2024). Identify and write the named reaction:       Aldol:  2CH3CHO (dil NaOH) → CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO (3-hydroxybutanal); on heating → CH3CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal) + H2O. This is how ethanal is converted to but-2-enal (2023).    Etard:  toluene + CrO2Cl2 in CS2 → chromium complex; + H3O+ → benzaldehyde    Wolff-Kishner:  >C=O + NH2NH2 → >C=N-NH2 (hydrazone); + KOH/ethylene glycol, heat → >CH2 + N2    Clemmensen:  >C=O + Zn-Hg / conc HCl → >CH2 + H2O (for example, butan-2-one → butane; acetophenone → ethylbenzene)    Cannizzaro  (only for aldehydes with no α-H): 2HCHO + conc KOH → CH3OH + HCOOK; 2C6H5CHO + conc NaOH → C6H5CH2OH + C6H5COONa. Of the four aldehydes in the 2025 MCQ, only (CH3)3C-CHO has no α-H.    Rosenmund:  RCOCl + H2 (Pd-BaSO4) → RCHO + HCl. This is how acetyl chloride is converted to acetaldehyde (2025, 2019).    Stephen:  RCN + SnCl2/HCl → RCH=NH; + H3O+ → RCHO. The reagent for ethanenitrile → ethanal is SnCl2 + HCl (2026).    Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ):  RCH2COOH + Cl2 / red P → RCH(Cl)COOH. This converts propanoic acid to 2-chloropropanoic acid (2023, 2017).    Decarboxylation:  RCOONa + NaOH/CaO (heat) → R-H + Na2CO3

title: Q60 · Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
text: Q60 ★ (2 marks, 2016, 2017, 2023, 2025, 2026, SQP). Distinguishing tests:       Aldehyde vs ketone  (propanal vs propanone): Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with the aldehyde; Fehling's solution gives a red-brown precipitate with the aliphatic aldehyde. The ketone gives neither.    Iodoform test  (I2 + NaOH, yellow CHI3 precipitate): given by CH3CO- compounds and CH3CH(OH)- compounds (ethanol, ethanal, acetone, butan-2-one, acetophenone). Not given by pentan-3-one, phenol or methanol (2020, 2017).   CH3COCH2CH3 vs CH3CH2CH2CHO: iodoform test is positive for the first; Tollens' test is positive for the second.    Acid vs aldehyde  (propanoic acid vs propanal; benzoic acid vs ethyl benzoate): NaHCO3 gives brisk effervescence (CO2) with the acid only.

title: Q61 · Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
text: Q61 ★ (3 marks, 2026, 2025, SQP). Give reasons:       Carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols  of similar mass: they form  dimers  through strong intermolecular H-bonding.    α-H of aldehydes/ketones is acidic:  the C=O group withdraws electrons, and the carbanion (enolate) formed is resonance-stabilised.    Ammonia derivatives do not add in strongly acidic medium:  strong acid protonates the NH2 group, so it is no longer a nucleophile. The best pH is about 3.5.    Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones  towards nucleophilic addition: they have fewer bulky groups (less steric hindrance) and fewer electron-releasing groups.   Order towards HCN (2026): di-tert-butyl ketone < acetone < acetaldehyde.   Ease of oxidation (SQP): HCHO > CH3CHO > C6H5CHO.    NaHSO3 purifies aldehydes:  it forms a water-soluble crystalline adduct, which gives back the aldehyde with dilute acid or alkali.

title: Q62 · Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
text: Q62 ★ (3 marks, 2025; 2026, 2015 similar)  A (C8H8O) gives a 2,4-DNP test, does not give Tollens' test, and gives a yellow precipitate B with NaOH + I2. Drastic oxidation gives C (C7H6O2). Identify A, B and C.    Ans:      A =  acetophenone, C6H5COCH3 : it is a ketone, it gives the iodoform test, and it has a CH3CO- group.   B =  iodoform, CHI3 : C6H5COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH → C6H5COONa + CHI3 + 3NaI + 3H2O   C =  benzoic acid, C6H5COOH  (from oxidation with KMnO4/KOH, then H+)

title: Q63 · Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
text: Q63 (5 marks, 2026)  C5H10O: draw X if it (I) does not give Tollens' test but gives a positive iodoform test; (II) gives neither Tollens' nor iodoform but does undergo aldol; (III) undergoes Cannizzaro.    Ans:  (I) pentan-2-one, CH3COCH2CH2CH3 (or 3-methylbutan-2-one). (II) pentan-3-one, CH3CH2COCH2CH3. (III) 2,2-dimethylpropanal, (CH3)3C-CHO (no α-H).

title: Q64 · Chapter 9: Amines
text: Q64 ★ (1-2 marks, 2015, 2017, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, SQP). Basicity:      In water: (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 > C6H5NH2. Increasing pKb is the same order (2025). The strongest base in the 2020 MCQ is  dimethylamine .    Aniline is weaker than NH3 / CH3NH2:  the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is less available for H+.    CH3NH2 is more basic than (CH3)3N in water  (2026): there is less steric hindrance and better H-bonding solvation of the cation (combined inductive, solvation and steric effects).   Boiling point: (CH3)3N < C2H5NH2 < C2H5OH (2015, 2019). Butane < butanamine < butanol (2020).

title: Q65 · Chapter 9: Amines
text: Q65 ★ (1-2 marks, 2017, 2023, 2025, 2026, SQP)       Aniline on nitration gives about 47% meta product:  in strong acid, aniline is protonated to the  anilinium ion (C6H5NH3+), which is meta-directing . NCERT figures: 51% para, 47% meta, 2% ortho (2026 MCQ).    Aniline is acetylated before nitration or bromination:  -NHCOCH3 is  less activating  than -NH2 (the N lone pair is shared with C=O). This stops multiple substitution, protects -NH2 from oxidation, and gives the mono (para) product. (2023 A-R: A true, R false → C.)    Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts:  it forms a salt with AlCl3 (a Lewis acid). The N becomes positive and deactivates the ring.

title: Q66 · Chapter 9: Amines
text: Q66 ★ (2 marks, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, SQP). Named tests and reactions of amines:       Carbylamine  (only 1° amines): R-NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH (alc) → R-NC (foul-smelling isocyanide) + 3KCl + 3H2O. 2025 version: C2H5NH2 → C2H5NC. SQP: nitrobenzene reduced → aniline, which gives this test.    Gabriel phthalimide  (only 1° aliphatic amines): phthalimide + KOH → potassium phthalimide; + R-X → N-alkylphthalimide; + NaOH(aq) → R-NH2 + sodium phthalate. (Aniline cannot be made this way.)    Hofmann bromamide:  R-CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → R-NH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O. The amine has  one carbon less . CH3CONH2 → CH3NH2 (2023 MCQ). C6H5CONH2 → aniline.    Hinsberg's test  (C6H5SO2Cl):   1° amine gives a precipitate  soluble  in NaOH. In 2025, C2H7N reacts and the product dissolves in NaOH, so X =  ethanamine, C2H5NH2 .   2° amine gives a precipitate  insoluble  in alkali. In 2026, C3H9N gives an alkali-insoluble product, so X =  N-methylethanamine, CH3NHC2H5  (2°).   3° amine does not react.

title: Q67 · Chapter 9: Amines
text: Q67 ★ (3 marks, 2020, 2024, 2025, SQP). Conversions using diazonium salts:      Diazotisation: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl (273-278 K) → C6H5N2+Cl- + NaCl + 2H2O    Sandmeyer:  C6H5N2+Cl- + CuCl/HCl → C6H5Cl; + CuBr/HBr → C6H5Br; + CuCN/KCN → C6H5CN (benzonitrile, 2026). C6H5CN + H2O/H+ → C6H5COOH.    Fluorobenzene (SQP):  nitrobenzene + Sn/HCl → aniline; + NaNO2/HCl (0-5 °C) → C6H5N2+Cl-; + HBF4 → C6H5N2+BF4-; heat → C6H5F + BF3 + N2    Phenol:  C6H5N2+Cl- + H2O (warm) → C6H5OH + N2 + HCl    Benzene:  C6H5N2+Cl- + H3PO2 + H2O → C6H6 + N2 + H3PO3 + HCl    Coupling:  C6H5N2+Cl- + phenol (OH-) → p-hydroxyazobenzene (orange dye). This is the test that distinguishes aniline from methylamine/ethanamine: aliphatic amines give N2 gas, not a dye.    p-Bromoaniline:  aniline + (CH3CO)2O → acetanilide; + Br2/CH3COOH → p-bromoacetanilide; + H+/H2O → p-bromoaniline    Benzoic acid → benzylamine (SQP):  C6H5COOH + NH3 (heat) → C6H5CONH2; + LiAlH4 → C6H5CH2NH2

title: Q68 · Chapter 10: Biomolecules
text: Q68 ★ (3 marks, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). Reactions of D-glucose:       HI (long heating) → n-hexane.  Shows that the 6 C atoms are in a  straight chain .    Br2 water → gluconic acid  (CHO → COOH). Shows the  aldehyde group .    Conc HNO3 → saccharic (glucaric) acid , HOOC-(CHOH)4-COOH. Shows a 1° alcohol group as well.    Acetic anhydride → glucose pentaacetate.  Shows  five -OH groups .    HCN → cyanohydrin; NH2OH → oxime.  Show the C=O group.   Glucose does not give the 2,4-DNP test or Schiff's test, and its pentaacetate does not react with NH2OH. This shows the free -CHO is absent: glucose exists in a  cyclic  form. (2026 A-R: A true, R false → C.)

title: Q69 · Chapter 10: Biomolecules
text: Q69 ★ (2 marks, 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). Linkages:       Peptide linkage:  the amide link -CO-NH- formed between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH2 of another, with loss of water. It joins amino acids into proteins.    Glycosidic linkage:  an oxide link (C-O-C) between two monosaccharide units, with loss of water. It joins sugars (for example, C1-C4 α-glycosidic links in amylose, 2023).    Essential amino acids  cannot be made in the body and must come from food (valine, leucine, lysine).  Non-essential  ones are made in the body (glycine, alanine, glutamic acid). SQP: HOOC-CH2-CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH (glutamic acid) is  acidic and non-essential .

title: Q70 · Chapter 10: Biomolecules
text: Q70 ★ (2 marks, 2016, 2020, 2025, SQP). Nucleic acids:      DNA vs RNA:   Sugar: DNA has 2-deoxyribose; RNA has ribose.   Bases: DNA has A, G, C,  T ; RNA has A, G, C,  U .   Strands: DNA is double-stranded (double helix); RNA is single-stranded.   Role: DNA carries heredity (replication); RNA makes proteins.    Nucleoside  = base + sugar.  Nucleotide  = base + sugar + phosphate.   The two DNA strands are  complementary  (not identical): A pairs with T (2 H-bonds) and G pairs with C (3 H-bonds), held by hydrogen bonds.   The third component of DNA, besides the sugar and base, is  phosphoric acid  (2024).

title: Q71 · Chapter 10: Biomolecules
text: Q71 ★ (1 mark each, 2015, 2016, 2024, 2026). Vitamins:      Fat-soluble:  A, D, E, K . They are stored in liver and adipose tissue.   Water-soluble:  B group and C . They must be taken daily because they are excreted in urine.   Deficiencies:   A: night blindness, xerophthalmia   B1: beriberi   B12: pernicious anaemia   C: scurvy (bleeding gums)   D: rickets (bone deformities in children)   E:  increased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness  (2026 MCQ)   K: increased blood clotting time

title: Q72 · Chapter 10: Biomolecules
text: Q72 ★ (2-3 marks, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2025, SQP). Carbohydrates and proteins, short facts:      Hydrolysis products:    Sucrose  → glucose + fructose. It is  non-reducing  because the glycosidic bond joins both reducing groups (C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose). It is called  invert sugar  because sucrose is dextrorotatory, but the mixture formed on hydrolysis is laevorotatory: fructose (-92.4°) outweighs glucose (+52.5°).    Maltose  → 2 glucose    Lactose  → glucose + galactose (β-D-galactose + β-D-glucose)    Starch vs cellulose:  starch is made of α-D-glucose units (amylose: unbranched, C1-C4; amylopectin: branched, C1-C4 + C1-C6). Cellulose is a straight chain of β-D-glucose units (C1-C4).    Anomers:  cyclic forms of a sugar that differ only in the configuration at C1 (α and β glucose).    Fibrous vs globular proteins:  fibrous proteins are thread-like and water-insoluble (keratin, myosin). Globular proteins are spherical and water-soluble (insulin, albumin).   Secondary structure: α-helix and β-pleated sheet. The α-helix is a feature of  polypeptides  (2023 MCQ).    Denaturation  (SQP: lemon juice in milk): a change in pH breaks the H-bonds, so the protein unfolds and loses its biological activity (the casein curdles). The primary structure stays the same.    SQP case:  a sugar that gives a positive Benedict's test (reducing) and gives only one monosaccharide on hydrolysis is  maltose .

title: 1. Exam at a glance (2026-27)
text: 1. Exam at a glance (2026-27)          Item   Details           Theory paper   80 marks, 3 hours (plus 15 minutes reading time)       Internal assessment (IA)   20 marks: Periodic Tests 10 (best 2 of 3) + Mathematics Activities 10       Total   100       Number of questions   38, all compulsory, with internal choice in some questions       Section A   Q1-18 MCQ + Q19-20 Assertion-Reason (A-R), 1 mark each =  20 marks        Section B   Q21-25 very short answer (VSA), 2 marks each =  10 marks        Section C   Q26-31 short answer (SA), 3 marks each =  18 marks        Section D   Q32-35 long answer (LA), 5 marks each =  20 marks        Section E   Q36-38 case study, 4 marks each =  12 marks  (two of them split 1 + 1 + 2, the third split 2 + 2)       Internal choice   2 questions in B, 3 in C, 2 in D, and one sub-part in 2 case studies of E       Calculator    Not allowed.  Take π = 22/7 if the question does not say.        Pass mark (theory)     26 out of 80  (CBSE minimum for 041 theory)        Pass mark (IA)     6 out of 20        Rule   Class XII: 33%  separately  in theory and in practical/IA, and 33% overall (CBSE pass criteria). Good IA marks  cannot  cover a theory score below 26.          The 2026-27 SQP says:  "There is no change in the Question Paper Design and Assessment Pattern for Academic Session 2026-27." So the pattern is the same as the 2024, 2025 and 2026 board papers.    Good news for weak students:  the official question paper design puts  44 of 80 marks (55%)  on "Remembering and Understanding" type questions. These are direct, textbook-style questions.    Activity marks (10) break-up:  activities done during the year + record file 5, year-end activity test 3, viva 2 (any 10 activities from the NCERT Lab Manual).    NOT in the 2026-27 syllabus. Skip old PYQs on these:      Binary operations; composition and inverse of a function   Properties of determinants (proof questions); inverse by elementary row/column operations   Rolle's theorem and Mean Value Theorem; tangents and normals; approximations   Integration as the limit of a sum   Forming a differential equation from a family of curves   Planes (all plane questions); scalar triple product   Random variable, probability distribution, mean and variance, binomial distribution (these appeared in 2016-2025 papers, but the 2026-27 syllabus text for Probability lists only conditional probability, multiplication theorem, independent events, total probability and Bayes' theorem; check with your teacher before skipping fully)

title: 3a. Study order (easiest and highest return first)
text: 3a. Study order (easiest and highest return first)       Linear Programming (5 marks).  Same method every year: draw lines, shade, find corner points, put in Z. Almost a free 5.    Matrices and Determinants (10 marks).  MCQs on order, transpose, |kA|, adj A; and the big one: find A⁻¹ and solve 3 equations. Asked every year we checked.    Probability (8 marks).  Conditional probability MCQs and one Bayes' theorem / total probability question (often a case study). Same table method every time.    Relations (5 marks) + ITF MCQs (3 marks).  The equivalence-relation proof is a fixed 3-step template (reflexive, symmetric, transitive).    Vectors (about 5 marks).  Magnitude, unit vector, dot product, cross product, area of parallelogram. Short formulas.    Differential Equations (5 marks).  Order/degree MCQ, integrating factor MCQ, one 3-mark DE (variable separable or linear).    AOD (9 marks).  Rate of change (2-3 marks) and the case study on maximum value (first 2 parts are easy).    Bonus if time:  C&D (chain rule, implicit, log, parametric), 3-D lines (direction ratios, shortest distance), easy integrals MCQs.

title: 3c. How internal assessment helps
text: 3c. How internal assessment helps      IA is  20 marks , given by your school: 10 from periodic tests (best 2 of 3 averaged) and 10 from activities (record 5 + activity test 3 + viva 2).   You need only  6 out of 20  in IA, but aim for 15+. Do all 10 lab-manual activities, keep a neat record file, and learn the viva questions for each activity. These are the easiest marks in the subject.   Remember: IA is passed  separately . Even 20/20 in IA will not save you if theory is below 26/80.
