title: 5. Must-do question bank (103 questions)
text: 5. Must-do question bank (103 questions)    Tags: (2019 OD) = Outside Delhi paper 2019; (2023 D) = Delhi 2023; (SQP 26-27) = CBSE Sample Paper 2026-27. "Similar" means the same idea was asked with different wording.

title: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants       Q1. (MCQ)  In a plant, the pistil matures several days before the stamens in all flowers. The most important result is that it: (A) guarantees self-pollination (B) promotes autogamy (C) ensures cross-pollination (D) leads to geitonogamy.  (SQP 26-27)      Answer:  (C) It ensures cross-pollination.        Q2. (MCQ)  An angiosperm embryo sac is located within the: (A) placenta (B) megasporangium (C) nucellus (D) ovary.  (2024)      Answer:  (C) Nucellus.        Q3. (MCQ)  An anther has 50 microspore mother cells and the ovary has 50 megaspore mother cells. Number of pollen grains and ovules likely formed: (A) 100, 25 (B) 200, 50 (C) 50, 50 (D) 200, 100.  (2025)      Answer:  (B) 200, 50. (Each microspore mother cell → 4 pollen grains by meiosis; each megaspore mother cell → only 1 functional megaspore → 1 embryo sac.)        Q4. (2 marks)  A mature embryo sac has 7 cells but 8 nuclei. Explain.  (2017 OD; similar 2019 D, 2020 D, 2023 D)      Answer:  The functional megaspore divides 3 times (free nuclear mitosis) → 8 nuclei. 3 nuclei at the micropylar end form the egg apparatus (2 synergids + 1 egg cell); 3 at the chalazal end form 3 antipodal cells; the remaining 2 nuclei (polar nuclei) stay together in one large central cell. So: 3 + 3 + 1 central cell = 7 cells, 8 nuclei.        Q5. (3 marks)  Explain the monosporic development of the embryo sac.  (2023 D; similar 2020 D)      Answer:  (1) The megaspore mother cell (MMC, 2n) in the nucellus undergoes meiosis → 4 haploid megaspores. (2) 3 megaspores degenerate; only 1 is functional — so it is called  monosporic  development. (3) The functional megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis 3 times (free nuclear, no walls) → 2, 4, 8 nuclei; then cell walls form → 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac (female gametophyte).        Q6. (2 marks)  Explain the development of the male gametophyte. Why is it called a male gametophyte?  (2023 OD; similar 2017 D, 2025)      Answer:  The microspore (pollen grain, n) divides by mitosis into a big  vegetative cell  (food store, irregular nucleus) and a small  generative cell  (spindle shaped, floats in vegetative cell). In ~60% of angiosperms pollen is shed at this 2-celled stage; in others the generative cell divides again into  2 male gametes  (3-celled stage). It is called the male gametophyte because it is the haploid structure that produces the male gametes.        Q7. (2–3 marks)  List and explain outbreeding devices.  (2018 OD, 2023 OD, 2024, 2026)      Answer (any three):       Pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised  — pollen is released before the stigma is ready, or the stigma is ready much before pollen release (SQP Q1 case).    Anther and stigma at different positions  — pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower.    Self-incompatibility  — a genetic mechanism that stops pollen of the same flower (or plant) from germinating or growing a tube in the pistil.    Unisexual flowers  — monoecious plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy; dioecious plants (papaya) prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy.          Q8. (2 marks)  Geitonogamy can be compared with both cross-pollination and self-pollination. Comment.  (SQP 26-27)      Answer:  Geitonogamy = pollen from the anther of one flower goes to the stigma of  another flower of the same plant . Functionally it is like cross-pollination because a pollinating agent is needed; genetically it is like autogamy (self-pollination) because the pollen comes from the same plant.        Q9. (3 marks)  Explain the steps a plant breeder takes so that only the desired pollen reaches the stigma of a bisexual flower (artificial hybridisation).  (2023 D; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD, SQP 26-27)      Answer:  (1)  Emasculation  — remove the anthers from the flower bud with forceps before the anthers dehisce. (2)  Bagging  — cover the emasculated flower with a butter-paper bag to stop unwanted pollen. (3) When the stigma becomes receptive, dust it with pollen collected from the chosen male parent, and  re-bag  the flower so the fruit develops. (In unisexual flowers like papaya, no emasculation is needed — only bagging.)        Q10. (5 marks)  Explain double fertilisation, starting from pollen on the stigma. Give the ploidy of the products and the role of synergids. Why does endosperm develop before the embryo?  (2024; similar 2018 OD, SQP 26-27)      Answer:      Pollen grain germinates on the stigma → pollen tube grows through the style → enters the ovule through the micropyle → enters one  synergid  (guided by the  filiform apparatus  of synergids) → releases 2 male gametes.    Syngamy:  male gamete 1 + egg cell →  zygote (2n)  → embryo.    Triple fusion:  male gamete 2 + 2 polar nuclei in central cell →  primary endosperm nucleus, PEN (3n)  → endosperm.   Two fusions happen in one embryo sac, so it is called  double fertilisation .    Endosperm develops first  because its cells store food, which nourishes the developing embryo. (SQP MS: the statement "zygote always divides before PEN" is false.)          Q11. (2 marks)  Why do farmers prefer apomictic seeds?  (2020 D, 2026; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD)      Answer:   Apomixis  = formation of seed without fertilisation (example: some Asteraceae and grasses). (1) If a hybrid is made apomictic, the hybrid characters do not segregate in the next generation. (2) So farmers can keep using their own seeds every year instead of buying costly hybrid seeds each year.        Q12. (2 marks)  When an orange seed is squeezed, many embryos are seen. Explain. Are they genetically similar?  (2017 D)      Answer:  This is  polyembryony . In citrus, some nucellar cells around the embryo sac divide and grow into extra embryos (without fertilisation). These nucellar embryos are genetically identical to the mother plant (clones); only the zygotic embryo differs.        Q13. (2 marks)  Differentiate between true fruit and false fruit, and give an example of a parthenocarpic fruit.  (2020 OD; similar 2018 OD, 2026)      Answer:  True fruit develops only from the ovary (e.g., mango). False fruit — the thalamus also contributes to the fruit (e.g., apple, strawberry, cashew). Parthenocarpic fruit develops without fertilisation and is seedless (e.g., banana).

title: Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction       Q14. (MCQ)  In humans, the secondary oocyte completes its meiotic division when: (A) it is implanted (B) it is released from the Graafian follicle (C) it is penetrated by the sperm (D) acrosomal enzymes break the zona pellucida.  (2024)      Answer:  (C) When the sperm enters it.        Q15. (MCQ)  The foetal ejection reflex triggers release of ____ from ____. (A) oxytocin, foetal pituitary (B) oxytocin, maternal pituitary (C) hCG, placenta (D) progesterone, corpus luteum.  (2026; similar 2015 D)      Answer:  (B) Oxytocin, maternal pituitary.        Q16. (Assertion–Reason)  A: The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a morula. R: The morula continues to divide and transforms into trophoblast.  (2026)      Answer:  (C) A is true but R is false. (The morula becomes a  blastocyst ; trophoblast is only its outer layer.)        Q17. (Assertion–Reason)  A: Spermatogenesis is continuous throughout a man's reproductive life, while oogenesis is discontinuous. R: Oogenesis begins in the embryo, is arrested at prophase I, resumes after puberty, and is arrested again at metaphase II.  (SQP 26-27)      Answer:  (A) Both true, R is the correct explanation of A.        Q18. (2 marks)  List the male accessory ducts in order.  (2020 OD; 2019 OD diagram; 2024 case)      Answer:  Rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens (→ ejaculatory duct → urethra).        Q19. (3 marks)  Explain spermatogenesis and the roles of LH and FSH.  (2024 case, 2020 D)      Answer:  In seminiferous tubules: spermatogonia (2n) multiply by mitosis →  primary spermatocytes (2n)  → meiosis I →  secondary spermatocytes (n)  → meiosis II →  spermatids (n)  → change into  sperms  (spermiogenesis). At puberty the hypothalamus releases GnRH → pituitary releases  LH , which acts on  Leydig (interstitial) cells  to secrete androgens (testosterone) that stimulate spermatogenesis, and  FSH , which acts on  Sertoli cells  to secrete factors that help spermiogenesis.        Q20. (3–5 marks)  Describe the menstrual cycle phases.  (2016 OD, 2019 D, 2025, 2026, SQP 26-27 case)      Answer:       Menstrual phase (days 1–5):  endometrium breaks down and bleeds out; happens only if the ovum is not fertilised.    Follicular/proliferative phase (days ~5–13):  FSH and LH rise; primary follicles grow into a mature  Graafian follicle ; follicle secretes  estrogen , which rebuilds the endometrium.    Ovulation (about day 14):   LH surge  causes the Graafian follicle to rupture and release the ovum (secondary oocyte).    Luteal/secretory phase (days 15–28):  the empty follicle becomes the  corpus luteum , which secretes  progesterone  to keep the endometrium ready for implantation. If no fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates → progesterone falls → menstruation starts again. (SQP link: no clear LH surge → no ovulation → no corpus luteum → low progesterone → irregular, heavy bleeding; heavy bleeding can cause  anaemia .)          Q21. (3–5 marks)  Trace the journey of the zygote from the fallopian tube to implantation.  (2023 OD; similar 2024, 2025, 2026)      Answer:  Fertilisation occurs in the  ampullary region  of the fallopian tube. The zygote divides by mitosis ( cleavage ) as it moves through the isthmus towards the uterus → 2, 4, 8, 16 daughter cells ( blastomeres ). Embryo with 8–16 blastomeres =  morula . Morula becomes a  blastocyst : outer layer  trophoblast  + inner group of cells, the  inner cell mass . The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium; uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst → blastocyst gets embedded =  implantation  → pregnancy. Inner cell mass becomes the embryo; trophoblast helps in nutrition and implantation (SQP Q3).        Q22. (2 marks)  How is polyspermy prevented?  (2024 OR)      Answer:  When one sperm touches the zona pellucida of the ovum, changes occur in the zona pellucida that block the entry of other sperms.        Q23. (2 marks)  Why is breast-feeding recommended in the first months?  (2016 D, 2018 OD)      Answer:  The first milk,  colostrum , contains many antibodies (IgA) that give the baby passive immunity, and breast milk gives complete nutrition and builds a healthy baby.

title: Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health       Q24. (MCQ)  A man undergoes an operation in which a small part of the vas deferens is cut and tied. The direct result is: (A) sperm transport into ejaculatory duct and urethra is blocked (B) testosterone stops (C) seminal plasma stops (D) spermatogenesis stops.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2023 OD, 2023 D)      Answer:  (A). This is  vasectomy  (tubectomy is the similar operation in females).        Q25. (2 marks)  Name two copper-releasing IUDs and state how they work.  (2024; similar 2020 D)      Answer:  CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375 (any two). Cu ions reduce sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms; IUDs also increase phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus. (Hormone-releasing IUDs like Progestasert and LNG-20 also make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.)        Q26. (2 marks)  Why is "Saheli" preferred by women?  (2020 D)      Answer:  It is a non-steroidal pill taken  once a week , with very few side effects and high contraceptive value. (Developed by CDRI, Lucknow.)        Q27. (2 marks)  What is amniocentesis? Why is it banned for sex determination?  (2026; similar 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2025)      Answer:  A sample of amniotic fluid around the foetus is taken and tested to detect  genetic/chromosomal disorders  (such as Down's syndrome). It is legally banned for finding the sex of the foetus because this misuse leads to  female foeticide  (killing of normal female foetuses).        Q28. (2 marks)  Why does the government have strict conditions for MTP?  (2017 OD)      Answer:  To stop illegal, unsafe abortions and the misuse of MTP for female foeticide (sex-selective abortion). MTP is safest in the first trimester (up to 12 weeks).        Q29. (3 marks)  A woman has blocked fallopian tubes but her ovaries make normal ova. Her husband has a very low sperm count. Which ARTs will help?  (SQP 26-27; similar 2015 D, 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2023 OD, 2024)      Answer:  (1)  ICSI (Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection)  — a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum in the lab; solves the low sperm count. (2)  IVF followed by IUT (Intra Uterine Transfer)  — embryo made in the lab (with more than 8 blastomeres) is placed directly into the uterus; this by-passes the blocked fallopian tube.        Q30. (3 marks)  Expand and explain ZIFT, GIFT and IUI.  (2023 OD; similar 2019 D, 2024)      Answer:       ZIFT – Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer:  zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) made by IVF is put into the fallopian tube.    GIFT – Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer:  an ovum from a donor is put into the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova but can give a suitable environment for fertilisation.    IUI – Intra Uterine Insemination (artificial insemination):  semen from the husband or a healthy donor is placed into the uterus; used when the man has a low sperm count.          Q31. (2 marks)  Name any four STIs. Which of them are not completely curable?  (NCERT fact; not seen in the papers read — learn as a 2-mark backup)      Answer:  Gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis B, HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV infections are not completely curable.

title: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation       Q32. (MCQ)  A woman with normal vision has a colour-blind father. She marries a normal man. The chance of their children being colour blind is: (A) 25% (B) 50% (C) 75% (D) 100%.  (2024; similar 2025)      Answer:  (A) 25% of all children (= half of the sons; no daughters affected). Woman is a carrier XᶜX; man XY.        Q33. (2 marks)  You have a tall pea plant. How will you find its genotype?  (2019 D; similar 2015 D, 2016 OD, 2017 D, 2023 D)      Answer:  Do a  test cross : cross it with a dwarf (homozygous recessive, tt) plant.     If all offspring are tall → plant is  TT  (homozygous).   If tall : dwarf =  1 : 1  → plant is  Tt  (heterozygous).          Q34. (5 marks)  Compare inheritance of flower colour in garden pea (violet/white) and snapdragon (red/white) up to F2.  (2024, 2025, 2026; similar 2019 OD)      Answer:       Pea (complete dominance):  VV (violet) × vv (white) → F1 all  Vv violet . F1 selfed → F2: VV : Vv : vv = 1 : 2 : 1 (genotype), violet : white =  3 : 1  (phenotype). Violet is dominant.    Snapdragon/Antirrhinum (incomplete dominance):  RR (red) × rr (white) → F1 all  Rr pink . F2: RR red : Rr pink : rr white =  1 : 2 : 1  for both genotype and phenotype.    Conclusion:  In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully dominant, so F1 shows an intermediate character and the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio.          Q35. (3 marks)  A woman with blood group O marries a man with blood group AB. Work out the cross and explain the pattern.  (2019 D; similar 2015 D, 2025)      Answer:  Woman ii × Man IᴬIᴮ. Gametes: i and Iᴬ, Iᴮ. Children: Iᴬi (blood group A) and Iᴮi (blood group B) in 1 : 1. No child is O or AB. ABO blood groups show  multiple alleles  (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) and  co-dominance  (Iᴬ and Iᴮ both express in AB); i is recessive.        Q36. (3 marks)  Mice: running R > walking r; black B > brown b. Cross Rrbb female × RrBb male. Give the phenotypic ratio and number of running-black mice out of 64.  (SQP 26-27)      Answer:  Gametes: female Rb, rb; male RB, Rb, rB, rb. Results: running black 6/16, running brown 6/16, walking black 2/16, walking brown 2/16 →  3 : 3 : 1 : 1 . Running black = 6/16 × 64 =  24 .        Q37. (Assertion–Reason)  A: Tissue culture is used when traditional breeding cannot keep pace with demand. R: Totipotency is the ability of a single plant cell/explant to regenerate a whole plant under sterile conditions.  (SQP 26-27)      Answer:  (B) Both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (One-line extra: a virus-free plant is obtained by culturing the  meristem  (apical/axillary), which is free of virus — 2026.)        Q38. (Assertion–Reason)  A: When two genes in a dihybrid cross are on the same chromosome, parental combinations are much higher than non-parental. R: This is due to crossing over between the two genes.  (2025; similar SQP 26-27)      Answer:  (C) A is true, R is false. (High parental combinations are due to  linkage ; crossing over produces the non-parental recombinants.)        Q39. (3 marks)  Explain linkage and recombination from Morgan's work.  (2018 OD, 2019 OD, 2020 D)      Answer:  Morgan worked with  Drosophila melanogaster  (short life cycle ~2 weeks, many offspring, easy to grow, clear male/female differences, many visible variations). In dihybrid crosses for X-linked genes, F2 ratios differed greatly from 9:3:3:1. Genes on the same chromosome tend to stay together =  linkage ; new (non-parental) combinations formed by crossing over =  recombination . Tightly linked genes (yellow body and white eye) gave very low recombination (1.3%); loosely linked genes (white eye and miniature wing) gave higher recombination (37.2%). Sturtevant used recombination frequency to map gene positions on chromosomes.        Q40. (2 marks)  Explain sex determination in honeybees. Why does a male bee have 16 and a female 32 chromosomes?  (2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2020 OD)      Answer:   Haplodiploid  system: a fertilised egg becomes a female (queen or worker), diploid, 32 chromosomes; an unfertilised egg develops by  parthenogenesis  into a male (drone), haploid, 16 chromosomes. Drones produce sperms by  mitosis . Males have no father and cannot have sons, but have a grandfather.        Q41. (2 marks)  How is sex determined in birds and how is it different from humans?  (2018 OD; similar 2015 D)      Answer:  Birds: female is  ZW  (heterogametic, gives two types of eggs), male is  ZZ . Humans: male is  XY  (heterogametic, two types of sperms), female is  XX . So in birds the female decides the sex of the chick; in humans the father's sperm decides it.        Q42. (2 marks)  Why do males suffer from haemophilia more than females? Give two differences between haemophilia and sickle-cell anaemia.  (2020 OD, 2024; similar 2017 D)      Answer:  Haemophilia is  X-linked recessive . A male has only one X, so one defective allele makes him ill. A female needs the defective allele on both X chromosomes, which is very rare (mother carrier + father haemophilic). Differences: haemophilia is sex-linked, more males affected, blood does not clot (a clotting protein is missing); sickle-cell anaemia is  autosomal recessive , males and females equally affected, caused by glutamic acid → valine change at the 6th position of the β-globin chain (GAG → GUG), RBCs become sickle shaped.        Q43. (3 marks)  How does a single gene mutation cause phenylketonuria (PKU)? What is pleiotropy?  (SQP 26-27)      Answer:  PKU is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. The person lacks the enzyme that converts  phenylalanine to tyrosine . Phenylalanine accumulates and is changed into  phenylpyruvic acid  and other derivatives; their build-up in the brain causes mental retardation (they are also excreted in urine).  Pleiotropy:  one gene shows many phenotypic effects (here: mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation, etc.), because it affects a metabolic pathway.        Q44. (3 marks)  Chromosomal vs Mendelian disorders; describe Down's, Turner's and Klinefelter's syndromes.  (2026; similar 2017 OD, 2019 D, 2024, 2025)      Answer:  Mendelian disorder = change/mutation in a  single gene  (haemophilia, sickle cell, thalassemia, PKU, colour blindness). Chromosomal disorder = absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of  whole chromosomes , usually due to  non-disjunction  (failure of chromatids/chromosomes to separate in meiosis).      Down's syndrome:  trisomy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes). Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with a characteristic crease, retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development.    Klinefelter's syndrome:  44 + XXY (47). Overall masculine but with feminine development (breast development, gynaecomastia), sterile. (Formed when an XX egg is fertilised by a Y sperm.)    Turner's syndrome:  44 + XO (45). Female, sterile (rudimentary ovaries), lacks secondary sexual characters.

title: Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance       Q45. (MCQ)  A DNA molecule is 160 base pairs long and has 30% guanine. How many adenine bases? (A) 48 (B) 64 (C) 96 (D) 192.  (2026)      Answer:  (B) 64. Steps: 160 bp = 320 bases. G = 30%, so C = 30%. A + T = 40%, A = 20%. 20% of 320 = 64.        Q46. (MCQ)  E. coli grown in ¹⁵N medium is moved to ¹⁴N medium. DNA after 60 minutes (E. coli divides every 20 minutes) will be: (A) 25% hybrid, 75% light (B) 50%/50% (C) 75% hybrid, 25% light (D) 85%/15%.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2016 OD, 2016 D, 2020 OD)      Answer:  (A). Steps: 60 min = 3 generations. Gen 1: all hybrid; Gen 2: ½ hybrid ½ light; Gen 3: ¼ hybrid ¾ light. This proved  semi-conservative replication  (Meselson and Stahl, 1958, using CsCl density gradient centrifugation).        Q47. (MCQ)  A stretch of euchromatin has 200 nucleosomes. Number of base pairs? (one nucleosome ≈ 200 bp)  (SQP 26-27; similar 2025)      Answer:  200 × 200 =  40,000 bp  (MS option C: 40,000 bp and 13,600 × 10⁻⁹ m, using 0.34 nm per bp).        Q48. (3 marks)  Describe the nucleosome and differentiate euchromatin and heterochromatin.  (2025; similar 2016 D, 2017 OD)      Answer:  Histones are positively charged proteins (rich in lysine and arginine). 8 histone molecules form a  histone octamer . Negatively charged DNA wraps around it →  nucleosome  (about 200 bp of DNA). Nucleosomes look like "beads-on-string" under the electron microscope and coil further into chromatin fibres (non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins help).  Euchromatin  = loosely packed, stains light,  transcriptionally active .  Heterochromatin  = densely packed, stains dark, inactive.        Q49. (3 marks)  Explain Hershey and Chase's experiment.  (2015 D, 2019 D; MCQ 2023 OD)      Answer:  They used bacteriophages. Some phages were grown with  radioactive phosphorus ³²P  (labels DNA), others with  radioactive sulphur ³⁵S  (labels protein). (1)  Infection:  phages infected E. coli. (2)  Blending:  a blender removed the phage coats from bacteria. (3)  Centrifugation:  bacteria settled at the bottom; phage coats stayed in the supernatant. Bacteria infected with ³²P phage were radioactive; with ³⁵S phage were not. So  DNA, not protein, enters the bacteria — DNA is the genetic material .        Q50. (2 marks)  Why is DNA a better genetic material than RNA?  (2020 OD; A-R 2024, 2023 OD)      Answer:  RNA has a reactive  2'-OH  group in every nucleotide, so it is labile, easily degraded and mutates fast (RNA viruses evolve fast). DNA is chemically more stable (no 2'-OH; thymine instead of uracil), so it is better for storing genetic information. RNA is better for expressing characters (protein synthesis).        Q51. (3 marks)  Draw a replication fork and explain why replication occurs within a fork. Role of DNA ligase?  (2026; similar 2019 OD, 2019 D, 2016 D)      Answer:  (Diagram in Section 6.) The two DNA strands cannot be separated along the whole length at once because it needs very high energy, so replication happens in a small opening of the helix =  replication fork . DNA polymerase works only in the  5'→3' direction , so the template with 3'→5' polarity gives  continuous  synthesis (leading strand), and the template with 5'→3' polarity gives  discontinuous  synthesis (lagging strand, short fragments).  DNA ligase  joins these discontinuous fragments.        Q52. (2 marks)  Draw/describe a transcription unit. Where are the promoter and terminator?  (2019 D, 2019 OD; MCQ 2024, SQP 26-27)      Answer:  Transcription unit =  promoter + structural gene + terminator . The promoter is towards the  5' end (upstream)  of the structural gene (with reference to the coding strand); the terminator is towards the  3' end (downstream)  of the coding strand. The template strand has 3'→5' polarity; the coding strand has 5'→3' polarity and the same sequence as RNA (T in place of U). In bacteria, RNA polymerase uses the  sigma factor  to start and the  rho factor  to stop.        Q53. (3 marks)  Why must hnRNA be processed? Name the processes. Why is only one DNA strand transcribed?  (2026; similar 2017 D, 2023 OD)      Answer:  In eukaryotes the primary transcript (hnRNA) has both  exons  (coding) and  introns  (non-coding). (1)  Splicing  removes introns and joins exons. (2)  Capping : methyl guanosine triphosphate is added at the 5' end. (3)  Tailing : 200–300 adenylate residues (poly-A tail) are added at the 3' end. Then it is mRNA and goes to the cytoplasm. Only one strand is copied because (a) if both were copied, the two RNAs would be complementary and pair to form double-stranded RNA, so no protein would be made; (b) two different RNAs/proteins from the same DNA segment would make genetic information transfer complicated.        Q54. (2–3 marks)  Name the three RNA polymerases in eukaryotes and what each makes.  (2023 OD)      Answer:  RNA polymerase I → rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); RNA polymerase II → hnRNA (precursor of mRNA); RNA polymerase III → tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.        Q55. (2 marks)  When is the genetic code said to be (a) degenerate (b) universal? Also unambiguous?  (2020 D; similar 2016 OD, 2017 D, A-R 2025)      Answer:  (a)  Degenerate:  some amino acids are coded by more than one codon. (b)  Universal:  the same codon codes for the same amino acid in all organisms, from bacteria to humans (some exceptions in mitochondria and a few protozoans).  Unambiguous/specific:  one codon codes for only one amino acid. Other features: triplet; 61 codons for amino acids; 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG has a dual role (codes methionine and acts as the start codon); read without commas.        Q56. (3 marks)  Describe tRNA. Why is it called an adapter molecule?  (2017 D; similar 2024, 2023 OD)      Answer:  tRNA looks like a  clover leaf  (2-D); in 3-D it looks like an inverted L. It has an  anticodon loop  (bases complementary to the codon on mRNA) and an  amino acid acceptor end  (3' end) where a specific amino acid attaches (charging/aminoacylation, which uses ATP). It "reads" the code on mRNA and also carries the matching amino acid, so it is an  adapter  between nucleic acid and protein. Translation stops when a release factor binds the stop codon. UTRs (untranslated regions) are on mRNA at both the 5' end (before the start codon) and the 3' end (after the stop codon); they are needed for efficient translation.        Q57. (5 marks)  Explain the lac operon (with inducer and without inducer).  (2024 OR, 2025 OR)      Answer:  The lac operon of E. coli has a regulator gene  i  (makes repressor), a  promoter (p) , an  operator (o)  and 3 structural genes:  z  (β-galactosidase),  y  (permease),  a  (transacetylase).      No lactose (no inducer):  the repressor made by the i gene binds to the  operator  → RNA polymerase cannot transcribe → genes switched  off .    Lactose present (inducer):  lactose (allolactose) binds the repressor and inactivates it → repressor cannot bind the operator → RNA polymerase transcribes z, y, a → enzymes made → lactose is used. Genes switched  on .   It is called  negative regulation  because the operon is controlled by a repressor.          Q58. (3 marks)  Give four goals of the Human Genome Project (HGP). Name one non-human organism sequenced.  (2023 D; similar 2020 D, 2017 D)      Answer:  HGP began in 1990 and was completed in 2003. Goals (any four): identify all the ~20,000–25,000 genes in human DNA; find the sequence of the ~3 billion base pairs; store this information in databases; improve tools for data analysis; transfer related technologies to other sectors such as industries; address the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI). Non-human organisms sequenced: bacteria, yeast,  Caenorhabditis elegans ,  Drosophila , rice,  Arabidopsis  (any one).        Q59. (5 marks)  Describe DNA fingerprinting steps and uses.  (2023 D; similar 2015 D, 2017 OD, 2018 OD, 2024 OR)      Answer:  Technique (Alec Jeffreys) uses  VNTRs  (Variable Number of Tandem Repeats — a satellite DNA that differs from person to person) as probe. Steps: (1) isolate DNA; (2) digest DNA with  restriction endonucleases ; (3) separate fragments by  gel electrophoresis ; (4) transfer (blot) fragments to nitrocellulose/nylon membrane; (5)  hybridise  with a labelled VNTR probe; (6) detect bands by  autoradiography . Uses: forensic science (identify criminals, identify dead bodies after accidents),  paternity disputes , studying population and genetic diversity.

title: Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Chapter 6 — Evolution       Q60. (MCQ)  Select the odd one in the context of convergent evolution: (A) eyes of octopus and mammals (B) flippers of penguins and dolphins (C) flying squirrel and flying phalanger (D) thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita.  (2026)      Answer:  (D) — these are  homologous  (divergent evolution); the others are analogous/convergent.        Q61. (MCQ)  If the frequency of allele A is 0.6 in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of Aa is: (A) 0.21 (B) 0.42 (C) 0.48 (D) 0.32.  (2024)      Answer:  (C) 0.48. Steps: p = 0.6, q = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, Aa = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48.        Q62. (2–3 marks)  Explain p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Which factors disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?  (2015 OD, 2017 OD, 2018 OD; similar 2020 OD)      Answer:  Hardy-Weinberg principle: allele frequencies in a population stay constant from generation to generation (genetic equilibrium) if there is no disturbance. p = frequency of dominant allele A, q = frequency of recessive allele a, p + q = 1. Then p² = frequency of AA, 2pq = Aa, q² = aa, and p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Five factors change it:  gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, natural selection.         Q63. (2 marks)  Differentiate homologous and analogous organs with examples.  (2016 OD, 2018 OD; similar 2015 OD, 2020 OD, 2024)      Answer:   Homologous:  same basic structure and origin, different functions →  divergent evolution  (forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human; thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita; vertebrate hearts/brains).  Analogous:  different structure/origin, same function →  convergent evolution  (wings of butterfly and bird; eyes of octopus and mammals; flippers of penguin and dolphin; sweet potato (root) and potato (stem)).        Q64. (3 marks)  Explain industrial melanism as an example of natural selection.  (2023 D; similar 2015 D, 2017 OD)      Answer:  In England, before industrialisation (before 1850), tree trunks were covered by white lichens, so  white-winged moths  were hidden from predator birds and were more in number. After industrialisation, smoke and soot darkened the trunks and killed the lichens. Now  dark (melanic) moths  were hidden and survived, while white moths were eaten → dark moths became more common. Nature selected the better-adapted (fitter) form → natural selection.        Q65. (2 marks)  Explain adaptive radiation with an example.  (2015 D; similar SQP 26-27 continental drift)      Answer:  Evolution of different species from one ancestor, spreading into different habitats in one geographical area. Examples:  Darwin's finches  of the Galapagos (different beak types);  Australian marsupials , which evolved from one ancestral stock within the island continent. (SQP: due to continental drift, South American mammals were overridden by North American fauna when the continents joined; Australian marsupials survived because there was no competition from other mammals.)        Q66. (2 marks)  Write the order of human evolution and one feature each.  (2025 MCQ, 2023 D MCQ, 2019 OD, 2017 D)      Answer:  Dryopithecus/Ramapithecus (~15 mya, ape-like) → Australopithecines (~2 mya, East African grasslands, stone weapons, ate fruit) →  Homo habilis  (first human-like, brain 650–800 cc, probably did not eat meat) →  Homo erectus  (~1.5 mya, brain ~900 cc, probably ate meat) → Neanderthal man (brain ~1400 cc, used hides to protect the body and buried the dead) →  Homo sapiens .

title: Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease       Q67. (MCQ)  The vector of dengue fever is: (A) female Aedes (B) female Anopheles (C) male Aedes (D) female Culex.  (2024; similar 2018 OD)      Answer:  (A) Female  Aedes  mosquito (also spreads chikungunya).        Q68. (3 marks)  "Plasmodium needs both mosquito and human hosts." Explain its life cycle.  (2023 D; similar 2023 OD, 2025)      Answer:  Infected  female Anopheles  bites a human and injects  sporozoites  (infective stage). In the human: sporozoites multiply in  liver cells , then attack  red blood cells , multiply and burst them, releasing  haemozoin  — a toxin causing chill and high fever every 3–4 days. Some parasites form  gametocytes  in RBCs. When a female Anopheles sucks this blood, gametocytes enter it;  fertilisation and development  happen in the  mosquito's stomach (gut) ; sporozoites form and are stored in the mosquito's  salivary glands . So the asexual phase is in humans and the sexual phase in the mosquito.        Q69. (2 marks each — learn as a table)  Disease table.  (typhoid 2017 D, 2023 OD; amoebiasis 2016 D; filariasis 2026; ringworm, ascariasis NCERT)           Disease   Pathogen   Spread   Key symptoms           Typhoid    Salmonella typhi  (bacterium)   contaminated food/water   high fever 39–40°C, weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache; Widal test confirms       Pneumonia    Streptococcus pneumoniae ,  Haemophilus influenzae    droplets, sharing glasses   alveoli fill with fluid, fever, chills, cough; lips/nails turn grey-bluish       Common cold   Rhino viruses   droplets, contaminated objects   nasal congestion, sore throat, cough (nose & respiratory passage, not lungs)       Malaria    Plasmodium  (vivax, malariae, falciparum — most serious)   female  Anopheles    chill and high fever every 3–4 days       Amoebiasis    Entamoeba histolytica    houseflies (mechanical carriers) contaminate food/water   constipation, abdominal pain, cramps, stools with mucus and blood clots       Ascariasis    Ascaris  (roundworm)   eggs in soil, water, vegetables   internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, blocked intestine       Filariasis (elephantiasis)    Wuchereria bancrofti ,  W. malayi    bite of female mosquito (Culex)   chronic inflammation and swelling of lymphatic vessels of lower limbs; genitals may be deformed       Ringworm    Microsporum ,  Trichophyton ,  Epidermophyton  (fungi)   towels, combs, soil   dry scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp, intense itching; heat and moisture help them grow              Q70. (3 marks)  Differentiate active and passive immunity; humoral and cell-mediated immunity.  (2026, 2024; similar 2019 OD, 2022)      Answer:       Active immunity:  the body itself makes antibodies after meeting an antigen (infection or vaccine); slow to develop, long-lasting.    Passive immunity:  ready-made antibodies are given (colostrum IgA from mother; antitoxin for tetanus or snake bite); quick, short-lived.    Humoral immunity (antibody-mediated):   B-lymphocytes  make antibodies that circulate in blood/lymph.    Cell-mediated immunity (CMI):  done by  T-lymphocytes ; responsible for  graft (organ transplant) rejection . T-cells also help B-cells make antibodies.          Q71. (2 marks)  Why does a vaccinated child not get the disease? Why don't people get measles/chickenpox twice?  (2020 OD, 2016 OD, 2019 D)      Answer:  The vaccine (weakened/killed pathogen or its proteins) or first infection produces a  primary response  and also  memory B and T cells . On the next exposure, these memory cells quickly produce a massive  secondary (anamnestic) response  that destroys the pathogen before disease develops.        Q72. (2 marks)  Explain cytokine barriers and the role of the spleen.  (2018 OD, 2025; spleen 2026)      Answer:   Cytokine barrier:  virus-infected cells secrete proteins called  interferons , which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.  Spleen:  a large bean-shaped secondary lymphoid organ with lymphocytes and phagocytes; it filters blood by trapping blood-borne microorganisms and is also a large reservoir of erythrocytes.        Q73. (4 marks — case)  Which cells does HIV attack? What happens inside? Test used?  (2024 case; similar 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2020 D)      Answer:  HIV (a retrovirus with RNA) first enters  macrophages : the enzyme  reverse transcriptase  makes viral DNA from viral RNA; viral DNA joins the host cell's DNA and the infected cell makes new viruses (macrophage becomes an "HIV factory"). HIV then enters  helper T-lymphocytes (TH cells) , multiplies and kills them, so the number of helper T cells falls → immunodeficiency → the patient dies from other (opportunistic) infections such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and  Toxoplasma . Test:  ELISA (Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay) . Treatment: anti-retroviral drugs, only partly effective (prolong life). Prevention: screen blood, use disposable needles and syringes, safe sex/condoms, awareness (NACO).        Q74. (3 marks)  Differentiate addiction and dependence. Why does a user increase the dose over time? Also name the source of heroin.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2018 OD, 2020 D, 2024, 2025)      Answer:   Addiction  = psychological attachment to the "high"/euphoria of a drug, even when it is not needed.  Dependence  = the body's physical need for the drug; stopping it causes  withdrawal symptoms  (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating). Repeated use raises the  tolerance  of body receptors, so they respond only to higher doses. Heroin ("smack", diacetylmorphine) is made by  acetylation of morphine , which comes from the latex of the poppy  Papaver somniferum ; it is a depressant. Cannabinoids ( Cannabis sativa ) affect the cardiovascular system; cocaine ( Erythroxylum coca ) interferes with dopamine transport and is a stimulant.

title: Chapter 8 — Microbes in Human Welfare
text: Chapter 8 — Microbes in Human Welfare       Q75. (2–3 marks)  Name the microbe used for each product.  (2015 D, 2016 D, 2017 D, 2019 D, 2022, 2026, MCQ 2024)      Answer (learn this table):          Product   Microbe           Curd    Lactobacillus  (LAB) — also increases vitamin B12, checks disease-causing microbes in stomach       Bread, ethanol, wine, beer    Saccharomyces cerevisiae  (baker's/brewer's yeast)       Swiss cheese (large holes)    Propionibacterium sharmanii  — holes due to large amount of CO₂       Citric acid    Aspergillus niger  (fungus)       Acetic acid    Acetobacter aceti  (bacterium)       Butyric acid    Clostridium butylicum  (bacterium)       Lactic acid    Lactobacillus        Penicillin    Penicillium notatum  (Fleming; Chain and Florey showed its full use)       Streptokinase ("clot buster" for heart attack)    Streptococcus        Cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant for organ transplant)    Trichoderma polysporum  (fungus)       Statins (lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting the enzyme for cholesterol synthesis)    Monascus purpureus  (yeast)         Whisky, brandy, rum are made  with distillation ; wine and beer  without distillation  (2025).        Q76. (3 marks)  Explain secondary (biological) treatment of sewage. What is BOD?  (2017 D; similar 2015 OD, 2016 D, 2017 OD, 2019 OD, 2022)      Answer:  Primary effluent goes into large  aeration tanks , where it is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped in → useful aerobic microbes grow into  flocs  (masses of bacteria with fungal filaments). They consume most of the organic matter, so  BOD falls . The effluent then goes to a  settling tank , where flocs settle =  activated sludge . A small part is pumped back to the aeration tank as  inoculum ; the major part goes to  anaerobic sludge digesters , where anaerobic bacteria digest it and produce  biogas  (methane, hydrogen sulphide, CO₂). The treated effluent is released into rivers.  BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand)  = the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria; higher BOD = more polluted water. (SQP A-R: the aim of sewage treatment is to reduce organic matter; high BOD means  more , not less, organic matter.)        Q77. (2 marks)  Biogas: which microbes, where found, which institutes developed the technology?  (2023 OD; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD, 2022)      Answer:   Methanogens  (e.g.,  Methanobacterium ) grow anaerobically on cellulose and produce methane with CO₂ and H₂. Found in anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment and in the rumen of cattle (so cattle dung, "gobar", is used). The technology was developed in India mainly by  IARI (Indian Agricultural Research Institute)  and  KVIC (Khadi and Village Industries Commission) .        Q78. (3 marks)  Why are baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus) good biocontrol agents? Name other biocontrol agents and biofertilisers.  (SQP 26-27 case; similar 2016 OD, 2020 OD, 2022, 2023 D)      Answer:  Baculoviruses (genus  Nucleopolyhedrovirus ) attack insects and arthropods. They are  species-specific, narrow-spectrum  insecticides with  no negative effect  on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects — so they are ideal for  Integrated Pest Management (IPM)  and ecologically sensitive areas. Other biocontrol agents:  ladybird  (eats aphids),  dragonflies  (mosquitoes),   Bacillus thuringiensis   (spores sprayed on plants kill butterfly caterpillars — toxin is released in the larval gut),   Trichoderma   (free-living fungus in root ecosystems, controls plant pathogens). Biofertilisers:  Rhizobium  (root nodules of legumes, fixes N₂),  Azospirillum  and  Azotobacter  (free-living N₂ fixers),  mycorrhiza  such as   Glomus   (absorbs  phosphorus  from soil, gives resistance to root pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought — SQP Q12), cyanobacteria  Anabaena ,  Nostoc ,  Oscillatoria  (fix N₂ in paddy fields, add organic matter).

title: Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology       Q79. (MCQ)  Which is NOT a feature of plasmids? (A) circular (B) self-replicating (C) single-stranded (D) extra-chromosomal.  (2024)      Answer:  (C) Plasmids are double-stranded.        Q80. (Assertion–Reason)  A: Chitinase is needed to separate DNA from yeast cells but not from  Spirogyra . R: Fungal cell wall is made of chitin.  (2026; similar 2024, SQP 26-27)      Answer:  (A) Both true, R explains A. (Use  lysozyme  for bacteria,  cellulase  for plant/algal cells,  chitinase  for fungi.)        Q81. (3 marks)  Explain naming of restriction enzymes and formation of recombinant DNA using EcoRI.  (2019 D; similar 2017 D, 2019 OD, 2020 OD, 2025)      Answer:   EcoRI:  E = genus  Escherichia , co = species  coli , R = strain RY13, I = first enzyme isolated from this strain. Restriction endonucleases recognise a  palindromic sequence  (reads the same on both strands in the 5'→3' direction), e.g. EcoRI site: 5'–GAATTC–3' 3'–CTTAAG–5' EcoRI cuts between G and A on both strands, a little away from the centre, leaving single-stranded overhangs =  sticky ends . If the vector and the foreign DNA are cut with the  same enzyme , they have matching sticky ends, which pair by hydrogen bonds;  DNA ligase  then seals them →  recombinant DNA .        Q82. (3 marks)  In pBR322, state the role of ori, ampR/tetR, rop and restriction sites. Explain insertional inactivation.  (2020 OD, 2024, 2026 case; similar 2016 OD, 2019 D, 2023 OD, SQP 26-27)      Answer:   ori  — origin of replication; any DNA linked to it can replicate in the host and it controls the  copy number .  ampR and tetR  — antibiotic-resistance genes (ampicillin, tetracycline) used as  selectable markers  to identify transformants.  rop  — codes for proteins involved in replication of the plasmid.  Restriction sites  — single sites (EcoRI, HindIII, ClaI, PvuII, BamHI, SalI, PstI, PvuI) where foreign DNA can be inserted. (BamHI and SalI are in tetR; PstI and PvuI in ampR; PvuII in rop.)  Insertional inactivation:  foreign DNA is inserted into one marker gene, e.g., tetR at BamHI — that gene stops working. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but  not  on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both. Easier method: insert the foreign DNA into the  β-galactosidase  gene — recombinants give  colourless/white  colonies; non-recombinants give  blue  colonies on a chromogenic substrate.        Q83. (2 marks)  How are bacteria made competent? Name two vector-less methods of gene transfer.  (2026, 2024; similar 2016 OD, 2025)      Answer:  DNA is hydrophilic and cannot pass cell membranes. Bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation,  calcium (Ca²⁺) , then placed on  ice , given a  heat shock (42°C)  and put back on ice → recombinant DNA enters. Vector-less methods:  microinjection  (DNA injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell);  biolistics/gene gun  (plant cells bombarded with high-velocity gold or tungsten micro-particles coated with DNA).        Q84. (3 marks)  Explain gel electrophoresis.  (2025; similar 2016 D, 2017 OD, 2024)      Answer:  DNA fragments are  negatively charged , so in an electric field they move towards the  anode  through  agarose gel  (from seaweed). The gel acts as a sieve:  smaller fragments move farther . Separated DNA is stained with  ethidium bromide  and seen as bright  orange bands under UV light . The bands are cut out and the DNA extracted ( elution ), then used to make recombinant DNA by joining with cloning vectors, in DNA fingerprinting, etc.        Q85. (3 marks)  Describe PCR. Role of Taq polymerase?  (2017 D; similar 2015 OD, 2016 D, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2023 OD)      Answer:  PCR = Polymerase Chain Reaction, used to make many copies of a gene in vitro. Each cycle: (1)  Denaturation  — high temperature separates the two DNA strands. (2)  Annealing  — two sets of  primers  (small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides) bind to complementary regions. (3)  Extension  — DNA polymerase extends the primers using nucleotides. Repeating ~30 times amplifies the DNA about  1 billion times .  Taq polymerase  is a  thermostable  DNA polymerase from the bacterium   Thermus aquaticus  ; it stays active at the high temperature of denaturation, so new enzyme need not be added in every cycle.        Q86. (2 marks)  Why are bioreactors used? Describe a stirred-tank bioreactor.  (2018 OD; similar 2015 D, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2025)      Answer:  Bioreactors (100–1000 litres) allow large-scale production of products by providing optimum growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen).  Stirred-tank  bioreactor: usually cylindrical with a curved base for mixing; a  stirrer  mixes contents evenly and increases oxygen availability; in the  sparged  type, sterile air is bubbled in. It also has a foam-control system, temperature and pH control, and sampling ports. (SQP: a fall in yield due to contamination is prevented by  sterile handling, sterilised equipment and aseptic transfer .)        Q87. (3 marks)  How was human insulin made by rDNA technology?  (2015 OD, 2015 D, 2017 D; similar 2018 OD, 2020 OD)      Answer:  Insulin has two short chains,  A and B , joined by  disulphide bridges . In the body it is made as  pro-insulin , which has an extra stretch, the  C-peptide , that is removed to make mature insulin. In 1983  Eli Lilly  prepared two DNA sequences for chains A and B, introduced them into  plasmids of E. coli , produced the chains separately, extracted them and combined them by creating disulphide bonds → human insulin ( Humulin ). It avoids allergy/reactions caused by insulin from cattle or pigs.        Q88. (2–3 marks)  Explain gene therapy for ADA deficiency. Why is periodic infusion needed?  (2025; similar 2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2019 OD)      Answer:   Adenosine deaminase (ADA)  is needed for the immune system; its deficiency (deletion of the ADA gene) causes immunodeficiency. In 1990 a 4-year-old girl was treated: her  lymphocytes  were grown in culture, a functional  ADA cDNA  was introduced into them using a  retroviral vector , and the cells were returned to her body. These lymphocytes are  not immortal , so periodic infusion is needed. Permanent cure: introduce the ADA gene isolated from bone-marrow cells into cells at  early embryonic stages . (Other options: bone-marrow transplant, enzyme replacement therapy — injecting functional ADA.)        Q89. (3 marks)  How was Bt cotton made pest resistant? Why does the Bt toxin not kill the bacterium?  (2023 D; similar 2017 D, 2017 OD, 2020 D, 2020 OD, 2022, 2024 OR)      Answer:   Bacillus thuringiensis  makes  Bt toxin  protein crystals that kill certain insects (lepidopterans like bollworms, coleopterans, dipterans). The toxin exists as an  inactive protoxin , so the bacterium is not harmed. When an insect eats it, the  alkaline pH of the insect gut  dissolves the crystals and activates the toxin; the active toxin binds to the surface of  midgut epithelial cells , makes  pores , cells swell and burst (lyse) → insect dies. The toxin is coded by   cry   genes;  cryIAc and cryIIAb  control cotton bollworms,  cryIAb  controls corn borer. These genes were introduced into cotton → Bt cotton.        Q90. (3 marks)  How was tobacco made resistant to the nematode  Meloidegyne incognitia ?  (2024; similar 2016 D, 2018 OD, 2023 OD, MCQ 2025, SQP 26-27)      Answer:  The nematode infects tobacco  roots  and reduces yield. Using   Agrobacterium   vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into tobacco so that the plant made both  sense and anti-sense RNA . These two complementary RNAs formed  double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) , which started  RNA interference (RNAi) : it  silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode  (stopped its translation). So the parasite could not survive in the transgenic plant.        Q91. (3 marks)  List benefits of GM plants. Give uses of transgenic animals.  (2016 D, 2019 OD, 2020 D, 2026; similar 2015 OD)      Answer:  GM plants: (1) more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat); (2) less use of chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops); (3) fewer post-harvest losses; (4) better use of minerals by plants (prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility); (5) more nutritional value — e.g.,  Golden rice , rich in vitamin A. Transgenic animals: study of normal physiology and development; study of diseases; biological products (e.g.,  α-1-antitrypsin  for emphysema; transgenic cow  Rosie  (1997) gave human-protein-enriched milk, 2.4 g/L α-lactalbumin); vaccine safety testing (e.g., polio vaccine on transgenic mice); chemical safety (toxicity) testing.        Q92. (1–2 marks)  What is biopiracy? What is GEAC?  (2015 D, 2016 OD, 2017 OD; MCQ 2025)      Answer:   Biopiracy  = use of bio-resources (and traditional knowledge) of a country by multinational companies or other organisations without proper authorisation from, or compensation to, the countries and people concerned (e.g., an American company got a patent on Basmati rice in 1997).  GEAC = Genetic Engineering Approval Committee  (Indian government body that decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public use).

title: Chapter 11 — Organisms and Populations
text: Chapter 11 — Organisms and Populations       Q93. (MCQ)  An interaction where one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited: (A) mycorrhiza (B) sea anemone and clownfish (C) Abingdon tortoise and goats (D) Cuscuta on hedge plants.  (2026)      Answer:  (B) Commensalism.        Q94. (3 marks — learn as a table)  Population interactions with examples.  (2016 OD, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2023 OD, 2024, 2026; SQP 26-27)           Interaction   Sign   Example           Mutualism   + / +   lichen (fungus + alga); mycorrhiza (fungus + plant roots); fig tree and wasp; orchid  Ophrys  and bee (pseudocopulation); plant and pollinator       Competition   − / −   Abingdon tortoise and goats in Galapagos (tortoises became extinct)       Predation   + / −   tiger–deer; Monarch butterfly is distasteful to predators due to a chemical it gets as a caterpillar by feeding on a poisonous weed       Parasitism   + / −    Cuscuta  on hedge plants;  brood parasitism  — cuckoo (koel) lays eggs in a crow's nest; eggs look similar, so the crow incubates them       Commensalism   + / 0   orchid growing on a mango branch; barnacles on whale; cattle egret and grazing cattle; sea anemone and clownfish       Amensalism   − / 0   one harmed, other unaffected          Gause's competitive exclusion principle (2026):  two closely related species competing for the same limited resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the competitively inferior one is eliminated. (MacArthur's warblers coexist by  resource partitioning  — feeding in different parts of the tree.)  Plant defence (2023 D):  cattle and goats do not browse  Calotropis  because it makes highly poisonous  cardiac glycosides . Other plants have thorns (Acacia, cactus) as mechanical defence.  Positive roles of predators (2024):  pass energy across trophic levels; keep prey populations under control (prickly pear cactus in Australia was controlled by a cactus-feeding moth); maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey (removing the starfish  Pisaster  led to extinction of more than 10 invertebrate species).        Q95. (3 marks)  Name population attributes, draw age pyramids and give growth equations.  (2017 OD, 2020 OD, 2022, 2025; similar 2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2017 D, 2019 D)      Answer:  Attributes of a population (not of an individual):  birth rate (natality), death rate (mortality), sex ratio, age distribution . Age pyramids:  expanding  (triangular — many young, growing population),  stable  (bell-shaped),  declining  (urn-shaped — fewer young). Density measured by counting, per cent cover,  pug marks and fecal pellets  (tigers), catch per trap (fish). Growth: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. Exponential growth dN/dt = rN gives a  J-shaped  curve (unlimited resources). Logistic growth dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K] gives an  S-shaped (sigmoid)  curve;  K = carrying capacity . r = intrinsic rate of natural increase. Example (2025): if density at t + 1 = 800, natality 200, immigration 200, mortality 150, emigration 100 → 800 = Nₜ + (200 + 200) − (150 + 100) →  Nₜ = 650 . Example (2019 D): 100 frogs, 20 born in a year → birth rate = 20/100 =  0.2 offspring per frog per year .

title: Chapter 12 — Ecosystem
text: Chapter 12 — Ecosystem       Q96. (2 marks)  Differentiate GPP and NPP. Calculate NPP when GPP = 3500 and R = 1300 g/m²/year.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2025, 2017 D, 2015 D)      Answer:   GPP (gross primary productivity)  = rate of production of organic matter in photosynthesis.  NPP  = GPP − R (respiration losses); it is the biomass available to consumers (herbivores and decomposers). NPP = 3500 − 1300 =  2200 g/m²/year . Productivity is expressed in g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹.        Q97. (5 marks)  Explain the steps of decomposition and factors affecting it.  (SQP 26-27 OR; similar 2020 D, 2024, A-R 2023 D, MCQ 2025)      Answer:  (1)  Fragmentation  — detritivores (earthworm, termites) break detritus into small particles. (2)  Leaching  — water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil and get precipitated as unavailable salts. (3)  Catabolism  — bacterial and fungal enzymes break detritus into simple inorganic substances. (4)  Humification  — forms  humus , dark amorphous material, highly resistant to microbial action, decomposes very slowly; it is a reservoir of nutrients. (5)  Mineralisation  — humus is further broken by microbes to release inorganic nutrients. Factors: decomposition is  slow  if detritus is rich in  lignin and chitin , fast if rich in  nitrogen and water-soluble sugars ;  warm and moist  conditions speed it up; low temperature, dryness and anaerobic conditions slow it.        Q98. (2–3 marks)  Differentiate grazing and detritus food chains. Why is the pyramid of biomass in the sea inverted? Limitations of ecological pyramids?  (2026; MCQ 2024)      Answer:   GFC  starts from green plants (producers), energy source is the sun (grass → goat → man).  DFC  starts from dead organic matter, with decomposers (fungi, bacteria — saprotrophs). In aquatic ecosystems GFC carries more energy; in terrestrial ecosystems more energy flows through DFC. Sea: biomass of fishes is  more  than that of phytoplankton (which reproduce fast but are small) →  inverted  biomass pyramid. The pyramid of  energy is always upright . Limitations: (1) does not consider the same species at two or more trophic levels; (2) assumes a simple food chain, not a food web; (3) saprophytes/decomposers are not given any place.

title: Chapter 13 — Biodiversity and its Conservation
text: Chapter 13 — Biodiversity and its Conservation       Q99. (MCQ)  Which fish led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in Lake Victoria? (A) Catla (B) Dogfish (C) Nile perch (D) African catfish.  (2026)      Answer:  (C) Nile perch.        Q100. (3 marks)  Explain the three levels of biodiversity with examples.  (2026; similar 2016 D, 2018 OD)      Answer:   Genetic diversity  — variation within a species:  Rauwolfia vomitoria  in the Himalaya differs in potency/concentration of reserpine; India has more than 50,000 strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.  Species diversity  — variety of species: the Western Ghats have more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats.  Ecological diversity  — variety of ecosystems: India has deserts, rainforests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, so it has more ecosystem diversity than Norway.        Q101. (4–5 marks)  Explain the causes of biodiversity loss ("Evil Quartet").  (SQP 26-27; similar 2017 OD, 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2025)      Answer:       Habitat loss and fragmentation  — most important cause; e.g., tropical rainforests once covered 14% of Earth's land, now only 6%; the Amazon is being cleared for soybean and cattle ranches. Fragmentation hurts animals that need large territories and migratory animals.    Over-exploitation  — e.g., Steller's sea cow and passenger pigeon became extinct due to over-exploitation by humans; many marine fish are over-harvested.    Alien species invasions  — Nile perch in Lake Victoria (200+ cichlid species lost); carrot grass ( Parthenium ),  Lantana  and water hyacinth ( Eichhornia ); African catfish  Clarias gariepinus  threatens native catfishes in Indian rivers.    Co-extinctions  — when a species becomes extinct, plants and animals obligately linked to it also become extinct (e.g., a host fish and its parasites; plant–pollinator mutualism). IUCN Red List (2004):  784 species  became extinct in the last 500 years ( 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, 87 plants ). Recent extinctions: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia), three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian).          Q102. (3–5 marks)  Explain in-situ and ex-situ conservation. What are hotspots and sacred groves?  (2016 D, 2017 OD, 2019 OD, 2025; similar 2015 OD, 2019 D, MCQ 2023 OD)      Answer:   In-situ (on site):  protect species in their natural habitat —  biodiversity hotspots  (regions with very high species richness and high  endemism ; 34 in the world; India has 3 that also cover neighbouring countries:  Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya ; hotspots cover less than 2% of the earth's land area), protected areas like  biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries , and  sacred groves  (forest patches protected by tribal communities for religious reasons — Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of MP/Chhattisgarh). Note: Jaintia Hills are a sacred grove area,  not  a hotspot (2023 OD MCQ).  Ex-situ (off site):  threatened species taken out of the habitat and protected in  zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks , and by  cryopreservation  of gametes, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture, and  seed banks .  IUCN Red Data List  records threatened and extinct species and helps decide conservation priorities.        Q103. (3 marks)  Why should we conserve biodiversity?  (2023 D; similar 2016 D)      Answer:  (1)  Narrowly utilitarian:  humans get food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicines (more than 25% of drugs sold come from plants);  bioprospecting  looks for useful products. (2)  Broadly utilitarian:  ecosystem services — the Amazon forest produces about 20% of the Earth's oxygen through photosynthesis; pollination by bees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasure. (3)  Ethical:  every species has an intrinsic value; we have a moral duty to care for them and pass them on to future generations.    Total: 103 questions in this bank (well above the minimum of 60).

title: 6. Quick revision sheet
text: 6. Quick revision sheet

title: 6.1 Key one-liners (high-frequency 1-mark facts)
text: 6.1 Key one-liners (high-frequency 1-mark facts)      Embryo sac: 7 cells, 8 nuclei. Filiform apparatus of synergids guides the pollen tube.   Pollen exine =  sporopollenin  (most resistant organic material; absent at germ pores). Intine = cellulose + pectin.   Tapetum = innermost anther wall layer; nourishes developing pollen.   Endosperm 3n; zygote/embryo 2n; perisperm = remains of nucellus (black pepper, beet).   Coconut: coconut water = free-nuclear endosperm; white kernel = cellular endosperm.   Fertilisation in humans: ampullary region of the fallopian tube. Implantation: blastocyst in endometrium.   hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens = hormones of pregnancy (placenta); relaxin (ovary) in later pregnancy. Parturition: oxytocin.   MTP Act: India legalised MTP in 1971 (amended later). Saheli: CDRI Lucknow, once a week.   Mendel: 7 pairs of traits in garden pea. Monohybrid F2 3:1, dihybrid 9:3:3:1, test cross 1:1.   Chromosomal theory of inheritance: Sutton and Boveri. Linkage: Morgan. Gene mapping: Sturtevant.   Colour blindness ~8% males, 0.4% females. Sickle cell: GAG → GUG (Glu → Val), 6th position of β-globin.   Thalassemia: α type — HBA1, HBA2 on chromosome 16; β type — HBB on chromosome 11. Too few globin chains (quantitative problem).   DNA: Watson & Crick (1953), using X-ray data of Wilkins and Franklin. Chargaff: A = T, G ≡ C. 0.34 nm between bp, 10 bp per turn (3.4 nm). Human haploid DNA 3.3 × 10⁹ bp; E. coli 4.6 × 10⁶ bp.   Griffith (1928) — transformation (Streptococcus pneumoniae, S and R strains). Avery, MacLeod, McCarty (1944) — DNA is the transforming principle. Hershey–Chase (1952) — ³²P / ³⁵S.   Meselson & Stahl (1958) — semi-conservative replication, ¹⁵N, CsCl.   Genetic code: George Gamow (triplet), Har Gobind Khorana (chemical synthesis of RNA with defined bases), Marshall Nirenberg (cell-free system), Severo Ochoa (polynucleotide phosphorylase).   HGP: 1990–2003; total bases 3164.7 million; average gene ~3000 bases; largest gene dystrophin (2.4 million bases); less than 2% codes for proteins; 99.9% bases same in all people; chromosome 1 has most genes (2968), Y fewest (231); ~1.4 million SNPs. Methods: ESTs (Expressed Sequence Tags) and sequence annotation; vectors BAC and YAC.   Miller (1953): CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800°C with electric discharge → amino acids.   Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1.   Types of natural selection: stabilising (mean favoured), directional (one extreme favoured — giraffe long neck, SQP), disruptive (both extremes favoured).   Lymphoid organs: primary — bone marrow, thymus; secondary — spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix; MALT (~50% of lymphoid tissue, lining of respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts).   Antibody = H₂L₂ (2 heavy + 2 light chains). Types: IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG. Allergy: IgE, mast cells release histamine and serotonin.   Cancer detection: biopsy and histopathology, X-ray, CT, MRI; treatment: surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy (α-interferon). Benign tumours stay in place; malignant tumours spread (metastasis).   First rDNA: Cohen and Boyer (1972), using a plasmid of  Salmonella typhimurium . First restriction enzyme: Hind II.   Retroviruses → animal vectors; Ti plasmid of  Agrobacterium tumefaciens  → plant vector (both "disarmed").   India: 2.4% of world land, 8.1% of global species diversity; one of 12 mega-diversity countries.   Species–area relationship (Humboldt): log S = log C + Z log A; Z ≈ 0.1–0.2 (small areas), 0.6–1.2 (very large areas/continents).   Earth Summit Rio (1992); World Summit Johannesburg (2002).

title: 6.2 Simple formulas / calculations
text: 6.2 Simple formulas / calculations      NPP = GPP − R.   Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)].   Birth rate = number born ÷ starting population (per unit time).   Exponential: dN/dt = rN. Logistic: dN/dt = rN (K − N)/K.   DNA base %: A = T, G = C, A + G = 50%.   Meselson–Stahl: after n generations in ¹⁴N, hybrid fraction = 2/2ⁿ (gen 1: 100%, gen 2: 50%, gen 3: 25%).   Nucleosome ≈ 200 bp; DNA length = bp × 0.34 nm.   Hardy-Weinberg: q = √(frequency of recessive phenotype aa); p = 1 − q; carriers = 2pq.

title: 6.3 Diagrams most asked — what to draw and label
text: 6.3 Diagrams most asked — what to draw and label    Draw neatly in pencil, label on the right side with straight lines, and give a heading.      Mature embryo sac  (2017 OD, 2019 D, 2020 D, 2023 D, 2023 OD): oval sac. Micropylar end (bottom):  filiform apparatus ,  2 synergids ,  egg cell . Middle: large  central cell  with  2 polar nuclei . Chalazal end (top):  3 antipodal cells .    T.S. of mature anther  (2020 OD): four pollen sacs (tetrasporangiate) around a central  connective . From outside in:  epidermis ,  endothecium ,  middle layers  (2–3),  tapetum  (innermost), and  sporogenous tissue/microspores (pollen grains)  in the centre of each sac.    Pollen grain (2-celled) : outer  exine  with  germ pores , inner  intine , large  vegetative cell  with its nucleus, small  generative cell .    Dicot embryo / monocot seed (L.S. of maize grain)  (2019 D, 2023 D MCQ): Dicot embryo —  plumule ,  cotyledons ,  hypocotyl ,  radicle ,  root cap ,  suspensor . Maize grain —  pericarp (fruit wall + seed coat) ,  endosperm ,  aleurone layer ,  scutellum  (single cotyledon),  coleoptile  around plumule,  coleorhiza  around radicle,  epiblast .    Human male reproductive system / accessory ducts  (2019 OD, 2023 OD MCQ): testis →  rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens  → ejaculatory duct →  urethra ; glands:  seminal vesicle, prostate, bulbourethral gland ; also urinary bladder, penis, scrotum.    Sectional view of seminiferous tubule  (2017 OD, 2019 D):  spermatogonia  (at outer wall),  primary spermatocyte ,  secondary spermatocyte ,  spermatids ,  sperms  (in lumen),  Sertoli cells ; outside the tubule:  interstitial (Leydig) cells  and blood vessels.    Human sperm  (2018 OD):  acrosome  (enzymes to enter ovum),  head/nucleus  (haploid DNA),  neck ,  middle piece with mitochondria  (energy for movement),  tail  (movement), plasma membrane.    Sectional view of ovary  (2019 OD OR):  primary follicle ,  secondary follicle ,  tertiary follicle  (with  antrum ),  Graafian follicle ,  ovum/secondary oocyte ,  ovulation (ruptured follicle) ,  corpus luteum , blood vessels.    Blastocyst / human embryo  (2023 OD, 2026):  trophoblast  (outer layer),  inner cell mass ,  blastocoel ; implantation in  endometrium .    Menstrual cycle graph  (2023 OD, 2025, 2026): x-axis days 1–28; LH and FSH peak around  day 14  (ovulation); estrogen rises before ovulation;  progesterone  high in luteal phase (days 15–28); endometrium thickest in luteal phase; menstruation days 1–5.    DNA replication fork  (2019 OD, 2026): parental helix opening;  leading strand  (continuous, 5'→3' towards the fork),  lagging strand  (discontinuous fragments, joined by  DNA ligase ); mark  3'  and  5'  ends on every strand; label  DNA polymerase .    Transcription unit  (2019 D, 2019 OD, SQP):  promoter  (upstream),  structural gene ,  terminator  (downstream),  template strand (3'→5') ,  coding strand (5'→3') ; in bacteria:  RNA polymerase, sigma factor (σ)  at start,  rho factor (ρ)  at end.    tRNA (clover leaf)  (2017 D, SQP 31B):  anticodon loop  (bottom),  amino acid acceptor end  (3' end, CCA),  T loop ,  D loop , variable loop.    Lac operon  (2024, 2025): genes in order  i – p – o – z – y – a ;  repressor  bound to  operator  (switched off);  inducer (lactose)  binding repressor → RNA polymerase moves → mRNA →  β-galactosidase, permease, transacetylase  (switched on).    pBR322  (2019 D, 2024, 2026): circle with  ori ,  rop ,  ampR ,  tetR ; restriction sites  EcoRI, ClaI, HindIII  (near top),  BamHI, SalI  in tetR,  PvuII  in rop,  PstI, PvuI  in ampR.    Antibody molecule  (2024, 2026): Y shape;  2 heavy chains ,  2 light chains ,  antigen-binding sites  at the tips,  disulphide bonds (S–S) , variable and constant regions.    HIV replication in host cell  (2020 D):  viral RNA  → ( reverse transcriptase ) →  viral DNA  → integrates into  host DNA  → new viral RNA and proteins → new viruses bud out; host cell = macrophage / helper T-cell.    Plasmodium life cycle  (2023 OD, 2025): mosquito bite →  sporozoites  →  liver cells  →  RBCs  (rupture,  haemozoin ) →  gametocytes  → mosquito  stomach (fertilisation)  → sporozoites in  salivary glands .    Biogas plant  (if asked):  dung + water slurry inlet ,  digester (sludge) ,  gas holder/floating cover ,  gas outlet ,  spent slurry outlet .    Age pyramids  (2016 D, 2017 OD, 2020 OD): three shapes —  expanding  (wide base),  stable  (bell),  declining  (narrow base, urn); bars for pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive ages.    Growth curves  (2020 OD, 2022):  J-shaped  (exponential) and  S-shaped/sigmoid  (logistic) with dotted line  K (carrying capacity) ; x-axis time, y-axis population density (N).    Pyramids  (2024, 2026): pyramid of numbers (grassland upright; tree inverted), biomass (sea inverted), energy (always upright).    Pie chart of vertebrate diversity  (2024): largest share  fishes , then  birds ,  reptiles ,  amphibians ,  mammals  (smallest).

title: 6.4 Practical viva quick answers
text: 6.4 Practical viva quick answers       Pollen germination:  sucrose (or sugar) + boric acid solution; pollen tube grows in a few minutes; seen under microscope.    Onion root tip mitosis:  fix in Carnoy's/acetic-alcohol, hydrolyse with dilute HCl (to soften), stain with  acetocarmine ; stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase; root tip is used because it is a meristem (cells divide actively).    Quadrat method:  density = total number of individuals ÷ number of quadrats studied; frequency (%) = (number of quadrats in which the species occurs ÷ total quadrats) × 100.    DNA isolation from spinach/banana/peas:  crush with salt + detergent (breaks membranes) → filter → add enzyme (meat tenderiser = protease) → add  chilled ethanol  → DNA appears as white threads, spooled on a glass rod.    Emasculation, bagging, tagging  — see Q9. Tagging = label with date and parents' names.

title: 7. Answer-writing tips and 30-day timetable

title: 7.1 How to grab step marks
text: 7.1 How to grab step marks       Write the keyword.  Marking schemes give marks for key words: "filiform apparatus", "triple fusion", "inactive protoxin", "alkaline pH", "sticky ends", "selectable marker", "insertional inactivation", "semi-conservative", "memory cells". Underline them.    2-mark answers = 2 points; 3-mark answers = 3 points.  Number your points. Don't write a story.    Draw whenever possible.  A labelled diagram often gets marks even if the explanation is weak. Even in a non-diagram question, a small sketch of a cross or a flow chart helps.    Crosses:  always write Parents → Gametes → Punnett square → F1/F2 → Ratio (phenotype and genotype). Each step carries marks.    Numericals (productivity, DNA bases, population):  write the formula first, then put values, then the answer with units.    Differences:  use a 2-column table with the same "basis" in each row.    Scientific names:  first letter capital for genus, underline (e.g.,  Bacillus thuringiensis ). Spell them correctly — learn the 15 names in Q69, Q75, Q78.    Assertion–Reason:  first decide if A is true, then if R is true, then check "because". If A is false, the answer is D (if R is true) — don't overthink.    Case-based questions (Section D):  answers are usually in the passage or are basic NCERT facts. Never leave them blank.    Attempt all 33 questions.  Start with Section A (16 marks). Then do the chapters you studied in Sections B–E. In internal choices, pick the option from your strong chapter.    Time:  Section A — 20 min; B — 20 min; C — 45 min; D — 20 min; E — 45 min; revise — 15 min.
