title: Q1 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q1. (MCQ)  In a plant, the pistil matures several days before the stamens in all flowers. The most important result is that it: (A) guarantees self-pollination (B) promotes autogamy (C) ensures cross-pollination (D) leads to geitonogamy.  (SQP 26-27)     Answer:  (C) It ensures cross-pollination.

title: Q2 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q2. (MCQ)  An angiosperm embryo sac is located within the: (A) placenta (B) megasporangium (C) nucellus (D) ovary.  (2024)     Answer:  (C) Nucellus.

title: Q3 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q3. (MCQ)  An anther has 50 microspore mother cells and the ovary has 50 megaspore mother cells. Number of pollen grains and ovules likely formed: (A) 100, 25 (B) 200, 50 (C) 50, 50 (D) 200, 100.  (2025)     Answer:  (B) 200, 50. (Each microspore mother cell → 4 pollen grains by meiosis; each megaspore mother cell → only 1 functional megaspore → 1 embryo sac.)

title: Q4 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q4. (2 marks)  A mature embryo sac has 7 cells but 8 nuclei. Explain.  (2017 OD; similar 2019 D, 2020 D, 2023 D)     Answer:  The functional megaspore divides 3 times (free nuclear mitosis) → 8 nuclei. 3 nuclei at the micropylar end form the egg apparatus (2 synergids + 1 egg cell); 3 at the chalazal end form 3 antipodal cells; the remaining 2 nuclei (polar nuclei) stay together in one large central cell. So: 3 + 3 + 1 central cell = 7 cells, 8 nuclei.

title: Q5 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q5. (3 marks)  Explain the monosporic development of the embryo sac.  (2023 D; similar 2020 D)     Answer:  (1) The megaspore mother cell (MMC, 2n) in the nucellus undergoes meiosis → 4 haploid megaspores. (2) 3 megaspores degenerate; only 1 is functional — so it is called  monosporic  development. (3) The functional megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis 3 times (free nuclear, no walls) → 2, 4, 8 nuclei; then cell walls form → 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac (female gametophyte).

title: Q6 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q6. (2 marks)  Explain the development of the male gametophyte. Why is it called a male gametophyte?  (2023 OD; similar 2017 D, 2025)     Answer:  The microspore (pollen grain, n) divides by mitosis into a big  vegetative cell  (food store, irregular nucleus) and a small  generative cell  (spindle shaped, floats in vegetative cell). In ~60% of angiosperms pollen is shed at this 2-celled stage; in others the generative cell divides again into  2 male gametes  (3-celled stage). It is called the male gametophyte because it is the haploid structure that produces the male gametes.

title: Q7 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q7. (2–3 marks)  List and explain outbreeding devices.  (2018 OD, 2023 OD, 2024, 2026)     Answer (any three):       Pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised  — pollen is released before the stigma is ready, or the stigma is ready much before pollen release (SQP Q1 case).    Anther and stigma at different positions  — pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower.    Self-incompatibility  — a genetic mechanism that stops pollen of the same flower (or plant) from germinating or growing a tube in the pistil.    Unisexual flowers  — monoecious plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy; dioecious plants (papaya) prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy.

title: Q8 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q8. (2 marks)  Geitonogamy can be compared with both cross-pollination and self-pollination. Comment.  (SQP 26-27)     Answer:  Geitonogamy = pollen from the anther of one flower goes to the stigma of  another flower of the same plant . Functionally it is like cross-pollination because a pollinating agent is needed; genetically it is like autogamy (self-pollination) because the pollen comes from the same plant.

title: Q9 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q9. (3 marks)  Explain the steps a plant breeder takes so that only the desired pollen reaches the stigma of a bisexual flower (artificial hybridisation).  (2023 D; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD, SQP 26-27)     Answer:  (1)  Emasculation  — remove the anthers from the flower bud with forceps before the anthers dehisce. (2)  Bagging  — cover the emasculated flower with a butter-paper bag to stop unwanted pollen. (3) When the stigma becomes receptive, dust it with pollen collected from the chosen male parent, and  re-bag  the flower so the fruit develops. (In unisexual flowers like papaya, no emasculation is needed — only bagging.)

title: Q10 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q10. (5 marks)  Explain double fertilisation, starting from pollen on the stigma. Give the ploidy of the products and the role of synergids. Why does endosperm develop before the embryo?  (2024; similar 2018 OD, SQP 26-27)     Answer:      Pollen grain germinates on the stigma → pollen tube grows through the style → enters the ovule through the micropyle → enters one  synergid  (guided by the  filiform apparatus  of synergids) → releases 2 male gametes.    Syngamy:  male gamete 1 + egg cell →  zygote (2n)  → embryo.    Triple fusion:  male gamete 2 + 2 polar nuclei in central cell →  primary endosperm nucleus, PEN (3n)  → endosperm.   Two fusions happen in one embryo sac, so it is called  double fertilisation .    Endosperm develops first  because its cells store food, which nourishes the developing embryo. (SQP MS: the statement "zygote always divides before PEN" is false.)

title: Q11 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q11. (2 marks)  Why do farmers prefer apomictic seeds?  (2020 D, 2026; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD)     Answer:   Apomixis  = formation of seed without fertilisation (example: some Asteraceae and grasses). (1) If a hybrid is made apomictic, the hybrid characters do not segregate in the next generation. (2) So farmers can keep using their own seeds every year instead of buying costly hybrid seeds each year.

title: Q12 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q12. (2 marks)  When an orange seed is squeezed, many embryos are seen. Explain. Are they genetically similar?  (2017 D)     Answer:  This is  polyembryony . In citrus, some nucellar cells around the embryo sac divide and grow into extra embryos (without fertilisation). These nucellar embryos are genetically identical to the mother plant (clones); only the zygotic embryo differs.

title: Q13 · Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
text: Q13. (2 marks)  Differentiate between true fruit and false fruit, and give an example of a parthenocarpic fruit.  (2020 OD; similar 2018 OD, 2026)     Answer:  True fruit develops only from the ovary (e.g., mango). False fruit — the thalamus also contributes to the fruit (e.g., apple, strawberry, cashew). Parthenocarpic fruit develops without fertilisation and is seedless (e.g., banana).

title: Q14 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q14. (MCQ)  In humans, the secondary oocyte completes its meiotic division when: (A) it is implanted (B) it is released from the Graafian follicle (C) it is penetrated by the sperm (D) acrosomal enzymes break the zona pellucida.  (2024)     Answer:  (C) When the sperm enters it.

title: Q15 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q15. (MCQ)  The foetal ejection reflex triggers release of ____ from ____. (A) oxytocin, foetal pituitary (B) oxytocin, maternal pituitary (C) hCG, placenta (D) progesterone, corpus luteum.  (2026; similar 2015 D)     Answer:  (B) Oxytocin, maternal pituitary.

title: Q16 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q16. (Assertion–Reason)  A: The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a morula. R: The morula continues to divide and transforms into trophoblast.  (2026)     Answer:  (C) A is true but R is false. (The morula becomes a  blastocyst ; trophoblast is only its outer layer.)

title: Q17 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q17. (Assertion–Reason)  A: Spermatogenesis is continuous throughout a man's reproductive life, while oogenesis is discontinuous. R: Oogenesis begins in the embryo, is arrested at prophase I, resumes after puberty, and is arrested again at metaphase II.  (SQP 26-27)     Answer:  (A) Both true, R is the correct explanation of A.

title: Q18 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q18. (2 marks)  List the male accessory ducts in order.  (2020 OD; 2019 OD diagram; 2024 case)     Answer:  Rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens (→ ejaculatory duct → urethra).

title: Q19 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q19. (3 marks)  Explain spermatogenesis and the roles of LH and FSH.  (2024 case, 2020 D)     Answer:  In seminiferous tubules: spermatogonia (2n) multiply by mitosis →  primary spermatocytes (2n)  → meiosis I →  secondary spermatocytes (n)  → meiosis II →  spermatids (n)  → change into  sperms  (spermiogenesis). At puberty the hypothalamus releases GnRH → pituitary releases  LH , which acts on  Leydig (interstitial) cells  to secrete androgens (testosterone) that stimulate spermatogenesis, and  FSH , which acts on  Sertoli cells  to secrete factors that help spermiogenesis.

title: Q20 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q20. (3–5 marks)  Describe the menstrual cycle phases.  (2016 OD, 2019 D, 2025, 2026, SQP 26-27 case)     Answer:       Menstrual phase (days 1–5):  endometrium breaks down and bleeds out; happens only if the ovum is not fertilised.    Follicular/proliferative phase (days ~5–13):  FSH and LH rise; primary follicles grow into a mature  Graafian follicle ; follicle secretes  estrogen , which rebuilds the endometrium.    Ovulation (about day 14):   LH surge  causes the Graafian follicle to rupture and release the ovum (secondary oocyte).    Luteal/secretory phase (days 15–28):  the empty follicle becomes the  corpus luteum , which secretes  progesterone  to keep the endometrium ready for implantation. If no fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates → progesterone falls → menstruation starts again. (SQP link: no clear LH surge → no ovulation → no corpus luteum → low progesterone → irregular, heavy bleeding; heavy bleeding can cause  anaemia .)

title: Q21 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q21. (3–5 marks)  Trace the journey of the zygote from the fallopian tube to implantation.  (2023 OD; similar 2024, 2025, 2026)     Answer:  Fertilisation occurs in the  ampullary region  of the fallopian tube. The zygote divides by mitosis ( cleavage ) as it moves through the isthmus towards the uterus → 2, 4, 8, 16 daughter cells ( blastomeres ). Embryo with 8–16 blastomeres =  morula . Morula becomes a  blastocyst : outer layer  trophoblast  + inner group of cells, the  inner cell mass . The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium; uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst → blastocyst gets embedded =  implantation  → pregnancy. Inner cell mass becomes the embryo; trophoblast helps in nutrition and implantation (SQP Q3).

title: Q22 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q22. (2 marks)  How is polyspermy prevented?  (2024 OR)     Answer:  When one sperm touches the zona pellucida of the ovum, changes occur in the zona pellucida that block the entry of other sperms.

title: Q23 · Chapter 2 — Human Reproduction
text: Q23. (2 marks)  Why is breast-feeding recommended in the first months?  (2016 D, 2018 OD)     Answer:  The first milk,  colostrum , contains many antibodies (IgA) that give the baby passive immunity, and breast milk gives complete nutrition and builds a healthy baby.

title: Q24 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q24. (MCQ)  A man undergoes an operation in which a small part of the vas deferens is cut and tied. The direct result is: (A) sperm transport into ejaculatory duct and urethra is blocked (B) testosterone stops (C) seminal plasma stops (D) spermatogenesis stops.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2023 OD, 2023 D)     Answer:  (A). This is  vasectomy  (tubectomy is the similar operation in females).

title: Q25 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q25. (2 marks)  Name two copper-releasing IUDs and state how they work.  (2024; similar 2020 D)     Answer:  CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375 (any two). Cu ions reduce sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms; IUDs also increase phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus. (Hormone-releasing IUDs like Progestasert and LNG-20 also make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.)

title: Q26 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q26. (2 marks)  Why is "Saheli" preferred by women?  (2020 D)     Answer:  It is a non-steroidal pill taken  once a week , with very few side effects and high contraceptive value. (Developed by CDRI, Lucknow.)

title: Q27 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q27. (2 marks)  What is amniocentesis? Why is it banned for sex determination?  (2026; similar 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2025)     Answer:  A sample of amniotic fluid around the foetus is taken and tested to detect  genetic/chromosomal disorders  (such as Down's syndrome). It is legally banned for finding the sex of the foetus because this misuse leads to  female foeticide  (killing of normal female foetuses).

title: Q28 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q28. (2 marks)  Why does the government have strict conditions for MTP?  (2017 OD)     Answer:  To stop illegal, unsafe abortions and the misuse of MTP for female foeticide (sex-selective abortion). MTP is safest in the first trimester (up to 12 weeks).

title: Q29 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q29. (3 marks)  A woman has blocked fallopian tubes but her ovaries make normal ova. Her husband has a very low sperm count. Which ARTs will help?  (SQP 26-27; similar 2015 D, 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2023 OD, 2024)     Answer:  (1)  ICSI (Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection)  — a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum in the lab; solves the low sperm count. (2)  IVF followed by IUT (Intra Uterine Transfer)  — embryo made in the lab (with more than 8 blastomeres) is placed directly into the uterus; this by-passes the blocked fallopian tube.

title: Q30 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q30. (3 marks)  Expand and explain ZIFT, GIFT and IUI.  (2023 OD; similar 2019 D, 2024)     Answer:       ZIFT – Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer:  zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) made by IVF is put into the fallopian tube.    GIFT – Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer:  an ovum from a donor is put into the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova but can give a suitable environment for fertilisation.    IUI – Intra Uterine Insemination (artificial insemination):  semen from the husband or a healthy donor is placed into the uterus; used when the man has a low sperm count.

title: Q31 · Chapter 3 — Reproductive Health
text: Q31. (2 marks)  Name any four STIs. Which of them are not completely curable?  (NCERT fact; not seen in the papers read — learn as a 2-mark backup)     Answer:  Gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis B, HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV infections are not completely curable.

title: Q32 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q32. (MCQ)  A woman with normal vision has a colour-blind father. She marries a normal man. The chance of their children being colour blind is: (A) 25% (B) 50% (C) 75% (D) 100%.  (2024; similar 2025)     Answer:  (A) 25% of all children (= half of the sons; no daughters affected). Woman is a carrier XᶜX; man XY.

title: Q33 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q33. (2 marks)  You have a tall pea plant. How will you find its genotype?  (2019 D; similar 2015 D, 2016 OD, 2017 D, 2023 D)     Answer:  Do a  test cross : cross it with a dwarf (homozygous recessive, tt) plant.     If all offspring are tall → plant is  TT  (homozygous).   If tall : dwarf =  1 : 1  → plant is  Tt  (heterozygous).

title: Q34 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q34. (5 marks)  Compare inheritance of flower colour in garden pea (violet/white) and snapdragon (red/white) up to F2.  (2024, 2025, 2026; similar 2019 OD)     Answer:       Pea (complete dominance):  VV (violet) × vv (white) → F1 all  Vv violet . F1 selfed → F2: VV : Vv : vv = 1 : 2 : 1 (genotype), violet : white =  3 : 1  (phenotype). Violet is dominant.    Snapdragon/Antirrhinum (incomplete dominance):  RR (red) × rr (white) → F1 all  Rr pink . F2: RR red : Rr pink : rr white =  1 : 2 : 1  for both genotype and phenotype.    Conclusion:  In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully dominant, so F1 shows an intermediate character and the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio.

title: Q35 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q35. (3 marks)  A woman with blood group O marries a man with blood group AB. Work out the cross and explain the pattern.  (2019 D; similar 2015 D, 2025)     Answer:  Woman ii × Man IᴬIᴮ. Gametes: i and Iᴬ, Iᴮ. Children: Iᴬi (blood group A) and Iᴮi (blood group B) in 1 : 1. No child is O or AB. ABO blood groups show  multiple alleles  (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) and  co-dominance  (Iᴬ and Iᴮ both express in AB); i is recessive.

title: Q36 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q36. (3 marks)  Mice: running R > walking r; black B > brown b. Cross Rrbb female × RrBb male. Give the phenotypic ratio and number of running-black mice out of 64.  (SQP 26-27)     Answer:  Gametes: female Rb, rb; male RB, Rb, rB, rb. Results: running black 6/16, running brown 6/16, walking black 2/16, walking brown 2/16 →  3 : 3 : 1 : 1 . Running black = 6/16 × 64 =  24 .

title: Q37 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q37. (Assertion–Reason)  A: Tissue culture is used when traditional breeding cannot keep pace with demand. R: Totipotency is the ability of a single plant cell/explant to regenerate a whole plant under sterile conditions.  (SQP 26-27)     Answer:  (B) Both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (One-line extra: a virus-free plant is obtained by culturing the  meristem  (apical/axillary), which is free of virus — 2026.)

title: Q38 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q38. (Assertion–Reason)  A: When two genes in a dihybrid cross are on the same chromosome, parental combinations are much higher than non-parental. R: This is due to crossing over between the two genes.  (2025; similar SQP 26-27)     Answer:  (C) A is true, R is false. (High parental combinations are due to  linkage ; crossing over produces the non-parental recombinants.)

title: Q39 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q39. (3 marks)  Explain linkage and recombination from Morgan's work.  (2018 OD, 2019 OD, 2020 D)     Answer:  Morgan worked with  Drosophila melanogaster  (short life cycle ~2 weeks, many offspring, easy to grow, clear male/female differences, many visible variations). In dihybrid crosses for X-linked genes, F2 ratios differed greatly from 9:3:3:1. Genes on the same chromosome tend to stay together =  linkage ; new (non-parental) combinations formed by crossing over =  recombination . Tightly linked genes (yellow body and white eye) gave very low recombination (1.3%); loosely linked genes (white eye and miniature wing) gave higher recombination (37.2%). Sturtevant used recombination frequency to map gene positions on chromosomes.

title: Q40 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q40. (2 marks)  Explain sex determination in honeybees. Why does a male bee have 16 and a female 32 chromosomes?  (2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2020 OD)     Answer:   Haplodiploid  system: a fertilised egg becomes a female (queen or worker), diploid, 32 chromosomes; an unfertilised egg develops by  parthenogenesis  into a male (drone), haploid, 16 chromosomes. Drones produce sperms by  mitosis . Males have no father and cannot have sons, but have a grandfather.

title: Q41 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q41. (2 marks)  How is sex determined in birds and how is it different from humans?  (2018 OD; similar 2015 D)     Answer:  Birds: female is  ZW  (heterogametic, gives two types of eggs), male is  ZZ . Humans: male is  XY  (heterogametic, two types of sperms), female is  XX . So in birds the female decides the sex of the chick; in humans the father's sperm decides it.

title: Q42 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q42. (2 marks)  Why do males suffer from haemophilia more than females? Give two differences between haemophilia and sickle-cell anaemia.  (2020 OD, 2024; similar 2017 D)     Answer:  Haemophilia is  X-linked recessive . A male has only one X, so one defective allele makes him ill. A female needs the defective allele on both X chromosomes, which is very rare (mother carrier + father haemophilic). Differences: haemophilia is sex-linked, more males affected, blood does not clot (a clotting protein is missing); sickle-cell anaemia is  autosomal recessive , males and females equally affected, caused by glutamic acid → valine change at the 6th position of the β-globin chain (GAG → GUG), RBCs become sickle shaped.

title: Q43 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q43. (3 marks)  How does a single gene mutation cause phenylketonuria (PKU)? What is pleiotropy?  (SQP 26-27)     Answer:  PKU is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. The person lacks the enzyme that converts  phenylalanine to tyrosine . Phenylalanine accumulates and is changed into  phenylpyruvic acid  and other derivatives; their build-up in the brain causes mental retardation (they are also excreted in urine).  Pleiotropy:  one gene shows many phenotypic effects (here: mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation, etc.), because it affects a metabolic pathway.

title: Q44 · Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
text: Q44. (3 marks)  Chromosomal vs Mendelian disorders; describe Down's, Turner's and Klinefelter's syndromes.  (2026; similar 2017 OD, 2019 D, 2024, 2025)     Answer:  Mendelian disorder = change/mutation in a  single gene  (haemophilia, sickle cell, thalassemia, PKU, colour blindness). Chromosomal disorder = absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of  whole chromosomes , usually due to  non-disjunction  (failure of chromatids/chromosomes to separate in meiosis).      Down's syndrome:  trisomy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes). Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with a characteristic crease, retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development.    Klinefelter's syndrome:  44 + XXY (47). Overall masculine but with feminine development (breast development, gynaecomastia), sterile. (Formed when an XX egg is fertilised by a Y sperm.)    Turner's syndrome:  44 + XO (45). Female, sterile (rudimentary ovaries), lacks secondary sexual characters.

title: Q45 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q45. (MCQ)  A DNA molecule is 160 base pairs long and has 30% guanine. How many adenine bases? (A) 48 (B) 64 (C) 96 (D) 192.  (2026)     Answer:  (B) 64. Steps: 160 bp = 320 bases. G = 30%, so C = 30%. A + T = 40%, A = 20%. 20% of 320 = 64.

title: Q46 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q46. (MCQ)  E. coli grown in ¹⁵N medium is moved to ¹⁴N medium. DNA after 60 minutes (E. coli divides every 20 minutes) will be: (A) 25% hybrid, 75% light (B) 50%/50% (C) 75% hybrid, 25% light (D) 85%/15%.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2016 OD, 2016 D, 2020 OD)     Answer:  (A). Steps: 60 min = 3 generations. Gen 1: all hybrid; Gen 2: ½ hybrid ½ light; Gen 3: ¼ hybrid ¾ light. This proved  semi-conservative replication  (Meselson and Stahl, 1958, using CsCl density gradient centrifugation).

title: Q47 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q47. (MCQ)  A stretch of euchromatin has 200 nucleosomes. Number of base pairs? (one nucleosome ≈ 200 bp)  (SQP 26-27; similar 2025)     Answer:  200 × 200 =  40,000 bp  (MS option C: 40,000 bp and 13,600 × 10⁻⁹ m, using 0.34 nm per bp).

title: Q48 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q48. (3 marks)  Describe the nucleosome and differentiate euchromatin and heterochromatin.  (2025; similar 2016 D, 2017 OD)     Answer:  Histones are positively charged proteins (rich in lysine and arginine). 8 histone molecules form a  histone octamer . Negatively charged DNA wraps around it →  nucleosome  (about 200 bp of DNA). Nucleosomes look like "beads-on-string" under the electron microscope and coil further into chromatin fibres (non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins help).  Euchromatin  = loosely packed, stains light,  transcriptionally active .  Heterochromatin  = densely packed, stains dark, inactive.

title: Q49 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q49. (3 marks)  Explain Hershey and Chase's experiment.  (2015 D, 2019 D; MCQ 2023 OD)     Answer:  They used bacteriophages. Some phages were grown with  radioactive phosphorus ³²P  (labels DNA), others with  radioactive sulphur ³⁵S  (labels protein). (1)  Infection:  phages infected E. coli. (2)  Blending:  a blender removed the phage coats from bacteria. (3)  Centrifugation:  bacteria settled at the bottom; phage coats stayed in the supernatant. Bacteria infected with ³²P phage were radioactive; with ³⁵S phage were not. So  DNA, not protein, enters the bacteria — DNA is the genetic material .

title: Q50 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q50. (2 marks)  Why is DNA a better genetic material than RNA?  (2020 OD; A-R 2024, 2023 OD)     Answer:  RNA has a reactive  2'-OH  group in every nucleotide, so it is labile, easily degraded and mutates fast (RNA viruses evolve fast). DNA is chemically more stable (no 2'-OH; thymine instead of uracil), so it is better for storing genetic information. RNA is better for expressing characters (protein synthesis).

title: Q51 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q51. (3 marks)  Draw a replication fork and explain why replication occurs within a fork. Role of DNA ligase?  (2026; similar 2019 OD, 2019 D, 2016 D)     Answer:  (Diagram in Section 6.) The two DNA strands cannot be separated along the whole length at once because it needs very high energy, so replication happens in a small opening of the helix =  replication fork . DNA polymerase works only in the  5'→3' direction , so the template with 3'→5' polarity gives  continuous  synthesis (leading strand), and the template with 5'→3' polarity gives  discontinuous  synthesis (lagging strand, short fragments).  DNA ligase  joins these discontinuous fragments.

title: Q52 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q52. (2 marks)  Draw/describe a transcription unit. Where are the promoter and terminator?  (2019 D, 2019 OD; MCQ 2024, SQP 26-27)     Answer:  Transcription unit =  promoter + structural gene + terminator . The promoter is towards the  5' end (upstream)  of the structural gene (with reference to the coding strand); the terminator is towards the  3' end (downstream)  of the coding strand. The template strand has 3'→5' polarity; the coding strand has 5'→3' polarity and the same sequence as RNA (T in place of U). In bacteria, RNA polymerase uses the  sigma factor  to start and the  rho factor  to stop.

title: Q53 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q53. (3 marks)  Why must hnRNA be processed? Name the processes. Why is only one DNA strand transcribed?  (2026; similar 2017 D, 2023 OD)     Answer:  In eukaryotes the primary transcript (hnRNA) has both  exons  (coding) and  introns  (non-coding). (1)  Splicing  removes introns and joins exons. (2)  Capping : methyl guanosine triphosphate is added at the 5' end. (3)  Tailing : 200–300 adenylate residues (poly-A tail) are added at the 3' end. Then it is mRNA and goes to the cytoplasm. Only one strand is copied because (a) if both were copied, the two RNAs would be complementary and pair to form double-stranded RNA, so no protein would be made; (b) two different RNAs/proteins from the same DNA segment would make genetic information transfer complicated.

title: Q54 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q54. (2–3 marks)  Name the three RNA polymerases in eukaryotes and what each makes.  (2023 OD)     Answer:  RNA polymerase I → rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); RNA polymerase II → hnRNA (precursor of mRNA); RNA polymerase III → tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.

title: Q55 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q55. (2 marks)  When is the genetic code said to be (a) degenerate (b) universal? Also unambiguous?  (2020 D; similar 2016 OD, 2017 D, A-R 2025)     Answer:  (a)  Degenerate:  some amino acids are coded by more than one codon. (b)  Universal:  the same codon codes for the same amino acid in all organisms, from bacteria to humans (some exceptions in mitochondria and a few protozoans).  Unambiguous/specific:  one codon codes for only one amino acid. Other features: triplet; 61 codons for amino acids; 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG has a dual role (codes methionine and acts as the start codon); read without commas.

title: Q56 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q56. (3 marks)  Describe tRNA. Why is it called an adapter molecule?  (2017 D; similar 2024, 2023 OD)     Answer:  tRNA looks like a  clover leaf  (2-D); in 3-D it looks like an inverted L. It has an  anticodon loop  (bases complementary to the codon on mRNA) and an  amino acid acceptor end  (3' end) where a specific amino acid attaches (charging/aminoacylation, which uses ATP). It "reads" the code on mRNA and also carries the matching amino acid, so it is an  adapter  between nucleic acid and protein. Translation stops when a release factor binds the stop codon. UTRs (untranslated regions) are on mRNA at both the 5' end (before the start codon) and the 3' end (after the stop codon); they are needed for efficient translation.

title: Q57 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q57. (5 marks)  Explain the lac operon (with inducer and without inducer).  (2024 OR, 2025 OR)     Answer:  The lac operon of E. coli has a regulator gene  i  (makes repressor), a  promoter (p) , an  operator (o)  and 3 structural genes:  z  (β-galactosidase),  y  (permease),  a  (transacetylase).      No lactose (no inducer):  the repressor made by the i gene binds to the  operator  → RNA polymerase cannot transcribe → genes switched  off .    Lactose present (inducer):  lactose (allolactose) binds the repressor and inactivates it → repressor cannot bind the operator → RNA polymerase transcribes z, y, a → enzymes made → lactose is used. Genes switched  on .   It is called  negative regulation  because the operon is controlled by a repressor.

title: Q58 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q58. (3 marks)  Give four goals of the Human Genome Project (HGP). Name one non-human organism sequenced.  (2023 D; similar 2020 D, 2017 D)     Answer:  HGP began in 1990 and was completed in 2003. Goals (any four): identify all the ~20,000–25,000 genes in human DNA; find the sequence of the ~3 billion base pairs; store this information in databases; improve tools for data analysis; transfer related technologies to other sectors such as industries; address the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI). Non-human organisms sequenced: bacteria, yeast,  Caenorhabditis elegans ,  Drosophila , rice,  Arabidopsis  (any one).

title: Q59 · Chapter 5 — Molecular Basis of Inheritance
text: Q59. (5 marks)  Describe DNA fingerprinting steps and uses.  (2023 D; similar 2015 D, 2017 OD, 2018 OD, 2024 OR)     Answer:  Technique (Alec Jeffreys) uses  VNTRs  (Variable Number of Tandem Repeats — a satellite DNA that differs from person to person) as probe. Steps: (1) isolate DNA; (2) digest DNA with  restriction endonucleases ; (3) separate fragments by  gel electrophoresis ; (4) transfer (blot) fragments to nitrocellulose/nylon membrane; (5)  hybridise  with a labelled VNTR probe; (6) detect bands by  autoradiography . Uses: forensic science (identify criminals, identify dead bodies after accidents),  paternity disputes , studying population and genetic diversity.

title: Q60 · Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Q60. (MCQ)  Select the odd one in the context of convergent evolution: (A) eyes of octopus and mammals (B) flippers of penguins and dolphins (C) flying squirrel and flying phalanger (D) thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita.  (2026)     Answer:  (D) — these are  homologous  (divergent evolution); the others are analogous/convergent.

title: Q61 · Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Q61. (MCQ)  If the frequency of allele A is 0.6 in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of Aa is: (A) 0.21 (B) 0.42 (C) 0.48 (D) 0.32.  (2024)     Answer:  (C) 0.48. Steps: p = 0.6, q = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, Aa = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48.

title: Q62 · Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Q62. (2–3 marks)  Explain p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Which factors disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?  (2015 OD, 2017 OD, 2018 OD; similar 2020 OD)     Answer:  Hardy-Weinberg principle: allele frequencies in a population stay constant from generation to generation (genetic equilibrium) if there is no disturbance. p = frequency of dominant allele A, q = frequency of recessive allele a, p + q = 1. Then p² = frequency of AA, 2pq = Aa, q² = aa, and p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Five factors change it:  gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, natural selection.

title: Q63 · Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Q63. (2 marks)  Differentiate homologous and analogous organs with examples.  (2016 OD, 2018 OD; similar 2015 OD, 2020 OD, 2024)     Answer:   Homologous:  same basic structure and origin, different functions →  divergent evolution  (forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human; thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita; vertebrate hearts/brains).  Analogous:  different structure/origin, same function →  convergent evolution  (wings of butterfly and bird; eyes of octopus and mammals; flippers of penguin and dolphin; sweet potato (root) and potato (stem)).

title: Q64 · Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Q64. (3 marks)  Explain industrial melanism as an example of natural selection.  (2023 D; similar 2015 D, 2017 OD)     Answer:  In England, before industrialisation (before 1850), tree trunks were covered by white lichens, so  white-winged moths  were hidden from predator birds and were more in number. After industrialisation, smoke and soot darkened the trunks and killed the lichens. Now  dark (melanic) moths  were hidden and survived, while white moths were eaten → dark moths became more common. Nature selected the better-adapted (fitter) form → natural selection.

title: Q65 · Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Q65. (2 marks)  Explain adaptive radiation with an example.  (2015 D; similar SQP 26-27 continental drift)     Answer:  Evolution of different species from one ancestor, spreading into different habitats in one geographical area. Examples:  Darwin's finches  of the Galapagos (different beak types);  Australian marsupials , which evolved from one ancestral stock within the island continent. (SQP: due to continental drift, South American mammals were overridden by North American fauna when the continents joined; Australian marsupials survived because there was no competition from other mammals.)

title: Q66 · Chapter 6 — Evolution
text: Q66. (2 marks)  Write the order of human evolution and one feature each.  (2025 MCQ, 2023 D MCQ, 2019 OD, 2017 D)     Answer:  Dryopithecus/Ramapithecus (~15 mya, ape-like) → Australopithecines (~2 mya, East African grasslands, stone weapons, ate fruit) →  Homo habilis  (first human-like, brain 650–800 cc, probably did not eat meat) →  Homo erectus  (~1.5 mya, brain ~900 cc, probably ate meat) → Neanderthal man (brain ~1400 cc, used hides to protect the body and buried the dead) →  Homo sapiens .

title: Q67 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q67. (MCQ)  The vector of dengue fever is: (A) female Aedes (B) female Anopheles (C) male Aedes (D) female Culex.  (2024; similar 2018 OD)     Answer:  (A) Female  Aedes  mosquito (also spreads chikungunya).

title: Q68 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q68. (3 marks)  "Plasmodium needs both mosquito and human hosts." Explain its life cycle.  (2023 D; similar 2023 OD, 2025)     Answer:  Infected  female Anopheles  bites a human and injects  sporozoites  (infective stage). In the human: sporozoites multiply in  liver cells , then attack  red blood cells , multiply and burst them, releasing  haemozoin  — a toxin causing chill and high fever every 3–4 days. Some parasites form  gametocytes  in RBCs. When a female Anopheles sucks this blood, gametocytes enter it;  fertilisation and development  happen in the  mosquito's stomach (gut) ; sporozoites form and are stored in the mosquito's  salivary glands . So the asexual phase is in humans and the sexual phase in the mosquito.

title: Q69 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q69. (2 marks each — learn as a table)  Disease table.  (typhoid 2017 D, 2023 OD; amoebiasis 2016 D; filariasis 2026; ringworm, ascariasis NCERT)          Disease   Pathogen   Spread   Key symptoms           Typhoid    Salmonella typhi  (bacterium)   contaminated food/water   high fever 39–40°C, weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache; Widal test confirms       Pneumonia    Streptococcus pneumoniae ,  Haemophilus influenzae    droplets, sharing glasses   alveoli fill with fluid, fever, chills, cough; lips/nails turn grey-bluish       Common cold   Rhino viruses   droplets, contaminated objects   nasal congestion, sore throat, cough (nose & respiratory passage, not lungs)       Malaria    Plasmodium  (vivax, malariae, falciparum — most serious)   female  Anopheles    chill and high fever every 3–4 days       Amoebiasis    Entamoeba histolytica    houseflies (mechanical carriers) contaminate food/water   constipation, abdominal pain, cramps, stools with mucus and blood clots       Ascariasis    Ascaris  (roundworm)   eggs in soil, water, vegetables   internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, blocked intestine       Filariasis (elephantiasis)    Wuchereria bancrofti ,  W. malayi    bite of female mosquito (Culex)   chronic inflammation and swelling of lymphatic vessels of lower limbs; genitals may be deformed       Ringworm    Microsporum ,  Trichophyton ,  Epidermophyton  (fungi)   towels, combs, soil   dry scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp, intense itching; heat and moisture help them grow

title: Q70 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q70. (3 marks)  Differentiate active and passive immunity; humoral and cell-mediated immunity.  (2026, 2024; similar 2019 OD, 2022)     Answer:       Active immunity:  the body itself makes antibodies after meeting an antigen (infection or vaccine); slow to develop, long-lasting.    Passive immunity:  ready-made antibodies are given (colostrum IgA from mother; antitoxin for tetanus or snake bite); quick, short-lived.    Humoral immunity (antibody-mediated):   B-lymphocytes  make antibodies that circulate in blood/lymph.    Cell-mediated immunity (CMI):  done by  T-lymphocytes ; responsible for  graft (organ transplant) rejection . T-cells also help B-cells make antibodies.

title: Q71 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q71. (2 marks)  Why does a vaccinated child not get the disease? Why don't people get measles/chickenpox twice?  (2020 OD, 2016 OD, 2019 D)     Answer:  The vaccine (weakened/killed pathogen or its proteins) or first infection produces a  primary response  and also  memory B and T cells . On the next exposure, these memory cells quickly produce a massive  secondary (anamnestic) response  that destroys the pathogen before disease develops.

title: Q72 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q72. (2 marks)  Explain cytokine barriers and the role of the spleen.  (2018 OD, 2025; spleen 2026)     Answer:   Cytokine barrier:  virus-infected cells secrete proteins called  interferons , which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.  Spleen:  a large bean-shaped secondary lymphoid organ with lymphocytes and phagocytes; it filters blood by trapping blood-borne microorganisms and is also a large reservoir of erythrocytes.

title: Q73 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q73. (4 marks — case)  Which cells does HIV attack? What happens inside? Test used?  (2024 case; similar 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2020 D)     Answer:  HIV (a retrovirus with RNA) first enters  macrophages : the enzyme  reverse transcriptase  makes viral DNA from viral RNA; viral DNA joins the host cell's DNA and the infected cell makes new viruses (macrophage becomes an "HIV factory"). HIV then enters  helper T-lymphocytes (TH cells) , multiplies and kills them, so the number of helper T cells falls → immunodeficiency → the patient dies from other (opportunistic) infections such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and  Toxoplasma . Test:  ELISA (Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay) . Treatment: anti-retroviral drugs, only partly effective (prolong life). Prevention: screen blood, use disposable needles and syringes, safe sex/condoms, awareness (NACO).

title: Q74 · Chapter 7 — Human Health and Disease
text: Q74. (3 marks)  Differentiate addiction and dependence. Why does a user increase the dose over time? Also name the source of heroin.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2018 OD, 2020 D, 2024, 2025)     Answer:   Addiction  = psychological attachment to the "high"/euphoria of a drug, even when it is not needed.  Dependence  = the body's physical need for the drug; stopping it causes  withdrawal symptoms  (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating). Repeated use raises the  tolerance  of body receptors, so they respond only to higher doses. Heroin ("smack", diacetylmorphine) is made by  acetylation of morphine , which comes from the latex of the poppy  Papaver somniferum ; it is a depressant. Cannabinoids ( Cannabis sativa ) affect the cardiovascular system; cocaine ( Erythroxylum coca ) interferes with dopamine transport and is a stimulant.

title: Q75 · Chapter 8 — Microbes in Human Welfare
text: Q75. (2–3 marks)  Name the microbe used for each product.  (2015 D, 2016 D, 2017 D, 2019 D, 2022, 2026, MCQ 2024)     Answer (learn this table):          Product   Microbe           Curd    Lactobacillus  (LAB) — also increases vitamin B12, checks disease-causing microbes in stomach       Bread, ethanol, wine, beer    Saccharomyces cerevisiae  (baker's/brewer's yeast)       Swiss cheese (large holes)    Propionibacterium sharmanii  — holes due to large amount of CO₂       Citric acid    Aspergillus niger  (fungus)       Acetic acid    Acetobacter aceti  (bacterium)       Butyric acid    Clostridium butylicum  (bacterium)       Lactic acid    Lactobacillus        Penicillin    Penicillium notatum  (Fleming; Chain and Florey showed its full use)       Streptokinase ("clot buster" for heart attack)    Streptococcus        Cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant for organ transplant)    Trichoderma polysporum  (fungus)       Statins (lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting the enzyme for cholesterol synthesis)    Monascus purpureus  (yeast)         Whisky, brandy, rum are made  with distillation ; wine and beer  without distillation  (2025).

title: Q76 · Chapter 8 — Microbes in Human Welfare
text: Q76. (3 marks)  Explain secondary (biological) treatment of sewage. What is BOD?  (2017 D; similar 2015 OD, 2016 D, 2017 OD, 2019 OD, 2022)     Answer:  Primary effluent goes into large  aeration tanks , where it is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped in → useful aerobic microbes grow into  flocs  (masses of bacteria with fungal filaments). They consume most of the organic matter, so  BOD falls . The effluent then goes to a  settling tank , where flocs settle =  activated sludge . A small part is pumped back to the aeration tank as  inoculum ; the major part goes to  anaerobic sludge digesters , where anaerobic bacteria digest it and produce  biogas  (methane, hydrogen sulphide, CO₂). The treated effluent is released into rivers.  BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand)  = the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria; higher BOD = more polluted water. (SQP A-R: the aim of sewage treatment is to reduce organic matter; high BOD means  more , not less, organic matter.)

title: Q77 · Chapter 8 — Microbes in Human Welfare
text: Q77. (2 marks)  Biogas: which microbes, where found, which institutes developed the technology?  (2023 OD; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD, 2022)     Answer:   Methanogens  (e.g.,  Methanobacterium ) grow anaerobically on cellulose and produce methane with CO₂ and H₂. Found in anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment and in the rumen of cattle (so cattle dung, "gobar", is used). The technology was developed in India mainly by  IARI (Indian Agricultural Research Institute)  and  KVIC (Khadi and Village Industries Commission) .

title: Q78 · Chapter 8 — Microbes in Human Welfare
text: Q78. (3 marks)  Why are baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus) good biocontrol agents? Name other biocontrol agents and biofertilisers.  (SQP 26-27 case; similar 2016 OD, 2020 OD, 2022, 2023 D)     Answer:  Baculoviruses (genus  Nucleopolyhedrovirus ) attack insects and arthropods. They are  species-specific, narrow-spectrum  insecticides with  no negative effect  on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects — so they are ideal for  Integrated Pest Management (IPM)  and ecologically sensitive areas. Other biocontrol agents:  ladybird  (eats aphids),  dragonflies  (mosquitoes),   Bacillus thuringiensis   (spores sprayed on plants kill butterfly caterpillars — toxin is released in the larval gut),   Trichoderma   (free-living fungus in root ecosystems, controls plant pathogens). Biofertilisers:  Rhizobium  (root nodules of legumes, fixes N₂),  Azospirillum  and  Azotobacter  (free-living N₂ fixers),  mycorrhiza  such as   Glomus   (absorbs  phosphorus  from soil, gives resistance to root pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought — SQP Q12), cyanobacteria  Anabaena ,  Nostoc ,  Oscillatoria  (fix N₂ in paddy fields, add organic matter).

title: Q79 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q79. (MCQ)  Which is NOT a feature of plasmids? (A) circular (B) self-replicating (C) single-stranded (D) extra-chromosomal.  (2024)     Answer:  (C) Plasmids are double-stranded.

title: Q80 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q80. (Assertion–Reason)  A: Chitinase is needed to separate DNA from yeast cells but not from  Spirogyra . R: Fungal cell wall is made of chitin.  (2026; similar 2024, SQP 26-27)     Answer:  (A) Both true, R explains A. (Use  lysozyme  for bacteria,  cellulase  for plant/algal cells,  chitinase  for fungi.)

title: Q81 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q81. (3 marks)  Explain naming of restriction enzymes and formation of recombinant DNA using EcoRI.  (2019 D; similar 2017 D, 2019 OD, 2020 OD, 2025)     Answer:   EcoRI:  E = genus  Escherichia , co = species  coli , R = strain RY13, I = first enzyme isolated from this strain. Restriction endonucleases recognise a  palindromic sequence  (reads the same on both strands in the 5'→3' direction), e.g. EcoRI site: 5'–GAATTC–3' 3'–CTTAAG–5' EcoRI cuts between G and A on both strands, a little away from the centre, leaving single-stranded overhangs =  sticky ends . If the vector and the foreign DNA are cut with the  same enzyme , they have matching sticky ends, which pair by hydrogen bonds;  DNA ligase  then seals them →  recombinant DNA .

title: Q82 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q82. (3 marks)  In pBR322, state the role of ori, ampR/tetR, rop and restriction sites. Explain insertional inactivation.  (2020 OD, 2024, 2026 case; similar 2016 OD, 2019 D, 2023 OD, SQP 26-27)     Answer:   ori  — origin of replication; any DNA linked to it can replicate in the host and it controls the  copy number .  ampR and tetR  — antibiotic-resistance genes (ampicillin, tetracycline) used as  selectable markers  to identify transformants.  rop  — codes for proteins involved in replication of the plasmid.  Restriction sites  — single sites (EcoRI, HindIII, ClaI, PvuII, BamHI, SalI, PstI, PvuI) where foreign DNA can be inserted. (BamHI and SalI are in tetR; PstI and PvuI in ampR; PvuII in rop.)  Insertional inactivation:  foreign DNA is inserted into one marker gene, e.g., tetR at BamHI — that gene stops working. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but  not  on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both. Easier method: insert the foreign DNA into the  β-galactosidase  gene — recombinants give  colourless/white  colonies; non-recombinants give  blue  colonies on a chromogenic substrate.

title: Q83 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q83. (2 marks)  How are bacteria made competent? Name two vector-less methods of gene transfer.  (2026, 2024; similar 2016 OD, 2025)     Answer:  DNA is hydrophilic and cannot pass cell membranes. Bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation,  calcium (Ca²⁺) , then placed on  ice , given a  heat shock (42°C)  and put back on ice → recombinant DNA enters. Vector-less methods:  microinjection  (DNA injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell);  biolistics/gene gun  (plant cells bombarded with high-velocity gold or tungsten micro-particles coated with DNA).

title: Q84 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q84. (3 marks)  Explain gel electrophoresis.  (2025; similar 2016 D, 2017 OD, 2024)     Answer:  DNA fragments are  negatively charged , so in an electric field they move towards the  anode  through  agarose gel  (from seaweed). The gel acts as a sieve:  smaller fragments move farther . Separated DNA is stained with  ethidium bromide  and seen as bright  orange bands under UV light . The bands are cut out and the DNA extracted ( elution ), then used to make recombinant DNA by joining with cloning vectors, in DNA fingerprinting, etc.

title: Q85 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q85. (3 marks)  Describe PCR. Role of Taq polymerase?  (2017 D; similar 2015 OD, 2016 D, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2023 OD)     Answer:  PCR = Polymerase Chain Reaction, used to make many copies of a gene in vitro. Each cycle: (1)  Denaturation  — high temperature separates the two DNA strands. (2)  Annealing  — two sets of  primers  (small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides) bind to complementary regions. (3)  Extension  — DNA polymerase extends the primers using nucleotides. Repeating ~30 times amplifies the DNA about  1 billion times .  Taq polymerase  is a  thermostable  DNA polymerase from the bacterium   Thermus aquaticus  ; it stays active at the high temperature of denaturation, so new enzyme need not be added in every cycle.

title: Q86 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q86. (2 marks)  Why are bioreactors used? Describe a stirred-tank bioreactor.  (2018 OD; similar 2015 D, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2025)     Answer:  Bioreactors (100–1000 litres) allow large-scale production of products by providing optimum growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen).  Stirred-tank  bioreactor: usually cylindrical with a curved base for mixing; a  stirrer  mixes contents evenly and increases oxygen availability; in the  sparged  type, sterile air is bubbled in. It also has a foam-control system, temperature and pH control, and sampling ports. (SQP: a fall in yield due to contamination is prevented by  sterile handling, sterilised equipment and aseptic transfer .)

title: Q87 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q87. (3 marks)  How was human insulin made by rDNA technology?  (2015 OD, 2015 D, 2017 D; similar 2018 OD, 2020 OD)     Answer:  Insulin has two short chains,  A and B , joined by  disulphide bridges . In the body it is made as  pro-insulin , which has an extra stretch, the  C-peptide , that is removed to make mature insulin. In 1983  Eli Lilly  prepared two DNA sequences for chains A and B, introduced them into  plasmids of E. coli , produced the chains separately, extracted them and combined them by creating disulphide bonds → human insulin ( Humulin ). It avoids allergy/reactions caused by insulin from cattle or pigs.

title: Q88 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q88. (2–3 marks)  Explain gene therapy for ADA deficiency. Why is periodic infusion needed?  (2025; similar 2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2019 OD)     Answer:   Adenosine deaminase (ADA)  is needed for the immune system; its deficiency (deletion of the ADA gene) causes immunodeficiency. In 1990 a 4-year-old girl was treated: her  lymphocytes  were grown in culture, a functional  ADA cDNA  was introduced into them using a  retroviral vector , and the cells were returned to her body. These lymphocytes are  not immortal , so periodic infusion is needed. Permanent cure: introduce the ADA gene isolated from bone-marrow cells into cells at  early embryonic stages . (Other options: bone-marrow transplant, enzyme replacement therapy — injecting functional ADA.)

title: Q89 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q89. (3 marks)  How was Bt cotton made pest resistant? Why does the Bt toxin not kill the bacterium?  (2023 D; similar 2017 D, 2017 OD, 2020 D, 2020 OD, 2022, 2024 OR)     Answer:   Bacillus thuringiensis  makes  Bt toxin  protein crystals that kill certain insects (lepidopterans like bollworms, coleopterans, dipterans). The toxin exists as an  inactive protoxin , so the bacterium is not harmed. When an insect eats it, the  alkaline pH of the insect gut  dissolves the crystals and activates the toxin; the active toxin binds to the surface of  midgut epithelial cells , makes  pores , cells swell and burst (lyse) → insect dies. The toxin is coded by   cry   genes;  cryIAc and cryIIAb  control cotton bollworms,  cryIAb  controls corn borer. These genes were introduced into cotton → Bt cotton.

title: Q90 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q90. (3 marks)  How was tobacco made resistant to the nematode  Meloidegyne incognitia ?  (2024; similar 2016 D, 2018 OD, 2023 OD, MCQ 2025, SQP 26-27)     Answer:  The nematode infects tobacco  roots  and reduces yield. Using   Agrobacterium   vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into tobacco so that the plant made both  sense and anti-sense RNA . These two complementary RNAs formed  double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) , which started  RNA interference (RNAi) : it  silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode  (stopped its translation). So the parasite could not survive in the transgenic plant.

title: Q91 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q91. (3 marks)  List benefits of GM plants. Give uses of transgenic animals.  (2016 D, 2019 OD, 2020 D, 2026; similar 2015 OD)     Answer:  GM plants: (1) more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat); (2) less use of chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops); (3) fewer post-harvest losses; (4) better use of minerals by plants (prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility); (5) more nutritional value — e.g.,  Golden rice , rich in vitamin A. Transgenic animals: study of normal physiology and development; study of diseases; biological products (e.g.,  α-1-antitrypsin  for emphysema; transgenic cow  Rosie  (1997) gave human-protein-enriched milk, 2.4 g/L α-lactalbumin); vaccine safety testing (e.g., polio vaccine on transgenic mice); chemical safety (toxicity) testing.

title: Q92 · Chapters 9 & 10 — Biotechnology
text: Q92. (1–2 marks)  What is biopiracy? What is GEAC?  (2015 D, 2016 OD, 2017 OD; MCQ 2025)     Answer:   Biopiracy  = use of bio-resources (and traditional knowledge) of a country by multinational companies or other organisations without proper authorisation from, or compensation to, the countries and people concerned (e.g., an American company got a patent on Basmati rice in 1997).  GEAC = Genetic Engineering Approval Committee  (Indian government body that decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public use).

title: Q93 · Chapter 11 — Organisms and Populations
text: Q93. (MCQ)  An interaction where one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited: (A) mycorrhiza (B) sea anemone and clownfish (C) Abingdon tortoise and goats (D) Cuscuta on hedge plants.  (2026)     Answer:  (B) Commensalism.

title: Q94 · Chapter 11 — Organisms and Populations
text: Q94. (3 marks — learn as a table)  Population interactions with examples.  (2016 OD, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2023 OD, 2024, 2026; SQP 26-27)          Interaction   Sign   Example           Mutualism   + / +   lichen (fungus + alga); mycorrhiza (fungus + plant roots); fig tree and wasp; orchid  Ophrys  and bee (pseudocopulation); plant and pollinator       Competition   − / −   Abingdon tortoise and goats in Galapagos (tortoises became extinct)       Predation   + / −   tiger–deer; Monarch butterfly is distasteful to predators due to a chemical it gets as a caterpillar by feeding on a poisonous weed       Parasitism   + / −    Cuscuta  on hedge plants;  brood parasitism  — cuckoo (koel) lays eggs in a crow's nest; eggs look similar, so the crow incubates them       Commensalism   + / 0   orchid growing on a mango branch; barnacles on whale; cattle egret and grazing cattle; sea anemone and clownfish       Amensalism   − / 0   one harmed, other unaffected          Gause's competitive exclusion principle (2026):  two closely related species competing for the same limited resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the competitively inferior one is eliminated. (MacArthur's warblers coexist by  resource partitioning  — feeding in different parts of the tree.)  Plant defence (2023 D):  cattle and goats do not browse  Calotropis  because it makes highly poisonous  cardiac glycosides . Other plants have thorns (Acacia, cactus) as mechanical defence.  Positive roles of predators (2024):  pass energy across trophic levels; keep prey populations under control (prickly pear cactus in Australia was controlled by a cactus-feeding moth); maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey (removing the starfish  Pisaster  led to extinction of more than 10 invertebrate species).

title: Q95 · Chapter 11 — Organisms and Populations
text: Q95. (3 marks)  Name population attributes, draw age pyramids and give growth equations.  (2017 OD, 2020 OD, 2022, 2025; similar 2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2017 D, 2019 D)     Answer:  Attributes of a population (not of an individual):  birth rate (natality), death rate (mortality), sex ratio, age distribution . Age pyramids:  expanding  (triangular — many young, growing population),  stable  (bell-shaped),  declining  (urn-shaped — fewer young). Density measured by counting, per cent cover,  pug marks and fecal pellets  (tigers), catch per trap (fish). Growth: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. Exponential growth dN/dt = rN gives a  J-shaped  curve (unlimited resources). Logistic growth dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K] gives an  S-shaped (sigmoid)  curve;  K = carrying capacity . r = intrinsic rate of natural increase. Example (2025): if density at t + 1 = 800, natality 200, immigration 200, mortality 150, emigration 100 → 800 = Nₜ + (200 + 200) − (150 + 100) →  Nₜ = 650 . Example (2019 D): 100 frogs, 20 born in a year → birth rate = 20/100 =  0.2 offspring per frog per year .

title: Q96 · Chapter 12 — Ecosystem
text: Q96. (2 marks)  Differentiate GPP and NPP. Calculate NPP when GPP = 3500 and R = 1300 g/m²/year.  (SQP 26-27; similar 2025, 2017 D, 2015 D)     Answer:   GPP (gross primary productivity)  = rate of production of organic matter in photosynthesis.  NPP  = GPP − R (respiration losses); it is the biomass available to consumers (herbivores and decomposers). NPP = 3500 − 1300 =  2200 g/m²/year . Productivity is expressed in g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹.

title: Q97 · Chapter 12 — Ecosystem
text: Q97. (5 marks)  Explain the steps of decomposition and factors affecting it.  (SQP 26-27 OR; similar 2020 D, 2024, A-R 2023 D, MCQ 2025)     Answer:  (1)  Fragmentation  — detritivores (earthworm, termites) break detritus into small particles. (2)  Leaching  — water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil and get precipitated as unavailable salts. (3)  Catabolism  — bacterial and fungal enzymes break detritus into simple inorganic substances. (4)  Humification  — forms  humus , dark amorphous material, highly resistant to microbial action, decomposes very slowly; it is a reservoir of nutrients. (5)  Mineralisation  — humus is further broken by microbes to release inorganic nutrients. Factors: decomposition is  slow  if detritus is rich in  lignin and chitin , fast if rich in  nitrogen and water-soluble sugars ;  warm and moist  conditions speed it up; low temperature, dryness and anaerobic conditions slow it.

title: Q98 · Chapter 12 — Ecosystem
text: Q98. (2–3 marks)  Differentiate grazing and detritus food chains. Why is the pyramid of biomass in the sea inverted? Limitations of ecological pyramids?  (2026; MCQ 2024)     Answer:   GFC  starts from green plants (producers), energy source is the sun (grass → goat → man).  DFC  starts from dead organic matter, with decomposers (fungi, bacteria — saprotrophs). In aquatic ecosystems GFC carries more energy; in terrestrial ecosystems more energy flows through DFC. Sea: biomass of fishes is  more  than that of phytoplankton (which reproduce fast but are small) →  inverted  biomass pyramid. The pyramid of  energy is always upright . Limitations: (1) does not consider the same species at two or more trophic levels; (2) assumes a simple food chain, not a food web; (3) saprophytes/decomposers are not given any place.

title: Q99 · Chapter 13 — Biodiversity and its Conservation
text: Q99. (MCQ)  Which fish led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in Lake Victoria? (A) Catla (B) Dogfish (C) Nile perch (D) African catfish.  (2026)     Answer:  (C) Nile perch.

title: Q100 · Chapter 13 — Biodiversity and its Conservation
text: Q100. (3 marks)  Explain the three levels of biodiversity with examples.  (2026; similar 2016 D, 2018 OD)     Answer:   Genetic diversity  — variation within a species:  Rauwolfia vomitoria  in the Himalaya differs in potency/concentration of reserpine; India has more than 50,000 strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.  Species diversity  — variety of species: the Western Ghats have more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats.  Ecological diversity  — variety of ecosystems: India has deserts, rainforests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, so it has more ecosystem diversity than Norway.

title: Q101 · Chapter 13 — Biodiversity and its Conservation
text: Q101. (4–5 marks)  Explain the causes of biodiversity loss ("Evil Quartet").  (SQP 26-27; similar 2017 OD, 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2025)     Answer:       Habitat loss and fragmentation  — most important cause; e.g., tropical rainforests once covered 14% of Earth's land, now only 6%; the Amazon is being cleared for soybean and cattle ranches. Fragmentation hurts animals that need large territories and migratory animals.    Over-exploitation  — e.g., Steller's sea cow and passenger pigeon became extinct due to over-exploitation by humans; many marine fish are over-harvested.    Alien species invasions  — Nile perch in Lake Victoria (200+ cichlid species lost); carrot grass ( Parthenium ),  Lantana  and water hyacinth ( Eichhornia ); African catfish  Clarias gariepinus  threatens native catfishes in Indian rivers.    Co-extinctions  — when a species becomes extinct, plants and animals obligately linked to it also become extinct (e.g., a host fish and its parasites; plant–pollinator mutualism). IUCN Red List (2004):  784 species  became extinct in the last 500 years ( 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, 87 plants ). Recent extinctions: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia), three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian).

title: Q102 · Chapter 13 — Biodiversity and its Conservation
text: Q102. (3–5 marks)  Explain in-situ and ex-situ conservation. What are hotspots and sacred groves?  (2016 D, 2017 OD, 2019 OD, 2025; similar 2015 OD, 2019 D, MCQ 2023 OD)     Answer:   In-situ (on site):  protect species in their natural habitat —  biodiversity hotspots  (regions with very high species richness and high  endemism ; 34 in the world; India has 3 that also cover neighbouring countries:  Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya ; hotspots cover less than 2% of the earth's land area), protected areas like  biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries , and  sacred groves  (forest patches protected by tribal communities for religious reasons — Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of MP/Chhattisgarh). Note: Jaintia Hills are a sacred grove area,  not  a hotspot (2023 OD MCQ).  Ex-situ (off site):  threatened species taken out of the habitat and protected in  zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks , and by  cryopreservation  of gametes, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture, and  seed banks .  IUCN Red Data List  records threatened and extinct species and helps decide conservation priorities.

title: Q103 · Chapter 13 — Biodiversity and its Conservation
text: Q103. (3 marks)  Why should we conserve biodiversity?  (2023 D; similar 2016 D)     Answer:  (1)  Narrowly utilitarian:  humans get food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicines (more than 25% of drugs sold come from plants);  bioprospecting  looks for useful products. (2)  Broadly utilitarian:  ecosystem services — the Amazon forest produces about 20% of the Earth's oxygen through photosynthesis; pollination by bees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasure. (3)  Ethical:  every species has an intrinsic value; we have a moral duty to care for them and pass them on to future generations.    Total: 103 questions in this bank (well above the minimum of 60).

Exam at a glance (2026-27)          Item   Details           Theory paper   70 marks, 3 hours (plus 15 minutes reading time)       Practical exam   30 marks       Total   100       Number of questions   37, all compulsory, with internal choice (OR) in some questions       Section A   Q1-21: 1 mark each, including MCQs, True/False, fill-ups, "write the output" and 2 Assertion-Reason (A-R) questions =  21 marks        Section B   Q22-28: very short answer, 2 marks each =  14 marks        Section C   Q29-31: short answer, 3 marks each =  9 marks  (usually text file, stack and output/function questions)       Section D   Q32-35: 4 marks each =  16 marks  (SQL queries on a table, CSV file, SQL on two tables, Python-MySQL)       Section E   Q36-37: 5 marks each =  10 marks  (binary file program, network case study)       Language   All programs must be written in  Python  only       MCQ rule   Write the  text  of the correct option, not only the letter (for example "c) Error").        Pass mark (theory)     33% of 70 = 23.1, so you need 24 marks         Pass mark (practical)     33% of 30 = 10 marks        Rule   In Class XII you must get 33%  separately  in theory and in practical (CBSE Controller of Examinations FAQ, March 2025).          The SQP note says:  "There is no change in the Question Paper Design and Assessment Pattern for Academic Session 2026-27." The pattern (37 questions, 21/7/3/4/2) is the same as the 2025 and 2026 board papers. The 2023 and 2024 papers had 35 questions, but the topics were the same.    Practical 30 marks break-up (2026-27 curriculum):          Part   Marks           Lab test: one Python program (60% logic + 20% documentation + 20% code quality)   8       Lab test: 4 SQL queries on one or two tables   4       Report file: at least 15 Python programs + at least 5 sets of SQL queries + at least 4 Python-SQL connectivity programs   7       Project (Python file handling or Python-SQL connectivity, in groups of 2-3)   8       Viva voce   3          What is NOT in the 2026-27 syllabus (skip old PYQs on these):  C++, classes and objects (OOP), inheritance, sorting algorithms (bubble/selection sort), queues, infix/postfix, Boolean algebra and K-maps, 3G/4G, cyber security topics (these are now in Class XI). title: 3. The 33-mark plan (target about 43% = 30 marks in theory)
text: 3. The 33-mark plan (target about 43% = 30 marks in theory)     Main idea:  Computer Science papers repeat the  same types  of questions every year. Only the names and data change. If you learn about 12 "templates" (patterns), you can pass. There is no negative marking, so attempt  every  question. Even half-correct code gets step marks.

title: 3a. Study order (easiest and highest return first)
text: 3a. Study order (easiest and highest return first)       Networks (10 marks):  pure theory with short answers. The 5-mark case study has the  same 5 answers almost every year  (server in the block with most computers, star layout, switch in every block, repeater if distance > 100 m, router/gateway at the server, VoIP/TELNET/FTP, optical fibre or satellite for long distance).    SQL queries (about 16 marks):  SELECT ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ... GROUP BY. These are simple English-like sentences. Learn 15 query patterns (Section 6c).    SQL theory 1-markers:  keys, degree, cardinality, DDL vs DML, COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column).    Python-MySQL connectivity (4 marks):  one fixed 8-line template. Learn it by heart (Section 6c).    Stack program (3 marks):  push with append(), pop with pop(), "Stack Empty"/"Underflow" message. The same every year.    Text file function (3 marks):  open, read, split, loop, count, print, close. One template.    Python output and built-in method questions:  practise 20 outputs from Section 5.    CSV (4) and binary file (5):  learn the two templates. Even writing the open(), writer()/reader() or pickle.dump()/pickle.load() lines correctly gives 1-2 marks.

title: 3c. How practicals save you
text: 3c. How practicals save you      Practical is a separate pass (10/30 needed), but most students get 24-28/30.  Do not lose these marks.     Report file (7) + project (8) + viva (3) = 18 marks  are decided before or on the exam day by your own work. Finish the file and the project in school, get them signed, and know what each program does.    SQL lab test (4):  4 queries on one or two tables. Practise CREATE, INSERT, SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, UPDATE, DELETE on the computer.    Python lab test (8):  usually one program from the practical list (text file count, binary search/update, CSV user-id/password, stack, random dice). 60% of marks are logic, 20% comments, 20% neat code. Always write comments (#) and use clear variable names.    Viva favourites:  difference between text and binary file; what pickle does; what a primary key is; what commit() does; LIFO; what a switch does; full forms (HTTP, SMTP, VoIP, LAN).
